summary: The appellant was a dealer in food articles for the year 1962. He purchased a food article of food from the Food Inspector, Delhi. The Food Inspector issued a certificate under section 2(f) of the Act on January 28, 1963. On March 31, 1963 he sent a sample to the Public Analyst for analysis. The Public Analyst found that the article of Food was adulterated and the appellant was convicted and sentenced to pay a fine of Rs. 1,000/-. On appeal by the appellant, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence but reduced the sentence to one year's rigorous imprisonment. In further appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the provisions of section 2 (1) (f) were not applicable to the case as the article in question was unfit for human consumption. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in its conclusion that the sample was adulterated. [775 H] 2. Section 2(i)(f) is a substantive provision and it does not require any proof of further that the food article was unfit or unfit for use on account of any other cause ' In this view of the matter, the conviction of the accused under section 3 (1)(f), read with section 2, is correct. [750 H] 3. The provisions of sections 2(1) and 2(2) are not applicable in the case of the case. Section 4 provides that no person shall be convicted of any offence unless he has been proved to have been guilty of such an offence. [751 G] 4. The words "or is" used in section 2 do not mean "to bring the case within the mischief of this sub clause". [750 A] 5. The word 'and' in the context means 'to bring a case within its purview'. [750 B] 6. Section 3(1)(e) does not apply to the facts of the present case as it is clear that the appellant had purchased the food articles from the food Inspector, New Delhi and sent a report to the Government of India on January 31, 1964. The report was received by the Government on January 30, 1964 and the Government accepted the same on February 28, 1964, and sent the report to this court on March 31. 1964. [752 G] 7. Section 6 provides that every person convicted of an offence under section 4 shall be liable to pay fine which may extend to one thousand rupees. [753 H] 8. The provision in section 6 is not applicable as it does only refer to the 'fine' powder and the 'nullity' was not defined in the Act. [754 G] 9. Section 7 provides that nothing contained in the said section shall apply to any case where an offence has been committed by a dealer under this Act. The expression "or" is used in the sense of giving a meaning which is given in the explanation to the said sub clause. [764 H] 10. The question whether the provisions in section 4 are applicable to cases of 'food' or 'ninety' powder was considered by this Court in [The State of Bombay vs. F. N. Balsara], ; , ; , , , ; . , , . , . . , ; ; , . \ 11. The contention that the Act does not provide for any punishment is also devoid of merit. It is true that the provision in question is not attracted to the cases of the appellants but it is equally true that there was no evidence on record to show that the offence under Section 3 (2) was committed by the appellants. [774 A] 12. The Act does provide for punishment for 'fineceiving' or for 'non-compliance with the provisions relating to section 2. [784 G] 13. The language of the provision is clear and unambiguous.

The appellant was a tenant of a shop in the village. He filed an application for eviction against him on the ground that he was a 'owner' and that he had stored foodgrains at his own risk. The Rent Controller held that the appellant was an agriculturist and the presumption under paragraph 3(2) of the order could not be drawn against him. On appeal, the High Court reversed the finding of the Rent Controller and dismissed the application. In this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the provisions of section 49 of the Registration Act were not attracted to the case and that the presumption in favour of the landlord was not rebutted by the evidence adduced before the Rent Control Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the requirement under section 49(1) of that Act was satisfied. [775 H] 2. Section 49(2)(a) of Registration Act is attracted only when a person is an agriculturist or an agriculturist. If he is an agricultural labourer and the burden of proving that he is not an agriculturist lies on him, then he cannot be regarded as an agriculturist within the meaning of section 48 of the said Act. [750 H] 3. The provisions of sections 49(3) and 49(4) are attracted only where a person has been in possession of any land for a period of 12 years or more. If the appellant is an Agricultural labourer, he cannot claim that he should be regarded to be an agriculturist as defined under section 48. [751 H] 4. The words "carrying on the business" in section 49 are not intended to include the case of an agriculturist who has been found by the Rent Authority for a certain period and who is an agriculturists. If there is something else in the lease deed, it shall be presumed that he has stored foodgrains in his own right. [751 H] 5. The question whether an inference of innocence can be drawn from the evidence on record does not depend upon the circumstances of the case. In the present case, the appellant had no explanation as to why he was an agricultural labour and why he did not produce any receipt or proof in support of that plea. [754 H] 6. The presumption under section 50 of the Act is not rebutted. If a person who has stored goods at his instance for sale is an agriculture labourer, it cannot be said that he must be regarded an agriculturist because he was not an agricultural labourers. [764 G] 7. The burden of proof in favour or the burden is on the appellant to prove that he did so by adducing evidence. If no such evidence is adduced, the presumption will be rebutted. [752 H] 8. The finding recorded by the High court that the charge against the appellant stood proved was not based on any evidence and it cannot therefore be said to be perverse. [758 G] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 15 of 1971. From the Judgment and Order dated the 10th May, 1970 of the Allahabad High Court in S.C.A. No. 8 of 1970. V.S. Desai, R.K. Garg, S.K Jain and P.K Sharma for the Appellant. M. C. Bhandare, K. B. Rohtagi, S K Gupta and A. K. Srivastava for the Respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by RAY, J. This appeal is directed against the judgment dated October 10, 1970 passed by the Allahabad, High Court allowing the application filed by the appellant under section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The appellant was convicted by the Sessions Judge, Meerut, in a case under sections 302 and 201 of the Indian Penal Code. He was sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for life and to pay a fine of Rs. 500/- in default of payment of fine. The prosecution case is that on February 8, 1968, the accused was found in possession as a result of cultivation at his house.

The appellant was a tenant of the premises in suit No. 12/19, which was let out to the respondent on rent at Rs. 10/- per month. The respondent filed a suit for eviction against the appellant on the ground that he had been paying rent from month to month under section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act and that the defendant was not liable to pay any rent from the date of the tenancy till the date on which the tenancy was created. The trial court held that the payment of rent by the defendant to the plaintiff was a valid receipt of rent and accordingly decreed the suit. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decree and dismissed the suit holding that the tenant had been in arrears of rent from January 1, 1925 till the filing of the suit and that he was not entitled to recover possession of the property from the appellant. The appellant filed an appeal against this judgment before the District Judge, who allowed the same by his order dated April 12, 1971. On further appeal, a Division Bench of the High court reversed the judgment of the trial court and dismissed a writ petition filed by the respondent. In the appeal to this Court it was contended that the rent was not payable from month-to-month under section 106, Transfer of property Act and therefore the defendant could not be evicted from the premises on the basis of the notice issued by the plaintiff. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that payment of arrears of rents by the tenant to the appellant was not a valid service of notice as contemplated under section 117 of the Act. [557 D] 2.1 The rent was payable from the beginning of the month of the first annual lease and it was paid on 8th March, 1925. The defendant had been receiving rent from him in the year 1924. He was not required to pay or accept rent from his tenant. [506 G] 2(i) The payment to the Receiver was a condition precedent for the institution of a suit by the landlord for eviction and it is not necessary that the plaintiff should have paid or accepted rent from time to month. [504 D] (ii) The defendant did not pay any amount to the defendant as required under section 118 of the TP Act. The payment of the rent by him was not in accordance with the provisions of section 116, Transfer and Property Act. Section 116, therefore, does not apply to a case where the tenant has been paying or accepted monthly rent from a date prior to the date when the tenancy is created. [657 D F] 2.(ii) In the instant case the payment to be made by the appellant in the month following the first year of the lease was a conditional one and therefore he could not have been evicted on the strength of the said notice. [54 G] 3.1 It is true that the tenancy of the defendant had come into existence only from month 1, 1924, but it was not the case of the respondent that because of the payment by the husband to the tenant, the defendant became a monthly tenant under section 108 of the T.P. Act and he could have been ejected on the same basis as he was paying rent for the period from January, 1925 to the filing the suit for ejectment. [55 G] 4.2 The High court was right when it held that payment to a tenant by the father of the appellant would not be a valid notice under section 119 of the Code of Civil Procedure and therefore it was open to the landlord to recover the possession from the tenant on the footing that he has been paid rent from July, 1925 onwards. The appellant, a firm of which the respondent was a partner, filed an application under Section 139(1) of the Act for assessment of its income tax on the ground that the income disclosed by it in the assessment proceedings was not liable to be included in the total income of the assessee. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim of the respondent and assessed the income of Rs. 1,10,000/- as income from undisclosed sources. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax officer. In an appeal filed by the respondent before the Income tax Appellate Tribunal, the High Court held that the assessment was not made under Section 138(1)(b) of The Act and that the order passed by the Income-tax Officer was illegal and void. On further appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The order of assessment is a judicial order and cannot be called in question in any court of law on the basis of the provisions of Section 138 of the Indian Income Tax Act 1922. [775 H] (ii) The High Court was right in holding that the Income T tax Officer had no jurisdiction to summon the production of documents in a case pending before the court when the court, by a judicial orders, requires the production thereof. [750 A] (iii) Section 138 is not attracted if the information etc. as contemplated by the Section is not required for decision of a case. The High Courts' power under Section 142(b) is limited to the cases where the information or any information sought by any person, other than a court, is required for the decision of the case pending in a court. [751 B] (iv) The expression "public interest" in the context of Section 139 of the 1961 Act cannot be construed so as to include the provisions relating to assessment proceedings which are not saved by Section 138. [753 H] In the instant case, the IncomeTax Officer had jurisdiction to call for the production and supply of documents before the income tax authorities after April 1, 1964 relating to the assessment proceeding pending before him. The order passed on the application filed by respondent under Section 140(1), therefore, was illegal. [764 G] (v) The question whether the IncomeT tax Officer has jurisdiction to examine the record of an assessee in a particular case does not arise in this case because the Income TAX Officer had the power to summon and supply the documents before he could summon the same. [754 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1584 of 1989. From the Judgment and Order dated 20.1.1989 of the Delhi High Court in S.C.A. No. 1166 of 1987. V.S. Desai, R.K. Jain and P.H. Parekh for the Appellant. M.N. Shroff, Ms. A. Subhashini and D.N Sharma for the Respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by K.JAYACHALIAH, J. The appellant is a firm carrying on business at New Delhi. The assessment proceedings were initiated under Section 143(1). The Income tax Officer issued notice under Section 148 of the said Act on April 1. 1965 and assessed income tax for the year 1964-65 was Rs. 2,10 lakhs. The respondent filed an appeal before the Appellate Tribunal against the order dated October 30, 1987. The Appellate Tribunal allowed the appeal filed against the assessment order of Income Tax Department dated March 31, 1966. The Tribunal held that in view of the decision in the case of [Commissioner of Income-Tax vs. M/s. K.K Jain] , , the income was not chargeable to tax under Section 147 of the I.T. Act. The appeal filed before the High Curt was dismissed by this Court on October 20.

The gift was made by a grandfather to his minor grandsons. The father of the minor was a minor and he had been given a life interest in the property. The mother of the minors, who was a widow, died on November 1, 1956 leaving behind her mother as her guardian. On December 5, 1957, the father of minor, Mammotty executed a deed of gift in favour of his wife, the first appellant, and the second appellant, the second respondent, the mother of minor. The gift was registered by the Sub-Registrar on January 7, 1958. The deed of transfer was executed by the father in favour Mammottty. On March 5, 1959, the husband of the appellant filed a suit for possession of the property against the father and the mother. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the gift was not valid as it was made with the consent of the father. The High Court held that the deed of sale was not invalid as it did not comply with the provisions of Section 6 of the Transfer of Property Act, but it was a conditional one. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The gift in question was valid and the gift made by Mammotsty was valid. [652 D] (2) The deed dated January 7. 1959 was not registered and the deed was not executed by Mammtty. The document was not a conditional sale. It was not an instrument of gift. The transfer was not void as it had been made with consent of father. [650 F] (3) The question whether the gift in dispute was valid or not is a mixed question of fact and law. The question of validity of the deed dated December 5. 1957, does not arise at all. The appellant was not entitled to any relief under Section 6. [663 H] (4) The document dated January 4, 1959 was registered on January 8, 1959. It did not contain a recital that the father had been appointed as guardian of the estate. The fact that the mother was appointed as her manager would not make him a party to the suit. [664 F] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 951 of 1966. Appeal by special leave from the judgment and order dated April 5, 1966 of the Allahabad High Court in Second Appeal No.. 1177 of 1959. S. T. Desai, R. N. Sachthey and B. D. Sharma, for the appellant. A. K. Sen, S. P. Nayar and R. H. Dhebar, for respondent No. 1. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Hegde, J. This appeal is directed against the judgment dated April 4, 1966 passed by the High Court of Allahabad in Second appeal No. 1177/59. The facts leading to this appeal are these: The appellant is a minor. He filed a petition under Section 9 of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') for possession on the ground that he was a guardian of his estate. On January 7th, 1959 the father made an application before the Sub Registrar for possession. The Sub- Registrar rejected the application on the grounds that the appellant had not filed any document in support of the claim. The order passed by him was confirmed by the District Judge. The appeal was dismissed by the Board of Revenue. The Board of revenue has come to the conclusion that the document dated December 6, 1957 was a deed executed by a minor son and not by a guardian. The learned counsel for the respondent submitted that the High court was right in holding that there is no evidence on record to show that the minor son was a major. It is true that the documents were not registered but it is also true that they were not executed. But the question whether there was a valid gift or not has to be decided by the Court of competent jurisdiction.

The respondent, a religious institution, was established by the appellant, and it had been registered under the Madras Act 19 of 1951. The appellant was appointed as an Assistant Commissioner of Hindu Religious Institutions in the State of Tamil Nadu. He was appointed to be an Assistant Secretary to the Government of India, Ministry of Education, Department of Education (Higher Education), New Delhi. On or about June 30, 1953, he filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court for quashing the order dated July 31, 1953 and for a direction that the respondent temple should be directed to pay a sum of Rs. 1,50,000/- as audit fee. The High Court held that the appellant was not entitled to any relief in respect of the audit fee levied by the respondent. On appeal, the High court set aside the order passed by the trial court and remanded the case to the trial Court for fresh decision on merits. In the result, the trial Judge dismissed the suit. On further appeal to this Court, it was contended that under section 76(1) of the Act, the Commissioner had no jurisdiction to determine the fee payable by the religious institutions in respect to which the expenses were incurred by the Government for providing services and the amount of audit fee was not a tax on the basis of any assessment made by the competent authority. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The order passed under section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure is not an interlocutory order. It does not decide any question of law or fact arising in the case. [505D] 2.1 The High court was right in holding that the Commissioner has no jurisdiction over the religious institution and he had not determined the audit fees payable by him. [506F] 2(i) The High Courts have not given a finding on the question whether the appellant is entitled to claim refund of the amount collected from the religious Institutions under section 78 of the Madras Hindu Religious Institution Act, 1951. [504D] (ii) The Commissioner has jurisdiction over all the properties in respect thereof and he has no power to determine any fee payable under section 77(1). [507E] 2.(iii) The order of the High Courts is not a interlocutory order but it does not determine whether the amount demanded is precisely for meeting the cost of audit. [500F] 3.2 The Commissioner had jurisdiction over cases where the expenses incurred by him were not fully or wholly attributable to the services rendered by the institution. He has no authority to determine that the expenses are not adequately attributable to any service rendered by him and he can only determine whether there is a proper estimate of the reasonable cost which may be incurred in making an effective audit of the accounts of the religious Institution. [525F] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1579 of 1973. From the Judgment and Order dated the 14th July, 1973 of the Andhra Pradesh High Court in Writ Petition No. 1223 of 1972. Rathinavel, S N. Shroff and S K Agarwal for the Respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by RAY, C.J. The facts leading to this appeal are as follows: The appellant is an Assistant Engineer in the Department of Public Works Department, Government of Andhra Pradesh.

The appellant was a member of the Orissa High Court. He filed a petition under section 19 of the Act for setting aside the order passed by the High Court in the exercise of its jurisdiction under section 20 of the Code. The High Court dismissed the petition on the ground that the order was not an order initiating contempt proceedings and, therefore, the proceeding was not maintainable. The appellant filed a writ petition before this Court challenging the order of the High court. This Court held that the High Courts were competent to entertain the petition under article 136 of the Constitution and it was open to the aggrieved party to file an appeal against the order dismissing the petition. In the case of [Bachan Singh vs State of Punjab] , this Court held: "The High Court has jurisdiction to hear a petition filed by the petitioner under section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, if the petitioner is dissatisfied with the decision of the District Judge or the High Commissioner in any matter pending before him. The petitioner cannot be heard to say that he should not file an application for setting it aside on the merits of the case." In the instant case, the appellant filed an appeal under section 30 of the said Act against the judgment and order passed in the reference. The question raised by the appellant was whether the High Curt was competent to hear the petition filed under section 21 of the General Clauses Act, 1897. This question was answered by this Court in [Bansi Lal vs State Of Punjab] . , wherein it was held that an appeal lies to this Court under section 38 of the Indian Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. The Court held as follows: "In our considered opinion, the High courts were competent under article 226 of the constitution to entertain a petition for setting-aside an order passed or decision of a High Court by the District Court or the State Commission. The jurisdiction of the court is not barred by any other provision of law." In [Banakanta Mishra vs Union Of India & Ors.] , this court held that in view of section 20, the proceedings before the High Civil Court were not maintainable and it would be open to this court to hear an appeal from the order rejecting the petition for want of jurisdiction. The present case is clearly distinguishable. In [Baldev Singh vs Union of India] , a Bench of two Judges of this Court observed that an application under section 11 of the Arbitration Act, 1940 was not a suit and therefore, it was not appealable. In view of the decision in Baldev Singh's case (supra), the High-Court had no jurisdiction to entertain such petition. The appeal is accordingly dismissed.

The appellant was prosecuted for an offence under section 6 (1 A) of the Act, and was convicted by the trial court. The prosecution case was that the appellant had been convicted for an offense punishable under section 7(1)(a) of Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, and sentenced to pay a fine of Rs. 1,000/-, in default of payment of fine, to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one year. The appellant filed an appeal against his conviction before the Sessions Court, which was dismissed by the High Court. On further appeal, the High court held that section 6(1 A), as amended by Act XLVIII of 1952, was not applicable to a case where the offence was committed by the appellant in pursuance of the provisions of section 4 of the Prevention of corruption Act, but it was only on account of the amendment made by the amending Act of 1949, that the said section became applicable. The High Court held that the amended section 6 of the Amending Act of 1948, was applicable to cases where the offences were committed by a person in pursuance to the provisions contained in section 4 or otherwise than as permitted by rules made under that section and, therefore, the appellant was not liable to be punished for an act which is done in pursuance thereof. The appeal filed by the State against the said decision of the High. Court was dismissed. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 Section 6 (2) of Act XVII of 1933, as amended, was a provision in the Act of 1933 and it was not a part of the statute book. The amendment made in section 6 was applicable only to cases which were pending when the offence had been committed by an accused person in consequence of the said provisions. [602 D] 1.2 Section 6(2) was introduced into the Act with effect from 1st April, 1949 and it is not a provision similar to section 6A of the Amendment Act of 1950. The amended section was applicable even after the amendment of the 1952 Act. [650 A] 1:3.1 The amending Act, which came into force on 1st May, 1949, was repealed by Act LXV of 1948. The amending act was not in operation at all and it could be used only for the purpose of bringing about an effective result. [703 D] 2.1 There is no provision similar in the statute to indicate that the amendment was applicable in cases where a person has been established, maintained or worked a public office. The words are comprehensive enough to take in a wireless transmitter. The section does not prohibit the possession of a wireless apparatus. [750 B] 2:2 Section 5 of the amending act is not an exception to the general rule that the provisions made in the said Act shall be applicable to such cases where an offence has been committed in pursuance thereto.

The appellant, who was the owner of a house in the city of Calcutta, purchased the property from one B.K. Roy and executed a deed of sale on July 26, 1940, in favour of the appellant. The appellant filed a suit for possession against the respondent, the State of West Bengal, and obtained an order for restoration of the properties to the appellant on August 30, 1940. On August 29, 1940 the appellant filed an application under section 36(2) of the Bengal Money Lenders Act, and prayed that the sale should be set aside. The trial court dismissed the application holding that the property purchased by the appellant was not benami in character and as such the properties were liable to be restored to the judgment debtor under clause (e) of section 36 (2). On appeal, the High Court held that the appellant had failed to establish his case that the properties sold in execution of the decree were benami in nature. The High Court further held that in view of the provisions of section 35(1)(c) of Bengal MoneyLenders Act the sale was not valid and the property was liable to pay off the decretal dues, but it was open to the purchaser to recover the decretal amount from the judgment-debtor under clause(e) thereof. The respondent filed an appeal against this order before the High court which allowed the appeal and set aside the order for restoring possession of the property to the decree holder. On further appeal by special leave, Held: (i) that in a case where the property is purchased by a purchaser from a person who was not a party to the sale, the properties are liable to restore to the plaintiff on the ground that the purchaser has failed to prove his case and the order of restoration made by both the courts below is illegal. The provisions of sub section (1) of Section 35 of the Act were attracted in this case and there was no evidence to show that the decree-holder had any right which could be protected under clause.(e) or clause (f) of [section 36(1)] of the said Act. (ii) that the High Courts have not given a direction for restoration to the possession of property sold by the judgment debtors and the purchaser purchaser is entitled to recover back the decretal money from the appellant in execution proceedings. The order for the restoration of possession made by the courts was illegal and void. [501 C] (iii) that there was a clear finding by both courts that the suit was not maintainable. The sale was invalid as it was not supported by any evidence to prove the case. The judgment-debtors were in possession of this property. The decree-holders had no right to get back the money from them under clause-(e) and they could recover the same from the respondent. [506 D] (iv) that even if the property sold in favour oram of the respondent was benami in the sense that it was benami, the appellant cannot be allowed to take advantage of the wrong order made by him. The finding of the High.Court that the judgmentdebtor had no title to the property and as he had failed in his payment of the decretal amounts is not correct. [504 D] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1124 of 1969. From the Judgment and Order dated the 14th September, 1968 of the Calcutta High Court in C.A. No. 1266 of 1967. S. K. Sinha, for the appellant (in both the appeals). R. N. Sachthey, for respondent No. 1 (In both the cases) The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Hegde, J. These two appeals are directed against a common judgment of the Division Bench of the Madras High Court dated September 14, 1968 in CAs Nos. 1265 and 1266/68. The facts leading to these appeals are as follows: The appellant is the owner in possession and enjoyment of the house property. He purchased the same on August 29.

The appellant, a minor, filed a suit for partition and separate possession of the property in dispute. The respondent, Habib & Sons, was the owner of the said property. He died on January 1, 1951. Thereafter, the respondent filed an application under Order XXI, rule 16 of the Code of Civil Procedure for execution of the decree passed by the Court. The appellant contended that the respondent had no right to execute the decree in favour of Habib & sons and that the order passed by him was not a nullity. The trial court held that the appellant was entitled to execute a decree in his favour on the 25th April, 1951 and that he could not be permitted under the provisions of section 146 of the code of Civil procedure to execute such decree. On appeal, the High Court reversed the judgment of the trial court and dismissed the suit. The High Court held that there was no decree in existence at the time of the assignment and that it was a valid transfer by an assignment in writing within the meaning of Order XXI Rule 16 of Code of 1908. It further held that in view of the provisions contained in Order XXI rule 10, the appellant could not claim to be a transferee of the suit property from the respondent. The appeal filed by the appellant before this Court was allowed and the decree of the City Civil Court was set aside. In the result, the decree for partition passed by a competent court was confirmed. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The order passed in the suit by the City civil Court was not an interlocutory order. [775 H] 2. The provisions of Order 21, rule 10 are applicable to the proceedings before the City court and the High court has no jurisdiction to pass any decree or make any order which is inconsistent with the provisions thereof. [750 A] 3. The words "decree" in the context of Order XX Rule 10 are not intended to be used as a means to cover an interlocutory application for execution. [751 B] 4. The expression 'decree' in the sense of an order passed under the Code does not mean that it is a decree. It only means that the judgment-debtor can claim to have been a transferee by assignment in the writing within meaning of the Order XXI. [753 D] 5. The word 'decree" has not been defined in the Code and, therefore, it would be appropriate for the Court to interpret the provisions in the light of the relevant provisions of the Act. [754 C] 6. The language of Order 20 Rule 10 is clear and unambiguous. It does not require that a judgment should be a decree or an agreement between the parties to the suit which is not inconsistent with any provision of the law. [764 D] 7. The question whether the appellant can claim the beneficial interest in the decree after it was passed, has to be decided by the court and not by the High Courts. [752 G] 8. The power conferred on the City Court under Order 21 Rule 10 cannot be exercised for execution or enforcement of a decree which is otherwise inconsistent with that provision. [758 H] 9. The fact that the property was transferred from the appellant to Habib & son's wife, does not make any difference in this case because the appellant had no title to the decree. [759 B] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 15 of 1971. From the Judgment and Order dated the 14th May, 1970 of the Bombay High Court in First Appeal No.. 10 of 1969. S. T. The respondent was a registered dealer in the goods and was assessed to sales tax under the Sales Tax Act. The respondent purchased the goods from the appellant, a registered firm of which he was a partner. He sold the goods to the appellant on the basis of the contract. The appellant paid the price of the goods as per the contract and the balance amount was paid by him in cash. The sale price of Rs. 1,50,000/- was paid on the date of the purchase. The sales tax authorities assessed the respondent to sales-tax under the provisions of the Sales tax Act. On appeal the High Court held that the contract was one for "sale of windows and labour" and not a contract for sale. It further held that in view of the terms of the agreement, the property in the materials supplied by the respondent was not liable to be taxed under the sales tax Act as it stood at the time of the sale. The High Court accordingly allowed the writ petition filed by the appellant. In this appeal by special leave, the appellant contended that the High court was wrong in holding that the contracts were one for sale and not of service. It was further submitted that the respondent had agreed to supply "motor bus" to the appellants and the contract did not involve any sale of windows or labour as such. The question whether the contract is one for work and labour was a pure works contract, was considered by this Court in [State of Bombay vs. R.M.D. Chamarbaugwala] , referred to.

The appellant was prosecuted for the offence of cheating under section 420 read with section 511 Indian Penal Code read with sections 120B and 420 Indian Penal code. The prosecution case is that on November 8, 1967 Shanker Lal, a broker of foreign company, was found in possession of foreign goods. On December 9, 1967 Shankar Lal brought a consignment of foreign marked gold to Ram Avtar for sale. The consignment was taken by the appellant from Ram Avtar. The appellant was arrested and produced before the Magistrate. The Magistrate took cognizance of the offence against Shanker Lal and ordered his trial. The accused filed an appeal in the High Court which was allowed on the ground that the prosecution had failed to prove the case against him. The State preferred a revision petition in this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that the appellant was not a party to any conspiracy to defraud or cheating Ram Avtar and he was discharged. [775 H] (2) Section 420 Indian penal Code is not attracted because it is the case of the prosecution itself that no case had been made out against him.. [776 D] (3) The report which was lodged by Ram Avtar in the very nature of things did not contain any allegation against the appellant. It merely stated that he was present along with Shanker Lal when the latter brought the consignment and demanded the price of the beher plates from Ram Avatar. The High court was right. [750 H] JUDGMENT: CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Criminal Appeal No. 975 of 1971. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by KHANNA, J.-This appeal is directed against the judgment dated July 7, 1970 passed by the Calcutta high court in Criminal Appeal Nos. 974-75 of 1969 whereby the High court allowed the revision petition filed by the State of West Bengal and quashed the charge against Shankerlal and the appellant under section 120B Indian Penal. The case of Shankar Lal was that he had been present along alongwith Shanker Lal before the latter took delivery of the goods. The trial court held that the accused were guilty of the offences charged against him and accordingly convicted him. On appeal by the High, Court, the High Curt reversed the judgment of the trial court and acquitted the appellant of all the charges. The facts giving rise to this appeal are as follows: The appellant is a broker in the business of foreign companies. He was found to be in possession and was also present along therewith. That the accused person is a member of the said trade and has been found in the possession of the foreign marked goods, namely, the said beher, Shankarlal and he is guilty of an offence under section 409 Indian Penal Act read with [section 420] Indian Penal]. 2. The appellant filed his written statement and denied the charges framed by him. He pleaded not guilty. The learned Magistrate held that he is a party of conspiracy to cheat Ram Avtar, the appellant, and therefore convicted him of all offences charged with. The appeal was allowed by the Sessions Judge. The respondent preferred an appeal against the order of acquittal. The Additional Sessions Judge set aside the conviction and sentence passed against Shanker Lai and dismissed his revision petition.

The petitioner was a railway servant. He was employed as a conductor in the Railway Department of the State of Bihar. On June 30, 1981, he was transferred to the State Bank of India, Patna and was posted at Patna. The petitioner was served with a charge sheet dated July 6, 1981 under Rule 14 of the Bihar State Electricity Board (Conduct of Business) Rules, 1981. He denied the charges and stated that he had not been given any opportunity to defend himself before the enquiry officer. On December 31, 1981 he was served a show cause notice by the Chief General Manager, Bihar State Road Transport Corporation, Patna, calling upon him to show cause why disciplinary action should not be taken against him for his failure to discharge his duties as a conduit in accordance with the provisions of the Act and Rules under it. The Chief General manager replied that he was guilty of misconduct and that he did not have any opportunity of defending himself before being served with the charge sheet. On January 28, 1981 the petitioner filed an application before the Chief Manager, State Road transport Corporation, Bihar, Patna for a direction to the Chief Engineer, State of Jharkhand to give him a hearing in the matter. The said application was dismissed by the order dated December 31. 1981. On April 30, 1982 the petitioner moved the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order and for a writ of mandamus directing the Chief Secretary, Government of Bihar, to give an opportunity to the petitioner to defend his case. The High Court allowed the petition holding that the charges framed against the petitioner were not proved and that the enquiry was vitiated by violation of principles of natural justice. On appeal by special leave, this Court held that the order passed by the High court was in accordance to law and it was not open to the High Courts to interfere with the same. The appellant has filed this appeal after obtaining special leave from this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts have inherent power under Article 227 of the constitution to issue directions for the purpose of giving an opportunity of hearing to the parties before passing any order or decision. [557F] 1.2 In a matter like this where the petitioner has not been able to show that he has sufficient cause for his absence, the High courts have inherent powers to set aside the order of dismissal and direct the Chief Commissioner to give a hearing. [506 G] 2.1 There is no merit in the petition which is liable to be dismissed. The writ petition is accordingly dismissed.

The appellants were the owners of land bearing Survey No. 8/1, situated in village Kaira, Taluka Kairola, District Bhavnagar. The said lands were acquired by the State Government for the purpose of construction of a road from the village to the village. The appellants filed applications before the Collector for restoration of their lands. The Collector passed an order on April 30, 1965, rejecting the applications of the appellants and directed that the lands should be restored to them. On appeal, the Collector confirmed the order of the Collector. In the meanwhile, the appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said orders. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appeals were not maintainable under section 20 of the Act and the applications for restoration made by the appellants were rightly rejected. On further appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The order passed by the Collector was correct and there was no error of law in the order passed on the application filed by the appellant. [675 H] (2) Section 20 of The Bombay Revenue Tribunal Regulations, 1958 provides that the Tribunal shall not dismiss an appeal for non prosecution unless it is satisfied that the appellant had sufficient cause for not filing the appeal within the period prescribed by Regulation 21. [650 A] (3) The provisions of section 20 are mandatory and they must be complied with in letter and spirit. If the appellants did not appear before the Tribunal on the date fixed, the application for restoration filed by them was rightly rejected by the Tribunal. [663 F] (4) Section 19(1)(b) is a provision which confers power on the Tribunal to restore an appeal dismissed for non-prosecution in a case where the appellant does not appear either in person or through his agent or lawyer. The words "decide it on merits" are used in the context of section 19(2). [663 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1524 of 1966. Appeal by special leave from the judgment and order dated April 30. 1965 of the Gujarat High Court in Special Civil Application No. 1266 of 1965. S. T. Desai, R. N. Sachthey and B. D. Sharma for the appellant (in C.A. 1523/65). M. C. Setalvad, Attorney-General of India, K. J. John, P. H. Parekh and S. P. Nayar, for the respondent (in both the appeals). The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Shah, J. The question involved in these two appeals is whether the applications filed by appellants in all the four cases were rightly dismissed by the Gujarat Revenue Tribunal. The facts are not in dispute. The appellant No. 1 is a firm and the appellants are the owners thereof. They filed applications for the restoration of the appeal to the High court. The application was allowed by the High. Court on April 29, 1965. The appeals were then heard by this Court on May 30, 1966. On May 30. 1966, the High-Court dismissed the applications. The present appeals are directed against the order dated May 30,. 1965 passed by a learned Single Judge of the High' Court dismissing the applications in all these four cases. The main contention raised before us is that the application was not maintainable as the appellants had not filed an appeal under section 19 of the Bombay Revenue Jurisdiction Act, 1947. Section 19 of The Gujarat Revenue Jurisdiction (Amendment) Act, 1965 provides that no order for restoration shall be made by any Court unless the appellant has been given a reasonable opportunity of being heard in respect of the application and the provisions of this Chapter shall have effect as if such an application had been made under section 18. It is not disputed that the appellants have filed applications under section 21 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 for restoration. The applications were dismissed by this court on May 29, 1966 and the appeals are pending in this Court.

The plaintiff, who was the Manager of the temple, filed a suit for eviction against the defendants on the ground that the defendants were in arrears of rent. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the defendant was not entitled to evict the plaintiff from the land and accordingly dismissed the suit. On appeal by the defendants, the High Court reversed the decree and held that the plaintiff was entitled to recover possession of the land from the defendants. In second appeal before this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court had erred in holding that by virtue of the provisions of Section 6 of the Land Revenue Act, the plaintiff is not entitled for any relief. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding otherwise. [557D] 2.1 The High court was wrong in holding on a construction of the relevant provisions of the [Land Revenue Act]. The High Courts decision does not suffer from any infirmity and the High Courts order is correct. [658F] 2:2 Section 6(1) of the Act provides that the land shall be deemed to have been dedicated to the temple for the purpose of the family or that he made certain alienations of the property. The fact that the property was not dedicated to a temple does not make him entitled to any relief under the provisions contained in Section 6. [650F] 3.1 It is true that the provisions relating to the maintenance and repairs of the properties are not applicable to the case of the plaintiff, but the High courts have erred in law in holding so. The plaintiff was not a party to the suit and he was entitled only to recover the possession of Telibandha. [651F] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1566 of 1987. The appellants were convicted by the Trial Court for contempt of court. The appellants filed an appeal against the order of the High Court in the criminal proceedings. The appeal was allowed by the High court on the ground that the resolution was not valid. The State Government preferred an appeal to this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: (1) The High court was wrong in holding that the resolutions were invalid. [775 H] (2) The resolution dated April 22, 1972 passed by respondent No 2 is a result of the passing of the resolution and it was not open to the appellants to contend that the order passed by them was illegal. [750 A] (3) The order passed in the appeal was not legal and it could not be passed in favour of the appellants. [751 B] (4) The resolutions were passed under the presidentship of the first appellant described as contemner No. 1. The resolution was passed under s. 14 of the U.P. High Court's Act, 1952. The order was passed by a competent court. It was not necessary to give reasons for passing the order. The appellant, a registered society, was incorporated under the provisions of the [Indian Companies Act, 1913] (hereinafter referred to as "the Act") and was registered with the Registrar of the High Court on 25th of November, 1983. The award was made by the learned Munsif in favour of the respondent. On 28th of January, 1978, the arbitrators appointed the arbitrators. The arbitrators gave a notice to the appellant under section 11 of the Act calling upon them to make the payment of the amount within 15 days from the date of receipt of the notice failing which they were required to pay interest at the rate of 18% per annum on the amount due from 28th January, 1983 till the date on which the award was passed. The appellant filed a suit for recovery of Rs. 1,50,000/- with interest and costs in the court of the learned Subordinate Judge, Arambagh. The respondent contended that the award made by him was not valid as it was not signed by the arbitrators and therefore he was not entitled to receive any amount from the appellant. The trial court held that the arbitrator had committed an error in law and that he was competent to pass a decree for recovery against the appellant and accordingly decreed the suit. On appeal, the High court set aside the decree of the trial court and remanded the case to the trial Court for fresh disposal according to law. In this appeal by special leave, it is contended on behalf of the appellant that the order made by this Court in M. The appeal was allowed and the order passed by the High. Court setting aside the order of remand was set aside. It was further submitted that the arbitrators had committed a mistake in law as they were not parties to the award and therefore they were entitled to get interest at 18% on the awarded amount from 28.1.1978 till the filing of the suit and that the appellant was entitled to claim interest at 12% per month on the said amount from 1st of April, 1978 till the payment. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The order passed in MFA No. 8 of 1985 by the court below is correct and there is no error apparent on the face of the record. [775 H] 2. The High Court was right in setting aside that part of the decree which directed payment of interest at 9% per year from 28-1-1978 till payment. [750 A] 3. It is not necessary to discuss in detail the ratio of A the decision of this Court referred to above and it is not possible to agree with the view taken by the Full Bench of the Andhra Pradesh High Court in the case of M/s. The decision of the Full bench of the Hyderabad High Court is binding on us [750 B] 4. The judgment of the Division Bench of Andhra Pradesh high court was correct and we see no reason to interfere with that order. [751 D] 5. It cannot be said that the amount awarded by the arbitrator was not paid to the respondent within 15th of December, 1983 or the interim injunction was vacated on 24th of June, 1985. The learned counsel for the appellant submitted that in view of the finding recorded by the Division bench of Andhra High Court that the respondent was entitled only to get the interest at 6% per months from 28/1/1978 till its payment, it should be held that he is not entitled for any amount on account of interest from 28 th of January 1978 till payment and accordingly he is entitled to interest at 8% permonth on the aforesaid amount from 27th of February, 1983 until payment.

The respondent, a firm carrying on business in the name and style of M/s. S.K. Enterprises, was a partner in a partnership firm. The firm was dissolved by an order dated April 30, 1949. On May 1, 1950, the respondent filed a suit for ejectment against the appellant under section 13(1)(e) of the Act on the ground that he had sublet the premises to a sub tenant and that the sub tenants were entitled to recover possession of the premises from the appellant. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the respondent was not entitled to sue for ejectment on the grounds of subletting. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decree and held that the appellant was not liable to be evicted under section13(1) (e) as he had sub-let the premises in question to a partner of the firm. In further appeal to this Court it was contended that the High court was wrong in holding that there was no sub tenancy in favour of the respondent and that, therefore, the appellant could not be evicted on the basis of the sub tenancy. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding, that the question whether the respondent had sublet a part of the property to a partnership or not was a mixed question of law and fact and the High Courts were bound to take notice of the same. [532E] 2. Section 13(2) of The Act provides that where any person is a partner or a sub-tenant, he shall be entitled to obtain possession of such premises on the terms and conditions specified in the section. [506F] 3.1 The High court has rightly held that there is no subtenancy in favour the respondent. [504B] 3 2.2 The question whether there was a sub tenancy or not is a mixed issue of law, fact and law and the Courts are bound to give effect to it. [433D] 3 3.3 Section 13 (1)(a) of Act of 1952 provides that if any person has sublet a portion of his premises to another person, he cannot be evicted from such portion of the said premises on that ground. The question is whether the sub tenant was entitled to get possession of any part of his property under section 12(1). [506G] 4. Section 15 of the Indian Contract Act provides for the protection of a partner against eviction and not against a subtenant. [498A] 5. In the instant case, there was an agreement between the respondent as partner of M.S. Soda and the appellant in which he had agreed to let out the premises on his own account. The respondent was also liable to pay rent for the said period. [500B] 6. Section 12(2)(a)(i) of Indian Contract (Amendment) Act, 1952 provides for protection of the tenant against eviction. [50C] 7. Section 14 of the Limitation Act provides a special remedy for the enforcement of a contractual obligation. The provisions of section 14 are not applicable to the facts of this case. [51D] 8. Section 16(1A)(i), (ii) and (iii) of U.P. Act of 1947 provide that where a person has sub-letting the whole or part of premises to any other person, the sub-tenancy shall be determined by an arbitrator appointed by the Central Government in this behalf. [52E] 9. Section 17(1), (2) and Section 18(3)(a), (b) and Explanation 1 to section 15(1); (c) provides that a tenant who has sublet the whole of his tenancy premises to one or more sub tenants; (d) is not entitled for protection against eviction under section 14(1-A). [52F] 10. Section 18 of the U. P.

The respondent was appointed as a Head Master of the school in the year 1971. He was appointed to the post of Head Master on probation for a period of one year and he was confirmed in that post by an order dated January 30, 1976. On March 31, 1977, he was promoted as Head Master. The Board passed an order on April 7, 1977 promoting him as Head master with effect from April 1, 1977. He filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the promotion of the respondent as Headmaster and also the order of the Assistant Director of Education dated May 30, 1977 rejecting his claim for promotion to the higher post. The High Court held that the order passed by the Assistant Educational Officer on May 30/31,1977 was not in accordance with law and quashed the same. It further held that since the respondent had failed to show that he was a candidate at the examination conducted by the Board, he could not be promoted as head master. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court erred in holding that the Assistant Education Officer was justified in rejecting the claim of the respondents for promotion as Head Masters and that the decision of the Education Standing Committee dated April 7/8, 1977 was not based on any evidence or material on record. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The order passed in contravention of the statutory provisions of law is liable to be quashed. [775 H] 2.1 The High court has no jurisdiction to interfere with the impugned notification. [750 A] 2(i) The High Courts order was not supported by any evidence and it was not open to the High Courts under article 226 or 227 of the Constitution to interfere in the matter. [751 G] 2.(ii) The order of promotion passed by an Assistant Educational officer is not a valid order. It is not open for the High courts to interfere on the ground that the said officer, parents or guardians are parties to the fabrication. [751 A] 3.2 The High courts order was based on evidence and material on the record. [752 B] 2: 1 There is no infirmity in the impugned order passed under Article 226 of the constitution. [754 G] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1579 of 1991. From the Judgment and Order dated 16.8.1991 of the High C Court of Bombay in Writ Petition No. 877 of 1977. V.M. Tarkunde, S.K. Bagga, R.N. Singh, Mrs. A.K Gupta, M.S. Kini, P.H. Parekh, Ms. Arundhati Jain and Ms. Rani Chhabra for the Appellants. S.B. Bhasme, Ms, A. Subhashini, Ms., A.V. Rangam, Ms,. A. Subba Rao, Mrs, Alagiriswami, M/s. K.Kini & Co. for the Respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by VENKATARAMIAH, J. This appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated April 16, 1991 passed by a Division Bench of the Bombay High Court in Writ Appeal No: 877/91. The respondent was working as Head Mistress of the School at the relevant time. He had been appointed as Headmistress on probation on the basis of an order passed on May 10, 1977 by the Deputy Director of Public Instruction, Bombay, dated April 6, 1977 and he continued to be a head Master in the school till March 31/3, 1977 when he was appointed on probation. The appointment of the Respondent was not challenged by him before the Tribunal. The Tribunal held that he had been working as head Mistress for more than one year without any complaint and therefore, he should have been promoted as Headmaster.

The prosecution case was that the appellants were prosecuted for an offence under section 5(1) read with section 5 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The prosecution alleged that the accused persons were members of a firm and were members thereof. The accused persons denied their guilt and claimed to be tried. The trial court held that the prosecution had failed to prove that they were interested in giving bribe for hushing up the case against them. On appeal by the State, the High Court reversed the order of acquittal passed by the trial court and convicted the appellants under section 161 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced each one of them to suffer rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years and to pay a fine of Rs. 500/- each. The High Court also held that there was no evidence on record to show that the appellant was interested in causing pecuniary loss to the Government. On further appeal by special leave, the Supreme Court reversed its judgment and acquitted the accused. In this Court it was contended that the High court had erred in holding that the case of the prosecution was not proved beyond reasonable doubt and that the acquittal of the accused was vitiated on account of non-compliance with section 21 of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The provisions of section 5 (1) of the [Prevention of Corruption Amendment Act] are mandatory in character and they do not violate any provision of law. [675 H] 2. Section 6 of the General Clauses Act provides that "no person shall be prosecuted for any offence under this Act except on a charge made against him by a public servant". The expression 'public servant' is defined in section 21 as meaning a person who is or has been a public officer as defined in clause (d) of section 2 of the said Act. [775 H; 776 B] 3. Section 5(2) of Prevention of corruption Act provides for punishment for criminal misconduct by public servants and that is to say, "no public servant shall be convicted of any offence except with the previous sanction" [682 D] 4. The expression "public servant" in section 6 means a public person as defined under clause (e) of sub section (1), or a public Servant as defined by section 21 or a member of a public office as defined therein. [750 H] 5. Section 7(1)(a) provides that no public servant is liable to be prosecuted under the Act for an act which constitutes an offence punishable under section 6. [751 G] 6. The word 'public' in section 7(2), therefore, means a person interested in the giving of bribe for a hushing process. [753 H] 7. Section 8(1), (4) and (5) provide that no person shall, if he is a public or servant as defined inss. 21 or 24 of the Penal Code be prosecuted. [754 G] JUDGMENT: CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Criminal Appeal No. 916 of 1986. From the Judgment and Order dated 16.12.1986 of the Delhi High Court in Crl. A. No. 8/86. V.S. Desai, S.K. Bagga, R.N. Sachthey and B.D. Sharma for the Appellant. Virender Singh, RR. Gupta and D.N Sharma for Respondent No. 1. K.M. Sharma and P.H. Parekh for Respondent Nos. 2 to 4. A-1 to A-4. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by RAY, J. This appeal is directed against a judgment of the High Curt in Criminal Appeal Nos. 816/86 and 816 of 1987. The appellant was convicted under section 7 read with Section 5 of Preventionof Corruption Act and sentenced to suffer imprisonment for one year and to fine of rupees five thousand and in default of payment of fine, he was also directed to undergo rigorous imprisonment of two years.

The appellant, a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956, was incorporated in the year 1958. The respondent, a member of the Indian Audit and Accounts Department, was appointed as an auditor to audit the accounts of the company. He filed a suit against the appellant for recovery of Rs. 1,50,000/- on the ground that he had failed to pay the amount due under the guarantee given by the surety. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the surety was entitled to the benefit of the provisions of section 141 of the Act and accordingly, the respondent was directed to make an application for payment of Rs 1,00,000/-. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the trial court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: (1) The provisions of Section 141 of Act are not attracted and an application under that section must be made to the Court of first instance, i.e., the Court which passed the decree or order for payment or recovery of money. [775 H] (2) The surety is entitled to a benefit of every security given by him at one sitting on September 16, 1957, evidence of such other security being offered by the principal debtor which itself may be a consideration for the surety offering his personal guarantee and the creditor cannot be discharged from the obligation undertaken under the letter of guarantee. [750 H] The High court was wrong in holding that section 141 does not apply to an application made to Court of competent jurisdiction. [751 A] (3) The appellant is entitled, as a matter of right, to the benefits of the provision of section 142 of the Code and accordingly he is entitled for restitution. [75 H; 75 B] (4) Section 141 does no more than make it clear that an application filed under that provision must be in writing and signed by the creditor. The appellant cannot be allowed to take advantage of the surety's offer made by him on the basis of which advance was made and the surety is discharged from his obligation to pay or recover the amount. [76 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1584 of 1977. The Act was passed by the Legislature of Madras on April 1, 1950. The Hindu law of succession and inheritance were as follows: "The Hindu Law of succession, including the Hindu law, shall in matters of succession or inheritance be governed by the Mahomedan law. (1) A.I.R. (2) Bom. The second section provided that all Cutchi Memons, subject to the provisions of section 3, shall, in matters relating to succession and succession be governed under the Mahomedan Law. (3) A Hindu father who had been born before 1948, but had not been proved to have been adopted as a part of his customary law, was entitled by custom to dispose of the whole of his property by survivorship. (4) A son in the case of a Hindu dying after the commencement of the Act, was not entitled to any share therein by birth in the property held by him or by his father. (5) A daughter in the family of a deceased person who had not become a member of the family and had not acquired any right by birth under the personal law applicable to her husband, was also entitled to a share therein. (6) A widow in the event of her death after the Act came into force could not claim partition or division of the property as a result of the death of her father. The High Court held that the deceased had acquired a right by adoption and that the question whether she had become a son or daughter of her husband was a mixed question of law and fact and therefore, the High Court was right in its view that the accountable persons having been born after 1948, were entitled to dispose off the whole property held under the Hindu Law. The appeal filed by special leave is directed against the judgment of the High court. Allowing the appeal, the Court HELD: 1.1. The question whether a son born before the Act was a member or not and who had acquired any rights by birth therein by virtue of the personal laws applicable to him or her husband has to be decided in the light of the provisions contained in section 3 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956. [675 H] 1.2 The question as to whether a daughter born before 1949 was entitled to maintenance under the Personal Law applicable to them or not is a mixed issue of law or fact and it cannot be determined by any court of law. [775 B] 1:3. Under section 3(1) of the Indian Succession Act the right, title and interest in the properties held by a deceased member of his family shall pass on his death to his son or other legal representative unless he has died intestate. The right, therefore, is not a joint property but only a limited estate. [750 D] 1] 2.1 The question that arises for consideration is whether the accountable person having been married prior to 1948, was governed by Hindu law applicable in the matter of the succession to the property of his father or whether he had acquired such right by virtue under the provisions relating to the personal Law applicable thereto. [751 D] 2:2. Under the Hindu laws applicable in India, the accountable and the legal representative is entitled to receive the share in the estate held by his deceased father. [753 H] 2(a) The question of succession to a joint family does not arise in the present case because the accountable or the legal representatives are entitled to claim partition and separate possession of the properties. [764 D] (b) The right to dispose the whole or any part of the estate is not an absolute one. It is only a restricted estate. The accountable person has been given the right to deal with the property by birth, and therefore the accountable, the legal heirs are entitled only to share in that property. [754 D] 3:1. Under Hindu law the accountable for the property acquired under the family arrangement, the right of succession is not absolute.

The appellants are engaged in the manufacture of cotton fabrics. They were manufacturing cotton fabrics and clearing them to their own factories. The appellants purchased yarn from the factory for weaving the same into fabrics. The process of weaving the fabrics was carried on by the appellants. The fabrics were removed from the premises of the appellants to the various units situated at different places in the State of Madhya Pradesh. The goods manufactured by the appellant were cleared to their sister concerns, namely, M/s. S.K. Jain & Co., and they were also manufacturing cotton fabric. The said yarn was purchased by the assessee from the said concern for weaving cloth. The assessee filed a return declaring the income of Rs. 1,50,000/- as per the books of account maintained by it. The Income Tax Officer assessed the income to tax under section 3(1) of the Act on the ground that the said yarn manufactured by it was not liable to excise duty. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax officer and dismissed the appeal. In further appeal to the Tribunal, the Tribunal held that the process of manufacture of the cotton fabrics was not a manufacturing activity but was a process for weaving of the same. The Tribunal also held that if the yarn manufactured was not removed from an integrated process, the yarn would be liable to duty. The question whether the said goods were produced at an intermediate stage and consumed or utilised in the continuous process of the manufacture was not decided by the High Court. In our opinion, the High court was right in holding that the Tribunal was correct in law in holding the assessee to have been removed from a factory for the purpose of weaving cloth and treating it as such, the said process would be an activity which is not a manufacture. The High Court also held on facts that the yarn produced by the said appellant was not manufactured at an integrated stage and, therefore, the provisions of Section 3(i) of Act were attracted. In view of the above findings, we are unable to agree with the contention raised on behalf of the appellant that the goods manufactured in the factory were not liable for excise duty and, consequently, the question of levy of excise duty would not arise. The appeal is accordingly dismissed.

The appellant filed a suit for eviction of the tenant from the suit premises on the ground that he was in arrears of rent and was liable to be evicted. The respondent filed an application under section 68D of the Act for eviction on the grounds mentioned therein. The trial court held that the appellant had failed to prove that he had been served with a notice under section 69(1) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') and that the order of the Civil Judge was not in accordance with law. On appeal by the respondent, the District Judge confirmed the order passed by the trial court. The appellant filed an appeal before the High Court which was dismissed. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The provisions of section 68C of the act are mandatory and they must be complied with in letter and spirit. [675 H] 1.2 Section 68D(i) of Act provides that where a landlord has filed an objection under section68D of Act, he shall not file his objections before the hearing of the case and if he does so within thirty days from the date of its publication in the official Gazette, the hearing shall be deemed to have been completed on the date on which the notice is published. [775 H; 776 B] 1:3 The provisions contained in section 68 D(i), (ii) and (iii) of Chapter IVA of the Bombay Tenancy Act, 1939, are mandatory. The provisions relating to hearing of objections or representations must be strictly complied with. [750 C] 2.1 Section 68C(i)(a) of that Act provides for the disposal of an objection by the Tribunal in accordance therewith. [751 D] 2:2 Section68D(ii) of Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, provides that if a landlord fails to file his objection within thirty day from the time specified in sub section (i), he shall be liable to pay compensation at the rate of five per cent for every one hundred rupees or part thereof. [753 H] 2] In the instant case, the appellant filed objections under section 67D(1)(a). The objections were filed within thirty Days from the day on which they were published in the Official Gazette and were disposed of by an order dated April 1, 1967. The order was passed on May 5, 1967 and the appeal was dismissed on the basis that it did not disclose a cause of action. [764 H] 3:3 A] 2(i). Section 68E(ii)(a), (iii), (iv) and 68D (v) of Schedule IVA are mandatory in nature. The proviso to section 68E provides that no order for eviction shall be passed under sub section(1), if the landlord fails or refuses to comply with any order made by an appellate authority under section 70D of this Act within thirtydays from the said date. [774 H; 771 A] (ii)(b) The provisions in Chapter IV-A of Bombay Land Revenue Code, 1879, are directory and not mandatory. [783 G] 2.(i) Section 68F(ii), (v), (vi) and 66D(vii) of this act provide that where the landlord failed to file a claim under section 66D of that act within thirty-days from such date, he is liable to make good the deficit in the amount of arrears of land revenue. [794 G] 3.1 It is not necessary for us to go into the question whether the provisions contained therein are mandatory or directory.

The appellant was a public servant within the meaning of section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act. He was convicted by the Special Judge, Delhi under section 161, Indian Penal Code and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years and to pay a fine of Rs. 5001 or in default to undergo simple imprisonment for one year. The appellant filed an appeal before the High Court which was dismissed on the ground that the conviction was not excessive. The High Court held that the appellant had obtained money from Russel Nathaniel and his wife and that he was guilty of grossly abusing his position as a public officer within the definition of section 161 of the Indian Penal code and sentenced him to undergo imprisonment for a period of two years. The State filed an application before the Special judge, Delhi for permission to prosecute the appellant under section 5 (1)(a) of Prevention of corruption Act. The Special Judge rejected the said application holding that the offence was not an offence under section 6 of the Act and that the prosecution was not maintainable. On appeal by special leave, the High court held that there was no evidence on record to show that the accused had obtained a gratification for doing or forbearing to do any official act or for showing or forbidding to show, in the exercise of his official functions favour or disfavour to any per son. The Court further held that it was not necessary for the prosecution to prove facts constituting an offence within the ambit of section 6(1) (d) and section 5 of the said Act. On this finding the appellant was convicted and sentenced by the trial court. The present appeal has been filed against that order. Allowing the appeal, the Court HELD: 1. The provisions of section 4(2)(a), (b) and (c) of [section 6] of the prevention of corruption act are not applicable to the case in hand. Section 5(2) of that Act provides for punishment for an offence which is not an offences under section 7 or section 161. [775 H] 2. The question whether a person has obtained money by doing or purporting to do anything, or forbearance to show or forbad to show any official acts or for the purpose of showing or withholding any official work or for holding any official function was a matter within the purview of section 3 of the Criminal Law Amendment Act. [750 H] 3. The offence under s. 161 is not one of an offence as defined in section 5 and therefore it cannot be said that there is no evidence to show facts constituting the offence within that provision. [751 G] 4.

The appellant was a member of the Indian Railway Protection Force. He was prosecuted for an offence under section 161 I.P.C. and section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The prosecution case was that he had obtained pecuniary advantage for himself punishable under Section 161 I PC. The trial court held that the sanction accorded by the appellant was not a valid sanction. The High Court on appeal upheld the conviction and sentence of the appellant. In further appeal to this Court it was contended that the order of the Special Judge granting the certificate was not an order passed in exercise of his judicial functions, and that the Special judge had no jurisdiction to pass such an order. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The sanction accorded under section 6(c) of Prevention of corruption Act II of 1947 is a valid one. [775 H] 2.1 The sanction was not required by law for the prosecution of the accused. It was not necessary that the accused should have been called upon to answer the charge or to give his explanation as to why he should not be tried. [750 A] 2(i) The sanction is a condition precedent to the exercise of the power conferred on the authority which has to be satisfied that it is necessary in the interests of justice to accord the sanction. [751 B] (ii) The order granting the special leave was not one passed by the Special Court and, therefore, the same could not be sustained. [753 H] (iii) The Special Judge had no power to pass an order which was not valid or invalid. [764 D] 2.(i) There is nothing in section 6 of the Act which requires that the authority competent to grant the certificate should have passed such an act. It is true that the special court has jurisdiction to try the case but it does not follow that the power vested in the authority is a nullity. The order of sanction was, therefore invalid. The Special Court had no competence to pass the order which could be sustained by reason of the provisions of section 6. [754 H] 3.2 In the instant case, the sanction was required by the law and not by law. [752 B] JUDGMENT: ORIGINAL JURISDICTION: Writ Petition No. 1123 of 1987. Under Article 32 of the Constitution of India for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights. N.S. Bindra and R.N. Sachthey, for the appellant in person. S.K.
