This is an appeal against a judgment of the High Court of Delhi dismissing a writ petition filed by the petitioner challenging the validity of the order passed by Special Judge on the ground that the said order was not passed by him in exercise or discharge of his duties as required by section 6 and was not in accordance with law. The facts leading to this appeal are these: The appellant is a member, Indian Railway, having been convicted for an act which was an offence punishable under section 5 (2) read with section 6, section 7(1)(a), section 8 of the said Act. He filed a writ application before the High court praying that the proceedings against him be quashed and he may be tried in accordance therewith. The appellant contended that he was not called upon by the authorities to answer charges under section 4 of the [Prevention of Corruption (Amendment) Act] II of 1956, as he had been convicted by the Court of Special Judge for an alleged offence punishable Under Section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The learned Single Judge dismissed the writ petition holding that the prosecution was not maintainable in view of the provision contained in section 5 and section 6 read with sections 6 and 7 of the General Clauses Act, 1897. The Division Bench held that there is no merit in this appeal and accordingly dismissed the same. Hence this appeal by special leave.

The appellant was the tenant of a building in which he had been residing. He filed a suit for eviction against the tenants on the ground that the landlord had let out the premises to the appellant and that the building was bona fide required by him for his own use and occupation. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the requirement of the landlords was not bona fide. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decree of the trial court and dismissed the suit. In this Court it was contended on behalf of the tenants that the tenancy in favour of the appellant was a permanent one and the landlord was entitled to recover possession of the building from the tenant. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The question whether the requirement for the landlords bona fide requires by the landlord for his personal use and/or occupation is bona fide or not has to be decided on the facts of each case. [675 H] 2.1 The requirement of a landlord for immediate purpose of demolishing the property in order to reconstruct it as that action would, per se, be not bona fides. [775 G] 2(i) The question as to whether there is any possibility or any objection from the daughters of the settlor or from any other remainder man cannot affect adjudication of the claim of the landlord against his tenants under the provisions of the Act. [750 H] (ii) The requirement for immediate demolition of the property was not a bona fide one and it was not bonafide required by the landlords. The requirement was not mala fide. [751 G] (iii) The High Court was wrong in holding that there is no possibility or an objection from any of the daughters to the landlord's need. [751 H] 3(i)(a) The requirements for immediate and urgent demolition of a house are not bona fulcrum, but only those which are required by a landlord under the Act for his residential purpose. [752 G] 3.1 In the instant case, the requirement was bona fides and it is not a bonafide one. [754 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 15 of 1976. From the Judgment and Order dated 16.5.1976 of the High court of Delhi in C.M.P. No. 1124/76. S.K. Mehta, R.N. Poddar and B.D. Sharma for the Appellant. V.S. Desai, S.C. Agarwal and P.H. Parekh for the Respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by KASLIWAL, J. The appellant was inducted as a tenant on a monthly rent of Rs. 500/- per month. He had been paying the rent regularly till the date of filing of the suit and that is why he has not paid any rent to the respondent. The High Courts orders are set-aside. The respondent, a bhumidhari land holder, was the owner of a grove. He had been in possession of the grove land for a period of five years from the date of his purchase. The grove land was acquired by the State Government under Section 6(a) of the Act. The respondent filed an application before the Collector for permission to sell the grove lands. The Collector rejected the application and granted permission to the appellant to sell them in the prescribed manner. On appeal, the Additional District Magistrate, Lucknow, held that the land was a part of the 'land' and as such the respondent was entitled to sell it in execution of decree. The appellant filed an appeal before the Board of Revenue which dismissed the same. The Board of revenue confirmed the order of the Collector. In the revision filed by the appellant, the Board held that since the grove was not a part thereof, the land could be sold in execution proceedings under Section 18(1)(a) and (b). On further appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The expression 'intermediary' is defined in section 3(13) of Act. It means a person who has been in continuous possession of any land for five years or more from the time of his holding as such. [605 H] 2.1 The word 'inter collector' is used in the sense of an expression which is capable of being understood in common parlance and understood in the ordinary sense. It includes a person whose interest is included in the whole. [650 D] 2(i) The words 'intermediate possession' and 'land', are not defined in the Act, but they have been used in section 18(2). Therefore, the word 'determine' has to be understood in its ordinary sense and understood according to the ordinary meaning of the term. [706 H] (ii) The expression "intermediaries" is defined by section 3 (13) as including a person holding any land or grove land. [750 A] 2.(iii) The word "inter collector" has been used for the purposes of section 18 which includes a sub-section of section 19. Therefore, it would be difficult to accept the contention that the words 'in the same sense' and the context in which they have to be interpreted are not capable of any precise or precise definition. [751 B] 2 (iv) The term 'interpret' is not defined either in the statute or in the rules framed thereunder. Therefore it would not be possible for us to accept this contention. [753 H] 3.1 It is well settled that a person cannot be said to have been in any manner included in a part, of the "land" and as he has been holding the land for the purpose of a large scale development, he is entitled to get the land in question in execution. [752 B] 3.(i) In the instant case, the respondent purchased the grove from the appellant on payment of Rs. 1,000/- per acre. The sale deed was executed by the respondent in favour of the appellant and the same was registered under Section 17(1) (a). Therefore the land cannot be sold for a price higher than the market value of the land. The High Court has rightly held that as the grove is not a separate property, the lands could be purchased in execution thereof. [754 G] 3(ii) In any event, the expression 'in his own right' and/or the context of Section 18 (2) are capable of only one meaning. [764 D] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 2041 of 1968. From the Judgment and Order dated the 9th July, 1967 of the Allahabad High Court in First Appeal No.. 1577 of 1966. S.K. Mehta, R.N. Sachthey and B.D. Sharma for the Appellant. V.C. Mahajan, M.M. K.

The appellants were convicted for an offence under Section 302 IPC and sentenced to suffer rigorous imprisonment for life. The prosecution case was that on the night of the occurrence, Suku had been murdered by all the four appellants. On the morning of the day of the incident, Suu, Suju and Preman were returning from their house. They were armed with deadly weapons. Suku was also armed with a chopper. The deceased Suku died as a result of the injuries caused to Suku. The accused persons were charged for an offences under Section 304 Part I IPC. The trial court convicted all the appellants for an offense punishable under Section 326 IPC and imposed sentence of one year rigorous imprisonment on each of them. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence passed against the first appellant Subran and Premen, but reduced the sentence to one year R.I. The State preferred an appeal before this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1. Section 149 IPC is a penal provision which provides for punishment of murder in certain circumstances. It is not a penal offence. [775 H] 1.2. The provisions of Section 302 read with Section 149 are mandatory and they do not provide for any punishment other than death or imprisonment for a period of three years. [750 A] 1:3.1 The High Court was wrong in holding that the appellants were guilty of an offence punishable under Sections 304 Part II IPC. [751 B] 2.1 There is no evidence to show that all the accused persons had shared the common intention of causing death of Suku and Suju or were sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death of the deceased Suu. The High court was wrong when it held that the injuries inflicted by them were on any vital part of the body, but the medical evidence shows that all these injuries were caused by the accused for which they were liable to be punished under Section 325 IPC. Therefore, the conviction of the appellants under Section 324 IPC is not sustainable. [753 H] 2:2 The High Courts have erred in holding otherwise. [754 A] 2] 1a. The evidence on record shows that Suku did not commit an offence of murder and it was not a case where the accused were armed and, therefore, they could be convicted under Section 323 IPC. There is nothing to show as to how the appellants are guilty for an act of murder punishable under [Section 302] IPC. In view of the circumstances of the case, the sentence imposed on Suku cannot be said to be excessive or disproportionate. [752 B] 3:3 The High courts have erred while holding otherwise and in convicting the accused under Section 307 IPC. It was not necessary for them to commit an act which is punishable under the provisions of [Section 326] IPC and they could also be convicted for the same offence. Therefore the conviction under Section 148 IPC cannot be sustained.

The assessee, a resident of U.K., was assessed to income tax on the basis that it maintained its accounts for the assessment years 1967 68 and 1968 69 and that it had maintained its account in the books of the Indian Company. The Income Tax Officer, however, held that the amount of royalty payable by the assessee was not taxable at all as it did not maintain any particular method of accounting regularly in respect of the said royalty amount. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax officer and dismissed the appeal. In further appeal to the Tribunal, the High Court held that there was no conflict or inconsistency between Section 5(2) and Section 145 of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The assessee is a debtor in respect to the amount which it has maintained for all its income. [557F] 2.1 The assessee was maintaining its accounts on mercantile basis and was liable to pay income tax only on its actual receipt under Section 5 (2) of the 1922 Act. [546G] 2(i)(a) The assessee had maintained the account books of Indian Company in respect whereof it maintained the accounts regularly. It was not a debtor within the meaning of Section 145. [547F] 3.1 There is no conflict between Section 145 and Section 147 of the 1961 Act. The High Court was right in holding that there is no inconsistency or inconsistency in the case of the assessee. [548G] 3(i) The expression "income tax" has not been defined in the Act and it must be held that it is a payment or receipt, but it must include income from other sources. [549F] (ii) Section 145 does not apply to the facts of the case. It only applies to an assessee who maintains accounts on his own account. [556G] (iii) The High court was right. [558C] 3.(i)(b) The amount of Rs. 1,000/- paid by the Indian company in cash is not taxable as it does not maintain a particular method or accounting regularly for all other income. It cannot be said that there has been any conflict or inconsistent or inconsistency with Section 145 or Section 147. [559F] 4.(i) There is nothing in the language of Section 5 of the 1918 Act which makes it clear that the assessee must be maintaining its account on mercantile system and if it maintains accounts regularly, it must also be held to have maintained a particular mode or accounting for all the income. The expression 'income tax' has not only been defined by the 1961 legislation but it was also used in the same sense as in Section 145 which is applicable to the case before us. [560F] 5.(i). The High Courts were right in taking the view that there must be a conflict or repugnant or inconsistency and that the expression 'Income Tax' has no application to the fact of the present case. [561G] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1566 of 1987. From the Judgment and Order dated 11.8.1987 of the Allahabad High Court in S.C.A. No. 8/87. V.S. Desai, R.K. Jain and P.H. Parekh for the Appellant. M.N. Shroff, Ms. A. Subhashini and D.N Sharma for the Respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by KASLIWAL, J. The respondent is a member of the Reserve Bank of India and is a creditor in respect thereof. The question involved in this appeal is whether there has not bee n any conflict between [Section 5(1)] of the 1973 Act and Section 5C of the 1908 Act.

The appellant was a member of the gang of dacoits. He was tried by the Additional Sessions Judge, Delhi for an offence under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The prosecution case was that on March 17, 1960, at about 6 p.m., the appellant was found in possession of a knife which he had used as a weapon in committing the murder of one Deoki Sahu. The appellant was arrested on March 18, 1960. He pleaded not guilty to the charge and claimed to be tried. The Additional Sessions judge held that the appellant had committed an offence punishable under section 34 read with sections 135(1) and 114 of the [Indian Penal Code] and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for a period of one year. On appeal by the State, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence but reduced the sentence to one year's rigorous imprisonment. The State appealed against the said order to this Court. HELD: (i) Section 114 of Indian Evidence Act provides that when any fact is especially within the knowledge of any person, it shall be presumed unless the contrary is proved, that he has committed an act which is inconsistent with the innocence of the accused and that he had taken all reasonable steps to prevent the commission of such act. [775 H] (ii) The appellant had not been convicted on the basis of the evidence adduced by him in his defence. He had been acquitted by the trial court. [750 A] (iii) The High Court was wrong in holding that the conviction of the appellant under section 304 Part II read with Section 34 of Indian Penal code is illegal and unsustainable. [751 B] (iv) The prosecution has not proved beyond reasonable doubt that the accused had committed the offence punishable by the first part of section 114 of IPC. [751 D] (v) The evidence adduced in defence was sufficient to prove that the deceased was murdered. [764 G] (vi) The conviction of an accused on the testimony of an accomplice cannot be sustained. [754 H] JUDGMENT: CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Criminal Appeal No. 9 of 1971. In an appeal to this Court it was contended that the appellant was not a public officer within the definition of section 2(1) (d) of Prevention of corruption Act. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The appellant was an officer in the service or pay of the Government and he was an Officer in the Service or pay or pay in the State. [675 H] 2. The words "public servant" include a person who is appointed to some office for the performance of any public duty. [775 B] 3. The word 'public' in section 21(9) of Act, 1947, means 'a public servant'. Therefore, an officer performing public duty must be a public or servant within a meaning of that section. [750 H] 4. The expression "public servants" includes a person holding any office under the Government or the Government. [751 G] 5. The term 'public servant' in the context of section 6(1), means 'an officer in an employment or pay, of the State'. Therefore the appellant is not a 'public officer' within the ambit of section 3(1). The appellant was a citizen of India. He was convicted by the trial court and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The prosecution case was that on November 1, 1966, the appellant was arrested in connection with an offence under section 3 of the Defence of India Act. On December 5, 1966 he was released on bail. On January 11, 1967, the respondent filed a petition before the High Court under Art. 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order of forfeiture and for a direction to the State Government to release him from detention. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the order passed by the appellant in respect of the contravention of the provisions of the Act was not an order made under section 43 of the, Defence of the India Act and therefore the order was not liable to be set aside. On behalf of the appellant it was contended that the High court had no jurisdiction to quash the order because the order had been passed by a competent authority and that the appellant had not challenged the validity of the order before the Court. HELD: (i) The order of the High. Court is not an administrative order made in exercise of its powers under Art.. 226 of Constitution. [775 H] (ii) The power conferred on the Central Government by s. 3 of Defence of a India Act is subject to the provisions contained in sub section (2) of that section and the notification issued thereunder. The notification issued under the said sub section is an administrative decision made by the competent authority. The order passed under the rules is not a quasi-judicial order. [750 H] In the instant case, the order dated December 5. 1966 was passed by an officer empowered to make such orders as are necessary for securing the defence of India and civil defence or in the interest of the security of India or for maintaining supplies and services essential to the life of the community. The appellant had no authority to challenge the validity or the legality of the said order before this Court. [751 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1566 of 1967. The appellant was convicted by the Additional District Magistrate, Delhi for an offence under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to undergo imprisonment for life. The prosecution case is that on the night intervening 1st and 2nd February, 1984 at about 10.30 p.m., the accused persons were armed with a gun and they were armed. On the same day at about 11.00 p. m., the appellant was armed with an axe and he fired two shots at the deceased. The deceased was also injured in the occurrence. The appellant was arrested on the next day at 10.45 p. M. The case of the prosecution is that the accused were found to have fired three shots at him. The trial court acquitted the accused. On appeal by the State, the High Court set aside the order of acquittal and convicted the appellant under Section 304 Part II of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The High Court held that the evidence of Dubey was not sufficient to sustain the conviction of Shri Ram. The learned counsel for the appellant contended that the High court was in error in interfering with the order passed by the trial court. In support of this contention, the learned counsel relied on the decision of this Court in [State of U.P. vs. Ram Chandra] and Ors., ; , referred to. (1) The evidence of a witness is not sufficient for sustaining the conviction. The evidence must be such as would satisfy the requirements of Section 84 of the Evidence Act that the witness was present at the time when the offence was committed. [557 C] (2) In the instant case, the appellant had been arrested on a very crucial date and he was also arrested on that day. The fact that he was arrested in the same night at about 12.00 noon, shows that he knew Shri Ram and was therefore able to identify him.

The appellant was convicted under section 302, read with section 34, of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to undergo imprisonment for life. The prosecution case was that on the night intervening 1st and 2nd June, 1967 at about 6 p.m., accused 2, 3 and 4 were armed with deadly weapons. Accused 2,3 and 4 attacked the deceased with their respective weapons. On the basis of the said attack, the appellant was arrested and sent to judicial custody. The appellant was also arrested on the same day. He was produced before the Magistrate on the next day. The learned Magistrate found that accused 1, 3, 4 and 5 were guilty under section 147, 302 read with sections 149 and 147, of Indian Penal. On appeal by the State, the High Court acquitted accused 2 and 4 but convicted accused 2 to 4 under section 148, I.P.C. and sentenced them to undergo rigorous imprisonment for a period of one year. The said conviction was confirmed by the High court. In further appeal by special leave, the only question that arises for consideration is whether the appellant can be convicted under sections 302, 307 read with [section 149], of the IPC. Section 34, Indian Penal code, provides that whoever intentionally caused grievous hurt to any person, shall be punished with imprisonment for either description which may extend to three years and shall also be liable to fine. The High Court held that the appellant had committed a serious offence under section 307, I PC and sentenced him to undergo simple imprisonment for one year and to pay a fine of Rs. 500/- in default to undergo further rigorous imprisonment. In appeal by certificate, the learned counsel for the appellant contended that the conviction of the appellant under section 324, I P.C., is not sustainable as he was not convicted under any other provision of law. The question whether the accused were guilty of an offence under sections 307, 307, and 149, IPG, was considered by this Court in [State of U.P v. Ram Singh] , referred to above. In that case, the accused had been acquitted on the ground that he did not commit a serious crime. The trial court found that the evidence adduced by the prosecution was not acceptable. The conviction of accused 2 under section 326, IPC was upheld. The State preferred an appeal against the said order of acquittal before this Court and the High Courts held that it was not necessary to consider whether the offence under [section 302], I PC was made out or not. In the present case, there is no evidence in that regard. The only question which arises for determination is whether accused 2 was guilty of a serious charge under section 304, IP. C., and sentenced accordingly. The contention of the learned Counsel for the State is that the High courts were wrong in holding that the offence committed by the appellant falls under section 325, Ipc. It is not necessary for us to consider this question as it is well settled that a conviction under section 323, IPP, can be sustained if the evidence on record shows that the accused was guilty under any of the sections of the Penal Code. The fact that the said offence was committed by an accused who had been convicted under Section 302, IPF, cannot be taken into consideration in view of the acquittal of accused 1 and 4. The appeal is accordingly allowed.

The petitioner was a citizen of India and was served with a notice under section 102 of the Act. The petitioner filed an application for refund of the duty paid by him on the ground that he had not paid the duty before the date of payment of duty. The Assistant Collector, however, rejected the claim of the petitioner on the grounds that the petitioner did not pay the duty after the expiry of the period of six months from the date on which the goods were imported and therefore, the question of refund of duty did not arise. On appeal, the Appellate Tribunal held that the appellant was entitled to a refund of Rs. 1,50,000/- under section 15(1)(b) of the Central Excises & Salt Act, 1944. The appellant filed an appeal before this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: (i) The High Court was right in holding that the petition for refund was not maintainable. [775 H] (ii) The petitioner had not made out a case under Article 32 of the Constitution and he could not be denied relief by way of refund. [750 A] (iii) The question whether the petitioner should be granted refund or not is a mixed question of law and fact and it cannot be decided in this petition under Article 226 of the constitution. [751 B] (iv) The appellant was not entitled to any relief under Article 142 of the Indian Constitution. [75 H; 75 A] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1579 of 1987. Shroff, Ms. A. Subhashini and Miss. Arundhati Gupta for the Appellant. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by KASLIWAL, J. This appeal is directed against the judgment dated October 20, 1987 of the High Court of Delhi dismissing the writ petition filed by the petitioner. The facts leading to this appeal are as follows: The petitioner was served on the date when the goods imported were cleared from the warehouse after the period specified in section 102(1) of The Act. He did not make out a clear case under [section 15] of the said Central Excises and Salt Act 1944. He filed an affidavit before the Assistant Collector of Customs, New Bombay, stating that he was willing to pay duty on the goods. On the basis of this affidavit, the petitioner filed a writ petition in the High court challenging the validity of section 102 (1) (b) read with section 15 of the General Clauses Act, 1897. The High court held that section 102 did not apply to the facts of the case and accordingly dismissed the writ application. In the appeal before us, it is contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Courts order was erroneous in law as the petitioner had made out an exceptional case under section 14(1). It is further submitted that the question whether there was a breach of fundamental right does not arise for consideration in this Court and therefore the writ jurisdiction cannot be invoked. The learned counsel for the respondent, however supported the judgment of the Delhi High Court on the basis that section 15 (1)(a) read along with section 14 of the general Clauses Act applies to the case. It is true that the goods are cleared from a warehouse after payment of the excise duty and they were cleared after the date mentioned in the notification dated 1st March, 1986 but the question as to whether there is breach of the fundamental right did not at all arise for decision in this appeal. The appellant, a Hindu undivided family, was the owner of a house property situated in the village of P.W. 1. The father of the appellant died on November 30, 1956 and his son, the respondent, was a member of the joint family. On December 31, 1957, the father of his son filed a suit for partition against the sons and the sons of the father. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the father had no right to make an (1) A.I.R. (2) (1887) L.R.. 14 I.A. (3) (1900) Lloyds' L. R. 13 I. A. (4) (1820) L,R. 15 I.P.C. and that the son of the respondent was entitled to make a partition in the joint Hindu family property. The appellant filed an appeal against the decree passed by the trial court. The appellate court dismissed the appeal holding that as the father died during the pendency of the suit, the sons were not liable to pay any debt or interest on the income of the family and accordingly decreed the respondent's suit. On further appeal, the High Court held that the appellant was entitled only to a share in the property which was purchased by him from his father and he could not make an application for partition under section 155 of the Indian Succession Act. The High Court also held that as there was no partition between the sons, the son could not be treated as a joint family and the father was liable to discharge the debts of the deceased father. On appeal to this Court, HELD: (1)(a) The right of the son to make any partition in his separate property is not an avyavaharika debt but is a question of fact in each case dependent upon what was the estate put up for sale, and where the estate was put up by the sons or the sons. [975 H] (b) The father had only a right to purchase the house property which he could make an assessment on the total income of his family. He could not have made an application under section 154 of the Act for partition in respect of the house properties. [999 G] (c) The son of respondent was a managing director and who was drawing a salary or a remuneration incurred as a result of negligence in the discharge of duties. [991 H] In the instant case, the appellant had no interest in the family property which could be termed as "replacement" within the meaning of section 155(2) of the Code. [1075 B] (d) The High court was right in holding that since the father did not draw any salary or remuneration for his share of the income he could only make an order for partition and therefore the son was liable for payment of any debt, interest on such a sum as well. The appellant, a motor vehicle carrying passengers and goods, was plying his vehicle on the route of the State of Rajasthan. The tax payable by him under section 7 of the Act was Rs. 1,000/- per month. The appellant paid a sum of Rs. 2,500/- as tax for the period from April 1, 1959 to March 31, 1960, and thereafter, he paid a further sum of rupees one thousand on January 30, 1961, and then paid a balance of rupees two hundred on February 28, 1962. The total amount payable by the appellant was Rs, 4,000/-. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court for quashing the order of assessment and also for refund of the tax. The High Court held that the proviso to sub section (3) of section 3 is extra territorial in nature and it does not apply to cases where passengers and persons are transported by motor vehicles. It was further held that as the proviso did not make the payment of tax on fares and freights attributable to the territory of another State when the route passes through Rajasthan, the amount payable under the Act is a tax on passengers and the said amount is calculated by the amount of fare and freight. The question for consideration in this appeal is whether the proviso applies to cases of taxation where passengers or goods are transported from one State to another within the meaning of section 2(3) read with section 3 of the Rajasthan Motor Vehicles Taxation Act, 1951. Section 3 provides that the tax payable under sub section 1 shall be paid by the owner of a motor car or a goods vehicle in respect of which the tax is payable by a registered owner. The proviso to subsection (3), however, makes it clear that the amount specified in the said proviso shall be calculated by deducting from the gross amount of the fare and the freights, if any, attributable to such territory when the bus terminates or ends in Rajasthan. It is not disputed that the appellant paid the tax under section 3 on the basis of actual fares and the maximum, Rs. 4,500/-. The proviso does not make it clear as to what the amount was payable by way of tax. In the absence of any material to show that the said sum was paid in lieu of the taxes attributable to territory of other States when the road terminates, the appellant cannot be held to be entitled to claim refund of tax under sub sections (3). The question is whether on a true construction of the proviso, the proviso does apply to a case where passengers are transported through a territory which is not available to the State Legislature when the journey starts and ends in the Rajasthan.

The appellant, a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956, was engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling cotton yarn. The respondent, a manufacturer of cotton yarn, was employed as a Director of the Company. He was paid Rs. 1,000/- per month as salary for the period from April, 1974 to March, 1976. On May 5, 1977, he was transferred to the appellant's factory. On June 30, 1978, he served a notice on the respondent under Section 25-F of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') terminating his services with effect from May 5. 1977. The notice was challenged by the respondent in a writ petition filed in the High Court. The High Court held that the termination of the appellant was illegal and directed the reinstatement of the respondent with 50% back wages. It further directed the appellant to pay 75% back-wages for the services rendered as Director, but without any compensation for the loss suffered by the company. On appeal by special leave, this Court held: "The question whether the termination is bad or not was a matter of fact and it was open to the respondent to show that he was in service. The appellant had no opportunity to explain why his services should not be terminated and, therefore, reinstatement was directed. It was also observed that the retrenchment compensation awarded by the Tribunal was wholly unjustified and the same was wholly unwarranted." In the appeal filed by the appellant against this Court's order, it was contended on behalf of the workmen that the High court was wrong in holding that the respondent was not a workman within the meaning of Section 2(s) of the Act. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The Tribunal had rightly held that there was no evidence to show as to why the services of the workman were terminated and that he should be given 50% of the back wages after deducting some sacrifice on management 's part. [775 G] 2.1 The High court has erred in holding otherwise. The award passed by the Industrial Tribunal is not sustainable. [750 A] 2:2 In the instant case, the appellant had worked for a period of more than 240 days and therefore, it could not be said that he had any opportunity to show cause against the termination. [751 B] 3.1 There was no material before the High. Court to hold that the appellant has suffered any prejudice by reason of the retrenchment. The order passed by it is wholly unjustified. [753 D] 2(i) The High-Court has erred on the ground that the workmen were not in service and, consequently, they are entitled to reinstatement with 50%. [751 G] 3:2 It was further contended that the award passed against the appellant is illegal and liable to be set aside. [752 B] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1533 of 1989. The accused was charged under sections 302 and 201 of the Indian Penal Code for causing death of Churi deceased. The prosecution case is that on the night of occurrence, Churi had been murdered by the accused. The accused was found in possession of a stolen property. The dead body of Chri was recovered from the house of Shri Mahajan. The police arrested the accused and produced him before the Magistrate who remanded him to judicial custody. On the basis of the information given by the deceased, the accused was arrested on the next day. The case was then sent for trial to the Court of Session. The Sessions Judge acquitted the accused but convicted the accused under sections 201 and 201 read with section 34 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence passed against the accused by its judgment dated April 30, 1986. On appeal to this Court, it was contended that the accused had committed a murderous act and that he was not guilty of any offence. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The evidence on record establishes beyond any manner of doubt that the deceased was with Churi and that the dead body was recovered after the accused left the house. [775 H] 2. The fact that the appellant had gone to see film shows that he had been born to Churi, is not a circumstance which would justify an inference that it was the accused who committed the murder of the deceased. [750 A] 3. The question whether the accused committed the offence under sections 304A and 201 IPC or not is a matter for the trial court to decide. It is not necessary for the accused to prove beyond any doubt that he committed the crime. The mere fact that he has been taken by the publicity Department from the bazar cannot be accepted because there is nothing to show that the police was aware of the murderous conduct. [751 B] 4. The appellant was a young boy and was in possession thereof. He had no reason to commit the offence. The act of the accused in abusing Churi did not amount to an offence under section 201 IPC. [751 D] 5. The circumstances established by the prosecution are sufficient to justify an order of acquittal. [764 G] 6. The position is well settled that the presumption of innocence of the person charged with murder or of his guilt is in favour of the offence and no other view is possible on the evidence adduced before the court. [754 D] 7. The principle of law regarding the burden of proof in a case of this nature is very much applicable to cases where the accused has committed an offence. It cannot be disputed that the prosecution must prove beyond reasonable doubt that it is the accused, who had committed the offences. The presumption of guilt is not in favour as against the person who is charged with the commission of the crime but against the other persons who are charged with such a crime. [752 D] 8. The provisions of section 201 of Indian Penal code do not apply to cases of murder or culpable homicide not amounting to murder. Section 201 IPC does not apply where the offence is committed by an unchaste wife. [758 G] 9. The burden of proving that the offence was committed by her husband lies on her and it is for her to prove that she committed the said offence. [759 D] 10. The facts established by evidence establish beyond reasonable doubts that the death of the appellant was caused by an act of murder. [761 E] 11. Section 304A IPC does apply where a person commits murderous assault. [762 G] 12. The offence under s. 201 IPC is not made out against the appellant.

The plaintiff, a partnership firm carrying on business in the name and style of M/s. S.K. Jain & Co., was incorporated with effect from 1st April, 1936, as a limited company under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The plaintiff was a partner in the firm. He was appointed as an auditor to audit the accounts of the firm for the period from 1.4.1941 to 31.3.1943 and he was also paid his remuneration on the basis of the agreement between the parties. On the death of the partnership, the plaintiff filed a suit against the defendants for recovery of Rs. 15,000/- as damages for breach of contract. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the plaintiff was entitled to recover Rs. 10,000/as damages from the defendants and also awarded interest at the rate of 12% per annum on the amount of Rs, 15,007-0 with effect on and from 1-4-1943 till payment. On appeal by the defendant, the High Court confirmed the decree passed by the trial court. In further appeal to this Court it was contended that the suit was barred by limitation as the plaintiff had not filed any suit for recovery against the defendant. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The plaintiff is entitled to get a decree for specific performance of contract in his favour. [775 H] (2) The agreement between parties was an agreement to sell and the terms of the contract were clear and unambiguous. The agreement was not intended to be binding on the defendant as he had not executed any document in respect of the property mortgaged at the time of the execution of the mortgage deed. [750 A] (3) The suit was clearly barred by law of limitation. [751 B] (4) The trial Court and the High court were right in holding that there was no cause of action for the plaintiff to file a suit for specific relief. [75 H; 75 D] (5) The contract between the plaintiff and the defendant was an independent agreement to sale and not a mortgage decree. [76 E] (6) The terms of contract were not capable of being enforced in law by the plaintiff as he was not bound by the terms thereof. [77 G] (7) The High Court was right in observing that the trial Court had jurisdiction to pass an order for specific Performance of the contracts and that the agreement was a mortgage. [78 H; 76 A] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1566 of 1967. Appeal by special leave from the judgment and decree dated April 10, 1967 of the Bombay High Court in First Appeal No.. 11 of 1966. S B G for the appellant. M. C. Bhandare, S. K. Kapur and R. N. Sachthey, for the respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Shah, J. This appeal is directed against the judgment dated April 20, 1967 passed by a Division Bench of the High 'Court in Second Appeal No...11 of 1966 whereby it allowed the appeal filed by the appellant and dismissed the suit filed by him. The facts leading to this appeal are as follows: The plaintiff firm was incorporated under the [Indian Companies Act] with effect form 1st May, 1936. It is a partnership business. The defendant was appointed an auditor in the year 1938. He had been paid his fees on the date of the filing of the suit. On February 9, 1942, he filed a written statement and took out notice of the plaint to be amended. The amendment was not allowed by the Court. The High court held that the amendment was necessary for the purpose of determining the question whether the agreement dated 1st March, 1936 was an arrangement between the defendant and the plaintiff firm. It was further held that it was not necessary to amend the plaint if the plaintiff wanted to amend his written statement. In the result, the suit came to be decreed in favour of the plaintiff.

The appellants were appointed as Assistant Engineers in the Public Works Department of the State Government on the post of Assistant Engineer (Civil) and they were selected for appointment to the posts of Assistant Engineers. The appellants applied for the post in the year 1986 and they had been selected by the Public Service Commission. They were selected and appointed as Junior Engineers on the basis of the written examination held by the Commission. On the basis thereof, a large number of candidates were selected but they did not join the posts. The State Government issued an advertisement in the Employment News dated 30th May, 1986 calling for applications from eligible candidates for appointment as Assistant Engineer in Public Works. The appellant was one of the candidates who applied for appointment on the said post. On his selection, he was appointed as a Asstt. Engineer (Mech.) in the public Works Department. He joined the posts on the same day and he was selected and he joined the duties. On completion of the training he was promoted to the post on the ground that he had not completed the required number of years of service. The Public Service Commis sioner, who was appointed by the State Govt., issued an order dated 24th May 1990 appointing the appellant Ashok Kumar Yadav as Assistant Executive Engineer (Mechanical) in Public Work Department. On receipt of the said appointment, the appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the aforesaid advertisement and also praying for quashing of the selection made by the Selection Committee. The learned Single Judge dismissed the writ petition holding that the selection was vitiated on account of violation of the mandatory provisions of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the appellant had not been selected in accordance with the Rules and as such he was not entitled to be appointed. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in dismissing the writ petitions. [523D] 2. The selection made was vitiated by mala fides. The Selection Committee was required to consider the cases of all candidates who had applied for a post. It is true that there are many other candidates who were selected on the posts but they have not joined the post and they did join the duties, but it is also true that the Public Services Commis tioner issued an appointment order in the name of the Public Work Deptt., which was subsequently cancelled by the Government. [506F] 3. The Rules do not provide for any appointment on a post which is not advertised. It only provides for a period of one year and no such period can be considered as they are not advertised for selection. [504D] 4. The rules do not prescribe any time limit for making appointments to the vacancies in question. The Government has already framed new rules, and as a result thereof it is not open to the appellant to challenge the validity or invalidity of the Rules. [423F] 5. The appointment of the appellant was made by way of selection and he had joined the services on the date of his selection. He was selected for the said posts. [406G] 6. The post of Asstt. Engineers (Civil), which is a post in Public works Department, is not a post advertised for appointment. It cannot be filled up by promotion from the post to which the appellant has been appointed. [405F] 7. The provisions of Article 233(2) do not apply to the selection of the present appellant. [404B] 8. The appointments were made in accordance therewith and as the Public works department was already in existence, it is open to them to make appointment on that post. [413D] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1320 of 1989. From the Judgment and Order dated 16.3.1990 of the High court of Orissa in W.P. No. 11058 of 1990. M.K. Garg, S.N. Jha, R.C. Sharma, P.K Singh, B.B.

The prosecution case was that the accused persons were arrested on 10th July, 1982 and they were produced before the Magistrate on 11th July. The accused persons pleaded not guilty to the charges framed against them. They denied their involvement in the murder of the Collector. The trial court held that the prosecution had failed to prove the charge beyond reasonable doubt and accordingly acquitted all the accused. On appeal by the State, the High Court reversed the order of acquittal and convicted Sadanand under section 302 read with section 34 IPC and sentenced him to undergo imprisonment for life. The State filed an appeal against the said judgment before this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The prosecution case is that the deceased was taken into custody by the police on 10-7- 1982 and he was produced before a Magistrate on 10.7.1982. He was also produced before him on 11-7. 1982. The High Court has rightly held that in view of the evidence adduced by the prosecution, it cannot be said that the appellant was guilty of conspiracy to kill the Collector through Yadav. [557F] 1.2 It is well settled law that if a person is acquitted by the trial court and the accused is convicted on the basis of circumstantial evidence, then it would not be hazardous to accept a part of the link as a complete one and on the same principle, the charge framed against him cannot be accepted. [506F] 2.1 There was no direct evidence in the case to show that the wife of the deceased had met Sadanand when she was taken by the accused person on 10/7-1982. The prosecution has not proved that P.W.4 had an interview with his wife and the fact that he met Sadananda at the jail, the story of bribing the jail authorities is false. [657F D] 2:2 There is no evidence to show conspiracy between Sadanand and Yadav. The appellant was arrested on 11/7/1982 and he produced before Magistrate on that day. The learned Sessions Judge has rightly acquitted him.

The appellant, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was an industrial undertaking of the Government of India. The respondent, a limited company, was engaged in the manufacture and sale of cotton and other products. The appellant was an employee of the respondent. On January 1, 1957, the respondent made an application to the Tribunal for fixation of wages and dearness allowance for the workmen employed by it. The Tribunal fixed the wage scale of the workmen at Rs. 10,000 per month. The company filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the fixation of the wage scales and dearness allowances. The High Court held that the minimum wage packet fixed by the Tribunal was not abnormal or so disproportionate as compared to the total wage packet in other comparable concerns. On appeal by special leave, the appellant contended that the Tribunal had erred in fixing the wage- scale at Rs 10,00,000 instead of Rs.10,000 and that the High court should have directed fixation of wage scales for clerical staff. The contention was rejected by this Court on the ground that the company was not engaged in any industry and it was not possible to fix the wage packet at a just figure. It was further held that there was no question of want of financial capacity and that it was open to the Company to fix wages and Dearness allowance for clerical and subordinate staff. In the present case, the Tribunal has given reasons for fixing the minimum wages packet in comparable concerns and thus arrived at a fair amount for basic wage. The first is with respect to the fixation by the High Courts of the question whether the minimum rate fixed by it was abnormal or not. The second is with regard to deduction from gratuity only to the extent of financial loss occasioned by misconduct in case of dismissal for misconduct. The third is with reference to the average of the total wages packet and the average is not abnormal. The question as to how much of the minimum packet should be taken into account for basic wages was considered by this court in [The State of West Bengal vs. Calcutta Tramways Ltd.] , ; , ; (1) where the Tribunal fixed a wage scale for clerical or subordinate staff, it was held that it would be open to this Court to fix a just amount for the financial loss arising from misconduct in such cases. The decision of the High courts was upheld by this. Court. In [The Central Bank of India vs. Its Workmen] , , , this court observed that the fixation is not arbitrary or unreasonable and that there is no question in the case of wantof financial capacity. The next is with regards to deduction of Rs 10 per month from gratuity. The learned counsel for the appellant submitted that the decision of this Court in [the State of Bihar vs. West Bengal Tramway Ltd.] ; , , was not correct. In support of his contention, he relied on a number of decisions of this court. He also referred to the decision in [State of West Punjab vs. The Workmen] . ; , and submitted that there has been no financial loss for which the company is liable to pay.

The appellants, who were the owners of an undivided interest in the joint family property, filed a suit for partition and separate possession of the properties. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellants had failed to prove that they were the tenants of the land. On appeal by the defendants, the Additional District Judge set aside the decree passed by the trial court and dismissed the suit. In second appeal before this Court, the judgment of the High Court was confirmed by this Court. The question for consideration in this case is whether the appellants are entitled to get possession of an interest in a joint family land on the basis of the provisions of section 74 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code as they stood at the relevant time. Section 74 of that Code provides that "a person who has become the owner by adverse possession of any property shall be deemed to have relinquished his rights in such property". The appellants filed an application for permission to file a suit under section 74 for partition of the joint property and for passing a decree for partition. This Court held that the provisions contained in section 74 were applicable to the facts of the case and, therefore, the appellants were entitled to obtain possession of their interest on the ground that they had failed in their written statement and, consequently, the suit was dismissed. The appellants then filed an appeal against the judgment and decree passed in their favour by the Additional Sessions Judge. The High Court allowed the appeal and set aside their order. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 Section 74 is applicable to a joint Hindu family property. [775 H] 1.2 In the instant case, the provisions relating to relinquishment of rights of both the brothers were not in dispute. The only question for determination in this appeal is whether a notice of relinquishment given by the appellants was a notice on behalf of all occupants or any particular occupant other than the 701 registered occupant. [750 H] 2.1 The High court was right in holding that a notice under section 73 of the Act was not necessary to be given to the appellants. [751 G] 1:2. Section 73 is applicable only to a case where there are more occupants than one, and the principal of such persons, must enter into a written agreement to become the registered occupant of the property. The provisions contained therein are applicable to cases where the interest in an estate does not pass on the death of any person other than one. [751 H] In the present case, there was no express pleading or cogent proof that a notices of relinquishment were given by all occupants other than those who had relinquished their rights in the property on behalf and that they entered into a registered agreement to be the registered occupants of the lands. The notice of abandonment given by them was not an act of surrender but only a notice to become a registered occupant within the meaning of section 73. [761 H; 771 A] 2:3. Section 75 is applicable in this matter and, as such, the notice of the relinquishment must be a notice in writing on behalf or for all occupants of an estate. [771 G] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1533 of 1987. From the Judgment and Order dated 16.8.1987 of the Allahabad High Court in Second Appeal No 1266 of 1987 and Civil Appeal Nos. 1534-1535 of 1987, arising out of S.L.P. (C) Nos. 11057-11009 of 1988. V.N. Ganpule, R.K. Jain, M.S. Kochar, A.K Gupta, S.K Srivastava and P.K Sharma for the Appellants. Virender Singh, S/o Late Shri Ram Chandra, R/o Village & Post Office-Bagrapur, District-Rohtas. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by VENKATARAMIAH, J. Leave granted. 2.

The appellant, a dealer in the sale of goods in the State of Orissa, filed a return for the period from April 1, 1966 to March 31, 1967. The Sales Tax Officer, who assessed the tax payable by the appellant under the provisions of the Orissa General Sales Tax Act, 1947, assessed the appellant to sales tax on the basis that "the said goods were not paper as defined in the said Act". On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the assessing authority. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court which was dismissed by reason of the judgment and order under appeal. The correctness of this decision is challenged in this appeal by special leave. Section 5(1) of the Act provides that "no tax shall be payable on the sale or purchase of goods specified in Schedule I, except as provided in sub-section (2) thereof." The appellant purchased the goods from the State Government and sold them to the State Trading Corporation. The sales tax was assessed by the Sales Tax authorities under the Orissa Sales Tax Rules, 1947. The respondent filed a petition for special leave before this Court which came to be dismissed by order dated April 27, 1967 on the ground that the said rules did not apply to the case of the appellant. On behalf of the State it was contended that the word 'paper' in the Notification issued by the State Legislature under section 5(2) of Act No. 1 of 1957 should be construed as a paper as understood in common parlance and in common sense meaning of the words "paper" and "paper "paper". The High Court held that the expression 'paper as defined by the said notification was not a paper but a printing machine and therefore, the appellant was entitled to claim exemption under section 4(1)(b) of Orissa General sales Tax Act. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The word 'papers' in Entry 42 of the Schedule to the Notification dated April 1. 1966 should be given its natural meaning and it must be construed in the light of what is meant by a typewriter ribbon. [675 H] 2. The expression "paper as well as paper" used in the notification issued under section 3(1), therefore, must be interpreted in the context of entry 42 of List II of Schedule VII to the Constitution and it cannot be construed so as to include 'paper printed or printed matter' which is not a printed matter. [650 D] 3. The words " paper" and 'paper " paper " are used in Entry 41 of the schedule to the notification dated April, 1, 1967 and they must be given their natural meaning. [663 H] 4. The use of the word "paper", as defined under section 2(f) of that Act, is not an expression of art. It is a book or paper which is used in connection with printing, writing or packing. [664 D] 5. The question whether the words 'paper" are to be construed or not must be determined having regard to the context and the purpose for which the said words have been used. [662 G] 6. The meaning of a printed article as defined is that it is a paper. It cannot be used in any other manner than what is mentioned in the Schedule. [775 H; 776 A] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1379 of 1967. Appeal by special Leave from the Judgment and Order dated the 14th July, 1967 of the High court of Orissa at Cuttack in Misc. Case No. 11 of 1966. S. K. Sinha, for the appellant (in C.A. No.1379/67). M. C. Setalvad, Attorney-General, V. N. Ganpule and R. H. Dhebar, for respondent No. 2 (In C. A. 1380/68) and respondent No 3 (In CA 1379/68). The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Sikri, J.

The appellant was employed by the respondents 1 to 4 as a Manager in the Sugar Mills at Amroha. He was appointed by the management of the Sugar Mill at Amroha on October 10, 1954. On November 30, 1955, he was transferred from one place to another and was posted at Amroha at the same place. On December 5, 1956, he served with a notice under section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') terminating his services. He challenged the validity of the order by filing a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant had no right to transfer the respondents from one branch to another. On appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The question whether an employee is entitled to transfer must be determined on the facts of each case and if it does not involve any substantial question of law within the meaning of section 7(1) of the Act, the question raised was one of law. [775 H] 2. Section 7(2)(a) of The Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950, provides that an employer who is a workman in an industry at the time of his employment shall be entitled to transferred his employee to any other establishment or to any person under the contract of service or under any statutory provisions. [750 H] 3.1 The question raised by the appellant was one relating to the right of an employer to transfer his employees from one concern to another, and that is whether in the circumstances of this case the appellant could be transferred to a new concern at a later date. [751 G] 3: 2. In the instant case, the appellant did not have the right to go to any place where he was working as Manager. The appellant had the right under section 7 (2) of that Act to transfer an employee to another establishment where he chooses to start (4) 926 a business subsequent to the date of his appointment. [751 H] 4. In view of the provisions contained in section 7 of the said Act, it was not open to the appellant to transfer him from one establishment to another without the express condition that the employer has the right at the relevant time to transfer such employees to any new concern. [754 G] 5. The contention raised by Mr. S. T. Desai, learned counsel for the respondent, that the question whether the appellant should be transferred must be decided on the basis of the facts and circumstances of each individual case is a matter which has to be determined in each case. [752 H] 6. In order to decide whether an employer has a right to transferring his employee from one office to another or not, it would be necessary for the appellant either to show that he had the said right at any stage of the proceedings before the State Industrial Tribunal or the Labour Appellate Tribunal. The respondent was also required to show how he had such a right. [764 H] 7. In considering whether an order of transfer is an order in writing, it is necessary for a Court to consider whether the order of transferring the employee is an act of discharge simpliciter. [758 G] 8. The Tribunal has jurisdiction to decide on the question as to whether the employer had the power to transfer a workman from one undertaking to another undertaking at a subsequent date. If the appellant has no such right, it can be said that he has the said power. [759 H] 9. In dealing with the question of transfer of an employee, it will be necessary to consider the nature and extent of the rights of an individual. The employer is entitled under section 8 of the Indian Contract Act to exercise his right to do so. [761 G] 10. The right of a workman to transfer is not an absolute right. It is a right which is conferred by statute. [762 H] 11.

The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1947 and it had a branch office at Bombay. The respondent, who was an employee of the appellant company, was employed by the appellant as a Manager in the appellant's factory at Bombay for a period of five years. He was paid contribution under the Employees' State Insurance Act, 1948 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') and he was also paid contribution towards the provident fund. The appellant company had a Provident Fund Account with the respondent. The Provident Fund account was opened in the name of the respondent on April 26, 1971. On May 31, 1973, the respondent made an application for payment of contributions under Section 7 of the Act to the Employees State Insurance Corporation (hereinafter called 'the Corporation') and the appellant Company filed a claim for contribution under Section 8 of the said Act before the Assistant Commissioner of Labour, Bombay. On June 30, 1974, the appellant filed an application before the respondent for payment by way of contribution under [Section 7] of the Payment of Contribution Act, 1952 (hereinafter to be referred to 'the said Act') for the period from May 31 1973 to March 26, 1973. The Assistant Commissioner, however, rejected the claim on the ground that the contribution was not a tax and that it had been paid by the respondent under Section 6 of the Employees Provident Fund Act, which was applicable to the appellant. On appeal, the order of the Assistant Commission was confirmed by the Appellate Authority. On further appeal, a learned single Judge of the High Court held that the amount payable by the employer under Section 5 of the aforesaid Act was not an income tax and it was not liable to be included in the total income of the assessee for the purpose of payment of contribution. The said order was confirmed in appeal by the Division Bench. On behalf of the appellants, Mr. S.K. Jain, learned counsel appearing on behalf of respondent submitted that the provisions of Section 7 were applicable to a case where the amount paid by an employer under the Act was less than the tax and not otherwise. It was further contended that the said provision did not apply to a situation where the benefit was not directly or indirectly derived from the employer. The learned counsel for the respondent submitted, therefore, that the question of payment by the appellants under Section 10 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 (hereinafter for short 'the 1961 Act') does not arise in this case and the said contention is liable to fail.

The petitioners were appointed as daily rated workmen in the year 1962. They were working on the rolls of the National Industrial Development Corporation Ltd., (hereinafter referred to as 'the NTCL') and they were continued on the roll of the NTCCL till their services were absorbed by the NTDR. The petitioners were paid regular wages in spite of their being no work for them. On the basis of the balance sheet, the NCCN was issued to the petitioners. The NTCG gave a notice dated December 6, 1987 to the workmen stating that they should be regularised and their services should be regularized as per the scheme of Voluntary Retirement Scheme framed by respondent No. 2. The said notice was challenged by the petitioners before the Industrial Tribunal, which allowed the claim of the petitioners and directed them to be absorbed in the NLCL. The Industrial Tribunal held that the petitioners were entitled to get the benefit of the VRS Scheme and they should have been regularised as per their scheme. The High Court has upheld the decision of the Industrial tribunal. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The scheme of voluntary retirement was framed in exercise of powers conferred under Section 25-F of the Act. It is not a statutory scheme but it is an independent scheme and it is a part of the statute. [652 D] 1.2 In the instant case, the petitioners are entitled to be regularised as regular workmen. They should have worked for more than 240 days in a year. The scheme was issued on December 6. 1987. The Scheme was not given effect to by respondent no. 2 and it was only a part time employment. [650 D] 2.1 There is no provision in the Act or any other statute which permits regularisation of a daily rated workman. The provisions of the Scheme are statutory in character. It cannot be said that there is no scheme for regularisation of the workmen. [663 F] 2:2 In view of the clear finding recorded by the Industrial Court, the question of directing their absorption and regu larisation does not arise. [664 D] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 979 of 1988. From the Judgment and Order dated 4.1.1988 of the Central Administrative Tribunal, Madras in O.A. No. 8 of 1987. S.T. Desai, P.H. Parekh and R.N. Poddar for the Appellants. M.K. Ramamurthy, Ms. A. Subhashini and K.R. Nambiar for the Respondents. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by B.P. JEEVAN REDDY, J. This appeal is directed against the judgment dated April 4, 1988 passed by the High Court of Madras in Writ Petition No. 1208 of 1987 whereby the High court allowed the writ petition filed by the respondents and quashed the order of the Tribunal dated December 5, 1987. 2 The brief facts necessary for disposal of this appeal are as follows: The petitioners are working on rolls of NTCML. They have been continued on their rolls till their service was absorbed by respondent Nos. 1 to 3 in the National industrial Development Corporation. On their absorption they were given regular pay scale in spite thereof. The respondents filed a writ petition before the High Curt challenging the order dated December 4, 1987 passed by respondent nos. 1 and 2. A Division Bench of the High Coupe Court allowed the said writ petition on April 4. 1988. The Division Bench held that there was no scheme or scheme for regularization of the employees as per which they were to be given regular wages. The learned Single Judge further directed that the respondents should regularise their services as per scheme of VRS. The appellants filed a Special Leave Petition before this Court against the order passed by it on April 5, 1988. This Court allowed that petition and quashed and set aside the order granting regularization of service. The matter was remitted to the Industrial court for fresh consideration.

The plaintiffs, who are the sons of Ismail and were in possession of the property under a lease granted in 1928, executed a mortgage deed in favour of the 1st defendant on April 18, 1931, and registered it as document No. 12(i) on April 17, 1931. The mortgage was executed by Ismail in favour Pir Baksh on April 19, 1931 and registered on April 20, 1931; and the sale was confirmed by the High Court on May 30, 1931 on April 21, 1931 after the sale. The plaintiffs filed a suit for declaration that they were entitled to a decree for a declaration that the mortgage deed dated April 18 , 1931, executed in favour them by Ismail was illegal and void. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the sale under exhibit 12(1) was not real and intended to pass title to PirBaksh and that the plaintiffs were 'not entitled to any further 2 as mentioned in the plaint. The High Court held that the sales made by Ismail were real and not real, and accordingly dismissed the appeal. In this appeal by special leave, it is contended on behalf of the appellants (i) that the High court was wrong in holding that a sale under a mortgage by the 1 st defendant in favour Air Bhism was illegal; (ii) that there was no mutation in the revenue records when the sale deed was executed and registered. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The sale under exhibits 12(l) is not real but intended to be passed title. [675 H] (2) The High court has rightly held that if the sale by Ismail had been made out of a benami transaction, the plaintiffs would be entitled to an order for the sale in execution of the mortgage decree. [775 B] (3) The fact that the property conveyed under exhibit12(1), was not intended to passing title to the plaintiffs, does not affect their right to this share. [750 D] (4) The question whether a sale is real or not does not depend upon the facts of each case. It depends on the facts and circumstances of the case. If the sale is not in favourof Pirbaksh, it would be open to the plaintiff to file a suit claiming a declaration of title to this property by way of a suit. [751 D] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1165 of 1968. Appeal from the judgment and decree dated April 20. 1967 of the Allahabad High Court in Second Appeal No, 12 of 1965. S. T. Desai, for the appellant. R. K. Garg, for respondent No. 1. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Shah, J. This appeal is directed against a judgment of the High Curt dated April 24, 1967 of that court dismissing the suit filed by the plaintiffs. The appellants are the plaintiffs in this appeal. They instituted a suit on July 18, 1934, for declaration and injunction restraining the defendants from interfering with their possession and enjoyment of the properties described in the schedule to the plaint and for recovery of possession thereof. The case was set up by the plaintiff that the properties were purchased under a registered sale deed dated May 30 , 1931 executed in 1928. The suit was filed on July 17, 1934. The defendants contested the suit. They pleaded that the suit was not maintainable as they had no right to file the suit and that they had not been impleaded as parties to the suit, and that therefore the plaintiffs could not have instituted a fresh suit for the same relief. The Trial Court decreed the plaintiff's suit on August 20, 1934 and dismissed the suit on April 24 , 1968. The First Appellate Court confirmed the decree of the trial court. The second appeal was filed by defendants 1 to 3 in this Court. The learned counsel appearing for the appellants contended that the findings recorded by the courts below were erroneous.

The appellant was convicted by the trial court under section 302 read with section 149 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to undergo imprisonment for life. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence passed against the appellant by the Sessions Judge, but reduced the sentence from one year's rigorous imprisonment to two years' rigorous imprisonment. The appellant filed an appeal before this Court, which was allowed by a Division Bench of the High Court holding that the provisions of section 173(4) of the Code of Criminal Procedure were not mandatory and that the accused persons had been prejudiced in their defence. It was further held that the omission on the part of police officers to fully comply with the provisions aforesaid did not amount to an offence under section 149, and that it was not necessary for the accused to have complied with the requirements of the said section. The Court, however, held that there was no substance in the contention raised by the appellant that the failure on the side of the prosecution to prove the charges against the accused was fatal. In this appeal, Mr. S. T. Desai, learned counsel for the appellant submitted that the High court had erred in holding that those provisions were not directory and that they did not apply to the case then before them. The question whether the omission by a police officer to fully complied with section 173 of the code was mandatory or only directory is a question of fact which can be decided only after the accused person has been given an opportunity to prove his defence. In the present case, the High Curt had not considered the provisions contained in section 173 (4) and (3) of Code of Civil Procedure. The learned counsel submitted that there were no materials on record to show that the appellant was prejudiced by the omission of the provisions mentioned above. It is further contended that the trial has not been vitiated by any error of law or procedure. In support of this contention, the learned counsel relied upon the decision of this Court in [State of Punjab vs The State of Punjab] , referred to and relied upon.

The appellant was a tenant of the premises in dispute. The respondent filed an application under section 153A of the Act for eviction of the appellant from the premises on the ground that the appellant had caused nuisance to the respondent. The Rent Controller, by his order dated December 31, 1966, held that the respondent was liable to pay damages to the appellant and directed him to arrange for the discharge of the effluent in the manner specified in the notice. On appeal, the appellate authority confirmed the order of the Rent Controller. In further appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the respondent that the order passed by the appellate Authority was not a speaking order and the High Court should have set aside the order. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The provisions of section 153 A of the Tamil Nadu Act are mandatory in character and do not require any judicial officer of the rank of District Judge to enquire into the dispute and make an inquiry into the matter. [675 H] 2.1 The provision of section 154 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is mandatory in nature and does not require a judicial officer to hold an enquiry into the complaint made by the respondent or to give any finding as to the existence of nuisance before a notice is issued to him. [775 D] 2:2 In the instant case, the appellant was required to comply with the requisition of the Municipality for discharging the effluent and he was also required to pay the damages in the form prescribed under section 154(1) of the said Act. The order passed on December 31 1966 by the Special Officer was not an order of assessment but a notice issued to the party concerned. [750 D] 3:3 In the circumstances, the order dated January 30, 1968 passed by a Special Officer is illegal and void. [751 G] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 877 of 1969. From the Judgment and Order dated the 9th July, 1967 of the Madras High Court in Writ Petition No. 1224 of 1966. S.T. Desai, R. Ganapathy Iyer and M. Veerappa for the Appellant. V.S. Mani, S.K. Bagga and A.V. Rangam for the Respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Shah, J. This appeal is directed against a judgment of the High court of Madras dated September 9, 1967 in Writ Appeal No.. 1224/66. The appellant is a tenant in the premises. He filed an eviction petition under section 13(1)(e) of Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control Act, 1960 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') against the respondent on the grounds set out in the application. The case was taken up for hearing by the High' Court on September 9. 1968. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the provisions of Section 153A were mandatory in respect of the notice issued under section 14(1). The appellant has come to this court by special leave. The only question which arises for consideration is whether the order dismissing the application filed by the appellant under section 15(2) of Act No. 1 of 1968 is an order passed under section 17(3)(a) of that Act. Section 17(4) of this Act provides that no order shall be made under sub-section (1) or subsection (2) unless the person affected thereby has been given a reasonable opportunity of being heard. The notice issued by the Rent Control Officer was served on the respondent and he filed an appeal against the order in question before the High 'Court. The appellate authority dismissed the appeal holding that there is no provision for giving any finding or finding as required under section 152 of the Indian Act. In this view, the High. Court held that there was no infirmity in the order made by it. It further held that if the appellant has been served with a notice under section14(1), he can be called upon to comply within the time specified therein.

The appellant was a railway servant. He was prosecuted for an offence under section 3 of the Indian Railway Act, 1890. The prosecution alleged that the appellant had purchased the property in question from one B.B. Singh who was the owner of the said property and that he had purchased it from the said B.D. Singh. The trial court held that the articles seized were railway stores within the meaning of section 2 of the Act and as such the goods were not liable to be confiscated under section 5 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954. On appeal by the appellant, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence but reduced the sentence to one year's rigorous imprisonment. The appellant filed an appeal before this Court. HELD: (1) The provisions of section 3 are mandatory in character and they do not require the prosecution to prove that the article seized was railway stores or that the goods in question were being used for construction or operation of a railway. [775 H] (2) The articles seized from the possession of the appellant were railway property within the definition of section2 of the act. The provisions contained in section 2 are mandatory and they must be proved to have been manufactured for such us, that the said goods were being manufactured for the construction or protection of a Railway. [750 H] JUDGMENT: CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Criminal Appeal No. 9 of 1971. Appeal by Special Leave from the Judgment and Order dated the 14th July, 1970 of the Orissa High Court in Criminal Revision Case No. 12 of 1970. S. K. Sinha and R. N. Sachthey, for the appellant. B. P. Singh, for respondent No. 1. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Shah, J. This appeal is directed against a judgment of the High court of Orissa at Cuttack dated November 14, 1970 in Criminal Appeal Nos. 9/70 and 10/70. The facts are not in dispute. The case of the prosecution was that the accused persons were carrying on business for which they had purchased property from B. D.
