Singh and that the seized articles were being produced for inspection by a railway administration. The accused were prosecuted for offences under section 4 read with section 5 read with sections 6, 7 and 8 of the Essential Supplies Act, 1955 (hereinafter referred to as the Act). The prosecution case was that on March 31, 1967, the appellant purchased the said properties from B D Singh who is the owner thereof. On April 1, 1967 the appellant filed a complaint against the accused for an alleged offence under sections 4 readwith section 5 and 6 of the aforesaid Act. The Magistrate took cognizance of the offence and issued process to the accused. The complainant filed an application before the learned Magistrate for quashing the proceedings on the ground that the provisions contained therein are mandatory. The High Court dismissed the revision petition holding that the offences were not committed by the accused in respect of which they were seized from their possession. On a further appeal to this Court, HELD: 1(i) The provision contained in sections 4 and 5 of Act is mandatory and it does not require that the prosecution should prove that goods are being manufactured or produced for construction. [875 H; 876 A] (ii) The words "and" used in section 3(1)(a) of the General Clauses Act, 1897, do not mean that the words "or" have to be read as "and". [878 B] (iii) The word "and", in the context, means "to produce a document or thing for inspection". [975 H-976 A; 877 D] (iv) The expression "and' used in the Act is not mandatory and the words 'or' used therein are not intended to be used in any other sense. [978 G] (v) The High court was wrong in holding that there was no evidence of the articles being manufactured by the appellants.

The appellants were inducted as tenants in the demised premises on a monthly rent of Rs. 100/- per month. The respondent filed an application under section 13(1) (a) of the Act for eviction of the appellants from the demised shop on the ground that the appellants had become entitled to remain in possession of the demised property till the date of filing of the suit as statutory tenants. The Rent Controller held that the tenancy was created by the tenant and the heirs of the tenants were entitled to enjoy the protection under the Act. On appeal, the Appellate Authority confirmed the order of eviction passed against the appellants. In second appeal, a Division Bench of the High Court reversed the judgment of the Appellate authority and restored the order passed by the Rent Controller. The appellants filed an appeal before this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The provisions of section 13 (1) of Act are not applicable to the facts of the case. [975 H] 1.2 The protection afforded to the tenant under the provisions of the Rent Act is a right which the Legislature has never intended to be caused by divesting their vested rights in the lease hold right. [999 G] 1:3. Section 13(i) of The Act provides that the heirs and tenants of a demised premises shall continue to enjoy protection against the eviction of such tenant if they are evicted under the tenancy law. [991 H] 2.1 In the instant case, the appellants were in possession as statutory tenant and tenancy rights were not heritable and the provisions contained in section 13 of the Transfer of Property Act did not apply to the fact of their being in possession. [19991 G] 2:2 The right conferred on the heirs under the Rent Control Act was a right that the tenants would have been entitled to retain the protection afforded by the Act and also subject to the rights in favour of the respondent created under section13(1)(a) to (k). [992 H] 3.1 Section 13 of Act is not applicable in the facts and circumstances of this case. The provisions contained therein are not attracted to the case and do not apply in the fact situation of the present case. There was no such protection afforded under the law as amended from time to time.

The appellant, a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956, was incorporated in the year 1948. The respondent, a Company incorporated under section 25 of the Indian Companies Act (hereinafter referred to as the 'Act') was incorporated on April 1, 1948. On May 30, 1949, the Board of Directors of the appellant company issued a notice under Section 29(1) of the Act calling upon the appellant to pay to the respondent an amount of Rs. 2,50,000/- towards interest on the loan advanced by it to the Board. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notice and praying for a direction that the respondent should be directed to make payment of the said amount to the appellant. The High Court held that the interest was payable under Section 59 of the Electricity Supply Act, 1948 and not under the provisions of the statute. It further held that as the interest had been paid by the respondent to the Government on the basis of the agreement between the parties, it was a clear case of breach of contract. On appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The High court was right in holding that the appellant was not entitled to any relief under Section 64 of the electricity supply Act,1948. [775 H] (2) The interest on loan advanced to the company by the Board is a statutory obligation and is a definite proportion and it is open to an ordinary commercial concern to credit any amount to depreciation reserve. It is open for an ordinary industrial concern to pay interest on loans advanced or deemed to be advanced to its shareholders under section 64 of Electricity Supply act, 1948, including arrears of such interest. [750 H] The High Courts were right in taking the view that as far as practicable and after giving credit for any amount payable by the company to the Electricity Board, it is a clear proportion and not a definite percentage. [751 A] (3) The appellant was entitled to claim interest under Section 61 of the Companies act, 1956 on the ground that the amount advanced by the appellant towards the loan was not in accordance with the provisions contained in the statute and was therefore a definite share capital. [751 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1566 of 1967. Appeal from the judgment and order dated April 10, 1966 of the Allahabad High Court in Misc. Writ Petition No. 1123 of 1965. S. T. Desai, R. N. Sachthey and B. D. Sharma for the appellant (in both the appeals). M. C. Setalvad, Attorney-General of India, K. J. John and P. H. Parekh for the respondent (in all the appeals) The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Hegde, J. These two appeals are directed against a common judgment of the High court of Allahabad dated April 20, 1966 in Misc.(Civil Writ Petition Nos. 1122 and 1123/65. The facts leading to these appeals are as follows: The appellant is a company registered under the Indian companies Act, 1913. It was incorporated under Section 25 of that Act. On June 30, 1950, the respondent issued a notification under Section 4(1)(a) of that section in respect of the undertaking of the company. The said notification was published on May 30. 1950. Under clause (b) of sub section (2), the Government of India has been pleased to direct that the said undertaking shall be transferred to and vest in the Central Government. Clause (c) of subsection (3)(a)(i) provides that the undertaking shall stand transferred to, and vested in, the Central Board of Direct Taxes. Under clauses (d) and (e), the undertaking is to be transferred by the Central Govt. to the Central Electricity Authority. Under sub section(4) of Section 4, the undertaking has been transferred to the State Government.

The appellant was married to one of the respondents, who is a minor. The marriage between the parties took place on 5th May, 1973. After the marriage, the respondent filed an application for maintenance under section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure before the Magistrate, but that application was dismissed by the Magistrate. On appeal, the High Court reversed the order and held that the appellant had failed to establish that he was impotent and unable to discharge his marital obligations. The appellant filed a petition for restitution of conjugal rights in the court of the Magistrate on the ground that the respondent was not entitled to live with her husband. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the wife was not a "false person" within the meaning of section 125(3) of the code of 1973 and accordingly allowed the appeal filed by the appellant. In this appeal, it is contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court erred in reversing the order of the learned Magistrate and allowing the petition for maintenance filed by her. The respondent was a minor at the time of the marriage and she had not been able to establish any such ground for the wife 's refusal to live together with her. It is further contended that the husband was not competent to maintain his wife. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 Section 125(4) of Code of 1973 provides that where a husband has contracted a marriage with another woman and the husband has not remarried or has been living forssing, the wife shall be entitled to maintenance from her husband according to his means. [675 H] 1.2 The expression "falsse person", in the context of section 488 of the Act, is wide enough to include a minor who is unable to maintain herself and her husband if she is not able to do so. [775 G] 1:3. Section 125 of Code is an enabling provision which provides that when a wife has contracted marriage with a woman, she shall be liable to pay maintenance from the husband according as he is unable or unwilling to maintain himself. [750 H] 2.1 The expression 'falter' in the explanation to sub section (3) means "a person who is not a minor" within that meaning. [751 G] 2:2. Section 488 of Code provides that if a husband is impotenti and unable or refuses to maintain her, he shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years or fine or both. [751 H] 3. The expression used in the Explanation to sub sections (3), (4) and (5) of section 498A of the Penal Code is wide and includes a minor, who has not been unable to pay his maintenance. [752 G] 4. In order that a husband may be liable under the said provision, he must be able to maintain wife and child-in-law. The Explanation to subsection (3)(a) of Section 498A provides that in case of a minor the husband shall be deemed to have contracted marriage if he has not married his wife within the period specified in the said section. [764 H] 5. In the instant case, the appellant was a major at the relevant time and she was unable to establish her case that she was not able or unwillingness to maintain the respondent. The husband was also not able and willing to live separately with his wife and children. [754 G] 6. Section 498-A of Code makes it clear that if the husband is found guilty of cruelty, he may be punishable under section 498- A of the Indian Penal Code. [758 H] 7. In a case where a wife is unable and unwillingness or refuses or fails to maintain any wife, she can be punished with imprisonment which may extent to three months or fine not exceeding one thousand rupees. [759 D] 8.

The plaintiff filed a suit for the eviction of the defendant from the land in question on the ground that he was in possession of the land as a tenant. The trial court held that the plaintiff had not proved his title to the land and accordingly decreed the suit. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decree and directed the trial court to pass a decree for possession of land in favour of the plaintiff. In second appeal before this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Municipality was entitled to take the land under Resolution No. 77 dated 29th February, 1948 and Resolution No, 10 of the Municipal Board dated 19th January, 1948. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the suit was not barred by limitation. [532E] 2. The plaintiff had failed to prove his title over the land. He could not be held to have acquired any interest in the land by virtue of the Resolution No., 10 of 1948. [506F] 3. The finding of the High court that possession of lands was taken by the Municipality on 7th July, 1952 and they were collecting the Revenue from the farmers is erroneous and that the land was vested in the Municipality subject to the condi tions mentioned in the letter dated 6th May, 1952. [504F] 4. The suit was barred by time. [633G] 5. The decision of the trial Court was correct and there was no question of law much less a substantial question of fact arising out of the pleadings or evidence adduced before the court. [434H] 6. The appellant had failed in his attempt to prove that he had acquired any right over the lands as claimed by him. He had also not proved that he ever acquired any rights in the lands. [498A] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 11 of 1972. From the Judgment and Order dated the 10th May., 1952, of the Gujarat High Court in First Appeal No, 8 of 1952. S. T. Desai, R. N. Sachthey and B. D. Sharma for the Appellant. M. C. Setalvad, Attorney-General of India, K. J. John, P. H. Parekh and R. Hathi for the Respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by FAZAL ALI, J.-This appeal is directed against the judgment dated October 10, 1952, passed by the High Courl in First Appeals Nos. 8/1952 and 8/1953. The facts leading to this appeal are as follows: The appellant is a tenant of the lands in question. He filed a petition for eviction on the grounds mentioned in paragraph 5 of the plaint. The case was taken up for hearing on the basis that the landlord had acquired the land on the date of the filing of the suit and that possession was not delivered to him by the Municipal authorities. The Trial Court held that possession could be delivered only after the plaintiff's evidence was recorded. On an appeal filed by the appellant, the learned Additional District Judge reversed the judgment of the Trial Court and decreed the respondent's suit for eviction. In this appeal, it is contended on his behalf that the High Courts in Gujarat and Gujarat had not followed the decision of this Court in the case of [Ganga Prasad v State of Bihar] , referred to above. It was further submitted that the appellant had not filed any application for condonation of delay in filing the appeal before the High.Court. The learned counsel for the respondent, however, supported the judgment and decree passed by both the Courts below. The only question which arises for consideration is whether the suit filed by a landlord for eviction of his tenant was barred under Section 13(2) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel & Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947.

The appellant was a public servant within the meaning of section 21(9) of the Penal Code. He was prosecuted for an offence under section 5(1)(d) read with section 21, Indian Penal Code and was convicted by the learned Judges of the Lahore High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 8 of 1949. The appellant was charged with having committed an offence punishable under section 7 of the Prevention of Corruption Act II of 1947. He pleaded not guilty to the charge but claimed that he was a Public servant within s. 21(1) of Indian Penal code and was, therefore, liable to be convicted under section 6 of the General Clauses Act. The learned Judges held that the appellant was an officer in the service or pay of Government and was therefore, a public servants within the definition of section 2 of the [Prevention of Corruption (Amendment) Act] II of 1948. On appeal by the State, the High Court reversed the decision of the learned judges of the Punjab High Court holding that the offence under s. 5(2) of Act II was not an offence as defined in section 21 of the Indian Penal. The High Court further held that since the appellant had been convicted for an act which is a public duty within the scope of section 6, he was not liable to suffer any punishment under that section. On behalf of the appellant it was contended that the provisions of s. 7 of Act I of 1947 were applicable to him and as such he was entitled to be acquitted. HELD: (1) The appellant had not been in the services or pay or employment of the Government but was a person who was an Officer of the State and was being paid by the Government. [775 H] (2) The provisions of section 7 were applicable only to persons who are public servants and not to persons whose duty it was to render any service or to give effect to any public duty. The words "any other person" in s. 6, which is similar to the words "public servant" in section 2, clearly indicate that the offences under section 3 of Act 1 of 1947 must be treated as offences under the said section. [750 H] In the instant case, the appellant did not fall within the ambit of section 5 (1)(a) readwith section 21 and therefore he was rightly convicted under s 5(l)(d). [776 H] The appellant could not be convicted for any offence under the provisions mentioned in section 6.

The Respondent was a tenant of the premises in dispute. He filed a suit for eviction against the appellants on the ground that he was entitled to recover possession of the said premises from the appellants. The appellants contested the suit and contended that the respondent was not entitled to evict the appellants under section 60 of the Code, as he had been residing with him and his family members and that the appellants were in arrears of rent for more than six months. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the Respondent was entitled only to the extent of half share in the said property. On appeal by the respondent, the District Judge confirmed the decree passed by the trial court. In second appeal before this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court had erred in law in reversing the judgment and decree of the trial Court. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court was wrong in holding that section 60(1) of the code is applicable to attachment and sale of property for recovery of revenue under the said Act. [652D] 2. Section 60(l)(c) of Code provides that the provisions of section 60 shall not apply to an attachment and sales made by a civil court. The words "such attachment or sale" in the proviso to sub section (1) are clear and unambiguous. The expression "such property as is so exempted by the said enactment" in clause (c) means "the property which is exempt from attachment and sold". [653F] 3. Section 62 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, provides that where a contract is made for the sale of immovable property for a price, the purchaser shall be entitled to receive from the vendor, the amount specified in the contract as the value of the property which would be liable to attachment or sold and the balance, if any, shall be paid to the vendor. [650F] 4. The proviso to section 60 (1)(c), however, does not apply where the property is exempt by the State Government under the proviso. [643D] 5. Section 63 of the Transfer of Property Act provides that no transfer of immovable properties for a consideration shall be made except with the previous sanction of the Collector or the officer authorized to adopt proceedings under the Indian Registration Act, 1908. The provisions of sub section 2 of section 62 are clear. [641F] 6. The language of the proviso is clear and explicit. It does not make any distinction between an attachment or sales and sale. [651G] 7. Section 65 of the Contract Act provides for the recovery of property by a Civil Court. [678B] 8. The Explanation to section 62(1)(b) makes it clear that where the immovable property is exempted from attachment, the provisions in sub section 1 of section 63 shall not be applicable. [693F] 9. Section 64 of the Act provides the mode of recovery of arrears of revenue and the proviso thereto does not provide for any such mode of recovering the amount as the property would be exempt from attached or sold. [70G] 10. The question whether the respondent is entitled to claim possession under section 62 of Code, doesn't arise in this appeal because the High court has erred in holding otherwise. [71B] 11. Section 61 of the Punjab Act provides a machinery for recovery and recovery of dues by attachment and detention and sale and sale in revenue recovery proceedings. The said provision is clear that the proviso applies to attachment of property. [72E] 12. Section 66 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930 does not lay down any such procedure. It only lays down that no sale shall be affected by reason of any attachment or detention or sale of the immovable properties of the defaulter. The effect of the provision is that the attachment and the sale in the revenue recovery proceeding would be subject to the provisions contained in section 65 of Code. [73F] 13.

The respondent filed a return of his income assessed by the Special Deputy Collector on the basis that he had acquired the lands in question for the purpose of construction of a building. The respondent claimed compensation at the rate of Rs. 1,000 per annum on the ground that the value of the land was not less than Rs. 2,500 per annum and that the amount of compensation fixed by the special Deputy Collector was inadequate. The Special Deputy collector held that the valuation made by the competent authority was correct and accordingly assessed the market value of lands at Rs. 3,000/- per annum. On appeal, the High Court set aside the order of the Special Assistant Collector and remanded the case to the Special Commissioner for determining the market price of the lands on the date of the death of the deceased. The High Court held that in view of the provisions of s.59(a) of the Act, the value fixed by a special Deputy collector was not correct and that as such the respondent was entitled to compensation at Rs 1,500/- per year. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The High court was right in holding that the Special Land Collector had adopted the valuation of the acquired lands on his own estimate and he assessed the value at Rs 3,500/per annum. [557D] (2) The respondent was not entitled to any compensation at all as he had not accepted the value as determined by the statutory authority. [506F] (3) The Special Commissioner acted in excess of his jurisdiction under s. 59(a). He could not be said to have adopted that valuation and, therefore, the respondent is not entitled for any relief. [504E] (4) The question whether the value was less than the market rate fixed by special Deputy Collectors or not was a matter of fact which was required to be determined by an expert body. It was not open to the respondent to contend that he was not liable to pay compensation at any rate higher than the amount fixed by his statutory authority and, in such circumstances, the Special Collector could not have adopted the value on the relevant date. [657F] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 15 of 1972. From the Judgment and Order dated the 10th May, 1971 of the Gujarat High Court in First Appeal No.. 11 of 1970. S. T. Desai, R. N. Sachthey and B. D. Sharma for the Appellant. V. C. Mahajan, M. K. Ramamurthi, A. G. Ratnaparkhi, S. P. Nayar and R. H. Dhebar, for the Respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by PATHAK, J. This appeal by special leave is directed against the judgment dated October 10, 1970 of the High court of Gujarat at Ahmedabad in First Appeals Nos. 11 of 1971 and 11 of 1972 whereby the High Curt has set aside an order passed by the learned Special Judge on a reference under ss. 66A of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') and remanded it for fresh determination. The facts giving rise to this appeal are these: The respondent filed an application before the Special Court under s, 66A(2) of that Act for enhancement of the value by the High Commissioner of Income Tax, Gujarat, Ahmedabad, in respect of his total income assessed at Rs 2,000/per year. The said application was allowed by the Additional Collector on a finding that the respondent had acquired land for the purposes of construction and development of building. On an appeal filed by the respondent before the High, Court, the same was allowed and the Special Judge enhanced the value to the extent of Rs 1.500/-per year from the date on which the special officer passed his order dated October 8, 1970. The appellant has come up in this appeal against that decision.

The appellant was a member of the Bombay Cooperative Bank Ltd. and he was elected as Director of the said bank on 31.3.1986. The appellant filed an election petition before the Assistant Registrar, Cooperation and Textiles, Nagpur, contending that the disqualification on account of his being a defaulter under section 73FF of the Act was not legal and proper. The High Court held that the appellant had committed default in payment of any instalment of loan granted to him; and that he was disqualified from being a member under section 78(1) of the act. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Section 78(2) of Act is not attracted to the facts of the case. The disqualification on the ground of default in paying any instalment or loan before the date of the notice is a legal and valid one. [675 H] 1.2 In the instant case, the appellant was elected by the Board of Directors of the Bank as Director on 18.8.1986 and he had paid the entire loan before his election. The question whether the disqualification was legal or not arose only in the context of the provisions in section 78 of the A.P. Cooperative Societies Act, 1964. [775 H; 776 B] 1:3.1 In the present case, there is no material to show that the petitioner had committed any default in making payment of instalments of loan before he was declared elected as a Director. The finding of the High Court that the penalty imposed on the appellant by the impugned order was legal and justified cannot be sustained. [750 H] 2:1. In the case of term lending society, a member who defaults the payment of instalment or loans after the date prescribed for the purpose is disqualified from continuing as Director or creasing to be Director on account. The penalty imposed by the High court in the present proceedings was not a disqualification under section78(2). [750 A] 2.2 The disqualification as provided in section 79(1)(b) of Bombay Cooperative Societies act, 1964 cannot be said to have been legal and correct. The appeal is accordingly allowed.

The respondent was appointed as a Sugar Inspector in the State of Maharashtra. He retired from service on September 30, 1966 and he was promoted to the post of Assistant Commissioner of Sales Tax. On December 31, 1967, he was served with a charge sheet under Rule 189 of the Rules. The charges were that while the respondent was in service he had committed serious misconduct during his service and the Government was competent to withhold or reduce the pension. The State Government issued an order dated October 16, 1968 reducing the pension by 50 per cent. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the said order. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the order passed by the Collector on December 4, 1982 was not in accordance with law and the order of the State Government was without jurisdiction. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 Rule 189 is a mandatory provision and it is not mandatory. It is only when a Government servant retired from the service on attaining the age of superannuation he could have been denied the pension or any part of it. [652 D] 1.2 The High court was in error in holding that since the respondent had already retired from services a lenient view should be taken and reduction of pension by fifty per cent was disproportionate to the charges proved against the respondent. [754 E] 1:3.1 The order passed on December 5, 1982 is not in consonance with Rule 189. [750 D] 2.1 There is no authority vested with the power to reduce or withhold the pension of a Government Servant for misconduct and negligence or financial irregularities which are serious in nature. The provisions of Rule 188 are mandatory and it cannot be said that the reduction of the pension was disproportionate. [751 G] 2:2 In the instant case, the respondent has retired from his service on October 31, 1966. He had already been retired a lenient opinion should have been taken and reduced to the extent of Re. 1 per month be made. [753 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1279 of 1987. From the Judgment and Order dated 4th February, 1987 of the Bombay High Court in Writ Petition No. 8 of 1986. S.K. Bagga, R.N. Poddar and B.D. Sharma for the Appellant. V.M. Tarkunde, Mrs. A.K Gupta and Ms. Arundhati Jain for the Respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by KASLIWAL, J. This appeal is directed against the judgment dated April 4, 1987 passed by a Division Bench of the High court of Bombay in Writ Appeal No: 8 of 1987 whereby it dismissed the appellant's writ petition and confirmed the order dated December 4/5, 1982 passed by respondent No. 1 imposing punishment on him. The facts leading to this appeal are as follows: The respondent was serving as a Clerk in the office of the Sugar Inspector, Government of Maharashtra, on October 16. 1967. He was promoted as Assistant Commissioner, Sales Tax, on September 29, 1968 and he had retired from that service on November 31, 1968. On February 13, 1970, he submitted an application for revision to the State Govt., which was rejected by the State. The appellant filed a Writ Petition in the High' Court of Bombay challenging the order imposing punishment. The learned Single Judge dismissed the writ petition holding: "The petitioner has not challenged the order under appeal and the same is without jurisdiction." The Division Bench held that the respondent having retired from Government service on December 31. 1967, the order was illegal and void. It was further held that since he had already completed his qualifying service of two years, he could not be denied pension for misconduct. The Division bench also held that in view of Rule 189, the punishment imposed by the respondent is disproportionate to his misconduct. In our opinion, the High 'Court has rightly dismissed the Writ Petition filed by the appellant.

The appellant was a tenant of the land in dispute. The respondent filed an application under section 3 (3) of the Act for permission to purchase the land from the landlord. The District Magistrate granted permission to the landlord to sell the land to him on condition that he will pay Rs. 1,000/- per month as rent to the appellant. On appeal, the High Court set aside the order passed by the District Magistrate and remanded the case back to the Commissioner for a fresh decision in accordance with law. The Commissioner, however, dismissed the application of the landlord under section 16(3) and 16(4). The appellant filed an appeal before this Court against the order of remand. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 Section 3 (4) of Act 17 of 1954 provides that the Commissioner shall hear the application made by the landlord for permission under sub section (2), if he is not satisfied as to the correctness, legality or propriety of the order. [652 D] 1.2 The High Court was in error in holding that the provisions of section 3(3)(a) and (b) were applicable to the case before it. [650 E] 1: 2.1 The Commissioner is not a court within the meaning of section 16 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. He can deal with the legality or the propriety of an order passed under the relevant provisions of the said Act. [663 F] 1.: 3.2 Section 3(4) provides that where the Commissioner has made an order on the application for permission, he shall hear and decide the application in accordance therewith. The words "in the opinion of the Commissioner" are clear enough to indicate that the power conferred on him by section 3 is not exercised by the Commissioner. [664 F] 2: 3.3 Section 16(1) provides for a revision against an order made under sub sections (2) and(4), but it does not provide for any appeal or revision against the said order. The High court was in wrong in holding otherwise. [662 D] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 15 of 1977. From the Judgment and Order dated the 10th May, 1976 of the Gujarat High Court in Special Civil Application No. 12 of 1976. S.V. Gupte, R.K. Mehta and M.N. Shroff for the Appellant. V.M. Tarkunde, K.R. Nambiar, P.H. Parekh, S.S. Khanduja, S.,B.D. Sharma, S,A. Shroff, S..C. Jain, S,.K. Dholakia, Setia, R K Jain and S.N Gupta for the Respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by RAY, J. This appeal is directed against a judgment of the High court of Gujarat dated October 10, 1976 in Special civil application No.12 of 1976 whereby the High-Court allowed the writ petition filed by the respondent and quashed the order dated November 30, 1976 passed by this Court in the Letters Patent Appeal. The appellant was appointed as a tenant on probation for a period of one year. On June 15, 1977, the landlord made an application to the District Judge under section 11(3), read with section 16 (1) of Bombay Rent Act, 1947 for permission for sale of the property. The application was rejected by the High. Court on the ground that the appellant had not challenged the order in appeal before the Supreme Court. The question whether the appellant could challenge the order dismissing his application under [section 11(2)] or section 16 was considered by this court in Special leave Petition No.11 of 1976 and it was held that the High Curt was right in holding, that the District Court had no jurisdiction to deal with an application made under section 12 of the Bombay Rent (Amendment) Act, 1954. The appeal is accordingly allowed. There will be no order as to costs.

The respondent filed a complaint under section 7 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 (hereinafter referred to as "the Act") against the appellant and two other persons alleging that they had committed offences punishable under sections 161, 165A and 166 of the Indian Penal Code. The trial was held in the Court of the Special Judge, Patiala House, New Delhi. The respondent filed an appeal before the High Court which was allowed by a learned Single Judge of the High court on the ground that the evidence of the witnesses who were examined by the prosecution was not relevant and that the charge against the respondent was not proved beyond reasonable doubt. The appellant filed a writ petition in this Court challenging the order of the learned Single judge. The learned single Judge dismissed the writ petition holding that the charges framed against the accused persons were not proved. On appeal, the Division Bench of the Punjab High Court held that the prosecution had failed to prove its case and accordingly quashed the proceedings. In further appeal to this Court it was contended by Shri Nariman that the order passed by the learned Judge was in violation of the principles of natural justice inasmuch as he had been given an opportunity to cross examine witnesses on those aspects of the matter. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court has not committed any error in quashing the proceedings and setting aside the order. [775 H] 2. The provisions of section 7(1) of the Act are mandatory in character and do not require that the accused should be given an oral hearing before the Special judge. It is only when the evidence is recorded by the Special Court that it can decide whether or not to proceed with the trial. [750 A] 3. In a case where the evidence consists of several witnesses, the court may have to consider the entire evidence and then pass an order for further inquiry on the basis of the evidence which the parties lead before it. The question whether the evidence should be recorded or not is a matter which the Court has to decide in a particular way. [751 B] 4. In the instant case, the Special court had no jurisdiction to go into the question as regards the admissibility or otherwise of the material evidence and that was done by the High Courts. The order passed on the application filed by the respondent under section 8 of the Criminal Procedure Code is not in accordance with law. [753 D] 5. In any event, the provisions of sub-section (1) are mandatory and do have no effect as regards its applicability to the facts of the case. [754 G] 6. The Special Judge was right in holding that it was open to him to decide whether the witnesses were examined or not. [764 D] 7. In view of the provisions contained in section 7, the order dated September 30, 1983 passed by a Special Judge is not an interlocutory order and the High Curt has no jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution. [752 G] 8. The power to issue prerogative writs under article 226 of Constitution is discretionary and the Court cannot sit as an appellate authority over the decision of the authorities. [758 H] 9. In this case, there was a delay in filing the writ application before the learned single judge. [759 B] 10. The special court has no power to go behind the order under section 11 of the Code. [761 D] 11. The right to cross examination is not a matter of procedure and does not require any interference by the Court. [763 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1579 of 1983. From the Judgment and Order dated 16.3.1983 of the Delhi High Court in C.W.P. No. 823 of 1982. V.S. Desai, S.K. Mehta, R.N. Poddar for the Appellant. M.C. Bhandare, K.R. Nambiar, P.H. Parekh and A.K Gupta for the Respondent.

The temple was dedicated to the public for the worship of a family idol. The members of the public were entitled to worship at the shrine and the deity was installed in the temple. The trustees of the temple were appointed by the Government as per the provisions of the Act. The temple was constructed by the members of a public trust, and the trustees were appointed under the provisions contained in the Act for the benefit of the family idol and the temple was installed by the trustees. The properties of the deity were dedicated to a family deity. The income from the property was not to be taken into account as a whole. The High Court held that the endowment was of a private nature and the members thereof were entitled, therefore, to worship in the said temple. It further held that there was no provision for offering offerings or contributions to be made by members of public to the temple and the recitals of the document show that the trustees had been appointed by members belonging to a particular community which shows that extensive properties were dedicated for the maintenance of the God. The finding recorded by the High Court is not based on any evidence, but it was based on an erroneous appreciation of the oral evidence led in the case. The findings recorded by both the courts below are concurrent findings of fact and do not call for interference under Article 136 of the Constitution. The appeal filed by the State of Bihar is accordingly dismissed. There will be no order as to costs. R.K.P.S. Appeal dismissed. (G.L. Sanghi)

The appellant was a member of the Indian Air Force. He was appointed as an Assistant Engineer in the Air Force on July 13, 1948. On August 14, 1949 he executed a deed of assignment in favour of the appellant. The appellant filed a suit against the respondents for recovery of money due to him under the bill dated July 19, 1948 and claimed a decree for Rs. 1,50,000/- as damages. The trial court decreed the suit on March 31, 1951. On appeal by the appellant the High Court held that there was no equitable assignment of the funds in favour the appellant and that the agreement between the parties was not an equitable assignment. In further appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondents that the power of attorney executed by Takhatmal in favourof the appellant was irrevocable. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The power of Attorney is a document of trust and is a contract between the lender and the borrower. [775 H] 2.1 The power to grant a loan under the deed dated July 13., 1948 was an equitable one and was irrevocable in nature. There was no transfer of the decree, or of the claim which was the subject matter of the pending appeal as the borrower continued to be the owner and the lender was only authorised to execute a decree then passed in favour him. [750 H] 3.1 In the instant case there was an agreement between Takhat Mal and the appellant that the debt due to it would be paid out of a specific fund of the borrower in the hands of the Government authorities. The agreement between them was not a contract but only a contract. The High Court was in error in holding that there is no equitable assignmen of the fund in favour. [751 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 979 of 1966. Appeal by special leave from the judgment and order dated April 20, 1964 of the Allahabad High Court in Second Appeal No.. 1123 of 1962. S. T. Desai, R. N. Sachthey and B. D. Sharma, for the appellant (in C.A. 980/66). A. V. Viswanatha Sastri, R., H. Dhebar, S. K. Kapur and R. H. Colagh, for respondent No. 1 (In C. A. 981/66) The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Hegde, J. This appeal is directed against a judgment of the High court of Allahabad dated April 21, 1964 in Second appeal No. 1123/62. The facts leading to this appeal are these: The appellant was an employee of the respondent-bank and was appointed on July 14, 1948 as an officer of the Bank. On September 15, 1949 the appellant made a bill for Rs.. 1,25,000/-. The appellant paid the amount due under the bills. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High' Court challenging the validity of the bill. The learned Single Judge dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant had not established any equitable assignment and that there were no equitable assignments. On further appeal by special Leave, the Division Bench held that the order passed by the learned Single judge was erroneous. In this appeal, it is contended on the basis of the decision of the Division bench that the High 'Court has jurisdiction to entertain a suit for recovery against the appellant in respect of the bills raised by him. The contention is that there are no equitable rights in favour or against the respondent and that as the agreement was not one of the parties, the agreement could be enforced. It is further contended that the contract between Takitmal and the respondent was an assignment of a decree passed in his favour by the Bank and he continued to hold the property as an agent of the bank. The Division Bench has held that it is open to the appellant to establish any equitable assignor right in respect to the bill raised by the respondent. In our opinion, this contention is without merit.

The appellant was a member of the Indian Income tax Appellate Tribunal, Madras. The respondent was assessed to income tax under section 10(1)(i) of the Income tax Act, 1961. He claimed that he was entitled to exemption from payment of tax in respect of his income for the assessment year 1962-63 and that the said sum of Rs. 27,948/ by way of interest on such contributions was not liable to be included in the total income under section 17(3) (ii). The Income tax Officer rejected the claim of the respondent and held that the amount of Rs 27,949/- was not income from other sources but income from house property. On appeal the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Incometax Officer. In further appeal to the Tribunal, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the sum of rupees 27,919/ by the respondent was not a salary and therefore he was not entitled to claim exemption under section 11(1) (i). The Tribunal held that in view of section 17 (3) of Act, the amount payable by the assessee for his income from House property could not be included. On behalf of appellant it was submitted that the High Court was wrong in holding that the receipt of Rs 20,000/- by the appellant with which we are concerned is exempt from tax under [section 11(2)] (ii) of Income tax. The Tribunal also held that there was no need to call into aid any of the rules of construction as was sought to be done by the High court and answered the question referred to it in favour of the Department. On the question whether the sum received by the Revenue from the respondent could be included under section 16(3)(ii) the Tribunal held, that the appellant had not claimed exemption under [sections 11(i)] and 17 (1) of The Act. The High Court also held on a reference made to it by the Tribunal that the assessee was entitled for exemption in respect to his income under sections 11(l), 17(2)(iii) and 17(4). On behalf, the appellant contended that the respondent had not produced any evidence before the Income Tax Officer to show that the receipts of Rs 10,000/by way of compensation were not income tax. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The question referred by the Appellate Tribunal was answered in favour or against the assessee and it is not open to the High Courts to interfere with the order passed by the Income-tax Officer on the ground that the income from which the sum was received by way o compensation was not taxable under section 12(1). [775 H] 2. The amount of interest paid by the Government in respect thereof cannot be treated as income tax and therefore it is exempt under section11(2) (iii) of [The Act]. [776 B] 3. Section 17(1), (ii), (iv) and (v) are mutually exclusive. They read together, they do not make any difference to the question of law referred to them in view or the decision of this Court in [P.K. Jain vs Union of India & Ors.] , ; , ; and the answer given by the appellate Tribunal is correct. [778 C] 4. The Income Tax Appellate Tribunal has jurisdiction to go into the question as to whether the amount received by it from the Government was not an income tax or not. [779 D] 5. Section 11(3), (iii), (v), (vi) and [section 17(5)] are mutually inclusive. [780 G] 6. The expression "income tax" is defined in section 2(b). It means "the total income of the assessee". In the case of a person who is not an individual, he is entitled to be assessed under section 15. [781 D] 7.

The Act was passed by the State Legislature in exercise of its powers under article 48 (1) (g) and (h) of the Constitution. The petitioners, who were members of the Indian National Congress, filed a petition before the High Court of Judicature at Bombay for a writ quashing the provisions of the Act on the ground that they infringed the fundamental rights guaranteed by article 19 (1)(g) of our Constitution. It was contended that the Act violated the fundamental right to slaughter animals and was therefore void as being violative of the fundamental freedom under article 19(1)(f). The High Court held that the impugned Act contravened the fundamental freedoms guaranteed by [article 19 (6)] and was, therefore, unconstitutional. On appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The Act is valid in so far as it prohibits the slaughter of cows of all ages and calves of cows, male and female, but we hold that it is constitutionally valid in respect of the slaughter, of a cow of all age and calf, or working bullocks (cattle and buffalo) which are useful for the purpose of the imposition of reasonable restrictions on the right to do so. [652 D] 2. The impugned Act was not violative of any fundamental right guaranteed by Article 19 (l)(g). It is a law made by the Legislature in pursuance of the Directive Principles of State Policy laid down in article 48 and it is valid. [650 A] 3. The provisions of article 19 are not unconstitutional as being in violation of the said fundamental rights. The restrictions imposed on the petitioners under article 14, if they infringed or are to be imposed, are void as offending the fundamental fundamental right of the petitioners. [663 F] 4. The restriction imposed by the impugned law is not a reasonable restriction within the meaning of article 14. It is not unreasonable and invalid. [664 D] 5. The question whether the restrictions imposed by section 3(1) are reasonable or not, does not arise in this case because the Act was enacted for the benefit of the people of the State. The right to carry on business under article 21 is a fundamental right. It cannot be denied that the petitioners have been carrying on their occupation or business without any test or requirement as to their age or usefulness, it is also not unreasonable. [665 F] 6. The law in question is valid and does not violate the fundamental Rights guaranteed by Part III of the constitution. [666 D] 7. The State Legislature has no power to impose reasonable restrictions under article 31 (1). The impugned law contravenes the fundamental provisions of articles 19 (2) and 19 (3), and is, therefore void. [667 G] 8. The petition is without merit and it should be dismissed.

The respondent was appointed as a workman in the Office of the Company on January 1, 1957. He was paid Rs. 10,000/- per month as salary for the period from February 1, 1958 to March 31, 1959. The respondent was served with a charge sheet dated December 5, 1960, and he was asked to submit his explanation within 15 days of the receipt of the said notice. On January 28, 1961, the respondent submitted his explanation. On April 29, 1962, the Company filed an application before the Labour Court under section 33A(2) of the Act for a declaration that the Standing Orders in question were not applicable to him and that he was entitled to be paid Rs 10,00/- per mensem as salary from February 5, 1959 to March 30, 1959, and that the respondent should be paid his salary from April 1, 1959 onwards. The Labour Court held that the said application was barred by limitation and dismissed the application. On appeal, the High Court reversed the order of the Labour court and directed the appellant to pay Rs 10 lakhs as salary to the respondent. In further appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that Standing Order No. (e) of Standing Orders was not applicable in the case of the respondent and that Standing Orders were not saved by section 30 of the local Act in the sense that no Standing Orders could be made for all employees except those who were in employment at the time when the Standing Order was issued, and therefore, the said Standing Orders applied to the appellant. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that Standing orders were saved by Section 30 of Act No. 13 of 1959. [775 H] 2.1 The Standing Orders are not saved under section 30. The Standing Order is a preliminary issue and it cannot be said to have been repealed or modified by the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. [750 A] 2(i) The Standing orders in question are saved by the proviso to sub-section (2) thereof. [751 B] 2.(ii) The respondent had not produced any evidence to show that he had been employed as a casual workman at the relevant time. [751 D] 3.1 There is no material on record to show whether the appellant was an employee of the Respondent or his service has been terminated in accordance with Standing Order. [752 B] 3.(iii) The High court was right, and the appeal must be dismissed. [754 G] 3(iv) The order passed by the Labour Commissioner, U.P., Lucknow, dated April 29 1962, is not a final order. [764 D] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1179 of 1966. Appeal from the judgment and order dated September 30, 1966 of the Allahabad High Court in Misc. Writ Petition No. 1223 of 1965. S. K. Sinha, for the appellant (in both the appeals). R. N. Sachthey, for respondent No. 1 (in all the appeals) The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Hegde, J. In this appeal by certificate, the only question that arises for consideration is whether the High court has jurisdiction to entertain a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution against an order passed in exercise of its powers under section 32(2)(b) of U. P. Act No, 13 of 1960. The appellant was appointed on January 28. 1957 as a temporary workman and he worked for more than 240 days in a calendar year. On December 5. 1959, the appellant filed an affidavit before the High Commissioner, Lucknow, stating that the appellant had not been employed by him at the date of his appointment. He also stated that he did not have any permanent employment at all. The learned Single Judge of the HighCourt held that there was no material to show as to why the appellant should be directed to pay wages from April 30, 1960 onwards.

The appellant, a Company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling of sugar. The respondent, Hindustan Steel Ltd., was an employee of the appellant. He was paid bonus at the rate of 8.5 per cent on the total paid up equity share capital of the company. On March 31, 1963, the Company filed a petition under section 33C(1) of the Act before the Industrial Tribunal, Delhi, for a declaration that the respondent was entitled to be treated as a separate establishment for purposes of computation of bonus under the Act. The Tribunal held that the appellant was not entitled to claim bonus at 8.05 per cent and accordingly directed the Company to pay bonus at Rs. 1,000 per annum. On appeal by the appellant, the High Court held that in view of the provisions contained in section 16(1), the respondent should be treated to be a separate unit for purposes other than those specified in the Act and, therefore, the Tribunal was right in holding that the claim of the respondent for bonus at 9.5% on the paid up capital was not maintainable. The appellant filed an appeal against this order before this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 Section 16(2) of The Act provides that the provisions of the said section shall apply to all the establishments in which the undertaking is owned, controlled and managed by the Company. [675 H] 1.2 The Tribunal was wrong in holding otherwise. It was not open to the Tribunal to hold that the company was a separate industrial establishment for the purposes other then mentioned in the statute. [775 G] 1:3 The proviso to section 16 (1) is applicable only to the separate establishments of the Company and not to all other establishments. [750 H] 2.1 The proviso does not apply to the case of the workmen of the Head Office where no separate profit and loss was worked out and the bonus was paid on the basis of consolidated accounts. [751 G] 2:2 Section 16 (2) is attracted only in respect of the separate establishment which is a separate and distinct establishment for purpose other than that specified in section 3(1). The proviso applies to all establishments where no specific profit and/or loss has been worked out or the bonus has been paid on any of the assets of the undertaking. [753 H] In the instant case, the appellant had not made any claim for bonus under section 16. [752 G] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1566 of 1967. Appeal by Special Leave from the Judgment and Order dated the 30th July, 1967 of the Delhi High Court in C.M. Application No. 11 of 1963. S.K. Bagga, for the appellant (In CA 1566/67). M.C. Bhandare, V.J. Francis, S.N. Mukherjee, K.R. Chaudhuri, R. N. Sachthey and B.D. Sharma, for respondent No. 1 (In C.A. 1568 of 1967). The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Sikri, J. This appeal is directed against the judgment dated October 30, 1967 passed by the High court of Delhi in Civil Miscellaneous Application No 11 of 1964. The facts leading to this appeal are these: The respondent-Company is a company incorporated under Indian Companies' Act, 1956. It has its factory at New Delhi. The Company was established with the object of carrying on the business as well as for the purpose of manufacturing sugar and it had its own factories in the State of Delhi. On April 1, 1963 the appellant filed a writ petition before the High C Court of Delhi challenging the validity of the notification issued by the Central Government under section 3 of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955 (hereinafter referred to as the 'Act') and also the notification dated March 31. 1963 issued by it under section 4 of the Central Act.

The levy of cess on the sale of goods produced in a factory is an industry as defined in Entry 15 of Schedule I. The levy of tax on sale of raw material and processing of goods manufactured by the assessee was challenged by filing a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court of Allahabad. The High Court held that the levy of excise duty on the manufacture of sugar produced by the petitioner was not an industry within Entry 15 but was an industry for the purpose of levying tax on the production of goods. It was further held that in order to bring an industry under Entry 15, it must be a manufacturing industry and since the entry in question was not intended to be included in the field of taxation, the levy was illegal. The State of Uttar Pradesh filed an appeal against the judgment of the High court. The Division Bench of the Allahabad High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the cess levied on the sales of raw materials and processing thereof by the appellant was not a tax on manufacture. In the circumstances, this Court held: "The levy is not an Industry as defined under Entry No. 15 but it is an Industry for certain purposes and vegetables are products of that industry. The entry in respect of goods must be construed as including all the activities which are incidental or ancillary to the main activity of the industry. In order to come within the Entry 15 the levy must be one which is an industrial product. It must be something which is made of or made of, or out of vegetable. " The High court held that sugar produced in the factory was not goods for the purposes of Entry 15 and a fortio ri the manufacture thereof was not only industry but it was an Industry within Entry No 15. In our opinion, the High Courts were right in holding that sugar producing industries are industries within Entry 14 of Schedule 1. The cess is not a levy on the activity of manufacturing sugar. It is an item of manufacture and therefore, the cess is a tax. The question whether the levy is an "industry" or not has to be decided by the statute in which it is occurring. If the entry is construed as an industry, then the levy would be illegal. In other words, if the entry itself is inclusive and not exhaustive, the tax is not leviable on the goods produced by that industry but is a levy of an industry.

The appellant, a tenant of a building in the city town of Hyderabad, filed a petition under Article 227 of the Constitution before the High Court of Andhra Pradesh challenging the validity of the Act. The respondent, who was the tenant of the building, filed an application for eviction on the ground that he required the premises for his own occupation and that the landlord bona fide proposed to start a business in the said building. The Rent Controller dismissed the petition holding that the requirement of the landlord was not bona fide. On appeal by the respondent, the High court held that the requirements of the provisions of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act were satisfied and accordingly allowed the petition. In this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Courts had erred in holding that there was no bona fide need for the landlord to start business in a building owned by an Advocate. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The expression 'business' is used in Section 10(3) (a) (iii) and it includes the practice of law as well as other statutes or in any manner alien to the context of the statute concerned. [775 H] 2.1 The word 'business ' in Section10(3)(a) is a wide expression which means that it should be construed in the context in which it occurs and not in the interpretation of the words used in the Act or other statutes. [750 A] 2:2 In the instant case, the requirement was bona fide for starting a business and was not the carrying on of a trade or business within the meaning of Section 10 (3) of the said Act. [751 B] 3.1 There is no merit in this contention. The High Court has erred in law in holding otherwise. [752 C] 2(i) The expression "business" in Section 9(3), (a)(iii) or (iv) means that the practice which a lawyer would be the carrying of a profession and was the carrying out of a business. [751 D] 3(ii) The word "business " in Section 11(3A) is not a wide definition and it should include any profession. [754 G] 3.(iii) The words "business", "business ". " or "business ", " or (v) The practice of a lawyer, as defined in Section 2(b)(ii), means that he must be the person who has a legal right to do business. The word business' is not an expression of the nature of a commercial or industrial occupation but it is a term of wide import and it cannot include any trade or profession. The words 'business', 'business'. [754 H] 3:1. Section 10 of the Madras Buildings (lease, Rent Control) Act, 1960, provides that no tenant shall be entitled to obtain possession of his building on the grounds specified in clause (i), (ii) and (iii). [776 B] 4. The question whether a person is the owner or not is a matter for determination by the Rent Controller. [758 C] 3I: 2: 2. Section 9 of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Control) Act provides that the provisions contained in the Madras Building (Lease Rent Control Act, and the rules made thereunder shall have effect notwithstanding anything inconsistent therewith contained in any other law for the time being in force or in the terms of any contract, express or implied, between the landlord and the tenant. [764 D] 4:3.

The respondent was a partner of the appellant. The appellant entered into an agreement with the respondent for the purchase of certain goods and services by the respondent. The respondent agreed to sell the goods to the appellant on condition that the appellant would pay Rs. 4,00,000 as advance to the respondent within one month from the date of the agreement. The balance amount was payable on 1st October, 1943. The total consideration for the sale of the goods was Rs. 2,50,000 and the balance amount of Rs. 3,006 was paid by the appellant in cash. The contract between the parties was that the respondent would pay to the appellants a sum of Rs 4,50.000 as an advance on or before 1st November, 1943 and thereafter the balance of Rs 3,20,000 was payable by the appellants to the respondents. The agreement provided for payment of interest at the rate of 18% per annum on the amount of the advance from the respondent to the date on which the sale was completed. The amount of advance was paid in cash on or after 1st December, 1943 but before the expiry of one month therefrom. The appellants were not liable to pay any interest on the said amount at the time of payment of the balance. The question whether the sum of money was an advance or a deposit was considered by this Court in [Kinglingappa vs The State of Mysore] , and it was held that there must be an agreement between the appellant and the respondent that the award in respect of Lakshmi Ratan Cotton Mills and India Supplies was paid on 1.10. 1943 and therefore limitation would start from that date. In the present case, the contract between both the parties is that the amount was to be paid by Lakshmi Ratan cotton Mills to the Government. The High Court held that the agreement dated 1st of October, 1942 was not a mortgage but an agreement for sale of certain articles. The transaction was between the appellants and the respondents and therefore the limitation would commence from that day. The contention of the respondent was that there was no agreement between them and the appellant as required by the terms of the contract. The learned Single Judge held that in view of the fact that the sum was paid before 1.11. 1943, the limitation will start from the said date. The Division Bench also held that if there was a demand for return of the amount deposited, the period of one year would commence on the date when the sale is completed and therefore, limitation would begin to run from that point of time. In this view, the learned Single judge held that it was not open to the parties to say that there could be an implied demand for a part of the sum before 1-11- 1943. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The agreement dated January 1, 1943 was not an agreement to sell and therefore it was a mortgage. [601 D] (ii) The contract in question was one for sale and not a loan or advance. The terms of agreement were that the money was to become due on the expiry date of one calendar month from that month. The period of two months would commence only from that time. The suit was filed within one year from the expiry period of three months. [650 D] In the instant case, there was an express demand for the entire sum before the limitation began to run, and therefore there could not be any implied demand in view ofs. 5 of the Limitation Act. [643 E] (iii) The suit filed by the respondents was within one calendar year from that period. The notice dated October 1, 1942 issued by the plaintiff was a valid notice under s. 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure and therefore no question of limitation would arise in view Of the fact, that there is an express agreement between both parties to sell certain articles and services were rendered to the plaintiff.

The petitioner was arrested on the basis of a criminal case registered against him under section 107 of the Customs Act. The petitioner was released on bail by the Magistrate on the ground that he had been in detention for a period of about six months and that he was not likely to get bail. On his conviction, he was released from custody on the allegation that he committed an offence punishable under section 108 of the Act. He was arrested and produced before the Magistrate and was remanded to judicial custody. The order of detention was passed against him on the same day. The detenu filed a petition in this Court for quashing the order of his detention. This Court quashed the order on the grounds that the detaining authority had not been satisfied that the petitioner was likely to be released on the date of his arrest and that there was no material before the detaining authorit y that he could get bail after the order was made. The Court held that the detenu was in custody when the order for detention was made and therefore, the question of his being released on furnishing a bail application did not arise. In the present case, the petitioner had been arrested and remanded to custody. On the facts of the present cases, there is no material to show that the detention of the petitioner in jail was necessary. The petition is accordingly dismissed. V.K. SHALI, J. ssm. W.P.(Crl.) No. 823 of 1986: This is a petition under Article 32 of the Constitution of India for quashing an order of preventive detention passed against the petitioner on the very same day and also to direct that he be released from detention. The grounds of detention show that on the next day, i.e., on 28th of February, 1986, the detenu had been detained in jail. On this ground alone, the petition is dismissed.

The petitioners were appointed as casual labourers in the Telecom Department of the Government of India. They were engaged on daily wages for a period of one year and five months. The respondents were paid wages at the rate of Rs.210 270 per month. On the basis of the recommendations made by the Pay Commission, the pay scales of the employees of the Telecom department were revised to Rs.260 350 and Rs. 260 350 respectively. The petitioners were working as casual labour in the Telecommunication Department of Government of Andhra Pradesh. They worked for a number of years in the said Department. On completion of the said period of six months, they were paid daily wages at Rs. 210 270 per year. On their failure to complete the said six months of service, they filed a writ petition before this Court challenging the action of the respondents in not paying them the arrears of wages. The High Court allowed the writ petition and directed the Union of India to pay to the petitioners the arrears due to the casual labourers from the date of their appointment till the date on which the first of the above two petitions, namely, Writ Petition No. It was further ordered that the said arrears shall be paid within four months from today. The Union of Indian filed an appeal against this order before this court and the same was dismissed by a Division Bench of the High Court. On behalf of the petitioners it was contended that the respondents were not entitled to the benefit of the revised pay scales as they had completed 720/1200 days in 3 years service. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The revision of wages is an administrative order and does not confer any right on the petitioners to claim the same benefits which the regular employees are enjoying. [535 G] 2.1 The respondents cannot be allowed to raise a new plea that they were not being regularly employed for more than six months in the Posts and Telegraphs Department. They cannot be permitted to agitate this issue before this Hon'ble Court. [506 B] 2(i) The petitioners are entitled to get wages at par with regular employees of Telecom Department. [504 G] (ii) The respondents have not been able to show that they had worked for more or less 240 days in a year and, therefore, they cannot be denied the same privileges which the regularly employed workers were enjoying. They could not be allowed the benefits of the revision of pay scales. [500 D] 2.(iii) The revision is an executive order and not an administrative one. [511 G] 3.1 It was open to the respondents to make a representation to the Union Government for the redressal of their grievances. If they were aggrieved by the decision of the Central Government, they could have filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution. The remedy of the petitioner lies in approaching this Court. There is no merit in the contention that the petitioners are not entitled for the same relief as the regular workmen of the Telecommunications Department. The writ petition was rightly dismissed by the High court and hence there is no need to interfere with the order passed by the Central Administrative Tribunal. [635 G-H] 3.(i) There is a clear violation of Article 14 of the constitution of India, inasmuch as the petitioners were not given any opportunity to show cause against the action taken by them. The impugned orders are liable to be quashed and set aside. [736 B] (iii) In the circumstances, there is merit in this appeal and it is accordingly dismissed.

The Income tax Officer issued a notice under section 22(2) of the Act on January 5, 1950, to the assessee. The assessee filed his return in response to the notice under [section 22(1)] and claimed that he was entitled to get the benefit of the proviso to sub section (3) of section 24 of the Income tax Act, 1961. The Income tax officer held that the assessee had not furnished a return within the period prescribed by section 22 of the said Act and therefore a notice for assessment under section 23(1)(a) of that Act was issued on January 6, 1950. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Incometax Officer. In further appeal to the Tribunal, it was contended that the proviso had no application in the case before the Income Tax officer. The Tribunal held that there was a failure or omission on the part of the assessee to make a return under section 24(1) and therefore the notice issued by the Income-tax Officer was not valid. On further appeal, Held: (i) that the notice for the assessment was issued in accordance with law and it was not necessary for the assessee either to file a return or to file an application under section 28 of the Indian Income tax act, 1922, for the purpose of making a return. The proviso had nothing to do with the question whether the assessee was entitled for the benefit under sub section(3) or sub section 4 of section 23 of the 1922 Act. (ii) that in the instant case the assessee did not file any return within time and therefore it was open to the Income -tax Officer to serve a notice on him under section 29(2)(b) of Income tax, 1961, for making a proper assessment. [557 H] The proviso to section 28(3), as amended by Act No. 1 of 1956, provided that if the assessee failed to file any such return within one year from the date of service of notice under sub-section (2) or subsection (4) of Section 29 of the 1961 Act, he was liable to be assessed to income tax. [506 H] In the instant cases, there is no question of a failure on the side of the appellant to file the return within two years from the relevant date. The notice for reassessment under section 34(1), therefore, could not be treated as valid and assessment could not have been made.

The appellant, a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956, was formed with effect from 1.4.1956 and it was registered as a nationalised bank under the provisions of the [Banking Regulation Act, 1949]. The scheme was framed by the Central Government in exercise of its powers conferred on it under Section 3(1) of the Act. Under sub clause (c) of Clause 3 of the Scheme, the Central Govt. had to make the following amendment in the Scheme to bring about a change in the procedure for appointment of the employees of the nationalised bank, namely:- "The provisions of this Scheme shall be deemed to have come into force on the 1st day of April, 1956." The appellant was appointed as an Assistant Manager with effect form 1.1.1956. He was promoted as Assistant Manager on 1.2.1957 and he was confirmed in that post by order dated 23.8.1982. On his appointment as an Asstt. Manager, he was appointed to the post of Assistant Manager in the nationalised Bank on 1st April, 1957. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the scheme. The High Court held that the scheme did not come into operation on the date when it came into force and that the Central government had no power to amend or alter the procedure prescribed by the Scheme. It was further held that as the Central Govern ment had no authority to amend the Scheme in question, the appellant was not entitled to any relief. The appeal filed by the appellant against the judgment of the High court was dismissed by this Court. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court HELD: 1. The scheme framed under Section 4(1)(c) is a statutory one and it has been enacted with the object of providing for election in the manner provided in Section 3 of that Act. [775 H] 2. Clause (c), (d) and (e) of Sub clause (b) of Section 3 are not applicable to the case on hand. The Scheme was framed under the Act by the State Government in terms of Section 4 of the said Act. It is not a statutory scheme but it is an independent scheme. [750 H] 3. Clause 3(c) and 3(d) of Schedule II are not attracted to the facts of the case. The Central Government had no jurisdiction to amend, alter or add to, amend, vary or rescind any Scheme framed under sub clause 2 of Clause (b). [750 A] 4. The object of the statute is to provide for election by nomination and it is not open to the Central Gov tain to amend/ alter the scheme in question. [751 H] 5. The Act does not make any provision for amendment or alteration of the procedure provided in the scheme, but only makes provisions for amending or altering the procedure laid down in the Act and the Scheme framed thereunder. [751 A] 6. Clause 4(c), 4(d)(i) is not attracted in the facts and circumstances of the present case. [752 H] 7. The question whether the Central Gover nment has power to add any provision or amendment of the provisions made under Section 5 of the Central Act, does not arise for consideration in this appeal. [754 A] 8. Clause 6(c)(i), (ii) and clause (e), (f) and 4(h) are not relevant for the purpose of determining whether the scheme framed by it is a 'statutory scheme' or a 'public policy'. The scheme has to be read as a whole and it cannot be said that the Scheme is not an 'statutory one' within the meaning of Clause 6. [761 A-B] 9. Clause 7(a) provides for election of the President and Vice-President of the Bank.

The appellant, a registered dealer in the State of Andhra Pradesh, was assessed to tax by the assessing authority under section 45(1) of the Act. The assessing authority levied a penalty of Rs. 1,000/- on the assessee for failure to pay the tax due from him. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of assessment and dismissed the appeal filed by the appellant. On an application made by the respondent, the Tribunal set aside the order passed by the appellate authority and remanded the case to the assessing officer for passing a fresh order in accordance with law. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order dated 30th March, 1986 of the Appellate Assistant commissioner. The High Court held that the provisions of section 255(5) of Act were not attracted to the facts of the case and accordingly set aside its order. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court erred in holding that the provision of section 254(5)(b) of The Act was applicable only to cases where an assessee had preferred an appeal, and that the power of stay by the Tribunal under section 255 (5) was not available to the Appellate Tribunal. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 Section 255(6) of A.P. General Clauses Act provides for a special procedure for the recovery of tax or penalties payable by or imposed on the assessees as a matter of course in view of the special nature of taxation and revenue. [775 H] 1.2 The provisions of sections 254(6), 255(8) and 256(6)(b), which are applicable to cases of assessment, are not attracted in the facts and circumstances of the present case. [750 A] 1:3. Section 255 (6) provides for an appeal against the order made by a Tribunal under sub-section (1) or sub- section (2). The power of the appellate Tribunal to stay recovery proceedings is not available in cases where the assessee has preferred an application before the Appellate Tribunals, but the Tribunal may consider whether to stay the recovery proceedings and on what conditions and the stay will be granted in most deserving and appropriate cases where successful from being rendered nugatory by allowing the appeal. [751 G] 1 D C D H H P Co. vs Commissioner of Income Tax, A.I.R. 1986 S.C. 869; referred to. 2.1 The provisions contained in section 255 of the Andhra Pradesh General Clauses act do not apply to cases wherein an assessee has submitted an appeal or a petition under sub section (6)(a) of section 256 is pending before the Tribunal. [75 H, 76 A] 2.2 In the instant case, the assessee had filed an application for stay of recovery proceedings against him and on that ground he was not entitled to any relief in terms of section 257(5). The High court was wrong in holding otherwise. [76 B] 1 S C D G H P CO vs Commissioner Of Income Tax , A.l.R., 1986 S C.

The respondent was a Police Officer in the State of Uttar Pradesh. He was appointed as a Police Constable in the year 1962 and was posted at the Police Station, Churhat, District Meerut. On September 6, 1963 he was served with a charge-sheet under section 7 of the Police Act (1) on the ground that he had committed an offence punishable under section 8 of the Indian Penal Code.
