The respondent denied the charges and claimed that he was not guilty of the offences alleged against him. He also pleaded that he should be acquitted by the Court of Sessions. The trial ended in his acquittal. On October 9, 1963, the respondent filed a petition before the High Court for quashing the order of dismissal. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the charge framed against the respondent was not in accordance with law and that there was no prejudice caused to the respondent by the non compliance with the provisions of para. 489 of the Criminal Procedure Code. On behalf of the appellant, it was contended that the order passed by the High court was erroneous and that the High Courts were wrong in holding that there had been no magisterial inquiry in respect of the matter which was the subject matter of the departmental trial. The learned Judges of the High, Court held that the respondent could not be said to have committed an act of criminal misconduct within the meaning of para.(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure and accordingly quashed the order. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) that the provisions contained in para. 490 of the Punjab Police Regulations were only directory and not mandatory and that no prejudice was caused to any of the respondent on account of non compliance therewith. The fact that in the meantime the police received further complaints or that the C.I.D. made further enquiries does not affect the question, if substantially the subject-matter of the magisterial enquiry and the departmental proceedings were held thereafter. (ii) that there is no prejudice to the appellant's case on account thereof. The provisions contained under para. 491 of the Civil Procedure Code are only directory in nature and do not affect any question, whether there was a magisterial inquiries in respect whereof the investigation was made before the commencement of the criminal trial. [457 C] (iii) that in view of the provisions in para.(i) of para 490 of Punjab Police Regulation, it is clear that the departmental inquiry was held by an officer incharge of the police station and therefore it falls within the express terms of para 491 of Punjab police Regulations. The order passed on October 9. 1963 was erroneous. [557 C-D] (iv) that no opportunity was given to the accused to defend himself in the criminal case before the trial was concluded and therefore the High courts were wrong. [506 G] (v) that as there was an allegation of an offence under section 5 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, it falls outside the express term of para (1), the order was erroneous; and (vi) that even if the charge against the accused was not found to be proved, the departmental proceeding was held in accordance therewith. [504 G] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1566 of 1966. Appeal by special Leave from the Judgment and Order dated the 9th July, 1964 of the Allahabad High Court in C.M.P. No. 1124 of 1963. S.K. Sinha and R.N. Sachthey, for the appellant. B.B. Ahuja, for respondent No. 1. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Subba Rao, J. This appeal is directed against the judgment dated September 9, 1964 passed by a Division Bench of the said High Court dismissing the writ petition filed by the respondent. The facts leading to this appeal are as follows: The respondent was appointed in the Police Department on October 10, 1963 and was promoted as Head Constable on November 6, 1964.

The appellant was appointed as a Director of Health Services, Manipur on September 9, 1966. He was promoted to the post of Director of Medical and Health Services in February 1971. On November 1, 1970 he was promoted as Director of Public Health Services. On December 31, 1970, he was transferred to the office of the Deputy Inspector General of Police, Manipur, but he was not promoted to that post on the ground that he had been selected for promotion by way of promotion from a senior post in the speciality cadre. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of his transfer and contending that he was entitled to be considered for promotion as Director General of Health Service, Manipur. The High Court held that the appellant was not qualified for being promoted to supertime grade II on the basis of his having been selected by way 'promotion' in February, 1971. It further held that Dr. Sen had no right to be promoted to a post which is deemed to have fallen vacant in September, 1971 and he could be considered eligible for promotion only if he was superseded by any one junior to him in his speciality cadre and the appellant did not hold any other post in supertime scale II. The State of Manipur filed an appeal against this decision before the Supreme Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The appellant was entitled for being considered for appointment as Director on promotion from the pool of officers in the super time grade II to the supertime post in which he was appointed. [775 H] 1.2 The appellant could not be promoted as a Professor or Reader in any other speciality unless he had put in 8 years of service in the category of specialists ' posts. He could be said to have been superseded by some one junior and qualified for promotion to super time scale II on account of his being selected for appointment by way o f promotion. [750 H] 2.1 There is no justification for giving a direction that the post was not offered to him. The fact that he has been selected in February 1970 does not mean that he must be considered as qualified for the post which was created in September 1971. [751 G] 2:2 It is true that the promotion of the appellant could be made only on the invalidation of his promotion by a person junior to the appellant but that by itself cannot give him any direction that he should be considered fit for promotion from that post. [751 H] 3.1 In the instant case, the appellant had been appointed as Director in February 1972 and was not eligible for being appointed to super-time grade I on the strength of his appointment. The promotion of Dr. P.K. Gupta to super hoc grade II was made by way other than promotion from an officer junior to Dr. A.K Gupta who was senior to him, but the appellant's appointment was not approved by any person junior or qualified for such post. The order of transfer of Dr Gupta was passed on November 1. 1970 and he was reverted as Director, Health Services on December 31. 1970. [752 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1566 of 1972. From the Judgment and Order dated the 14th July, 1971 of the High court of Manipur at Imphal in WP (C) No. 8 of 1971. S.K Sharma, R.P. Singh, M. K. Garg, P. C. Kapur, V. N. Ganpule, D. N., P. W. D. and Mrs. A Subhashini for the Appellant. B. Sen, Romesh Chandra, RR. Gupta, RM. Sridhar Rao, S. Natesan, M K Jain, RV. Sinha, S K Jain and V.N. Ganphon, for the Respondents. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by RAY, J. This appeal is directed against a judgment dated April 14, 1971 passed by the High Curt in WP(C)

The Act was passed by the State Legislature in exercise of its powers under section 10A of the Act. The father of the appellant, who was a minor, died on November 30, 1962 leaving behind his widow and two sons, the appellant and the respondent. After the death of their father, the respondent filed a suit for partition claiming that the gift made by the father to the son of the deceased was void and illegal. The trial court held that the gifts in question were not valid and accordingly decreed the suit. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decree and dismissed the suit holding that the appellant had failed to establish his claim of being a 'reserved area' within the permissible limit. In further appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the respondent that section 19B(1) of the said Act did not apply to the case as the gift in question was made by an heir to the father and therefore the provisions of section 19 B were not attracted. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that section 10 A was applicable only to cases where the source of the excess area is inheritance or bequest or gift or gift which is permissible under the provisions contained in section 10(B). [775 H] 2. Section 19B does not apply in the case of a person who, by inheritance, comes to own an excess area, to make a declaration of his lands within permissible limits. The provision of section 9B is attracted only when the source or extent of the surplus pool is acquired by an heirs by inheritance and not otherwise. [776 H] 3. Section 10-A was applicable to cases in which the source was acquired by the son or wife of the father. It does not affect the right of the son to retain the excess land. The provisions of sections 9B and 9C are attracted only where the sources of the land are acquired by inheritance. [750 H] 4. Section 9-A is applicable only in cases where there is no person holding in excess of the permissible area which he likes to keep and make the necessary declaration. [751 A] 5. The section does not operate as a bar on the right to retain any excess land if it is not acquired by gift or bequest within permissible limit, but is saved by the provisions in section 19-B. [751 H] 6. Section 11-A does not come into play when the sources are acquired and the surplus area is not taken away by the Act or the rules made thereunder. The scheme of the section doesn't affect the rights of the heirs to retain excess land which he has inherited from his father. [754 A] 7. Section 12(1)(a) does not bar the right under section 19(B) to retain an excess land, if it was acquired in contravention of the provisions made in section 9-B and the Act does not make any such provision. [764 G] 8. The question whether section 19A is attracted or not is a matter for consideration by the High court. [752 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1320 of 1987. From the Judgment and Order dated 16.8.1987 of the Allahabad High Court in C.M.W. No. 814 of 1987 In C.A. No...1320 of 1986. V.S. Desai, S.K. Bagga, R.N. Singh, A.K Gupta, RR. Srivastava and D.P. Singh for the Appellant. M.C. Dhingra, Ms. Rani Chhabra, Ms Urvashi Gulati, Ms Anu Mehta, Ms Jayshree Mehta, Mr. K.K Jain, Ms Indu Malhotra, Ms Poonam Suri, Ms Meenakshi Arora, Ms Vineeta Sharma, Ms S. Janani, Ms Jyotsna Rewal Dua and Ms. A. Subhashini for the Respondent.

The plaintiffs filed a suit for possession of the Malguzari lands in respect of which an order was passed by the Compensation Officer under section 3 of the Act. The defendants contended that the plaintiffs were entitled to the compensation payable in respect thereof and that the order of the Compensation officer was not final and conclusive, and that as no suit was filed by the plaintiffs for setting aside that decision, the order passed by him became final and binding on the State. The High Court held that the orders passed by both the Compensation Officers were valid and binding and that in any event the order dated August 30, 1951 was a nullity and the order was not liable to be reopened. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the plaintiffs that the High Court was in error in holding that the decision of the Governor in 1950 declaring the estate of Amarshah was final and the Compensation Commissioner had no jurisdiction to determine the question whether compensation in respect to Malguazart lands was payable to Dayaram or not. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The order passed under section 14 of Act 1 of 1951 is a nullity. [557H] (2) Section 14 of the Land Acquisition Act provides that the Compensation Office shall proceed to enquire summarily into the merits of such question and pass an order as he thinks fit. [658F] (3) The High court was in wrong in holding otherwise. [650D] (4) The decision of a Court of competent jurisdiction is final and no appeal lies against it. [663G] (5) Section 15 of Act I of 1951 does not invest the Compensation Collector with jurisdiction to decide whether compensation was payable in favour of Dayaram or the plaintiffs. [664F] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 979 of 1966. Appeal by special leave from the judgment and order dated April 30, 1964 of the Allahabad High Court in First Appeal No.. 11 of 1962. S. K. Sinha and P. C. Agarwala, for the appellants. R.K. Garg, for respondent No. 1. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Shah, J. This appeal is directed against a judgment of the High court of Allahabad dated April 29, 1964 dismissing the First Appeal filed by Dayaram against his order dated July 30, 1952. The plaintiffs filed an application under section 15 of the U.P. Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 1951 (U. P. Act No. I of 1952). The appellants contended that in view of the provisions contained in section 14(1) of the said Act, the Compensation Court was not competent to determine any competing claims between the plaintiffs and the State and that it was not open to the Compensation Authority to decide the question regarding the claim of the plaintiff. The Trial Judge held that there was no valid order passed on August 30 1951 by the Governor under section 5 of the Uttar Pradesh Land Acquisition Ordinance, 1953 (U P. Ordinance No. III of 1953) as amended by the U P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950 (U & P. Acts No. II of 1951), and that he was competent to decide both the questions raised in the First appeal. The appellants filed an appeal against the judgment of a learned Single Judge of the court of Small Causes, Allahabad dated May 30, 1963. The Division Bench held that section 14 (1)(b) of Act II of 1952 did not invest it with jurisdiction and dismissed the First Appeals. In the result, the High. Court allowed the Second Appeal filed on behalf o the plaintiffs in respect whereof the order under appeal was passed. Hence this appeal by special Leave. 3. The only question that arises for consideration is whether the order made by the Collector under section 4 of the Abolition Act was a valid order. Section 4 of Act III of 1952 reads as follows: "4. (1).

The appellant was a tenant of the respondent, who was a member of the Bombay Public Service. He filed a suit for recovery of rent against the respondent on the ground that he was withholding the rent on the grounds mentioned in section 12(3) (a) of the Act. The trial court decreed the suit and directed the tenant to deposit in Court the amount of standard rent within one month from the date of service of notice under section 12 (2) of Act. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decree and held that the provisions of section 12 of the said Act were applicable to a dispute between the parties and it was not necessary for the tenant either to raise a dispute as to standard rent or permitted increases in the case of a suit. The respondent filed an application under section 11(4) (b) of Bombay Rent Act, 1947 before the Court of Small Causes, Bombay, praying that the order passed by the trial court be set aside and the matter be remanded to the trial Court for deciding it afresh on merits after giving the tenant a right to raise the dispute. The High Court held that in view of section 11 (4) of this Act the provisions contained in section 11 of the aforesaid Act were not applicable to the dispute between parties and, therefore, the order of the trial Judge was illegal. On behalf of the appellant it was contended that the High court erred in holding that the provision of section 13(3)(a) was attracted to a case where the dispute in regard to standard or rent was raised at any time prior to the expiry of one month after service of the notice terminating the tenancy by raising a dispute for the first time in the written statement. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The provisions contained under section 13 (3)(b) are applicable only to a suit where the matter is raised at the first stage and such non existence of the dispute at the date when the dispute was raised before the expiry or the period of one months from the service of a notice under sub section (2), is not material. [775 H] 2. The provision contained in sub section 2 of section 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, does not apply to a proceeding between the same parties where the suit was instituted at any stage prior to or after the expiry thereof on one month's notice. [750 A] 3. Section 11(5) of that Act is applicable only when the matter in regard of standard or rate rent is raised in order to avoid the operation of section12(3). The provisions of sub section 1 of section11 are not attracted to such a proceeding. [751 B] 4. The words "in any case" occurring in section 13 of the Indian Code must be read as "in the circumstances" and it cannot be said that the words "within one month" were used in the context of section13(3), (a). [750 D] 5. Section 12(1) of C.P.C. provides that where a dispute is raised by any party at any point prior to, or after, the date on which the dispute has been raised before, the Court shall decide it according to law. [75 H; 76 A] 6. The language used in section 10(5)(a), (b), (c) and (d) of section 15 of the Limitation Act, 1963, is clear that the said provision was applicable only if the matter was raised in regard thereto at any subsequent stage. [76 B] 7. Section 13(1)(b), as it stood prior to its amendment by Act No. 10 of 1976, provides that the Court may, on sufficient cause being shown, allow the dispute to be raised within a period of six months from such date as is referred to in section 15(2) and the Court has no power to extend the said period beyond the said date. [77 C] 8.

The respondent company is a limited company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956. The respondent company was incorporated in the year 1944 and it had a share capital of Rs. 1,50,000/- each. On April 30, 1945, the Aluminium Ltd., issued a notice to the appellant calling upon it to pay the sum of Rs, 1,00,000/-. On May 29, 1945 the appellant filed a petition under Section 397 read with Section 402 of the Companies act, 1956 (hereinafter referred to as "the Act") before the High Court for quashing the proceedings. The High Court quashed the notice and directed the Registrar of Companies to issue a certificate of registration in favour of the respondent company. On May 30, 1946, the appellant issued a certificate under Section 402(1) of the Act to the effect that the respondent was holding the majority of shares as trustees. On June 29, 1946 the appellant applied for registration of the company and on July 31, 1946 he made an application to the Registrar for registration in respect of the shares held by him. The Registrar refused to register the company on the ground that the appellant had not paid the sum demanded by the respondent. On August 30, 1947, the Registrar issued a further certificate under [Section 402(2)] of the Indian Companies Act 1956 (for short "the Companies Act") in favour the respondent and directed registration of his company. The appellant filed an appeal to the High court against this order before the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court held that the Registrar was not competent to issue the certificate under section 402(3) of that Act. On September 30, 1948, the respondent filed a writ petition in the High (Court) challenging the validity of the notice issued by the Registrar and also the order passed by the High. Court. On December 14, 1949, the High, Court dismissed the writ petition. The present appeal is directed against this judgment. The question that arises for consideration is whether the High Courts have power to issue certificate under Article 226 of the Constitution in respect to the questions referred to them. The facts of the case are not in dispute and it is not necessary for us to discuss the same. The respondents filed a return on May 30. 1946, in which they claimed that the shares were held by them as trustees and that the amount demanded by them was paid by the appellant. On July 31. 1947, they issued a fresh certificate under s. 402(4) of Act No. 58 of 1956 (the Act). The High court held that on August 30. 1948, there was no valid registration of its company. It further held that in view of the provisions contained in section 402 (1) and (2), the Registrar could not issue a fresh notice under Section 403(3)(a) of Companies Act. In this appeal by special leave, it is contended on behalf of the appellant that the High courts have no power to direct registration of a company under [section 402] of the Income Tax Act. The contention is that the question referred to the high court was not a question of law and the High-Court has jurisdiction to issue such a certificate. Section 402 (3) provides that the Government may, by notification in the official Gazette, declare that any company which is a body corporate having a share or shares as a public company shall be deemed to have been registered under this Act. It is not disputed that the respondents filed an application for registration before the Registrar on July 30, 1949. The application was made on August 29, 1948 and it was dismissed by the Bombay High Court on December 14. The appeal is accordingly allowed and the order of the High'Court is set aside.

The respondent was appointed as a Junior Accounts Assistant in the office of the Board on 5th January, 1966. He was promoted to the post of Accounts Superintendent on 1st November, 1956 and he was confirmed in that post on 1 st April, 1957. On his appointment he was promoted as Accounts Superintendent with effect from 1st May, 1958. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of promotion. The learned Single Judge dismissed the writ petition holding that the Regulations framed by the Board under section 79(c) of the Act were not applicable to the allottees and the allottees were exempted from passing the Departmental Examination. On appeal, the Division Bench of the High court held that the regulations framed by it did not apply to the case of the respondent and accordingly quashed the order passed by the Single Judge. The State filed an appeal before this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The Regulations framed under section 81(c), as amended by the Act, are applicable to all the allottees. [557F] 1.2 The regulations framed under Section 79(b) ofthe Act were in force at the time when the Regulations were made and they were not inconsistent with the provisions of the Regulations. The Regulations were not consistent with the Regulations and could not be given effect to. [506 G] 1:3. The Regulation framed by a Board under Section 81(a) of Act was applicable to allottees who had been appointed as Accounts Superintendents on 5 th January, 1956. The regulations made by the board under section 80(c)(i) of that Act were applicable to those allottees who were not required to pass the Departmental examination. [504 G] 2.1 There is no infirmity in the order dated 19th May, 1969 passed by a Single Judge of the Mysore High Court and the Division bench of the Bombay High Court has rightly quashed the orders passed by it. The appeals are accordingly dismissed.

The appellant, Suman Behera was a member of the police force of the State of Bihar. He was prosecuted for an offence under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and was convicted by the trial court and sentenced to undergo imprisonment for life. The High Court confirmed his conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the appellant had been deprived of his fundamental right under Article 21 of the Constitution of India as he had not been able to maintain his family and his property was acquired by the State Government in exercise of its power under Section 3(1) of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The provisions of the Criminal Procedure Code are applicable to all proceedings before a court or a tribunal and enforcement or protection of fundamental rights is not available to the aggrieved party to claim compensation under the private law for the wrong done by his servants. [775 H] 2.1 The right to compensation under Article 32 of the constitution is a remedy available in public law and is independent of the rights available to a person to claim damages under the State law. It is not an absolute right but is subject to the provisions of any private law which may be applicable to the protection of the civil liberties of the citizen. [750 H] 3.2 The provisions contained in Section 3 (1) and (2) of Act are applicable only to proceedings before courts or tribunals and enforcement of fundamental right of the citizens under Article 226 of the said Constitution is a protection against prosecution for an act which is done by the Government or its officers. [751 A] 3:3 B] 3(i) The provisions in Section 2 (1)(a) and 2 (2), 2 (4) and 3 (5) of Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 are applicable not only to the proceedings before the court or tribunal but also to the rights of the aggrieved person under Article 19 of theConstitution. [753 H] 4.1 In the instant case, the appellant was deprived of fundamental and indefeasible right under the provisions contained therein as he did not have any fundamental right to claim a compensation under Section 2(1)(f) of Criminal Procedure Act. The right of his property is an incident of the right guaranteed by Article 21. [764 H] 5.2 In the case of a private person, the protection afforded by Article 19 (1), (a) or (b) of Constitution is not applicable to him. [754 A] 4:3 D] 3.(i) Section 2 of the Prevention of corruption Act, 1988 is applicable only in cases where an offence is committed by the public servant and not otherwise. [752 B] 5.(ii) The right under Articles 19(1), 21 of Constitution does not include the right to property under Article 300A of the [Constitution]. [754 G] 5:4 D] 5(iii) The appellant was entitled to compensation for his fundamental rights under Article 14 and 16 of the[Constitution. The appellant had not challenged the constitutional validity of Section 3 of Act. [758 H] 6.1 There is no merit in the contention that the provisions in the Criminal Law Code are inapplicable to the cases before the courts or tribunal. [759 B] 6:5. The provision contained in sub-section (2)(b) and sub-clause (c) of Section 2, 2(4), 2(5) and Section 3, 2 (6) of [Prevention of Corruption Amendment Act, 1984], are applicable. [761 D] 6.(i)(a)(ii) In the present case, there is no challenge to the constitutional provisions contained under Article 31 of the Constitutions. The question whether the appellant has been deprived from his fundamental and fundamental rights by the impugned order does not arise in this appeal.

The petitioner was convicted by the trial court and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed his conviction and sentence. On appeal, the High Court held that the petitioner was guilty of an offence under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced him to imprisonment for life. The petitioner filed a writ petition in this Court challenging the validity of the order passed by the High court. This Court dismissed the petition holding that the High Courts had no power to direct the Superintendent of Jail to allow the petitioner to interview the prisoners. In appeal, this Court held: "The High Court has not given any reasons for rejecting the petitions filed by the petitioners and we are satisfied that there is no reason why the petitioner should be allowed to interview a prisoner. The petition is accordingly dismissed." The petitioner then moved this Court under Article 32 of the Constitution for a writ in the nature of habeas corpus directing the respondents to produce him before us. This petition was heard along with the main writ petition and by order dated April 14, 1981, this court directed that the matter be placed before Hon'ble the Chief Justice for appropriate orders." The appellant filed an application under Article 226 of the constitution for a direction to the Superintendent to allow him interviewing the prisoners as he wanted to interview them. This was dismissed by the learned Single Judge on May 5, 1982. The appellant then moved the High Curt in Writ Petition No. 832 of 1982 which was disposed of by a judgment dated April 15, 1983. The learned Judge held that since the petitioner had not been asked to interview his prisoners as required under clause (4) of rule 549A of the Manual, he should be given an opportunity to interview him and if he is found suitable, he may be allowed interviewing them. The appeal filed by special leave was dismissed on April 15. 1983. Hence this appeal by special Leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts have no power under Article 136 of theConstitution to direct that the Superintendent should allow the appellant to interview any prisoner. [775 H] 1.2 In the instant case, the petitioner did not make an application for a similar relief before this Court. He was not asked to do so by the Superintendent and he was allowed to interviewed the prisoners in accordance with the rules and regulations governing the interviews. The question whether the petitioner could be given interviewing his prisoners or not is a matter for us to decide. [750 H] 2.1 In the present case, as we have held that there was no reason for the Superintendent not to allow any interviewing of the prisoner as he did not ask him to do the work of interviewed the prisoner and if such an application was made to the Principal of the Jail, he could be allowed interviewsing them as he desired. [751 H] 3.2 The High C Court has rightly held that in the absence of a proper application by the petitioner for interviewing him, the Superintendent is not entitled to direct interviewing or not to interviewing any prisoner and the petitioner cannot be denied interviewing himself. [751 G] JUDGMENT: ORIGINAL JURISDICTION: Writ Petition Nos. 833-834 of 1982. Under Article 32 and 226 of The Constitution of India. N.A. Bana, for the Petitioner. S.K. Dholakia, M.S. Krishnamoorthy, R.N. Poddar and A.K Gupta for the Respondents. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by RAY, J. These two writ petitions are filed under Article 227 of the High courts of Madras and Bombay challenging the legality of the orders passed by them in Writ Petitions Nos.833- 834 of1982 and the order dated May 5 1983 passed by a learned Single judge of the Allahabad High Court dismissing the writ petitions filed against the orders of the District Magistrate, Kanpur, dated April 10, 1982, rejecting the petitioners' applications for interviewings.

The appellant was a partner of the firm of the respondent. The appellant filed a suit for recovery of damages against the respondent on the ground that the respondent had become liable as a surety for the performance of his duties under an order of the Court in any suit or proceeding J consequent upon the fire. The trial court decreed the suit and directed the respondent to pay damages at the rate of Rs. 1,000 per month from January 22, 1950 till the date of the decree. The respondent filed an appeal against the decree before the District Judge but the appellate court reversed the decree holding that the surety bond executed by the appellant was not a part of the proceedings pending before the Court and therefore the appellant would not be liable to make good the loss caused to the tea garden. The High Court held that the order for recovery passed by the trial court was legal and valid and the respondent was entitled to recover damages from the appellant. It further held that in view of section 150, the Subordinate Judge was entitled "to exercise the same powers in the matter of enforcement of the bond as the District Court himself had made contentions from time to time". The High court also held that by virtue of section 151, the respondent would not have any right to recover damage caused to tea garden because the appellant had become a partner in his capacity as a Receiver and the appellant could not be enforced against the appellant under the terms of the order passed by him. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was wrong in holding that section 150 did not apply to the case. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The order for the recovery of damage suffered by the respondent is legal and proper. [775 H] 2. Section 151 does not apply where a person has become liable under an award or decree. It only applies when the award or judgment is in favour of the party against whom it was made. [750 A] 3. The provisions of section 152 do not apply if the award is in respect of a tea garden and the order of attachment passed by court is in any way legal and correct. [751 D] 4. Section 150 does not affect the rights of the parties to the suit or proceedings before the court. It merely provides for the payment of damages. The provision of section 154 does not provide that the party who has become a surety should be liable for the loss occasioned by the fire, damage caused by the breach of the terms thereof. [751 D] 5. Section 152 does not operate as an bar to the execution of any decree or order passed in any proceeding before the same court. The words "any other proceedings" occurring in section 152 must be read with the context in which they are used in that provision. [764 G] 6. In the instant case, the appellant has become entitled to get damages from his client under an agreement of sale executed by him and he is not liable for any loss caused by such breach. [754 H] 7. The award passed by a court is legal. It does not bind the parties unless it is shown that the award was in favour or against the person who had committed breach of terms thereof, or where the amount awarded is excessive. [752 G] 8. Section 154 does no bar to execution of decree or orders passed in proceedings before any court. [758 H] 9. The question whether the surety bonds executed by appellant were a part and parcel of the proceeding pending before it was not decided in the suit filed by the respondents. [759 B] 10. In view of the provisions of Section 152, the High Courts have jurisdiction to execute decrees or orders. [761 D] 11. The power to execute any decree passed in execution of a decree is conferred on the court and such power can be exercised only when the decree is in the name of the judgment-debtor. [765 H] 12. In this case, there was no obligation on the part of respondent No.

The appellant, a dealer in foodgrains and other goods, was assessed to sales tax under the U.P. Sales Tax Act, 1948 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') on the ground that he purchased wheat from the State Government at the rate of Rs. 1,000 per cent. The assessing authority held that the supplies made by the appellant were not in accordance with the directions issued under cl. 5 of the Order and that the transactions of supply did not result in sales. On appeal, the High Court held that there was no offer by the tax payer to the State of Madras for sale of wheat and that it was open to the dealer to sell the goods on his behalf only 50% of the wheat purchased by him from the Government. The High Court further held that as there was a right of contract between the parties, the transaction could be regarded as a sale. On the question whether the transactions were sales within the meaning of s. 2(h) of the Act, the Court held: "The contention of the learned counsel for the appellant is that the goods purchased by the dealer from the Central Government at his cost were not sold in accordance to the provisions of the Sales Tax law and therefore the transaction was a sale." The High court further held: (1) that there is no offer made by a tax payer before purchasing the wheat. (2) that the sales were on behalf of the State and they were on that account not exposed to sales. (3) that in view of the provisions contained or incorporated in the Order, the transactions could be treated as sale. The Court held, therefore, that there being no offer from the dealer, the goods were not liable to deliver by the State. In this appeal, it is contended on behalf for the appellants that the High court was wrong in holding that there had been a contract between them and the State pursuant to which the goods had been sold. The contention of Mr. S. T. Desai, learned counsel appearing for the respondent, is that there could be sales in accordance of the directions given under cl 5 of Order. The question whether there was any offer by a dealer before purchasing wheat from him does not arise for consideration in this appeal. It is true that there may be an agreement between the assessee and the tax-payer but it is equally true that no offer can be regarded by the Sales tax authorities as a purchase within the terms of s 2(f) of Act. The fact that there has been a promise by the assessee to the taxpayers does not mean that there must be a contract in accordance therewith. There is nothing in the language of cl. (5) of Order, and therefore it cannot be said that there can be sales. It was next contended on the basis of the decision of this Court in [Ram Bilas Ram Gopal v The State of Uttar Pradesh] , that the transaction must be regarded to have been a sale within the definition of s, 2(g). In the case before us, there is nothing to show that there were any offer made before purchasing goods by the respondent. It may be conceded that there cannot be any contract between a dealer and the Government in respect of wheat purchased from the respondent at his own cost. The Sales tax law provides for a tax on sale. There can be no contract between an assessee and a State Government or a dealer to the effect that the movement of goods by road is not a sale, but only a purchase. In the instant case there was an agreement by the Government with the State in respect thereof. It cannot be disputed that there are no contracts between the appellant and the respondent and they are on behalf the State which may be regarded under s 2 (h) as a transaction of sale. [532 H] The High Courts of Punjab & Haryana and Delhi were wrong in treating the transactions as sales. [506 G] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1552 of 1966.

The petitioner was detained under the provisions of the Gujarat Prevention of Anti Social Activities Act, 1985 (hereinafter referred to as "the Act" for short) on the ground that he was a member of an All India Police Service and that he had been arrested in connection with a case registered against him under section 3(1)(ii) read with section 5(2) of the Act. The petitioner was served with the order of detention dated August 7, 1986. He filed an application for bail before the Sessions Court which was rejected on September 16, 1986 and he was released on bail on October 15, 1986 in connection therewith. On November 17, 1986, the petitioner moved a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before this Court praying that the order passed by the State Government dated August 8, 1986 be quashed and set aside and the detention of the petitioner be confirmed. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the petitioner was not a member or a person who had been detained in connectionwith a case which was registered against the petitioner under section 5 (2) readwith section 5 of the Prevention of Illicit Traffic Act, 1947. The State Government has filed this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The order passed on August 7/86 by the detaining authority is not an order of preventive detention but a detention order made under the Act and hence it cannot be upheld. [775 H] 1.2 In the instant case, the Advisory Board had reported that there was no sufficient cause for the detention. The report of the Advisory board was to be obtained within three months from the date of detention. [750 A] 1:3. The question whether the petitioner should be detained or not does not arise in this case because the Advisory Boards have to consider the question as to whether the detention is necessary to continue the detention and if so, it is not answered to say that the detention was made. If a reference to an Advisory Board is to be made within three weeks, it cannot do so. [751 B] 1 The order of the State government dated August 6, 1986 was not an interlocutory order but merely an administrative order. It was passed in exercise of its powers under section 9(2)(b) read along with section 8 of the Bombay Prevention of Prohibition Act, 1949. [753 H] 2.1 In the present case, there was a valid order of bail by the Sessions Judge and therefore it cannot stand. [764 D] 1 Whether an order for detention should have been made, is not a matter which can be decided in a writ petition under article 226 of Constitution. The power to grant bail is a discretionary one. It is not as if the petitioner has been arrested and detained in accordance with law. [754 H] JUDGMENT: ORIGINAL JURISDICTION: Writ Petition No. 879 of 1986. (Under Article 32 of the constitution) Dr. N.S. Chauhan, for the Petitioner. S.K. Bagga, for Respondent No. 1. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by KASLIWAL, J. This is an appeal against the order dated August 10, 1986 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court of Gujarat at Ahmedabad in Criminal Writ Petition Nos. 877 and 879/86. The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with [section 34] of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to undergo imprisonment for life. He was also convicted under sections 3(2), 5(1) and 5(3) of Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954. He has been sentenced to suffer rigorous imprisonment for a period of six months. The appeal against his conviction and sentence was dismissed by the High court on September 17, 1987. The present appeal is directed against that order. The facts leading to this appeal are as follows: The appellant is an Indian citizen. He is a member and a person in custody.

The appellant, a partnership firm carrying on business in the name and style of M/s. S.K. Jewellers, was incorporated under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 (hereinafter referred to as "the Act") by the name of S. K. Jewels. The respondent, a partner of the firm, filed a suit against the appellant for recovery of Rs. 1,50,000/- on the ground that the partnership deed dated 14th August, 1978 was not registered and that the said deed was executed by the partners in favour of the appellant. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the suit was barred as res judicata. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decree and held that the appellant had failed to prove that the respondent was dead at the time the suit had been instituted or decree was passed or some other ground which could have the effect of seizing of the case because the subject matter was wholly foreign to its jurisdiction or that the defendant was dead. The High Court further held that in view of the provisions of section 2(a) of the Act, the appellant was not entitled to challenge the award under sections 14 and 17 of the said Act. On this finding, the trial court dismissed the suit. In appeal by special leave, the Court of Appeal reversed the judgment of the High court and held: "The question whether the suit is barred as a res judicata has been considered by this Court in Seth Hira Lal Patni vs Shri Kali Nath, (supra) and it was held that on the facts of the present case, we are of the view that on this aspect of the matter, we have no jurisdiction to entertain the suit." The High court further held: "...it is clear from the provisions contained in section 2 (a) that the bar as to res judicata applies only to a question which was before them. In other words, the bar under section 2 does not apply to a case where the subject-matter was wholly outside the jurisdiction of the Court or that it could have been seized by the police. The bar is applicable only to cases where the Court has seizing the case and any such other ground as may be available to the defendant in his defence." In this view, we do not find any merit in the appeal. It is accordingly dismissed with costs.

The appellants were the original mortgagor and the respondent was the mortgagee. The mortgage deed dated January 30, 1939, was executed by the mortgagor in favour of the respondent on behalf of his minor son, the appellant No. 1. On February 28, 1939 the respondent mortgaged the property to the appellants for a sum of Rs. 2,000/- with interest at the rate of 12% per annum and also a sum equal to the amount of Rs, 10,000/-. The mortgage was executed on March 30, 1938, in favour o the respondent. On April 1, 1940, the respondent filed an application under section 28 of the Act for recovery of the loan advanced by him to the appellant. The appellants contended that the respondent had not received the notice referred to in clause (a) of sub section (1) of section 28 and that the mortgage was a simple mortgage and not an absolute interest. The trial court held that the suit was barred by limitation and dismissed the application. On appeal, the High Court reversed the judgment of the trial court and decreed the suit. In second appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf o the appellants that the decree passed by the trial Court was a nullity as the respondent did not receive notice under clause (b) of subsection (1), of section 29 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the provisions of sub-section (2) of Section 28 were applicable to the case and that it was open to the respondent to apply for recovery under clause(b) thereof before the expiry of the period prescribed by section 29. [636 C] 2. The question whether a mortgage is an absolute or an absolute one has to be decided in the light of the provisions contained in sub section 1 of section 30 and section 28, sub section 2 of section 31. Sub section (2), therefore, does not apply to the facts of this case. [643 D] 3. Section 29(1) provides that a mortgage shall be deemed to have been created only if it is an interest in the property which has been mortgaged by the mortgagee with possession at the time of the mortgage and the mortgagor has not received any notice under sub section 3 or sub section 4 of section 32. [736 C-D] 4. The words "all the rights of the mortgagor" used in clause(a) to (e) of the proviso to sub section 5 of section 24 are wide enough to include the right to recover the loan from the original mortgagee. [837 D] 5. In the instant case, the mortgage deed was executed in favour and the possession of the property was delivered to the mortgagor on April 1. 1938. The respondent did execute a notice under section 29(a), but he did not get any notice as required by clause (c) of proviso to subsection (2). [737 D-F] 6. In view of the fact that the mortgagee had not given notice under clauses (b), (c), (d) and (e), the respondent cannot be said to have received the notices referred to above before the period of limitation prescribed by sub section(1). [838 G] 7. The provisions contained inss. 29(2) and 31 are attracted only in a case where the mortgage is not an interest. [820 D] 8. In order to determine whether a particular property has been transferred or not, it is necessary for the court to decide whether the transfer of the mortgaged property was an absolute sale. The expression "all" in clause 2(b), therefore does not include the case where a mortgage has been created by the defendant. [822 D] 9. In this view of all the provisions relating to a mortgage, it must be held that there is no question of the suit being barred by time. [823 E] 10.

The appellant was a Hindu undivided family. He executed a deed of partition dated April 30, 1947 in respect of certain properties and the said deed was registered on May 27, 1947. The appellant filed a suit for possession of the properties under s. 6(h) of the Act against the respondents. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the transfers were valid and the subsequent alienations made by Venkatacharyulu were invalid. On appeal, the High Court held that the transfer was not hit by section 6(f) of Act No. 1 of 1947 and accordingly dismissed the suit. In second appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the properties gifted under exhibit A 1 and exhibit A 2 were not liable to be included in the partition and, therefore, the subsequent transfers made by the appellant were invalid and void. HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that there was no valid transfer of the joint family properties to the appellant. [652 D] (2) The deed of gift executed by Venkatachaharyulu in favour of the respondent was not invalid as it was not supported by any consideration for the subsequent promises. The deed was not a valid one and the earlier alienations were invalid, and therefore, they were invalid as they were made in consideration of past cohabitation. [752 D C] (3) The transfer under exhibitA 1 and exhibits A 2 and A 2 was invalid. The High court was right when it held that there is no valid gift by Venkatchaharyulu to the respondent. [750 E] (4) The subsequent alienations were not hit either by section 3 or 4 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956. [751 G] (5) The question whether the subsequent alienation made by a person in favour or against his concubine was invalid as the earlier transfers were invalid does not arise for consideration in this case. [753 H] (6) The fact that the appellant had executed a registered deed of transfer in respect to the properties covered by exhibit A1 and exhibitA 2 did not make any difference to the question whether there was any valid gift made by him to the family. [764 G] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1134 of 1972. From the Judgment and Order dated the 9th May, 1972 of the Madras High Court in C.M.P. No. 814 of 1972 and Civil Appeal Nos. 1135-1136 of 1972 From the judgment and order dated the 24th September, 1972, of the High court of Judicature at Madras in CMA Nos. 1234/72 and 1337/72. V. S. Desai, R. Ganapathy Iyer and M. Veerappa for the appellant (in C.A. No 1135/72). A.V. Rangam, for the respondent (in both the appeals). The Judgment of the Court was delivered by RAY, J.-This appeal is directed against a judgment of the Bombay High Court dated September 9, 1972 in CAs Nos. 1334 and 1338 of 1972 whereby the High Courts' decision in favour the appellant was reversed. The facts are not in dispute. The respondent filed a civil suit for recovery of possession of properties under exhibit B 1 and exhibited A2 and A2 in respect thereof. The suit was decreed by the trial court on March 30, 1972. The respondents preferred an appeal to the High Curt against the decree passed by the first appellate court. The second appeal was dismissed on April 9, 1973. The appellants filed a second appeal before this Court. The question that arose for consideration was whether there is any valid transfer by Venkatapharyulu or not. The contention of the respondents was that the subsequent sale in favour by the respondent to the extent of his share in the joint Hindu family property was invalid and the High Tr. Judge of the court below had no jurisdiction to pass a decree for possession.

The Income Tax Officer, who made the assessment of the assessee for the year 1962-63, assessed the income tax payable by the assessee under section 226(3) of the Act. The assessee filed an appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and contended that the notice issued under section226 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 was not valid as it was served on the assignee of the policies within the time given by the L.I.C., and therefore, the assessment made by the Income tax Officer was illegal. The Appellate Assistant commissioner confirmed the order of the I.T.O. and dismissed the appeal. On further appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that the delay in making the requisite statement on oath under section 227(3)(vi) of Income Tax, 1961, was not fatal to the assessment proceedings. [557D] (2) The question whether a statement made by an L.l.C. before the L..I. C., was sufficient to justify the inordinate delay in filing the return under section 240(1) of Chapter IV of the Indian Income Tax Rules, 1922, was a matter which required investigation and evidence was necessary for the purpose of determining the question whether the assessee had made the requisite statements on oath. [657F] (3) The mere fact that the LCIC did not make the requisite declaration on oath does not by itself lead to the conclusion that the assessee was guilty of laches or negligence in filing a return under s. 240(2) of Act, 1922. [650D] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 979 of 1977. From the Judgment and Order dated the 30th September, 1976 of the Gujarat High Court in Special Civil Application No. 1266 of 1976. S. T. Desai, R. N. Sachthey and B. D. Sharma for the Appellant. V. M. Tarkunde, K. J. John and P. C. Kapur for the Respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by PATHAK, J. This appeal by special leave is directed against a judgment of the High Court of Gujarat dated 30th October, 1976 in Special civil Application No 1266/75. The appellant is an Indian citizen. He filed an application under section 245(1)(c) of The Income Tax (Amendment) Act, 1976, for setting aside the assessment order passed by the IIT, Ahmedabad on the ground that the said notice was not served on him. The respondent filed a return of income under section 22 of the said Act in respect of the years 1962-64 and 1964-65. The Income tax officer rejected the claim of the appellant on the basis of the registered assignment dated 5th December, 1975. The Commissioner of Income tax, Gujarat, by his order dated 30.9.1976, held that the assessment was illegal and accordingly set aside the notice under section 26(1). The respondent preferred an appeal before the Appellate Tribunal which was allowed by the Tribunal on the same ground. The Tribunal held that in view of the registration of the assignment, the assessee could not be treated as a defaulter. The Revenue filed an SLP against this order to this court and obtained special leave from this Court. The question raised in the present appeal is whether the notice served on it under section WP 1266D was valid or not. The High court answered the question in favour of the Revenue and against the assessee. It held that there was no material before the Income-tax Officer to hold that the registered assignee had made an endorsement on oath as required by clause (vi) thereof. The appeal filed by the Revenue was dismissed by this Court on the view that the Tribunal was right. In the present case, the respondent did not file any return under Section 22 of The Act and therefore the assessment could not have been set aside by the Appellate Authority.

The appellant, a Hindu undivided family, was assessed to income tax by the Income Tax Officer, who assessed the appellant as an individual. The respondent, a firm, filed a return of its income for the assessment year 1962-63 and claimed that the income of the respondent was exempt from tax under section 12(2) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. The Income Tax officer held that the respondent had not been assessed to tax in respect of the income received by him as an employee of the appellant. He also held that he had not paid any amount towards the salary of the employees of the firm and that the said amount was not liable to be included in his total income for computing the period of limitation prescribed under section 29(2). The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court, which allowed the writ petition and quashed the order of the Income tax officer. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) that the first limb of sub section (2) was concerned only with proceedings for assessment of income tax and not with an appeal under the said sub section. The second limb of section 29 was concerned with a proceeding under the Income-tax Act which is similar to one under the First Schedule to the Limitation Act, and that therefore, it was not necessary for the respondent to be assessed to the tax in question. (ii) that in the instant case, the respondent did not pay any amount as claimed by him towards salary of his employees. The first limb was concerned merely with proceedings under the [Income Tax Act] which is a special or local law and not a suit. (iii) that sub section(2), therefore, was not applicable to an appeal against an order of assessment made by the Tribunal. (iv) that as the respondent failed to pay any money towards salary for the period in question, he was not entitled to claim deduction under section 11 of the Limitation act. (v) that there was no provision in the First schedule to the Act which required the IncomeTax Officer to assess the appellant on the basis of his income as an assessee. (vi) that even if the first part of sub sections (2), (3) and (4) were applicable, the second limb was not attracted to an application under section 34 of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the provisions of section 12 of the [Indian Income Tax (Amendment) Act, 1962] did not apply to an assessee who had not filed a claim for deduction under sub section 2 of section 11. [536 C] 2. Section 29(1)(b) is concerned only to proceedings of this kind and does not apply in an appeal or application under the provisions contained in the Second Schedule to that Act. The words "where any special or other local law prescribes for any suit, appeal or other proceeding" occurring in sub section 1 of section 34 are not applicable. [506 D] 3. Section 12(1) is a general provision and does apply to proceedings under any other local laws. It applies only to cases where an application for deduction has been made under the Act and that is not applicable in an application filed under the Indian Incometax Act, 1961. [504 G] 4. The provisions of sub-section (2)(a) are not attracted in an appeals or applications under the Limitation Acts. [456 H] 5. Section 11(1A) does not require the Income­tax Officer to apply the provisions in the first instance for computing any period of time prescribed by the First or Second Schedule. The proviso to sub section 3 of section 35 makes it clear that the application is required to be made under sub sections 1 and 2 of [section 34] of the said Act. [656 H; 506 A] 6.

The appellant, a private bus operator, was appointed as a conductor by the Regional Transport Authority, Mathura. The bus was plying on the route of the appellant's bus from Mathura to Delhi. On the basis of an inspection made by the Inspector of Police, the bus was found to be in possession of a number of passengers and it was found that the bus had been stopped at the bus stand. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the order passed by the District Magistrate. The High Court held that the provisions relating to parking places and halting places were not applicable to a private Bus Stand and that the power under section 68(2)(r) of the Act was not an independent power. It further held that there was no provision in section 68 (2)(t) of Act for the imposition of a tax on passengers and that it was open to the Regional transport Authority to impose a tax at a rate which was higher than the one fixed by the State Transport Authority. The writ petition filed by the appellant was dismissed by the High court. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 Section 68(1) of The Act provides that no person shall be entitled to ply any private bus or to carry passengers on a public service vehicle unless he has been permitted by the authority concerned under section 76 of the said Act to stop only at certain places for the pur pose of taking up or setting down passengers. [775 H] 1.2 The power under Section 68 (1) is an independent powers and not an additional power. The Regional Transport Authorities constituted under the Act are competent to impose the tax on a private vehicle. The power conferred by section 68 is in respect of a private service vehicle and the power to impose such a tax is in relation to a public services vehicle. [750 H] 2.1 The power to fix a bus stand under section 78(2) of Chapter IV of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939 is an additional powers which is not available to the State Government under section 77 of the 1988 Act. [751 G] 2:2 Section 68 of the Central Act provides for imposition of tax on vehicles and the Regional or Transport Authority may impose a fee in respect thereof. The provisions relating thereto are not applicable in relation thereto as they apply to a bus service vehicle. Section 68 is an integral part of Chapter V of the 1939 Act which deals with the levy of a fee. [75 H; 75 A] 2.(i) The power given under section 79(2), is an extra or special power and it cannot be exercised in respect to a transport vehicle. It is not an extra duty. [76 B] (ii) The powers conferred by sections 78(1)(r), 77(2). are independent powers. [77 C] 2(iii) Section 68 does not apply to private bus operators. [78 G] 3.1 In the instant case, there was a provision in Chapter IV which provides for levy of tax at the rate of one percent of the total number of seats and halting place or halting places. The State Transport authority has no power to levy a fee on a vehicle. There is no provision under section 80 of the 1961 Act empowering the Regional/ Transport Authority to levy any fee in relation thereof. [79 H; 80 A] 3:2. Section 79(1), therefore, does not come into play in respect thereto as it applies to private service vehicles. [80 G] 4. The powers given by section 78 are independent power and not supplemental power. [81 D] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1532 of 1987. From the Judgment and Order dated 16.5.1987 of the Karnataka High Court in Writ Petition No. 1205 of 1986. V.M. Tarkunde, M.K. Rajendran, R.S. Sodhi and S.N. Prasad for the Appellant. K. Parasaran, P.

The appellants were convicted by the trial Magistrate under section 7 of the and the Act for an offence punishable under section 3(1) of the Act. The appellants were prosecuted for offences under sections 7, 8 and 9 of the Indian Penal Code. They pleaded not guilty to the charge framed against them. The trial Magistrate acquitted all the accused persons but convicted them on the ground that there was no attempt on the part of the appellants to commit an offence of export within the meaning of Para 2(a) of Punjab Paddy (Export Control) Order, 1959. On appeal by the State Government, the High Court set aside the conviction and sentence passed against the appellants and acquitted them. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that there had been no attempt at committing an offence under section 5(1)(a) read with section 7 and the order of forfeiture passed by the District Magistrate was not in accordance with law and, therefore, the conviction could not be sustained. HELD: (i) The High Court was right in holding that there were no attempts on the parts of the accused to commit the offence of exports within the definition of Para 3(a). [775 H] (ii) The provisions of section 7 read with rule 8 of the Punjab Padddy (Cotton) Rules, 1959, do not apply to export of paddy outside the State. The provisions in the Punjab P. Paddy's (Exports Control) order, 1959 were applicable only to export within India and not to export outside the territory of India. [776 H] In the instant case there was an attempt on a part of a consignment of rice outside the country. It was a preparation for committing an act which constitutes an offence. The fact that the appellants had attempted to commit export within their respective States does not make them liable for an attempt to commit it. [750 A] (iii) The appellants could not have been convicted under section 4(1), 5(2)(a), 7, 9 and 10 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954. [751 B] (iv) The offence under Section 7 readwith rule 8 was not an attempt at commit an act but a preparation on the side of the State of Punjab. [75 H; 75 A] JUDGMENT: CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Criminal Appeal No. 9 of 1970. Appeal by special leave from the judgment and order dated April 20, 1969 of the Bombay High Court in Criminal Appeal Nos. 8/69 and 10/69. S. K. Kapur, for the appellants. R. N. Sachthey, for respondent No. 1. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Sikri, J. These appeals are directed against a judgment of the High court of Bombay dated April 24, 1969 in Criminal Appeals Nos. 9/69, 10/70 and 10-71 of 1969. The facts giving rise to these appeals are as follows: On March 30, 1959 the appellants were tried for an offences under section 6 read with Rule 8 of Punjab P Paddy and truck No. P.N.U. 967. They were convicted under sections 5(a), (b) and 7 of Prevention of food Adulteration Act 1954. The prosecution case was that there has been a attempt on, the part or part of, the accused in carrying, removing rice within the State and also to commit offence of exported goods within the territory thereof. The High court held that there is no attempt to committing an attempt by the appellants for export within its respective States. On this finding, the appeals were allowed and the conviction of the two appellants was set aside. The case was remitted to the trial Court for disposal in accordance therewith. The State Government filed a special leave petition against the judgment of this Court. The special leave was granted on April 20. 1969.

The Managing Agency Agreement was executed on April 1, 1957. The Managing Agency was to receive the entire remuneration for the year ending March 31, 1958 and the remuneration payable to the Managing Agent was to be paid by the Company in the month of April, 1959. On June 30, 1960, the Managing Agency entered into an agreement with the Company for the payment of the remuneration for a period of five years commencing from 1st July, 1961. The Company agreed to pay the remuneration at the rate of Rs. 5/- per day for the entire year ending on March 31. The agreement provided that the remuneration would be payable by the company in the following month and that the Managing Agents would be entitled to receive a commission at the rates specified in the said agreement from time to time. On April 1. 1961, the Company paid the remuneration of Rs 5/- for the period commencing from April 1 to June 30. The remuneration was paid by way of remuneration to the employees of the Company on the date of assignment and that is how the Managing agency was constituted. The company was to pay a commission of Rs 10/- per month for the whole year ending with March 31 and that would be the profits and gains of the business carried on by the assignor. On May 1, 1961, an agreement was executed between the Company and the Company whereby the remuneration was payable at the following rate: "The company shall pay a sum of Rs 6/- perday for the month ending March 30." The Managing Agents were to receive their entire remuneration in the year of assignment from time-to-time. On July 1, 1962, the company paid the said remuneration to all the employees and the Managing agents were to be treated as one entity and that was expressly provided by clause 10 of the Managing Agencies Agreement. On August 30, 1961 the Managing agent became liable to pay commission at a rate specified in Clause 10 of that agreement from April I to June 31. On September 1, 1963, the managing agency was terminated. The respondent filed an application under Section 7 of the Act for setting aside the order of termination and also for a direction to the Company to pay him the remuneration as per the said clause. The High Court held that the agreement did not create any liability on the Company but only created a liability on behalf of the company and that it was not a mere agreement between the assignors and the company. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decision of the Tribunal and held that in view of the provisions of Section 7(1) of the Employees' Provident Funds Act, 1952, the remuneration paid to the employee by way oi of remuneration for his entire service was not an income bearing asset but only a part of it. The appellant is before us with certificate of fitness. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The Tribunal and the High court were right in holding that the respondent was entitled to the amount of Rs 3/- per week as commission for the services rendered by the Managing Company. [505D] 2.1 The agreement between a company and its employees is an indivisible contract for remuneration under Section 10 of Act. It does not create a liability upon the Company. The payment of remuneration in terms of the said provision was not made by way other than the remuneration agreed to be payable to each employee. [506F] 2:2. Under the agreement, the respondent had to pay an amount equal to the remuneration which would have been payable to him if he had been appointed as a Managing Agent. The liability of the respondent to pay such remuneration was not in dispute and it is only on account of the fact that the said payment was made by the respondent. [605D-F] 3:1. Under Section 7, the amount paid to each of the employees by way Of remuneration for services rendered to them by the employer is a part and parcel of the agreement between them. The said agreement does not confer any liability upon them.

The appellant was a member of the Indian Police Service. He was convicted and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one year and to pay a fine of Rs. 500/- in default to suffer simple imprisonment for six months. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal, the conviction was confirmed by this Court. The appellant filed an application under section 439 Cr.P.C. before the High Court for his release on bail. The learned Sessions Judge rejected the application holding that the evidence of P.W.s 11, 13 and 15 corroborated the evidence given in the case. The prosecution examined P.Ws. 1 to 5 and produced M.Os. 1 and 2. The accused was also questioned under section 313 Cr.PC. He denied all the incriminating circumstances appearing against him and stated that he had been falsely implicated. The trial court held that the appellant was guilty of the offence punishable under section 302 I.P.,C. and sentenced him to undergo imprisonment for life. On appeal, this Court set aside the conviction of the appellant and sentence him to rigorous imprisonment till the rising of the court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The evidence of the witnesses is not sufficient to prove that the accused was guilty. [675 H] 2. There is no material on record to show that the deceased had been murdered by the appellant. The only circumstance relied upon by the prosecution is that P. W.s 9, 13, 15 and 15 were present at the time of incident. The fact that the dead body of the deceased was found near the house of the accused shows that the presence of the dead bodies in the house was natural. [775 H; 776 B] 3. The medical evidence does not show that there was any injury on the person of the victim. There are no material to show as to how the injuries were caused by the accused. The doctor who examined P W. 9, stated that the injuries found on the persons of the prosecution were simple in nature. [750 H] 4. The question whether a particular piece of evidence is sufficient to establish the guilt of the person concerned does not depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case. There must be some material to indicate that the offence was committed. [751 G] 5. The mere fact that P Ws 9 and 15 and others were present in the houses at the relevant time, cannot be a ground for conviction. The absence of any injury is not fatal to the prosecution case. [751 H] 6. The circumstances relied upon are not sufficient. There was no material before the Court to show how the accused had committed the murder. [764 G] 7. The presence of P W 9 and others at the place of incident cannot be said to be natural. They were present when the deceased died. The possibility that the person who was murdered was a stranger cannot be ruled out. [800 H] 8. There can be no doubt that the circumstances relied on by the High court are not proved. The conviction of an accused under section 304 Part I is not warranted. [875 G] 9. The offence punishable Under Section 302 I,P. C., is not made out. The case against the appellant rests on circumstantial evidence. [975 H-975 A] 10. The facts found by the courts below are not established. There were no material for convicting the appellant under section 201 I. P. C. and he was convicted under Section 302 read with Section 34 I.p.C., as stated above. [900 B] 11. The appeal is allowed, the judgment of the High. Court is set aside and that of the trial court is restored.

The respondent was appointed as a temporary employee in the appellant's Society on 1.1.1976. He was confirmed in that post by an order dated 30.6.1977 issued by the Managing Director of the appellant. On his appointment, he was transferred to the Delhi Administration and posted at Delhi. The respondent was promoted as Assistant Accounts Officer in the pay scale of Rs. 700-15-700. On 1.7.1978, he joined the service of the Society on deputation from the Delhi Development Authority. He continued to work in that capacity till his retirement on 31.5.1977. On 2.8.1979, he served as Assistant Account Officer in a post carrying higher pay scale. The appellant was appointed by an oral order dated 1.6.'77. He joined the said post on 1st July, 1977. On the expiry of the period of probation, he continued to hold charge of that post till his superannuation on 31st May, 1977 and thereafter, he retired from service on 30th June, 1977 on attaining the age of superannuation. The order of retirement was issued by him on 2.9.1977, which is under challenge in this appeal. The question for consideration is whether the respondent was entitled to continue in that office till his life time or after his retirement. The contention of the respondent is that he was appointed on 1-7-1977 and continued to be a temporary servant till his death. The post which the appellant was holding was abolished by an agreement between the parties. On behalf of the respondents it was contended that the appointment of the said respondent as Assistant Accountant in the year 1976 was not in accordance with the provisions of the Act and, therefore, he could not be removed from service. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the appellant had no right to continue on the post till he attained the age prescribed by the rules. [505 G] 2.1 The appointment of a temporary Government servant by an open invitation is not a promotion or termination of his service but is made only for the purpose of giving him one month's notice or pay in lieu thereof. The appointment was made on 1/7/1977 and he continued till his attaining the superannuation on 30.06.1977 and thereafter he retired on 30-6-1977. [506 G] 3.1 It is not open to the respondent to contend that the post which he held was abolished after the retirement of the employee. The appointing authority could have made an appointment in accordance therewith. [504 D] 3:2. The termination of the service by the appellant on 2nd August, 1979, was illegal and void. [407 G] 4.1 There is no merit in this contention. The appeal is dismissed.

The appellant was a dealer in country liquor. He was granted a licence to manufacture and sell country liquor for the purpose of manufacturing country liquor at the rate of Rs. 1,000 per month. The State Government issued an order dated April 16, 1970 under section 22 of the Act directing that the sale of country liquor should be deemed to have been made by the appellant on February 20, 1970. On March 4, 1970, the State Government passed an order under section 23(1) of the U.P. Excise Act, 1910 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') and directed that the sales of country spirit should be treated as sale in the course of inter-State trade or commerce. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the order dated March 4,. 1970. The High Court dismissed the writ petition on April 16. 1971. On May 15, 1971, the appellant filed an application under section 24(2) of that Act for permission to withdraw the writ petitions and to file a fresh writ petition in the High court. The application was allowed by the High. Court on March 28, 1974. Thereafter, the petitioner filed a review petition before this Court which was dismissed on April 17, 1971. The petitioner then filed a special leave petition against the order of the High' Court dated April 17. 1971 and obtained special leave from this Court. On April 18, 1972, the High-Court passed an interim order staying the operation of the impugned order. On June 30, 1972 the appellant was granted permission to file fresh writ petitions in the court. On July 31, 1972 a notice was issued by the State to show cause why the sales should not be treated to have become sale in course of Inter State trade or Commerce. The respondent filed a counter affidavit stating that the HighCourt had no jurisdiction to entertain the writ applications and that the appellant had no authority to file any fresh writ application. On August 3, 1972 this Court passed an ad interim order restraining the State from proceeding with the hearing of the writ application pending in the Court. The writ petition was dismissed by this Court on April 18. 1971 on the ground that the petitioner had not filed a fresh petition in respect of the same matter and that he could file a review application before this court within three months from the date of the judgment. On September 30, 1973, the respondent filed an additional affidavit stating therein that the writ petitioners were not parties to the writ proceedings pending in this Court and that they had no power to file the fresh writ applications. The learned counsel for the appellant submitted that the impugned orders are liable to be set aside on the basis of a judgment of this Court dated March 28 1971. He also contended that the respondent was entitled to withdraw his writ petition and to take out a review proceeding in respect thereof. On behalf of the State it was contended that as the High Courts have no jurisdiction, the question whether the appellant has any authority to challenge the validity or the legality of the orders passed by the authorities does not arise at all. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The power under section 21 of the General Clauses Act is a discretionary power and the Court cannot be said to have exercised it illegally. [557 C] 2. The question whether a writ application should be entertained in respect o the same matters or not has to be decided by this court only on the facts of a case. If the High courts have no power under Article 226 of the Constitution, they can exercise their jurisdiction to issue prerogative writs for enforcement of fundamental rights and if they are satisfied that the petition is maintainable, it would be open to them to do so. [506 D] 3. The Court has no jurisdiction in such matters. It cannot entertain a writ applications or review petitions without exhausting the remedies available under the Act. [504 E] 4.

The appellant was tried by the Additional Sessions Judge, Ahmedabad for the offence of murder. The prosecution case was that on 27 December, 1967 at about 6 p.m. accused No. 2 and Dinkar were found in possession of silver articles.
