On 27 December 1967 at 6 a.m., accused No 1 was arrested and he was produced before the Magistrate. Accused No. 3 was arrested on 28 December, 1968. The appellant was arrested by the police on 29 December, 1969. He was sent to the Chemical Analyser's Laboratory for analysis. The report of the chemical analyser showed that the articles in question were found to be of silver and that the accused No 2 and 3 were guilty of the offence. On 28 December 1967 the appellant was produced by the prosecution before the Judicial Magistrate, First Class, Ahmedabad. The Judicial Magistrate after considering the evidence held that there was sufficient corroboration of the evidence of Dinkar and accused No 4 and 5 and that they were guilty. The Sessions Judge also found that there were no circumstances to connect accused No 3 with the murder. On appeal by the appellant, the High Court set aside the order of conviction and sentence passed against him. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The evidence of the two witnesses is not sufficient to connect the accused with the crime. The fact that the appellant had a silver article in his possession was proved by the evidence on record. [775 H] 2. The High Court rightly held that the prosecution case could not be relied upon as it was found that the chain of circumstances was complete and there was no infirmity in the evidence adduced by the defence. [750 A] 3. The question whether there was any infirmity in evidence or not is a mixed question of fact and law. It cannot be decided on mere appreciation of evidence. There must be some other evidence to connect an accused with murder. [751 B] 4. The circumstances relied upon by the High court are not sufficient for holding that there is no infirmity. [751 D] 5. The case of the prosecution was that the silver articles were given by accused No, 2 and accused Nos. 3 and 4 to the deceased. The articles in the gunny bag which he had kept in his godown were found with the gold articles. The accused No., 2 and the deceased were found dead. [761 D G] 6. The circumstance that there are no circumstances connecting him with murder is not a sufficient ground for holding him guilty of an offence, In view of the fact that there has been substantial compliance with the provisions of Section 100 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, it cannot be said that the High Courts below have committed any error in convicting accused No,. 2 and 5. [754 D] 7. The appeal is accordingly dismissed.

The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the Act and the Rules. The appellant was a member of the Town Planning Scheme. He had been allotted plots on the basis of the final scheme prepared by the Town planning Officer. On the basis that the scheme was sanctioned, he made an application to the Town Development Officer for sanction of the scheme. The Town Planning Officer rejected the application and directed the appellant to pay the amount of compensation as per the final Scheme. The respondent filed a revision petition before the High court which allowed the same by order dated April 30, 1976. On further appeal to this Court it was held that the Act does not provide for a principle of compensation and that the provisions of section 65 (1) (f) were applicable to the scheme framed under the Act. It was further held that in view of the fact that the Town Plan prepared by Town Planning officer was approved by the Government, the appellant could not claim compensation from the local authority or from any person benefited or partly from the Local Authority and partly from such person as the Town development Officer was entitled to obtain compensation from him under section 66 (1)(f). It was held by this Court that the High Courts were right in holding that the decision of the District Planning Officer determining the amount payable to the owner of a plot on the date of declaration of intention to make a scheme as provided in section 64 (1), was not appealable. The question whether the Town and Country Planning Scheme prepared by a Town Planning Authority is an Act or a rule framed under Article 309 of the Constitution was considered by this court in [State of U.P. vs Ram Chandra] , referred to above. In that case, the Town Planner had approved the scheme and the appellant filed an application for sanction before the Town plan officer. The High Court held that since the Town Improvement Officer had not determined the amount as required under section 65(1) of the act, he was entitled only to get compensation from a local authority. Allowing the appeal by special leave, HELD: 1. Section 65 (2) of Act No. 67 of 1976 is applicable to cases where the Town or Country Planning Authority has made an order determining the compensation payable to a person under section 64(1). [775 H] 2. The provisions of sections 65(2), 66 and 69 are not applicable to a case where the scheme prepared is approved by Government. Section 67 provides for a scheme which is an act or a Rule framed under article 309 of Constitution. [776 G] 3. In view of section 64, the High courts were right. The decision of this court was affirmed by this appeal. [750 A] 4. The scheme framed by the appellant was not an Act and it was not a rule made under Article 310 of the constitution. [751 H] 5. Section 66 (2)(f) is applicable only to cases in which the Towns Planning Authority makes an order as provided therein. [751 G] 6. The provision of section 67(2) is not applicable in a case when the scheme is approved under section 63. [764 D] 7. The Act does provide for compensation payable by a local or other authority to the person interested and that is the position in law. [754 H] 8. Section 64 (2), 65 (3) and 69(1)(e) are not attracted to cases of acquisition under section 71. [752 G] 9. The object of the provisions contained in sections 65 (4), 66 (5) and 70 is to provide for an appeal against the decision on a scheme prepared under section 67. [758 H] 10. Section 69(2)(e), does not apply to cases which are covered by section 64. [759 A] 11.

The appellant, the father of the appellant, executed a will on July 1, 1956, in favour of his brother Seetharama. The testator died without making any selection and he was nominated by the testator to make the selection. On the death of Seetharaman, the appellant filed a suit for partition claiming that the properties were devised to the daughters of the deceased. The trial court held that the will was not valid and that the appellant was entitled to select the house himself and to allot the same to his brother. The High Court on appeal by special leave reversed the decree of the trial court and dismissed the suit. In this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the testator intended to select a house for the daughters and that he intended to make selection in respect of the houses which he wanted to select. It was further submitted that the words used in the will were not such as would lead to the inference that the intention of the testator was to select and give the land to the two daughters. Held, that the language of the will is clear and unambiguous and it is not possible to read the words from which it can be inferred that the Will was intended to be a gift to the daughter. The words used are plain and simple. The intention of a testator intended that each daughter should select the land in question to the one who wanted to make a selection, but the other son must have been nominated by him to make such selection. The language of s. 89 is clear enough and it cannot be held that there was no express words in the document from which the intention was to appoint the daughters. The will was intended only to select persons who were entitled to be given the land devised to them taking into account the good and bad quality of the land. The construction put by the High Court is clearly erroneous. The deed was not a valid one. The appellant had no authority to select any land for the purpose of selection.

The respondents filed a suit for partition of the properties in dispute on the ground that they were co-sharers in the land in question. The appellant was the co-sharer in the property and she was entitled to be in possession thereof. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the plaintiff was not entitled to get any share out of the produce and, therefore, the plaintiff's right to get a share out from the joint family properties was not affected by the consolidation operations. The respondents filed an appeal before the District Judge which was allowed by the Additional District Judge on the finding that the appellant had failed to prove that she was ousted from possession of the property in dispute. The High Court held that the trial court was right in holding that there was no evidence on the record to show that any fraud was committed on her by giving her an assurance that her share would be properly looked after by them and on this basis, decree for partition was passed. In second appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court erred in law in holding the respondents to be co-owners in the properties and that the finding of fact recorded by the District judge was perverse. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The findings recorded by both the courts below are correct. [557D] 2. The question whether a person is excluded from possession or not was a mixed question of law and facts and it was not open to the High court to interfere with the finding on that ground. [506F] 3. The finding of the District Court that there were no evidence to show as to which of the defendants was entitled in any manner to get share out is not correct. It is true that the findings recorded are perverse and do not suffer from any infirmity. But, it is also true that in second appeal the High Courts have reversed concurrent findings of fact on the basis of the evidence adduced by the parties. [504F] 4. The first question whether the plaintiff had given her an undertaking to give her share out or not is a mixed issue of lawand fact and the judgment of the High C Court is perverse. [54E] 5. The second question whether there was any fraud on the consolidation authorities was a pure question of fact. It was not necessary for the appellant to prove by evidence that she had given an assurance to the plaintiff that her claim would be summarily rejected. [55F] 6. The judgment of both the Courts below are perverse. The courts below were right in law and on facts in second appeals. [56G] 7. The third question whether any fraud has been committed on the Consolidation authorities was not a mixed one of law or fact and it could be proved only by evidence. [57F] 8. The concurrent findings recorded against the appellant are based on no evidence. The appeal is accordingly allowed, the judgment and decree passed by the High. Court are set aside and the suit filed by the plaintiff is dismissed.

The petitioner was appointed as Deputy Prime Minister of India in the year 1962. He was elected to the Legislative Assembly from the State of Haryana on the basis of a resolution passed by the House of People, which was adopted by the President of India. The petitioner was elected as a member of the Legislative Council of the State. On the basis that he was elected, Respondent No. 1 filed an election petition before the High Court of Punjab and Haryana challenging the appointment of Respondent No 1 as Deputy Chief Minister of Haryana contending that the petitioner had been duly elected as Deputy Speaker of the Assembly from a constituency in the State where he was functioning as the Chief Minister. The High Court held that the petition was not maintainable since it was filed by the petitioner himself, and dismissed the writ petition. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The petitioner is entitled to succeed on the ground of non-compliance with the provisions of Article 173 read with Form VII A. [675 H] 1.2 The petitioner has not been able to show that he had been elected as the Deputy Prime Ministers of Haryana. He has also not been shown to be a member in the Council of Minis tions, nor is there any evidence on record to show whether he was a member or not. [775 H; 776 B] 1:2 The petition was filed after the expiry of the period prescribed under Article 173 and the petitioner was required to file an affidavit stating that he has been duly nominated as a candidate. [750 D] 1.:3 2.1 There is no merit in this appeal and it is dismissed.

The appellant, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling cotton yarn. The appellant was an employee of the respondent. On 1st November, 1948, the appellant issued a notice to the respondent calling upon him to show cause why his services should not be terminated on the ground that he had been dismissed for misconduct by the management. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notice and also praying for a direction to the appellant to reinstate him with effect from 1st December, 1948. The High Court held that the notice was illegal and quashed the order of termination. On appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The Labour Appellate Tribunal has jurisdiction to decide whether an industrial dispute is or is not a 'strike' within the meaning of section 2(q). [775 H] (2) The Industrial Tribunal has no power to decide any question of law in respect of the construction of the section. It is open to the parties to raise this contention before the Labour Appellate Court and it is for the Labour Court to decide that question. [776 B] (3) The appellant had not given a notice under section 10(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, nor was he heard by the Industrial Tribunal in the matter. The Industrial Tribunals have no power or jurisdiction to determine any question which is an illegal strike and it cannot be said that they have exercised their powers under section 9A of the Act. [750 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1123 of 1966. Appeal from the judgment and order dated April 8, 1966 of the Madras High Court in Writ Petition No. 1224 of 1965. S. T. Desai, R. Ganapathy Iyer and B. Sen, for the appellant. M. C. Setalvad, Attorney-General of India, K. N. Rajagopal Sastri and P. D. Menon, for respondent No. 1. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Shah, J. The question involved in this appeal is whether the Labour Courts have jurisdiction to hear the case on the point decided by the Labour appellate Tribunal. The facts leading up to this appeal are as follows: The appellant, an employee, was employed in the respondent's factory at the time of his dismissal from service and he had given a written notice under [section 10(1)] of the [Industrial Disputes Act] that he should be deemed to have been dismissed from service. On January 1, 1961, the respondent filed an application before the Industrial Court for permission to withdraw the appeal. The said application was allowed by the Tribunal on the finding that the appellant had failed to prove that he was entitled to reinstatement with effect form 1st January, 1948 and that the order passed by the respondent was illegal. On this finding, the Labour Officer held that there was no evidence to show that the respondent had been guilty of misconduct. The Labour Court found that the charge against the respondent did not fall within the definition of the word "strike" as given in section 2 (q) of Industrial Disputes. The Tribunal also held that it was open to a workman to withdraw his appeal and that he could not be heard to say that he would not be entitled to any relief under the Act on the basis of the said finding. On these findings, the Industrial court dismissed the application filed by the appellant for permission under section 11(2)(b) of The Industrial Disputes (Amendment) Act, 1961. The appeal was allowed and the order dismissing the application was set aside. The matter was carried to this court by special leave. HELD: The Labour Courts are not competent to decide on the question whether an employee is entitled to be reinstated with effect on the date of his reinstatement or not.

The appellant was a film producer. He filed a writ petition in the High Court of Madras challenging the validity of the notification issued under section 5A of the Act and also the order passed by the Central Board of Film Censors, acting within their jurisdiction. The High Court quashed the notification on the ground that it was not based on any evidence or material. It held that the film produced by the appellant was obscene and therefore prohibited by section 79 of the Code. The appellant filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the notification. The learned Single Judge dismissed the petition holding that the certificate issued under the Act is valid and the certificate granted thereunder is not conclusive. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) Section 79 of I.P.C. confers power on the Board to make a declaration in respect of any film as suitable for public exhibition. The notification issued by the Government under section 4(2) of the said Act does not confer any right on the producer or any other person to shower of prosecutions for an offence under section 292 I. P.C., nor is it based on evidence or materials which are sufficient to prove that the certification was granted under section 3A of that Act. [566 F] (2) The notification dated April 1, 1962 issued under sections 5A and 79 of that Code does not create any right in favour of the producer to showers of films as suitable to be public exhibition by means of a declaration under section 6(1). The notification is not based upon any evidence. [506 G] (3) Section 4(1)(a) of Act provides for certification of films. It is not necessary that the person who has been granted certificate should have made an application and obtained it. If, as here, the certificate was issued by a competent authority under section 7 of the Central Act, the producer and connected agencies do enter the statutory harbour and are protected because section 79 does not empower the producer, or any person to make an offer for exhibition of films, as the case may be. [666 D] (4) The certificate granted under the said section is a conclusive evidence that the certificates were granted under sections 4(3)(a), 4(4)(b) and 4(5). [506 F] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 15 of 1986. From the Judgment and Order dated 16.12.1986 of the Madras High Court in C.R.P.(C) No. 12 of 1986 and C.M.A. Nos.

The petitioner, a High Court Judge, was appointed as the Chief Justice of the Madras High Court. He held the office of the Chief justice of the High Court and was paid a salary of Rs. 1,000 per month. The Chief Justice issued a notification under section 4(1) of the Act declaring that the petitioner's appointment as the President of the Calcutta High Court was illegal. The petitioner filed an application before the High court for a writ in the nature of mandamus directing the State Government to appoint him as the Judge of the Delhi High Court, and also prayed for a direction to the State of Madras to appoint a person who is not qualified to be appointed as Judge of that High Court or to direct the Chief Justices of the other High Courts to act as Judges of that court. The petition was dismissed by the High. Court on the ground that it was barred by limitation. The appellant filed an appeal against the order of the learned Single Judge before this Court, which was allowed by a Division Bench of the said Court by its judgment dated April 14, 1981. The matter was carried to this Court by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The High Court has no jurisdiction to issue a writ of mandamus or any other appropriate writ in respect of a public office. [775 H] 1.2 The power under section 5(3) of Act is not absolute and is subject to the limitations imposed by Article 14 of the Constitution. It is not open to the Government Pleader to plead that the appointment of a person as Judge was illegal or contrary to law. [750 A] 1:1. Under section 5 (3), the Government may appoint a Judge of any High Court to be a Judge thereof, and in addition to the power conferred by this Code on the Chief Judge of a High court, the Chief Secretary shall have the same powers as are vested in a civil court under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. [751 B] 1 The power conferred on the Government pleader under section 6(1)(b) is absolute and subject to any limitations imposed thereby, the office must be held to be an office within the scope of a quo warranto proceeding. [753 D] 2.1 There is no merit in the contention that the power under Article 14 is not exercised by the Government Pleaders or Courts subordinate to it. The power to appoint the Judge is absolute. It cannot be exercised by any other person. [764 G] 1 Whether a person is qualified to hold office as Judge, he must be holding an office of profit under the State and having regard to the various functions and duties to be performed by him, the Office must be a public officer within the meaning of section 5. [754 D] 1 2 The power of appointment conferred on a High Courts under section 7(1), is absolute in terms and subject only to any limitation imposed thereby. [752 B] 3.2 In the instant case, as the petitioner was appointed by the State, he was paid salary of an amount equal to the salary of the Government Advocate for the period from 1st April, 1966 to 31st March, 1967. The order of appointment is illegal and contrary to the provisions of section 6 (1) (b).

The Bank of India, the Mills of which the shares were offered by the Bank of Indian, was a shareholder in the Mills. The Mills had a market value of Rs. 100 for acquiring the new issue of the Bank. The Mill had a stock of about 50,000 shares of the Mills and the Mills had an offer to purchase the said shares. The mills had a share of about Rs. 1,50,000 in the Bank and the Mill had an interest in the said amount. The mill was assessed to income tax by the Income Tax Officer on the basis that the value of the right to apply for the shares had a monetary value of more than Rs. 50,00,000. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax Officer and dismissed the appeals filed by the Mills against the orders passed by the Incometax Officer. The Tribunal held that the distribution of the rights to the Bank was not a distribution of dividend within the meaning of section 2(6A) of the Act and accordingly set aside the order passed by him. On further appeal, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court was in error in holding that the said distribution amounted to distribution of dividends within the definition of section2(6C). The Tribunal rejected the contention. It held that since the shares offered by Bank of the mills were not the value payable for acquiring a new issue, the question of distribution of such right did not arise and accordingly it was set aside. On behalf of Mills, it is contended that the decision of the High court in the case of [Commissioner of Income Tax vs. The Bharat Heavy Electricals Ltd.] , referred to above, does not lay down correct law. It was further urged that the Tribunal had erred in holding otherwise. The question whether the distribution amounted for distribution of a dividend within section 2 (6A), was decided by the High Courts on the facts and circumstances of the case. In the result, it must be held that there was no distribution of any dividend within [section 2(06)] of the Indian Income Tax Act.

The appellant was a candidate for the post of Assistant Teacher in Government High School, Palai. He was appointed as an Assistant Teacher on 1.7.1971 and he joined duty on 2.8.1972. The respondent was selected by the Selection Committee for appointment to the post. On the basis of the selection made by the Committee, the appellant was appointed to the said post. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of his appointment as Assistant Teacher. The learned Single Judge dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant had failed to show that he was not entitled to be heard for procuring the presence of the respondent and that the party was unable to produce him on his own under Rule 1A of Order XVI, but he was able to keep his witnesses present when the evidence of the witness was being recorded and that he could not produce him before the Court. The Division Bench held that the order passed by the learned Single judge was in accordance with law and it was not necessary for the appellant to show as to why he should be permitted to examine the witnesses who were called to give evidence under Rule I of Order XVIII, but the respondent did not file any list of witnesses before the Selection committee. The High Court held that there was no infirmity in the order dated 11.8.'1977 passed by learned Single Jude in Writ Petition No. 823/77 and that it was a fit case for interference with the order under appeal. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Rule 1 of Order XVII of the Code of Civil Procedure is not applicable to the facts of the present case. The provisions of Order XIX of the code of Civil procedure are not applicable in the facts and circumstances of the case. [775 H] 1.2 In the instant case, the respondent was appointed by the selection committee as an assistant teacher on 1st July, 1971. He joined duty after obtaining a certificate from the District Education Officer that he had been selected for appointment as an ad hoc Assistant Teacher and was also confirmed in his service. The order of appointment passed by him was not challenged by the appellant before the High court. [750 H] 2.1 There is no infirmity or illegality in the impugned order passed on 11th August, 1977. [751 G] 2:2 In view of the fact that the respondent had failed and kept his witnesses in the Court on the date fixed for recording evidence, it was obligatory on the part of learned Single Judges to have examined the witnesses produced by the respondent. The appeal is accordingly dismissed.

The appellant was appointed as a Head of Institution in the year 1981. He was appointed to the post of Head of an Institution by the Managing Committee of the Institution on April 27, 1981. The appointment of the appellant was approved by the Director of the institution on May 1, 1981 and he was paid salary for that period. On June 30, 1982, the appellant made a representation to the State Government that he should be given appointment as Head of the Institutions in accordance with the provisions of the Act. The State Government rejected his request and directed the Committee of Management to make appointment of appellant on April 28, 1981, but the Committee did not make any appointment. On May 29, 1982 the appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of the State government dated June 30. 1982. The High Court dismissed the writ petition by its judgment and order dated August 14, 1983. The appellant then filed a Writ Petition in this Court which was allowed by the High court on September 5, 1984. The matter was carried to this Court by special leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The appointment made by the Committee was illegal and invalid. [1080D] 1.2 The appointment was not illegal but was only a stop gap arrangement. The order of appointment was passed in contravention of the provisions contained in the Act and the Rules. [1181F] 1:3. The power to make appointments is vested in the State. The Committee of management had no power to appoint any person as Head or teacher of an institution in contravention with the provision of the statute. [1282D] 2.1 There was no power of appointment, nor was there any power of termination of service. The provisions contained under the Act were not complied with by the State and the Committee had no authority to make the appointment. [1385E] 1.:4. The appointments made were illegal and void. [1466F] 2:2. The approval of the Director was necessary for making appointment as per the provisions in the statute and the State could not make appointment without complying with the requirements of the Statute. [1566G] 2.(i) The power of the Committee to make an appointment is vested only in the Government or the Committee, as the case may be, and not in the Director. [1667F] (ii) The appointment is made by way of a stop-gap arrangement. [1768D] (iii) The State government was bound to hear the appellant before making any appointment and it was not open to the Committee or the Institution to make any appointments without complying the provisions relating to the Act, the Rules and the Regulations. [1866F D] 2(i) There is no power in the appointment of a Head or Teacher of an educational institution in accordance With the provisions under the statute to make such appointment. The Government or Committee of a private institution cannot make appointments without following the procedure prescribed by the Act or the Rules or the Regulations and the appointment was made in contravention thereof. [1966F F] 2 (ii)(a) The order passed by the Vice-Chancellor is not an order of termination simpliciter but only an order for recovery of amount paid to the appellant under the provisions mentioned in the order. [2066G D] 3.1. The action taken by the Government and the Director cannot be said to have been done without following any procedure prescribed under the Statute or the rules. [21C] 2] (b) The Vice- Chancellor is bound to act as per law. [22D] 3:2.(i)(a). The power conferred on the State Govt. by Section 11 of the Bihar Act is not a power of control vested in it and the power of removal or termination of services of teachers, officers and employees of an aided institution.

The appellant, a manufacturer of cotton yarn, was assessed to sales tax under the Central Excises and Salt Act, 1944 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') on the ground that it had purchased cotton from its purchasers "in the same way as is being done by the first petitioner. The first petitioner claimed exemption from payment of sales tax on the basis of the purchase price paid by it in respect of cotton fabric manufactured by it. The Assistant Collector of Central Excise, who assessed the appellant's claim, held that the "textile" fabrics was a "cotton fabric" and not for any other kind of fabric. On appeal to the Appellate Tribunal, the Appellate tribunal confirmed the order of the Assistant Collector. In further appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the cotton fabric was an "c Cotton fabric" as defined in Section 2(f) of the Act and, therefore, the "paper fabrics" manufactured by the appellant could not be said to constitute a fabric within the meaning of Section 2 (f). Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The question whether the "Textile" fabric is an "artificial" fabric or not was a question of fact and not a question Of law. [675 H] 2. The expression "textiles" in Section 3(1) of Act means "any other kind or fabric". It does not include any other type of fabric, but it includes only such fabric which is the end product for the Delhi Cloth Mills. [775 G] 3. The word "cool" has been defined in the Act to mean "any kind of cloth." [682 H] 4. The words "totton fabrics" are not used in Section 6 of the Central Excise and Salt (Amendment) Act, 1972. Therefore, the question whether cotton fabric is a textile fabric or an article of cotton fabrics does not fall within the scope of Section 3 of the said Act. [650 D] 5. The High Court was right in holding that the appellant had purchased the cotton from the purchasers " in the same manner as is done by it" and, accordingly, the tax authorities were justified in treating the cotton fabrics manufactured by them as a "paper fabric". [691 H] 6. The decision of the Appellate Assistant Commissioner is correct. [663 G] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1566 of 1972. From the Judgment and Order dated the 10th May, 1971 of the Delhi High Court in S.C.A. No. 814 of 1970. V.M. Tarkunde, K.K. Venugopal, R.B. Datar, P.H. Parekh and M.N. Shroff for the Appellant. A.S. Nambiar, Mrs. Rani Chhabra, Ms. Rani Jethmalani, Ms Urvashi Agnihotri, Ms Indu Malhotra, Ms Anu Mehta, Ms Poonam Suri, Ms V.K Jain, Ms S. Janani, Ms Jayshree Pandey, Ms P. Gupta and Ms. Aparna Srivastava for the Respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by KASLIWAL, J. This appeal is directed against the judgment dated October 10, 1971 passed by the Delhi high Court in its order dated October 15, 1970. The appellant is a manufacturer and has purchased cotton fabrics from the buyers " in this case" and has filed this appeal on November 16, 1971. The facts of the case are that the respondent manufactures cotton fabric under the name of "Textiles" and "Totton fabrics". The question for consideration is whether the appellant was entitled to exemption from sales tax as claimed by it or not. [662 H; 663 A] 2(i) The question which arises in this appeal is whether cotton fabrics is a "trading" fabric. [664 D] 3(ii) The expression 'textiles' has been used in the context of Section 6(1)(b).

The appellant, a workman in the year 1962, was appointed as a clerk in the office of the Assistant Electrical Engineer, Dhanbad. He was transferred to the office at Dhanbad on August 8, 1962. On September 9, 1963, he was transferred from Dhanbad to Dhanbad. On October 10, 1964, he joined the service of the appellant as an Assistant Electrical Inspector. On November 1, 1966, he served in the appellant's office for a period of one year and thereafter, he worked as an assistant Electrical Inspector in the Office of the Chief Engineer, Public Works Department, Government of Bihar. On December 9, 1966 he was promoted to the post of Assistant Electrical Inspectors. On January 10, 1968, he filed a petition before the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order of transfer and also for a direction to the State Government to transfer him from Dhanbad. The High Court held that the transfer was in violation of section 5(7A) of the Act and quashed the order. On appeal by special leave, this Court held: "The question whether the transfer is in contravention of section 6(1)(b) of Bihar Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, or not, has to be decided on the facts of each case. The power vested under section 5 (7A), therefore, vests in the Commissioner of Income Tax and the Central Board of Revenue, which is empowered to make rules for carrying out the purposes of this Act. Section 5(6) of this section provides that the State Govt. may transfer any employee from one office to another without hearing him or representing his views on the question and the reasons for such transfer shall be reduced accordingly. The proviso to sub-section (7) of section 127 provides that where an order of transferring an employee is made by the Commissioner, he shall not be transferred under this section unless he has given a reasonable opportunity of being heard in the matter." In the instant case, the appellant was transferred on October 10 and his transfer was quashed for violation of Section 5 (6) read with Section 127 of the Income Tax Act. The appellant filed a writ petition before this Court challenging the order dated August 8. 1988. This Court held; "The power vested in the State to make rule under section 127 of that Act is not exercised by the State or its officers, but only by the Central Government. It is true that the power vested by section 5 of the Bihar Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946, is exercisable by the appropriate Government and if the appropriate government does not give a reasonable hearing to the assessee in the matters, it has no jurisdiction to refuse to transfer the case. But where an authority subordinate to the Central Govt., exercises powers under section 6 of the said Act, it must be held that such power vested with the Commissioner is exercised by him " The appellant was also directed to file a return and the same was done in accordance with law. In the circumstances, we allow this appeal, set aside the order passed by the High court and restore the writ petition filed by the appellant before the Patna High Court."

The dispute between the appellant and the respondents was as follows:The appellant is a society registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860. The appellant is an association of persons who are members of the said society. The management of the appellant's hotel was taken over by the Government of India on October 7, 1955. On October 8, 1955, the Government issued a notification in exercise of powers conferred by section 10(1) of the Act declaring that the appellant was an industrial dispute within the meaning of the provisions of the [Industrial Disputes Act]. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court of Delhi challenging the validity of the notification. The learned single Judge dismissed the writ petition holding that the notification issued by the State Government under section 10 (1) was not in accordance with law and, therefore, it was not open to the appellant to challenge the said notification. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The notification issued under section10(1), is not in conformity with the provisions contained in the Act as it is not a mere administrative order or an executive order but is in accordance therewith. The notification is not an administrative order and does not comply with the requirements of the statute. The Government must, of course, have sufficient knowledge of the nature of the dispute to be satisfied that it is an industrial matter within the purview of the Central Act. (ii) The appellant was a society which was registered under section 7 of the Societies' Registration Act. The order passed by the Commissioner of Labour was not an executive or administrative order but was an administrative one and, as such, it could not be challenged in any court. [775 H] (iii) The order dated October 8 1955, is a quasi judicial order and the appellant cannot challenge the same on the ground that it relates to retrenchment or reinstatement. The question whether the order passed under section 11(1)(b) of Act is an administrative or executive order does not arise in this case because the Government has no sufficient knowledge about the nature and the dispute between employer and the workmen before the tribunal. [750 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 879 of 1966. Appeal by special Leave from the Judgment and Order dated the 9th July, 1966 of the Delhi High Court in C.W.P. No. 1123 of 1965. S. K. Sinha and P. C. Agarwala, for the appellant. M. C., Sharma and R. N. Sachthey, for respondent No. 1. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Sikri, J. This appeal is directed against a judgment dated September 9, 1966 passed by a Division Bench of the High court of Delhi in Civil Writ Petition No. 1023 of 1964. The facts leading to this appeal are as follows. The petitioner is an Association registered under Section 7 of Act No. 16 of 1961. It has its office at New Delhi. The dispute between it and the management was referred by the Central Government for adjudication to the Industrial Tribunal, Delhi. On November 8, 1957, the appellant filed an application before the Labour Court, Delhi under section 33C(2) of that Act praying that the order dated December 10, 1955 be quashed. The said application was dismissed on October 9, 1956. Thereafter, the management filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution in the High' Court of Punjab and Haryana at Chandigarh for quashing the said order. On September 8, 1966, the High-Court passed an interim order staying the operation of the order of reference dated December 8, 1956, which was subsequently vacated on October 10, 1956 by the Labour court. The High Court quashed the said interim order. It is against this judgment that the present appeal has been filed. The main contention of Mr. Sharma is that the impugned notification issued in exerciseof powers conferred under section 3(1).

The appellant, a manufacturer of motor vehicles, filed a declaration under Section 14 of the Central Excise Act, that they are parts of the engines and are parts thereof. The appellant claimed exemption from payment of duty on the ground that the bushes, which have been imported by them, are parts and parts of their engines. The Assistant Collector of Customs held that the trees in question were parts of internal combustion piston engines, as mentioned under Heading No. 84.06. He also held that they were parts and accessories of the engine and not parts thereof, and accordingly rejected the claim for exemption. On appeal to the Tribunal, the appellant contended that the goods in question are parts or accessories of a motor vehicle and, therefore, the benefit of the Notification should be extended to them. The Tribunal held that "the parts of engines which have already been imported, are part of internal fire pistons, as described under Heading 84.6". The Tribunal also held, relying on the decision of the Bombay High Court in the case of [Commissioner of Customs vs. M/s. K.K. Modi & Co.] ; that "it is not necessary to decide whether the parts of a particular engine or engines are parts, of internal or combustion pistson engines". The appellant contended before the Tribunal that the words "part" and "parts" in the Notification were used in order to avail of the exemption under the Notification. The High Court held that these words were not relevant for the purpose of determining whether the bushes imported by the appellant, are components or accessories thereof. In view of this finding, the appeal was allowed and the order passed by the Tribunal was set aside. Hence this appeal.

The plaintiffs filed a suit for partition of the properties in respect of which the defendants claimed to be the owners. The trial court held that the plaintiffs were entitled to 1/3rd share in the suit properties and accordingly decreed the suit. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decree and dismissed the suit holding that the defendants had not acquired any right by adverse possession against Fathima Bee. In further appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High court was wrong in holding that there was no question of any knowledge to Fathina Bee as well as the plaintiffs. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding the suit for a partition of properties in 1957 and the plaintiffs had not claimed any share in those properties. [675 H] 2. The defendants were entitled only to 1⁄2 share in their respective shares in the said suit. [775 B] 3.1 The question whether the plaintiffs are entitled to any share or not was a mixed question of law and fact and it was not open to the High Curt to interfere with the findings of fact recorded by the trial court on the basis of the evidence adduced before it. [750 D] 3:2. The question as to whether the defendants were in possession of the suit property or not is a mixed issue of law, fact and law and the same cannot be decided in a regular civil proceeding. [751 G] 3(i) The High court has rightly held that there is no question about any knowledge of Fathim Bee as such the plaintiffs could have filed a separate suit for possession of their respective share in respect to the suit lands. [751 D] (ii) The defendants had failed to prove that they were entitled under Muslim Law to 1 1⁄4 share in management or possession of any share therein. [762 G] (iii) The plaintiffs could not have claimed any right in the properties which were allotted to them by the High Courts in India. [754 A] 3.(i) There is no merit in the contention that the question as regards the defendants being entitled to a share in profits of the Dargah does not arise at all. [752 B] (iv) The finding recorded by both the courts below that the right of Fatima Bee was specifically denied on any particular occurence, cannot be sustained. [758 G] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 879 of 1987. From the Judgment and Order dated 11.8.1987 of the HighCourt of Madras in C.M.A. Nos. 912-913 of 1986. V.S. Desai, S.K. Bagga and R.N. Poddar for the Appellants. M. Veerappa, A.K Gupta, B.D. Sharma, K.R. Nambiar, P.H. Parekh, Ms. A. Subhashini, Mrs. Arundhati Roy, Ms V.Kowli, Sreedharan, M.V. Goswami, R.B. Singh, M/s. Vam Organic and Co., and M/S. Vaman & Co. for the Respondents. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by K. RAMASWAMY, J. These appeals by special leave are directed against the judgment dated 11th August 1987 passed by the Division Bench of the Madras High Court in CMA No. 913 of 1987 filed by the plaintiffs in the above suit. The facts leading to these appeals are as follows: The plaintiffs were members of the joint Hindu family and they had been living separately for a period of five years from the date of their marriage. They were entitled for 1/4th share each in the joint properties. The plaintiffs claimed that they have become owners of the said properties by adverse title.

The appellant was a member of the Indian Railway Establishment. He was appointed as a clerk in the office of the 1st respondent on January 10, 1957. On December 31, 1958, he was transferred to the office at Bombay. On March 30, 1959, he joined the service of the appellant. On April 28, 1960, he resumed his duties at Bombay and was posted at Bombay from that date. On May 29, 1961, he filed a suit for recovery of house rent allowance from the 1 st respondent in respect of the house rent paid by him to the appellant on January 30, 1960. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the house-rent allowance was not payable under the terms of the contract between the parties and that the appellant was entitled to the house rate allowance. On appeal, the High Court held that the House Rent Allowance was not a part of the terms and conditions of the agreement between the appellant and the 1St respondent and that it was not an allowance in respect thereof. The High Court further held that in view of the provisions of section 23 of the Act, the house allowance could not be claimed by the 1rd respondent under the provisions contained in sections 7 and 11 of the said Act. On behalf of the appellants, Mr. S. T. Desai, learned counsel for the 1nd respondent submitted that the High court was wrong in holding that house rent allowances were not payable to the 1th respondent under section 23(1) of the Contract between the employer and the employee. The contention on behalf of both the parties was that the provisions in sections 6 and 11 were applicable to the case and that section 23 did not apply to the facts of the present case. It was further submitted that section 7 of the Payment of House Rent Act, 1947, was a complete code in itself and that as soon as he was offered Government quarters for his accommodation, he ceased to be entitled to house rent Allowance. The question whether house rent is payable under section 3 or 4 of the [Payment of House-rent Act, 1952] did not arise for consideration before the High Courts. It is true that section 11 of this Act does not apply in the facts and circumstances of the case but it is equally clear that section 6 of the payment of house-tax allowance was applicable to cases where house rent was payable under a contract between employer and employee. In our opinion, the contention on the basis of section 7 cannot be accepted. The House Rent Allowances Act, 1948, was enacted by Parliament in exercise of its powers under Article 246 read with Entry 54 of List I of Schedule VII of the Constitution. Section 23 of that Act provides for payment of House rent allowance to every employee who is entitled to a house-rate allowance. It does not provide for any exemption from payment of such house-rates. The provisions contained therein are applicable only in cases where the house is not payable by the employer under the contract or the agreement. In the present appeal, it is clear that the question whether the house was not paid under section 7 or 11 of Act did not really arise for determination before the Court. It may be noted that section 3(1)(a) of this act does not confer any absolute right in the employee to the House rent Allowance as a matter of law. The appellant's contention that section 4 of this enactment does not create any absolute rights in the employees is, therefore, without substance. Section 7 of this legislation provides for an exemption from the payment by the employee of house rate allowances. It reads: "7. Exemptions.- (1) Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law, no deduction shall be made under section 8 or section 9 of this Chapter."

The petitioner, who was detained by the order of detention dated March 3, 1980, under section 3(1) of the Conservation of Foreign Exchange and Prevention of Smuggling Activities Act, 1974, (hereinafter referred to as "the COFEPOSA") read with section 8 of the Preventive Detention Act, 1950, was ordered to be detained in pursuance of the order passed by the Central Government on March 31, 1980. The grounds of detention served on the petitioner were that he was a member of the Indian National Congress Party and was a Member of the Legislative Assembly of the State of Gujarat. He had been arrested on April 3,1980 and was released on bail on May 4, 1980 in connection with the case registered against him under section 8(1)(b) of COFEPOSA. The petitioner filed an application for release of his detention on March 30, 1980 before the Central government praying that he should be released on the ground that the grounds of his arrest were not supplied to him and that he had been detained in contravention of the provisions of the COFEPOSA. On April 3. 1980, the Central Govt. rejected the petitioner's request for release on the grounds that the detention was illegal as it was not made by a person who was not a member or a Member or a member thereof. The order passed on March 3.1980 was confirmed by the State Government and the same was communicated to the detenu. On May 4. 1980 the petitioner filed a writ petition in this Court challenging the validity of the detention. This Court dismissed the petition holding that the order dated March 31. 1980 was not an order made by the detaining authority under section 9(1), sub-section (2) of section 8 and that the said order was passed without giving any opportunity to the petitioner to make a representation against his detention. The Court held that the provisions contained in section 9 of the Act were mandatory and that it was open to the State Govt. to withhold the supply of the grounds on which the detention had been made. In the present case, the petitioner challenged the validity and the legality of the orders passed by both the authorities. Allowing the writ petition, HELD: 1. The provisions contained under section 11(1A) of Conservation of foreign exchange and Preventionof Smuggled Exchange Act, 1973 are mandatory in character and they cannot be read into the provisions as they are not mandatory in nature. [557 C] 2. The power to withhold supply of documents is a discretionary power vested in the detaining authorities. It is not necessary that the detenu should have been given an opportunity to make representation against the detention before he can make a full and effective representation at the earliest. [506 D] 3. The right to be released under section 10(2) is a valuable right which is guaranteed by Article 21 of the Constitution. The obligation to supply the grounds upon which the order is made does not extend to the making of any such order. It only means that the State has the right to withhold or withheld the supply. [504 D] 4. The failure to supply copies of the basic materials and documents to the detenus within the period prescribed by section 11 (1A), sub section (2), is fatal to the detention, and it cannot be said that the detaining Authority was not given an adequate opportunity to meet the case of the detenu before he could make a valid order of release. [457 D] 5. The question whether the grounds are required to be supplied to the person concerned does not depend upon the nature of the documents which were in his possession and which were relied upon by the authorities, but on the basis of the record of the case, it cannot also be said to be a valid ground for detention. [498 E] 6. The detenu was entitled to make an effective representation against such detention. If he made a full representation, the detainingauthority should have given him an opportunity of making a representation and if he had not done so, he could have made a representation.

The appellant was convicted by the trial Court of an offence under section 419 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one year. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence passed against the appellant. On appeal by the State, the High Court set aside the order of acquittal passed by the Sessions Judge and remanded the case back to it for decision on merits. The State filed an application before the High court under section 439(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure for a direction that the appellant should be heard on the merits. On the basis of the judgment of the High, Court, the appellant was acquitted by the Additional Sessions Judge. The appellant filed an appeal to this Court and contended that the High Courts were wrong in holding that the joint appeal by State against several accused persons was not maintainable. Allowing the appeal, HELD: (1) The High Courts have jurisdiction to hear the appeal on merits and it is not open to a joint appeal to admit it only on a question of sentence and that such a restricted order of admission being invalid, the trial court should be held to have been valid. [775 H] (2) In the instant case, the Sessions Court hearing an appeal filed by the appellant against several persons convicted at one trial was competent to hear it. The Sessions Judge hearing an application for revision filed by some of the accused persons did not have the advantage of hearing them on merits but only on the question of conviction and sentenced them to undergo imprisonment for life. [750 H] JUDGMENT: CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Criminal Appeal No. 9 of 1972. Appeal by special leave from the judgment and order dated April 10, 1973 of the Gujarat High Court in Criminal Revision Application No. 8 of 1973. S.V. Gupte, R.N. Sachthey and B.D. Sharma for the appellant (in Cr. A. Nos. 9/72 and 9/73). V.S. Desai, S.K. Mehta and P.H. Parekh for the respondent (In both the appeals). The Judgment of the Court was delivered by RAY, C.J.-This appeal by special Leave is directed against the judgment dated April 11, 1973 passed by a Division Bench of the Bombay High Court allowing the criminal revision application filed by one of the appellants and setting aside the conviction of the appellant under section 420 of the Penal Code. The facts giving rise to this appeal are as follows: On March 12, 1968, the Deputy Superintendent of Police, Ahmedabad City, received information that the accused were involved in a criminal case at the instance of the complainant. He was also informed by the complainant that the said accused had been acquitted by a competent court and that he was required to be tried on the basis thereof. The complainant filed an affidavit before the trial Magistrate stating that the complainant was not interested in prosecuting the accused. On March 13, 1968 the Deputy Inspector of Police lodged a complaint against the accused for offences under section 467 and 468 of the penal Code. On that complaint, the learned Magistrate took cognizance of the offence on the same day. The case was then committed to the Court of Sessions. The learned Additional Sessions judge framed charges against the appellants under sections 419 and 420 of Indian Penal code. The charge against the said appellant was that he had been convicted by a court of competent jurisdiction. The accused pleaded not guilty to the charge and claimed to be heard. The trial Magistrate, however, acquitted the accused on the ground that the complaint filed by him was not in accordance with law. On an appeal preferred by the accused, the Additional Session Judge set aside his conviction and directed the case to be sent back to the Sessions court for disposal according to law. The appellants then filed a revision application before a Division bench of the Calcutta High Court which allowed the revision application and remanded it for fresh decision on the point of sentence. On remand, the case was transferred to the Additional District Judge, Ahmedabad for trial.

The assessee, a resident of the United Kingdom, was assessed to income tax under the 1918 Act. The Income Tax Officer assessed the income of the foreign firm for the assessment year 1949-50 and assessed the same to income-tax in respect of the income from house properties owned by the foreign company. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax officer. In further appeal, it was held that the assessee was entitled to exemption under section 25(3) of the 1922 Act with regard to interest on securities as well. The High Court held that in view of the provisions of the 1918 (Act) and the 1922 (Amendment) Act, the assessee is not entitled to relief under section25(3). It was further held by this Court that the income- profits and gains of business, profession or vocation were not taxable under the Income tax Act. In the result, the High Court allowed the appeal filed by the assessee and dismissed the writ petition filed by him. The Revenue is in appeal against the judgment of the High court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The provisions of section 25 (3) are general. It is well settled that the exemption under the said section is a general one and the conditions of the applicability of the exemption are general; but the exemption is not general. [652 B] 2. Section 25(1)(a) of 1922 Act provides for exemption from tax in respect to income on which the tax was payable by an assessee. The expression "income" has been defined in section 2 (b) of that Act as meaning "any income, profits or gains accruing or arising to a person". [653 C] 3. Section 24(3)(a), (b), (c) and (d) are special provisions relating to the computation of income under the 1922-Act. The object of the 1961-Act is to provide for the computation and recovery of income tax in cases where the assessee has not claimed exemption under [section 25(2)] of the Act. [650 D] 4. Section 26(3), (4) and 28 of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922 are special provision relating to computation of total income. The section provides for the payment of interest on such securities as is mentioned in section 24(1). [654 G] 5. In order that the provisions contained in section 25 may be applied to the case it must be shown that the amount of tax payable by the appellant under the Act was not a part of the total income of his previous year. The assessee was not entitled, therefore, to claim exemption under Section 25 (1) of [section 24(2)]. [655 B] 6. The words "income", "profits and gains" have been defined by section 2(b) in the General Clauses Act, 1897. [613 D] 7. The language of section 26(4) is clear and unambiguous. It provides that where any income, loss or other income has accrued or arisen to a foreign company, then, notwithstanding anything contained in the Indian Incometax Act, 1961, the provisions relating thereto shall apply to such income. [625 C] 8. Section 27 of the General Clause Act provides that if any income is chargeable under the head "Profits and gains", the assessee shall be entitled to claim deduction under section 80-O of the said Act. Section 28(3A) provides that in case where any amount has been paid by an Indian company, the Income-tax Officer may, if he is satisfied that the sum payable by such Indian company under the provisions referred to in sub-section (1), shall be allowed as a deduction under [ section 80G] of the Incometax Act 1961. [643 D] 9.

The appellant, a contractor, was appointed by the Government of India in the year 1962 as a contractor for supply of bricks to the buyers under the contract. The appellant entered into an agreement with the State Government on April 1, 1963 for supply and manufacture of bricks. On or about May 31, 1964, the appellant supplied the bricks to its customers under the contracts. The contract was executed by the appellant in favour of the State of U.P. The contracts were executed between the parties on April 30, 1964. The agreement provided that the contractor would be responsible for the payment of the price of the bricks at the rates mentioned therein and that the said payments would be made within a period of six months from the date of execution of the contract and in case the contractor fails to make the payment within the stipulated period, the contract shall stand terminated. The State Government issued a notification on April 27, 1964 under s. 6(1) of the U. P. Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') for the purpose of determining the rates of the goods sold by the contractor. On May 31. 1965, the State government issued a Notification under s, 6(2) of that Act in respect of the supplies made to the buyer under the said contract. On June 30, 1966, the Government issued another notification under s..6(1). The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the said notification on the ground that it was not within the competence of the Government to make a declaration under s 6(3) of Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The notification issued by the State in respect to the supplies of bricks was valid and binding on the appellant. The notification dated April 27 1964 was not a contract of sale but only a works contract. [775 H] (ii) The High court was right in answering the question in favour o the assessee. The decision of the purchaser in Chandra Bhan Gosain`s case (supra) was not applicable to the facts of the present case. The fact that the appellant had inspected and approved, the goods after the date specified in the notification did not make him liable for payment of price at the rate mentioned therein. [750 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1579 of 1966. Appeal by special Leave from the judgment and order dated the 9th July, 1964 of the Allahabad High Court in Special Appeal No.. 10 of 1965. S. T. Desai, S. K. Bagga and R. N. Sachthey, for the appellant (in both the appeals). A. V. Viswanatha Sastri, S., P. Varma, S, C. Agarwal and D. N.. Gupta, for respondent No. 1 (In both the cases) The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Shah, J. These two appeals are directed against a common judgment dated September 9, 1964 passed by the Allahabad, High Court allowing the writ petitions filed by the appellants. The facts leading to these appeals are as follows: The appellant is a contractor who had entered into a contract with the respondent for supply, manufacture and sale of bricks in the State. On April 30. 1964, he supplied the goods under the terms of the contracts and paid the price thereof. On July 31, 1966 the respondent issued a notice to the appellant calling upon him to pay the amount specified therein within six months of the date fixed by the respondent. The respondent filed a suit for specific performance on May 31,. 1965. The trial court decreed the suit on June 30. 1965. On August 30, 1965, an application was made under s 11(5) of Arbitration Act, 1940 (hereinafter called 'the 1940 Act') and the appellant filed an objection to that application. The learned Subordinate Judge dismissed the application holding that the respondent had not complied with the provisions of s. 11(6).

The President of India issued a Proclamation on the 3rd December, 1971 under Article 352 of the Constitution declaring that the life of the Lok Sabha was extended for a period of one year from the date appointed for its first meeting and thereafter on the 25th day of June, 1975. The proclamation of emergency was in force at the time when the House of the People (Extension of Duration) Act, 1976 was passed. The President issued a proclamation under Article 356 of the constitution declaring that it was necessary to dissolve the Lok-Chance Assembly from the said date and also to declare that the said dissolved Lok Sabha shall be deemed to have been dissolved on the expiry of two months from the day appointed for the first meeting. The Proclamation of Emergency issued on the 4th December, 1972 was challenged by the petitioners in a writ petition filed under Article 226 of the said Constitution before the High Court of Jammu and Kashmir. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the proclamation of Emergency was not valid as it was not published in the official Gazette. The petitioners filed a special leave petition against this judgment which was also dismissed by this Court on 2nd February, 1976. The petitioner filed a writ appeal to this Court which was allowed by a learned Single Judge of the High court by his order dated 5th February, 1977 and the matter was remitted back to the President for reconsideration of the proclamation in accordance with law. The Union of India filed an application under Article 32 of the Indian Constitution before this Court praying that the President should be directed to hold an enquiry into the alleged irregularities committed by the Lok Dal (Extension) Act 1976 and to pass appropriate orders thereon. This Court held that the Proclamation of emergency issued on 3rd January, 1975 was valid and accordingly quashed the proclamation. The Court further observed that the period of five years in relation to the then House of Parliament would be extended for one year and thereafter it would be deemed that the Lok proclamation had been duly published in accordance therewith. In the meanwhile, the President passed an order on the 5th March, 1976 declaring that a Proclamation of the Emergency issued by the President on the 6th December 1971 was valid. The petition filed by the petitioner under Article 136 of the Act was also allowed and the proceedings were quashed. The matter was then taken up in appeal to the Supreme Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1. The order passed by the High Courts dismissing the writ petitions is not sustainable. [775 H] 1.2. The Presidential Order issued on 4th January, 1976 is valid and it cannot be questioned in a court of law. [750 A] 1.(i) There was no material before the President to hold that the dissolution of the House was not in accordance With the provisions of the Ordinance. [751 B] (ii) The proclamation dated 3rd February, 1975 issued by a competent authority under Article 359(1) of theConstitution is valid as the Proclamation was duly published and the proclamation was also in force on the date when the President issued the Proclamation. [753 H] 2.1 The Presidential order issued on 5th January 1976 is not invalid because it is not in conformity with the provisions contained in Article 356. [764 D] 2.(i)(a) The Presidential Orders issued by this court are valid and they cannot be challenged in a Court of law; (ii)(b) The President has no power to issue an order under Article 357(1); (iii) The Proclamation is not valid because it was published in terms of the provisions made in Article 359 of the Constitutions.

The appellant was the owner of a house in which he had been residing. He was assessed to income tax by the Income Tax Officer, who assessed him to income-tax for the assessment year 1950-51. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax officer and dismissed the appeal. On further appeal, the High Court held that the property in dispute was a private or a public temple and that the appellant was entitled to claim exemption under section 8(1) (a) of the Madras Act 19 of 195 1. The appellant filed an application for leave to amend the plaint to include the property as a private one. The High Court allowed the application and dismissed it. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The High court was right in holding that the properties were private or public temple within the meaning of Madras Act 20 of 195I. [675 H] (ii) The appellant was not entitled to any exemption under the said section. He could claim exemption only if he had a private property which is capable of alienation and the question whether the property was a public or a private temple does not arise in this case. [775 G] (iii) The property was not a private trust within the scope of Madras. [750 A] (iv) The respondent was entitled under 0. 1,126 6 0 in 1950 to claim an exemption from income tax for the period prior to the date of the application for permission to amend his plaint. [751 G] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1124 of 1966. Appeal by special leave from the judgment and order dated April 20, 1966 of the Bombay High Court in Special Civil Application No. 923 of 1965. S. T. Desai, R. N. Sachthey and B. D. Sharma for the appellant. M. C. Setalvad, Attorney-General for India, K. J. John and P. H. Parekh for the respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Shah, J. This appeal is directed against a judgment of the High court of Bombay dated April 24, 1966 in Special Appeal No.. 923/66. The facts are not in dispute. The respondent filed an appeal before the High (1) [1962] Supp. 2 S.C.R. 19. Court on May 20, 1967. The question for decision was whether the properties in dispute were private property within the ambit of Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951 (hereinafter referred to as the Act). The appellant contended that the respondent was not liable to pay any exemption from payment of income tax under section 10(1)(a) or (b) of that Act. The trial court held that there was a valid lease in favour of the appellant for a period of five years and that it was open to the respondent to claim the benefit of section 8 of the Act. On appeal, this Court reversed the judgment of that court on the ground that the High Curt had no jurisdiction to direct the grant of exemption under [section 10(2)] of the said Act. In the present case, the appellant contended (1)[1962] 1 S. C R. 19 that the suit was not maintainable in view of section 10 of the Hindu Religious & Charitable Endowments act, 1951 and that as the respondent had failed to establish that the said property was private property, the question of exemption did not arise. The learned counsel for the respondents submitted that the appeal should be allowed and the order passed by the High. Court should be set aside. We have heard the learned counsel on both sides. Section 10(3) of Madras City Civil Courts Act, 1908 (hereinafter called the Act') provides that no suit shall be instituted in any civil court to set aside or modify any decree or order passed therein by the Court which passed it. The section provides for a remedy of appeal against an order of assessment made under the Act and not against an appellate order. Section 8(2)

The appellant was an employee of the respondent company. He was appointed as a clerk in the office of the appellant on July 1, 1957 and he was paid Rs. 5/- per day. The appellant was working as a Clerk with effect from August 1, 1958. On December 6, 1959, the appellant was served with a notice under s. 80 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') calling upon him to show cause why he should not be dismissed from service. The respondent filed an application before the Tribunal on January 5, 1960 for a direction that the appellant should be paid Rs 10/- per month as salary and dearness allowance. On March 31, 1961, the Tribunal passed an order in favour of the respondents directing them to pay Rs. 10/- p.m. towards the wages of the employees. The respondents filed an appeal before the High Court on April 5, 1962. The High Court held that the Tribunal was not justified in holding that the re employment of the retired persons was only a mode of recruitment and that the said arrangement was not based solely on humanitarian grounds. On further appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The appellant is entitled to get Rs.10/- p., as salary for the period from August I, 1958 to March 31. 1961. [775 H] (ii) The Tribunal has erred in holding otherwise. It was not open to the appellant to contend that the decision of the Tribunal should be set aside on this ground alone. The Tribunal had no jurisdiction to go into the question whether the re employed persons were entitled to any relief under the Act. [750 A] (iii) The order passed by the Tribunal is erroneous and unsustainable in law. The appeal is allowed, the judgment of the High court is set aside and that of the learned Single Judge restored.

The appellant was a member of the Indian Railway Administration. He was appointed as an Assistant Manager in the Railway Department of the Northern Railways on January 1, 1962. On March 31, 1963 he was promoted as Chief Accounts Officer in the scale of pay of Rs. 700-15-700. On April 30, 1964 he was transferred to the Reserve Bank of India and was posted at Calcutta. He retired from service on June 30, 1966. On May 29, 1967 he was served with a notice under section 3 of the Act by the Railway Administration asking him to show cause why action should not be taken against him for his failure to pay the amount due to him. The appellant submitted his reply to the said notice. He also submitted that he had paid the money in cash and that he was entitled to receive the money on his behalf. On June 30. 1967 he filed a suit in the Court of the District Judge, Alipore, for recovery of Rs., 1,10,000/- from him. On July 31, 1968 he filed an application under section 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the attachment and for restoration of the amount to him on the ground that the amount was not due to the railway administration as the agent of the Railway administration for conversion into sterling and was liable to be attached. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the appellant had failed to show that he paid the amount in cash to the Bank. On appeal, the District Court held that the money was not payable to the appellant because the amount lying with the Reserve bank of India was insufficient to maintain the application for removal of attachment and accordingly directed the appellant to pay it within one month from the date of receipt of the order. The High Court also held that in view of the provisions of section 3(3) of the Limitation Act, 1963, the period of limitation prescribed by the said section is three years from the time when the amount became due and not six months from the day on which it was originally paid. On further appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The High court was in error in holding that by sending the two cheques to the bank as the agents of the railway Administration for conversion of the amounts into sterling, the debt was discharged. [775 H] (ii) The amount lying in the hands of the ReserveBank of India in performance of the manner of Payment prescribed by section 3 is a trust fund money and is liable to attachment. The provisions of sections 3(1)(a), 3(2) and 4 are mandatory in character and they do not affect the rights of the appellant under section 5 of the said Act. [750 H] In the instant case, the amount deposited by the appellant was not a part of the deposit made by him as agent of Railway Administration for converting sterling and therefore he could not be attached to the application filed by the Bank under section 7 of the Court Fees Act. The appeal is allowed and the order passed by the High Court is set aside.

The respondent was employed as a clerk in the appellant-Bank. He was dismissed from service on the ground that he had been guilty of misconduct by the management. The respondent filed an application before the Labour Court for reinstatement with back wages and compensation. The Labour Court held that the termination of his services was not a colourable exercise of power but was a result of victimisation or unfair labour practice. On appeal, this Court set aside the order of the Labour Appellate Tribunal and remanded the case to the Labour court for fresh disposal in accordance with law. In the meanwhile, the respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order passed by the Labour Officer. The High Court held against him that the order was not an interlocutory one but was merely an administrative order and it was not open to the Tribunal to go behind the evidence or to set aside such an order. It further held that in any event, the Industrial Tribunal had no jurisdiction to go into the question whether the termination was a colourable or mala fide exercise of powers by the employer. The appellant filed a special leave petition against this judgment and obtained special leave from this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The order passed on the basis of the finding recorded by the trial court is not an order of dismissal simpliciter but is a result thereof. [775 H] 1.2 In the instant case, the Labour Commissioner has found that the respondent was guilty of victimisation and unfair labour practices. He had no material and if so advised, to proceed against the workman for misconduct. The management cannot be permitted to go on the question of dismissal merely because it is a fact finding and set aside by the High court. [750 H] 2.1 There is nothing in the order dated December 14, 1982 that shows that the Labour Authority had lost confidence in the employee. It was not necessary for the respondent to disclose to the Court the grounds of his impugned action so as to enable him to be tested judicially. The order of termination passed by him was not one of dismissal simplicitor but was an administrative one and it is only a camouflage or an act of victimisation. [751 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 879 of 1982. From the Judgment and Order dated 16.1.1982 of the Andhra Pradesh High Court in W.A. No. 955 of 1982 and Writ Petition No. 1123 of 1982, T.S. Krishnamoorthy vs The State of Tamil Nadu & Ors. .

The appellants, who were the members of the All India Services (Medical Attendance) Service, were appointed as Assistant Surgeon in the Government Medical College, Meerut. They were appointed to the post of Assistant Surgeon on contract basis for a period of one year and thereafter they were transferred to the District Hospital, Meerut, and subsequently to the State Medical Board. The appellants were appointed by the State Government as Assistant Surgeons on contract. On the basis of the recommendations made by the Medical Board, the services of the appellants were terminated with effect from 1st April, 1988. The respondents filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the termination of their services and also praying for a direction to the appellants to pay them the amount of Rs.5,000/- as interim relief. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellants had not been appointed by way of contract basis and they were entitled to receive the additional payment from the State. Hence this appeal by special leave.
