Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The High court was right in holding that there was no infirmity in the order passed by the learned Single Judge as well as the Division Bench of the High court. [557F] 1.2 The appellants had been appointed on contract for a specified period and they could not be said to have been appointed under any of the existing schemes now in force in the State, their cases should be considered for appointment by way o f interim relief and the State should make suitable arrangements for providing aid to the aged, the disabled, and the destitute, sub ject to the condi tions of the scheme. [506F] 2.1 There is no infirmity with the order of the learned Judge as he was not a party to the writ proceedings. The appeals are accordingly dismissed.

The appellant was elected as a member of the Samiti from the Byabasthapika and Karyapalika. The appellant filed an election petition before the High Court challenging the election of the appellant as a Member of the Parishad. The High Court held that the appellant had ceased to be a member and therefore he was not entitled to continue in office until he attained majority. It was further held that since the appellant was holding the office of a member, he was entitled to hold office till he attained the majority. The election petition filed by the appellant before the District Judge was dismissed. The appeal filed by him against the order of the High court was also dismissed. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The term 'member' in Article 19(1)(c) is a term which means that the person constituting an association must have been formed for the purpose of promoting or maintaining any association or for maintaining or improving any existing or future affairs of the society. [675 H] 1.2 The term "member" in Article19(1) (c) has to be read as if it was a term of the nature of 'service' and not as a term in the sense that it means service. Therefore, the appellant ceased to hold the office by virtue of his membership. [775 H; 776 A] 1:3 The term of office of the President is a tenure which means the appointment of a person who has been elected as such by the State Government and in this view of the matter we are of the opinion that the term of 'member', in Article[19(2)] does not include the term 'office bearer' in the context of the Constitution. The widow of a Hindu widow, who was the daughter of a widow, filed a suit for partition in respect of the properties given to her as stridhana and for possession of the same. The trial court held that the gift made by Sumitra Devi at the time of the marriage of Kamala Devi was not valid and that the plaintiffs respondents were entitled to the reliefs which they claimed. The High Court, however, reversed the decree of the trial court and dismissed the suit. In this appeal by special leave, it is contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court was wrong in holding that there was a moral or religious obligation of giving a portion of the joint family property for the benefit of the daughter and son in law. The learned counsel for the respondents submitted that the question whether Sumitra Devi was competent to make a gift of a reasonable portion of her estate was not a question of law, but a question which arose out of the said provision. It was further contended that the trial Court had erred in holding otherwise. The first contention of the learned counsel is that the finding of the High court that there is a moral and religious obligation on the part of the widow to make an gift for or at the date of the death of her husband, is not correct. The second contention of learned counsel was that the suit filed by Sumitra was barred by limitation as the plaintiffs had failed to prove that she made a "sankalpa " at the relevant time. It is further contended on their behalf that the findings recorded by the High Curt are erroneous and contrary to law. On behalf of respondent No. 1, it was submitted that there were no legal obligations on the appellants as they did not make any gift for the purpose of the family. The question whether there was any moral or social obligation of the plaintiffsrespondents was a question arising out of a contract between them and the daughter. The suit filed in respect thereof was barred under section 14 of the Act. It may be mentioned that the first contention raised by learned counsel, namely, that there could not be a religious duty on the death or in law, was also not accepted by the trial Judge as correct. In the alternative, it may be stated that the second contention raised before us was not accepted and the High Courts decision was reversed.

The appellant was a candidate for the election to the Punjab Legislative Assembly from the constituency of village Bana, District Sangrur. The first respondent filed an election petition against the appellant alleging that he had been guilty of corrupt practices under section 123(2) of the Act and that the result of the election would have been materially altered. The appellant contested the said election. He was declared elected by a margin of votes between the contesting candidates (the returned candidate) and the second respondent. The High Court held that the appellant had committed an offence under section 100(1)(d) read with section 77 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 (hereinafter referred to as "the Act") and that he was guilty of the said offence. On appeal by special leave, the High Court reversed the order of the trial court and held that Tej Singh had committed corrupt practices within the meaning of section 123 (2) readwith section 77(1) of The Act. In this view, it allowed the appeal and quashed the election of the first respondent. It is against this judgment that the present appeal has been filed by special Leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The result of a trial under section 101 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 (hereinafter called "the Evidence Act") is that the returned candidate was guilty and sentenced to imprisonment for life. [675 H] 2. The question whether Tej Singh was guilty or not was a mixed question of law and fact. It was not necessary for the appellant to prove beyond reasonable doubt that Tej singh had committed any corrupt practice within the mischief of section 100 of the Code. [775 G] 3. Section 123(1), as it stood at the relevant time, provided that if in any case it is proved that a candidate or his election agent was guilty by any other person with the consent of the returned candidates or any other candidate with the permission of the court, the result shall be materially altered and that would have come to an end. [750 H] 4. The object of section 101 is to prevent the commission of corrupt practice which is likely to have been committed in the interests of the general public by a person who has committed such corrupt practice. It cannot be said that the consequence of the corrupt practices mentioned in section 123 is not a mere irregularity but a total failure on the part of the candidate or the returned agent to comply with the provisions of section 77 and 78 of the Evidence Act. [751 H] 5. The burden of proving that the election petitioner had committed such an offence lies on the person who alleges it. In the instant case, Tej Singh has not been proved to have committed any such corrupt practices. Therefore, the appellant was not guilty of any offence under sections 123(3) and 77 of The Representation of People Act. The appeal is allowed and the judgment of the High court is set aside. [751 H] 6. Section 100 of The Code provides that if a candidate has been guilty by an other person of corrupt or illegal practice, he shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months or with fine or with both. [764 G] 7. In view of the provisions contained in section 77, it is not necessary to examine the effect of the provision as it stands at the material time. The election petition was filed by Tej Singh and the appellant has failed to prove that Tej Kaur had committed the corrupt practice under section 77. [771 H; 771 A] 8. Section 101 provides that where in any trial under this Act, a candidate is guilty of an offence punishable under section 102, he may be punished for the said offences with imprisonment which may extent to six month or with a fine or both.

The appellant was a member of the Indian Administrative Service. He was appointed as an Assistant Engineer in the year 1962 and he was promoted to the post of Superintending Engineer on 1st January, 1963. On his appointment he was transferred to the State Government. The State Government issued a notification dated 30th June, 1964 under section 19(1) of the Act appointing him as an Executive Engineer. He challenged the validity of the said notification by filing a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant had not been served with any notice or order for contempt and that he was not entitled to be heard before the order of dismissal was passed. In this appeal, it is contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court erred in holding that there was no violation of section 19 (1) read with section 19 of the act. The learned counsel appearing for the respondent submitted that the provisions of section 6(2)(i) of Act were not applicable to the case and that the order passed by the High, Court was erroneous. Section 6(3) of this Act provides that no person shall be entitled to appeal against any order made by the State or its officers under section 6 (1). The appellant had been appointed as a Superintending Engineer in 1962 and his appointment was confirmed on 1.1.1963. He filed a writ application in the Calcutta High Court challenging the validity and correctness of the notification dated 1st June, 1965 issued under section 16(1)(b) of that Act. The said petition was dismissed by the learned Single Judge. On appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) Section 6 (3) is not applicable in the case of a person interested in maintaining the dignity of the court. [775 H] (ii) The High court has erred in not holding that section 6 of Act was applicable to cases where there were only two parties, namely, the court and the contemnor. The appellant was not interested in keeping the dignity and the right of the Court under Article 215 of the Constitution. [750 A] (iii) Section 19(2) of act is a provision which provides that every person who is interested in the maintenance of the institution shall be heard by the court before any order is passed against him. The provisions of sub section (3), therefore, are applicable to such cases where the High Courts have not been conferred with jurisdiction or power under Article 226 of the constitution. [751 B] (iv) Section 7(2A) of Ordinance No. 1 of 1964 provides that nothing in this Act shall apply to any person who has been appointed to be an Executive Officer of a State Government and whose appointment was made by or on behalf or for the time being in force in connection with the affairs of the State. [753 H] The High Courts were not competent to pass orders under section 7(1). Section 7 (2A), therefore. does not apply to cases wherein there are only two persons, namely the court or the contemnor and it is one of them.

The appellant was the tenant of a shop in the ground floor of the building situated at Bombay. The respondent filed a suit for ejectment against the appellant on the ground that he was a tenant under the landlord and that the tenancy was not terminated by the tenant. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the tenant had failed to prove that he had been in possession of the shop since the date of the notice. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decree and held that the appellant was entitled to relief against forfeiture of the lease under section 111 (g) of the Act. In second appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the tenant that the provisions of section 111(g) were not applicable in the case of a landlord who had been given notice by the landlord before the coming into force of the, Act and that in view of the decision of the Bombay High Court in Tatya Savla Sudrik vs Yeshwanta Kondiba Mulay (1), the tenant was entitled for relief against the forfeiture of lease under [section 111(h)] of the Transfer of Property Act. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The provisions of sections 111(k) and 111(l) are not applicable to a landlord whose tenancy is terminated by his denial of the landlord's landlord's title. The section does not require that the landlord must be going to obtain the forfeiture in case of non payment of rent. [775 H] 2.1 The provisions contained in section 111 of the Tenancy Act, 1939, are not attracted in the present case and the tenant is entitled for a decree against forfeiture under section 114(g). [776 B] 2:2 Section 111 (k) of Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, provides that if the tenant has been in occupation of any land after the date on which the Act came into force, he shall be liable to pay rent at the rate of two hundred rupees per month. The proviso to section 111 makes it clear that the court is not required to grant relief against a forfeiture for non payment or non payment by the person who has been given a notice before the commencement of the tenancy. [750 H] 3:3 A] 2(i) The provisions in section 112(g), (h) and (j) are applicable to cases where the tenant, after the coming in force of this Act, is a landlord. [751 G] (ii) The proviso does not apply to a person who had given notice before coming into operation of the law. [75 H; 75 A] (iii) The provision contained in sections 111 (h), 112(j) and 114 are not relevant for determining the lease. [76 H] (iv) The tenant is not entitled to claim relief against an forfeiture under clause (g). The provisions relating to forfeiture of tenancy are not made applicable to such cases. [77 G] 2.(i) Section 111(j), (k), (l) and Section 112(h) are inapplicable to a case where the landlord has been granted notice before commencement of tenancy. The provision in section 113(h)(h) is not attracted to a tenant who had not given notice prior to the coming within the mischief of clause (f). [76 G] 3.1 In the instant case, the appellant had been granted a notice by his landlord on the date when the Act was brought into force and that he did not have any knowledge of the provisions contained therein. The appellant was not entitled for the relief against such forfeiture under Section 111 of Bombay Rent Act, 1947. [78 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1524 of 1972. From the Judgment and Order dated the 10th May, 1971 of the Gujarat High Court, Ahmedabad in Special Civil Application No. 923 of 1970. S. T. Desai, V. M. Tarkunde, R. N. Sachthey, for the appellant. B. D.

The appellant was employed as a driver in the respondent-Corporation. He was dismissed from service on the allegation that he had committed misconduct by abusing his position as a conductor of the bus. The respondent filed an application before the Labour Court under section 33A(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') for setting aside the order of dismissal passed against him. The Labour Court held that the termination of the services of the respondent was illegal and directed reinstatement of the appellant with back wages. On appeal by the Corporation, the High Court set aside the award holding that the order terminating the services was not in accordance with law and it was not open to the Labour court to interfere with the punishment imposed upon the respondent. The appellant filed a writ petition before this Court challenging the validity of the order passed by the Labour Commissioner. The learned Single Judge dismissed the writ petition holding that there was no violation of principles of natural justice as the termination was in accordance to the provisions of the Act and that the High court was not justified in interfering with the award. On behalf of the Corporation it was contended that the respondent had been guilty of misconduct by using his position in the bus and, therefore, he was entitled to reinstatement with back-wages. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The order passed against the appellant is liable to be set aside. [775 H] 2.1 The High Court has not properly appreciated the evidence on record and has rightly interfered with the finding of fact recorded by the learned Single judge. [750 A] 2(i) The Labour Commissioner was not competent to enter into merits of the case or interfere with punishment imposed by the Management. [751 B] 2.(ii) The High court has not correctly appreciated the facts on which the inquiry was held to be invalid. [751 D] 3.2 The order of termination passed against Rama Shankar and Burma Pradhan is illegal and void. [764 G] 3(i)(a) The order terminating services of Rama Shankar is bad in law as it does not disclose any misconduct on his part. [754 A] 3.(ii)(b) The award passed by Labour Court is liable for interference with the quantum of punishment imposed on the respondent and, accordingly, we do not find that there is any infirmity in the order. [752 B] 3 (iii)(a)(i) There was no breach of principles or natural justice in passing the order by the High. Court. [758 C] 4.(i)(b)(ii) There is nothing on record to show that the Labour Officer had any jurisdiction to enter upon the merits of his case or interference with punishment awarded by the management. [759 D] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1079 of 1973. From the Judgment and Order dated the 9th July, 1972 of the Andhra Pradesh High Court in Writ Petition No. 1223 of 1972. V. S. Desai, for the appellant. R.K. Garg, for respondent No. 1. M.C. Bhandare, for respondents Nos. 2 to 4. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by RAY, J. This appeal is directed against the judgment dated September 9, 1972 passed by a Division Bench of the High Curt in Writ Appeal No: 1079/73. The facts leading to this appeal are as follows. The first respondent was working as a Conductor in the appellant-Corporation at the relevant time. He worked for about two years and completed more than 240 days of service. On June 30, 1973, he made an application to the management for reinstatement with continuity of service and back wages and other benefits. The management did not accept the said application and reinstated him. Thereafter, on September 9. 1974, the appellant filed an appeal before the Industrial Tribunal, Andhra Pradesh at Hyderabad against the order dated October 10, 1972. The Industrial Tribunal dismissed the said appeal.

The Kerala Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1969, was passed by the Kerala Legislature on the basis of a registered deed purporting to be a lease deed executed by a tenant in respect of the land of another at the commencement of the Kerala Land Reform (Amendment ) Act, 1970. The said Act came into force with effect from 1st April, 1970 and the Kerala Stay of Eviction Proceedings Act, 1957, was repealed by the [Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963]. On or about 11th April, 1957 the Kerala Revenue Tribunal, on an application made to it under section 6 of the said Act, passed a decree for possession of the lands of another and continued in possession of such land till the commencement o f the Kerala Lands Reforms (Second Amendment) Act. The Kerala Land Tribunal held that the tenant had not surrendered his leasehold right to the landlord within a period of 10 years from the date of the lease deed. On or before the said date, the tenant was deemed to be in occupation of the property and continued to be so in possession till the date on which the lease was executed. The tenant filed an application under section 5 of the Act for delivery of possession of his land. The Tribunal held, inter alia, that the tenancy had not been terminated by the landlord before the commencement or at any time after the 11th day of April, 1958, but continued in occupation by the tenant till the expiry of the period fixed under the said lease deed and accordingly the tenant became a tenant. On appeal, the High Court held that as the tenant did not surrender his leasehold rights within 10 years of the date when the lease had been executed, the tenancy was liable to be terminated. The High Court further held that since the tenant continued in actual possession after the expiry or at least from the 11 th day of the relevant date, he became a deemed tenant and the provisions of section 6 were not applicable. On behalf of the appellant it was contended that as there was no surrender of the leasehold right by the lessee within 10 year from the said period, the provisions contained in section 6 would be inapplicable to the facts of the case. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The lease deed dated 11th of April 1957 was not a lease but only a lease and therefore the provisions relating to the tenancy were applicable to the case on hand. [505 G] 2. The question whether the tenant has surrendered his lease or not is a mixed question of fact and law and it cannot be decided in an application for delivery under section 7 of the Tamil Nadu Land Reforms(Amendment)Act, 1969. [506 H] 3. Section 6 of Act does not apply to the circumstances of the present case. The provisions contained therein are applicable to cases where the tenant surrendered his tenancy within a certain period and continued as such after the said 11th date. [504 G] 4. The words "or" occurring in section 5(2) of the Amendment Act, 1968, must be read as "or", so that the words "and" occurring therein are not used in any other provision of the statute. [407 H] 5. Section 7 of Act is applicable to a case where the tenancy has been terminated before the date specified under the lease. The word "or". [506 G] 6. The expression "or " must be construed as " or" occurringin section 6. [500 D] 7. The language of section 5 is clear and unambiguous. It does not require that the provisions in question should be read in any manner. [525 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1704 of 1972. From the Judgment and Order dated the 14th May, 1973 of the High court of Kerala at Ernakulam in O.P. No. 1124/75. S.T. Desai, V.K. Francis, M.M. Kurian, P.C. Kapur, R.N. Sachthey, for the appellant.

The appellant was prosecuted for the offence of smuggling gold and diamonds, watches, etc. under Section 135(1)(ii) of the Act. The appellant was convicted by the trial court and sentenced to pay a fine of Rs. 1,000/- in default to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one year. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence but reduced the sentence to a period of six months. In further appeal to this Court it was contended that the goods were not smuggled or imported into India and therefore, the appellant could not be convicted under Section 111(d) of The Act. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The provisions of Section 123 of the Evidence Act are mandatory in nature and they must be complied with by the prosecution. [652 H] 1.2 In the instant case, the goods in question were seized from the possession of the appellant. They were smuggled goods. Therefore, the burden was on the appellant to prove that the said goods were smuggled or importable. The onus was on him to show that he knew that the articles were illegally imported and that he had a chance of getting the benefit of doubt. [752 H; 753 A] 1:3. Section 106 of the Indian Evidence Act is mandatory in character and it is not necessary for the prosecution to prove the place from where they came, or when they were imported or brought into India. The burden was upon the appellant who had been convicted under Sections 135(2) and 114 of the Customs Act. [750 B] 1.(i) The provisions contained in Section 123 are mandatory and it cannot be said that the appellant knew that he was an innocent receiver of such goods without knowing that they were illegally import or imported. [751 H; 751 A] 2.1 In the present case, there was no evidence to enable the Court to come to the conclusion that the appellants were in possession of such articles. The fact that the accused were found to be smuggled goods does not mean that they must have been known to the appellant as a result of which he could have got the benefit under Section 123. [753 H] 2:2 In view of the provisions contained under Section 106, it is only if the appellant proves that he has a chance to get the benefit thereof, that the Court can go further and assume them to be illegally imported or import or import of such article in contravention of law.

The appellants, who were the members of a registered Association, filed a suit in the Court of the District Judge, Chhindwara against the respondent for recovery of contributions made by the appellants and also for accounts. The appellants contended that they had a right to bring a suit for accounts of the Association and that the suit was maintainable under section 69(3)(a) of the Act. The trial court held that the appellants were not entitled to bring the suit for account of the profits made by them and accordingly, dismissed the suit. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decree passed by the trial court and decreed the suit in favour of the respondent. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The provisions of section 69 (3)(b) of The Partnership Act, 1932, are not applicable to a firm which is dissolved in February 1948. [675 H] 2. Section 69(1) of that Act provides that where a plaintiff comes to court on allegations which on the face of them show that a contract has been made by law, but the defendant in respect of the partnership transactions, it is competent to the defendant to resist the suit on the ground of illegality. [775 H; 776 B] 3. The provision in section 69 of the Partnership Act is not applicable in a case where a suit is filed by one member of an illegal association against another in respect to the firm which was dissolved in March 1948. Section 70(3) of this Act provides for the institution of suits by or against any person for recovery, damages or costs and also provides that the provisions of sub section (2) shall not apply to a suit instituted by or on behalf of a firm for accounts or for accounts and also to a case in which an unregistered firm is registered. [750 H] 4. The words "any other" occurring in section 70(1)(b), therefore, refer only to the cases where a partnership firm has been dissolved in accordance with sub section 2 of section 70 of the Indian Partnership Act. [751 G] 5. Section 71 of the Trade and Merchandise Marks Act, 1958, is not attracted to a proceeding under section 70. The suit was filed by the respondent on the basis that the appellant had a valid partnership with the respondent and that he was entitled to sue for accounts in respect thereof. [753 H; 75 B] 6. Section 72 of the Contract Act provides as follows: "72. (1) Where a contract is made by a person who is not a member of any illegal association or is a partner of such association, he may apply to the court for an order that the said association or the members thereof be dissolved and that it shall be lawful for the court to make an order directing that the association or members be dissolved. (2)(a). Where a suit has been instituted by a firm against any member of a illegal association, the court may direct that the firm or any member thereof be reconstituted in accordance therewith, but where a decree is passed in favour or against the firm, the Court shall make an application to the Court for an injunction restraining the said firm from proceeding with the business of the said partnership. (b) Where the suit is instituted by the firm against a member, he shall apply to that court for the order directing the dissolution of the firm and the court shall make such order as it may direct. [764 H; 76A] (c) The provisions in section 72 of The Indian Partnerships Act, 1939, are applicable to cases where accounts have been filed and also in cases in which a suit was instituted by an unregistered association against any other person for accounts, and also the case in respect whereof the suit has not been instituted.

The respondents were prosecuted for offences under secs. 498A, 406 and 506 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. The learned Magistrate took cognizance of the offence on the basis that the respondents had committed an offence punishable under sec. 498 A of the IPC. The respondents filed a criminal complaint against the respondents for the alleged commission of offences under sections 498A and 406 of the I.P.C. The trial court held that the prosecution was not maintainable in view of the provisions contained in section 195(1)(b) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (hereinafter referred to as "the Code") and accordingly issued summons to the respondents. On appeal by the State, the High Court set aside the order of the learned Magistrate holding that the complaint filed by the respondents was not competent. The State of Madras has come up in appeal against the said order. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 Section 195(l)(b), Cr.P.,C. provides for an offence which is punishable under section 498A or section 406 of IPC. [557F] 1.2 In a case where the acts alleged to constitute an offence under section 499 of IPC are punishable as contempt of court, High Court can take cognizance of such offences and direct issue of summons to any person who has committed an act which constitutes an offence. The expression "the same offence" in the context of the provision contained in sub section (1) of section 195 Cr. P.C., means that the said offence is punishable as a contempt of Court. [506F] 2.1 In a proceeding under section 482 of the Criminal Procedure Code, 1973, the question whether an act constitutes an offense for an act or not, has to be determined by the High Courts in the exercise of their powers under Article 226 of the Constitution. The High Courts have no power to issue summons to a person who is alleged to be guilty of an offence and, therefore, the said provision does not apply to cases where the offences are punishable under sections 499A and 500 of IPC only. [657F G] 2:2 In the instant case, the respondents were convicted for an offenses under section 500 of the Penal Code and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for a period of one year and to pay fine of Rs. 1,000/- each in default to suffer simple imprisonment for six months. The order of conviction was passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge on 1.7.1986. [504F] 3.1 The High Court has not given any reason as to why the said provisions contained therein should be held to apply to a case under section 9(1) read with Section 50 of the Act.

The appellant was convicted by the trial court for an offence under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court confirmed his conviction and sentence on the ground that he had a good moral character and was not likely to abscond from justice, and that he was released on bail. The appellant filed an appeal against his conviction before this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1. Section 439 of the Code is a special provision which confers power on the High Court to release on bail in cases where the accused is in custody or has been arrested and detained in custody for more than one year. [775 H] 1.2. The provisions of Section 437(1) of the code are not mandatory but directory. It is only a procedural provision which can be used to protect the accused from being punished for an alleged offence. [750 A] 1:3. The power conferred on the court by Section 439(1)(b) is discretionary and it cannot be said that the power to release the accused on bail includes the power of the court to release him on bail, but not to release a person on his own bond without monetary sureties or financial security. [751 B] 1.(i) The power under Section 437 (1) is an inherent power which can only be exercised in exceptional circumstances and for reasons to be recorded by it in writing. It cannot be used as a substitute for the ordinary procedure of bail. [753 H] 2.1 The power to grant bail includes both release on the accused person's own bond and financial security and also bail bonds to ensure that the 'bailee' does not flee justice. [754 D] 1(ii) Section 437A is an enabling provision which empowers the court, if it thinks fit, to release any person on bail who has been in custody, for a period of one year or more, on his personal bond without surety or financialsecurity and without sureties. The discretion conferred on a court by this section is not arbitrary but is subject to judicial review. [764 D] 2.(iii) The powers conferred on an appellate Court under Section 439 are discretionary in nature and it can be exercised only in exceptional cases and for good reasons. [752 B] 3.1 In the instant case, the High court has not recorded any finding that the appellant was not a 'satisfied' with his personal bonds or financial sureties or he was likely to commit a breach of the conditions of bail as required by Section 437 of the Cr.P.C. [758 C] 3.(i)(a) The order passed by the High. Court is clearly unsustainable in law and it is accordingly set aside. [759 D] (ii) The appellant has been released on his executing a bond for Rs. 50,000/- with one surety of the like amount to the satisfaction of the trial Court. [761 F] 3(i)(b). The High court was not justified in setting aside the order passed under Section 438 of the Criminal Procedure Code.

The appellant, a registered firm carrying on business in the name of M/s. S.K. Jain & Co., Bombay, was assessed to income tax by the Income Tax Officer under section 66(1) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') for the assessment year 1951 52, and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax Officer. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order passed by the Appellate Tribunal. The High Court held that the income of the assessee was not taxable under section 11(1)(a) of Act, but it was assessed as income from other sources and that the Income-tax Officer had no jurisdiction to assess the income from the business in question. The appeal filed by the appellant before this Court was allowed by a Division Bench of the High court on the ground that the order made by the Tribunal was erroneous and that it was not open to the Court to interfere with the finding of fact recorded by the appellate authority. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Appellate Commissioner had no power to review his own decision under section 35(1). Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (i) The High court was right in holding that the Tribunal had jurisdiction to call upon the Tribunal to state a case and to refer it. [775 H] (ii) The order of assessment passed by an Income tax officer is not final and conclusive. It is open to this court to examine whether the finding recorded by him is erroneous or not. If the finding is based on some evidence, it cannot be regarded as a finding not given by the High Tribunal. [750 H] In the instant case, the Appellate Deputy Commissioner had acted upon the findings of fact and the Incometax Officer was justified in rejecting the claim of the respondent for exemption under section 10(1), and that order was confirmed by the Commissioner of Income tax. [751 G] (iii) The finding recorded on the basis of which the Appellate Authority had relied is not a finding of law. It has been held by this Court in the case of [S.K Jain & Company vs Union of India & Ors.] , that the High Courts have the power to interfere in cases where the findings are based on no evidence, and in such cases it cannot also be regarded either as a decision not given under section35(1); or even as a result of an erroneous finding of facts. [753 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1566 of 1968. Appeal by special leave from the judgment and order dated September 16, 1967 of the Allahabad High Court in Special Appeal No.. 14 of 1967. S B. Sen, J. B. Dadachanji, O. C. Mathur and Ravinder Narain, for the appellant. A. K. Sen and R. N. Sachthey, for respondent No. 1. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Hegde, J.-This appeal is directed against the judgment dated September 15, 1967 passed by a learned Single Judge of the said High Court allowing the writ petition filed by respondent No 1. 2. The facts leading to this appeal are as follows: The appellant is a registered partnership firm and has its office at Bombay. The respondent was appointed as a partner in the business of manufacturing and selling of sugar. He was assessed under section 3(1A) of Central Excise Act, 1944 (hereinafter called 'the said Act') on the total income of Rs. 1,50,000 for the year 1951-52. The Income tax authorities were of the view that the respondent had not paid any amount in respect of the assessment years 1951-53 and 1953-54. On appeal by the assessee, the Commissioner (Appeals) set aside the order under section 5(1B).

The appellant was appointed as a Sub-Inspector of Police in the Punjab Government. He was posted as Assistant Sub Inspector of Police, Punjab State. On January 29, 1974, he was promoted as Sub- Inspector of police. The appellant was promoted to the post of Sub-inspector of police on February 18, 1975. On March 31, 1975, the appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of his promotion. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the order passed by the Government dated January 29. 1974 fixing the seniority of the appellant as Sub Inspector was illegal and void. The State of Punjab filed an appeal against the judgment of the High court before this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The power to appoint a Sub Inspector under Rule 3(a) of the Punjab Police Rules is vested in the Government. The power conferred on the Government by Rule 3 (b) is not subject to any limitation or restriction. [775 H] 1.2 The High court was right in holding that since the Minister concerned had dealt with the matter directly and by passing the impugned order dated February 18 1975, he had dealt in the matter, the High Courts were in error in directing that the Minister was impleaded as a party. [750 A] 2.1 Rule 3 of the Rules provides that the Government may appoint an officer as a sub-inspector or Sub- inspector of police to assist the State Government in the investigation of any case relating to the service of the Government and such officer shall be deemed to be a public servant within the meaning of Section 21 of the Indian Penal Code. [751 B] 2:2 The power under Rule 4(a)(i) is subject to the provisions of Rule 3. It is not open to the State to make any appointment which is contrary to the statutory provision. [75 H; 75 A] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1207 of 1975. From the Judgment and Order dated the 9th February, 1975 of the Bombay High Court in Writ Petition No. 11 of 1975 S. T. Desai, R. N. Sachthey and B. D. Sharma for the Appellant. V. M. Tarkunde, Mrs. A. K. Verma, P. C. Kapur, RR. 1-2, R-1 and R-3. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by RAY, J.-This appeal by special leave is directed against the order dated January 18, 1976 passed by a Division Bench of the Gujarat High Court dismissing the writ application filed by the appellant. The facts giving rise to this appeal are as follows: The appellant is an Assistant Sub-Inspectors of Police posted at the Punjab State and was promoted on February 17, 1975 as SubInspector of police in the year 1974. On April 18,1975, he made a representation against his promotion to the Government of Punjab. The Government rejected that representation by its order dated March 31. 1975. The appeal filed by him was dismissed by the High Curt. The order passed in the writ proceedings is not challenged by the State of Haryana. The only question which arises for consideration in this appeal is whether the Minister, who had dealt With the matter and the respondent before us, was a public officer within the definition of Section 2(h) of The Punjab Police Act, 1951 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') and that the power to make appointment under Rule 5 of the said Rules was not delegated to the appellant by the Governor. The question is whether in view of the provisions contained in Rule 3, the Minister had acted on behalf of the State and therefore, the order of the government dated March 30, 1975 fixing the date for making the impugned promotion was illegal. The respondent filed a counter affidavit in which he stated that the Secretary to Government of the Department of Home Affairs, Punjab issued an order dated April 18. 1975 fixing his seniority as Sub Inspectors of police with effect from February 18.1975.

The Act was passed by the Punjab Municipal Act, 1911 (hereinafter referred to as "the Act") and it received the assent of the President on April 1, 1911. The Act provided for recovery of arrears of rent and other dues by a Board or a Military Estates Officer under the Act. Section 259 of the Act provides that no suit or proceeding shall be instituted in any civil court against a Board, or a Government servant or a member of the Board or the Government servant in respect of anything done or to be done under the provisions of the [Punjab Municipal Act] and the rules made thereunder. The respondent filed a suit for recovery by way of arrears on the ground that he was entitled to recover the rent due from him under the Punjab Land Revenue Act, 1887 (hereinafter called "the Code") and that the notice issued by the Board was illegal as it did not comply with the provisions contained in section 259 of that Act. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the respondent was a tenant within the meaning of section 259 and that he had been evicted from the land on the basis of the notice served upon him under section 259. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decree and held that the provisions were not applicable to the case. In second appeal before this Court it was contended by Mr. S. T. Desai, learned counsel for the appellant, that the Act did not provide for recovery in respect to arrears of any tax or water rate or other money recoverable under any express provision of the statute and that since the respondent had been a tenant under the management of the Cantonment Authority, he was not entitled to claim the rent from him. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The provisions contained inss. 259 and 259 of Indian Penal Code are applicable to cases where rent is payable by a person who is not a tenant but is recovered by a local authority under this Act or the rules framed thereunder. [457 D] 2. Section 258 of the Punjab Act provides for recovery as provided in section 260 of the Code. The words "any arrears of tax, water rate, rent or fee" are defined in section 261 of the Indian Penal code which is reproduced below: "261. Recovery by a Police Officer of certain offences.- (1) Any offence punishable under this Chapter shall be tried by a Magistrate. (2) No Court shall take cognizance of any offence punishable Under this Act except upon complaint made by a police officer, or on his own knowledge or suspicion, and no Court inferior to that of a Magistrate of the first class shall try such offence." [456 H] 3. The word "shall" used in section 258 of Indian penal Code is not defined in the Code but it has been construed in the context of the provisions relating to recovery of rent by a Local Authority under this section. [557 C] 4. Section 260 of Punjab Act, 1913 does not provide that the provision contained ins. 259 of Criminal Procedure Code will apply to cases in which rent is paid by a contractor or a local fund. The language used in the section is "any offence punishable" under any other law. [506 G] 5. The expression "any sum due" in the Act means only the amount due from an occupier and not the amount of arrears. [504 D] 6. Section 261 of Punjab Municipal Corporation Act, 1956 does not confer jurisdiction on a Magistrate to take cognizance. It merely provides for the recovery of dues by the local authority. [500 G] 7. The High Court was right in holding that since no complaint was made against the respondent under section 258, the provisions are applicable. [511 D] 8. Section 256 of the Haryana Municipal Act is not attracted to cases arising under the Indian penal code. It does not make any distinction between cases where a notice served by a private person or a public servant is not an offence punishable U/s 259 of IPC.

The appellant was employed as a conductor in the respondent company. He was appointed to work for a period of two years on contract basis. On his appointment, he was transferred to the service of the company. The company terminated his services by an order dated December 31, 1973. The appellant challenged the termination of his services before the Labour Court and the Labour Appellate Tribunal allowed the appeal filed by the company and set aside the order of termination. The respondent company filed a writ petition in this Court challenging the order passed by the Labour court. During the pendency of the writ petition, the appellant was appointed as a driver on contract for a fixed period. On December 31. 1973, the company terminated the services of the appellant. Thereafter, the respondent filed an application before the Tribunal under section 33C(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act claiming that the termination was illegal and the order terminating his services was without any notice or compensation. The Tribunal held that the appellant is a workman within the meaning of the [Industrial Disputes Act] as it stood in 1973 when the appellant's services were terminated, and therefore, he is not a workman under the said Act. On appeal by the respondent, the High Court set aside that order and directed the Tribunal to consider the question whether the termination is illegal and if so, whether the appellant can be held to be a workman. The High Court further observed that the question of law raised in this appeal was not required to be decided in view of our finding that the respondent was a workman as defined under the Industrial Employment Act. In the circumstances, we are of the opinion that no interference is called for with the decision of the High court. The appeal accordingly fails and it is dismissed.

The Company was a lessee of the land in question. The Company had leased out the land to the Government for a period of 99 years and the Company continued to remain in possession of the said land as a lessee. On the expiry of the lease, the Company filed an application under section 181 of the Code before the Collector for eviction of the Company from the land. The Collector passed an order on 1.10.1977 holding that the Company was not a 'pakka' tenant within the meaning of the Madhya Bharat Act No. 66 of 1950 and that the company continued to be in possession as a tenant under the Government lessee. The application for eviction was filed by the Company before the Assistant Collector, who passed an Order on 1st October 1977 holding that it was not necessary to hold any lease from the Government or to continue to remain with the Government. On appeal, the Appellate Authority confirmed the order of the Assistant Commissioner and dismissed the appeal. In the meanwhile, the company filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the Order of the Collector dated 1st10 1977. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that since the Company had been holding over under the old lease or under the newly stipulated terms agreed upon between the Company and the Government, it was a 'Pakka'. It was further held that the order passed by the Assistant Commissioneer on 1/10/1977 was not an order of eviction but an order for eviction. The appeal filed by special leave was also dismissed. Hence this appeal by special Leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The High court was right in holding that as the Company has been holding the land on lease from Government and it is a 'public lessee' within the definition of the Act, the order for possession passed by him is not an illegal order. [652 H] 1.2 In the circumstances, the impugned Order of eviction passed by Assistant Collector was not sustainable in law. The order of Assistant Collector dated 30th October 1977 was not illegal and void. [754 D B] 1:3. Under Section 181 of The Code, a 'Public lessee' is defined as a person who holds land from the State Government or the Collector and who is not entitled to hold land as an owner under the new lease or any other law in force at the time of the grant of that lease. [750 D] 1.:4. Under section 181(1) of the old Code, the 'Public Lessee' has been defined as meaning a person holding land from Government or by whom he is granted by the State or the Central Government or any local authority and includes a Government lessee in respect of such land. [751 G] 2.1 In the instant case, the appellant was holding over as a licensee under the original lease. The question whether the Company could be deemed to be holding over on the expiry or after the expiry thereof does not arise for consideration in this appeal. [753 H] 2:2. Under sub section (1) read with section 181, the Collector is empowered to make an order directing the eviction of a tenant from the said lands and the Collector has no power to make any order for the recovery of possession of such lands. The appellant was not entitled either to continue in possession or to remain as a 'owner' under the fresh lease. Under subsection (2) of section 181 the Collector can make an application to the Collector within the period prescribed by sub section 2 of section 182 and the said period has been extended by the Government by notification. [764 G] 3.1 Section 181(3) of The old Code provides that a 'Private Company' is deemed to have been holding land under the State.

The Travancore Act 14 of 1124 (M.E.) was passed by the State Legislature on July 1, 1949 and it received the assent of the President on August 15, 1949. The Madras Legislature passed the Travancore Act 13 of 1125 (M..E.) in exercise of the powers conferred by section 1(3) of the principal Act. Under section 1 (3), the Government of the United State was empowered to make rules for carrying out the purposes of this Act and that power was exercised by the Governor of the State on August 16, 1949, and was repealed by the Madras Legislature on August 17, 1950. The second proviso to article 31A(1) was in operation on July 11, 1949 when the United States was formed. The third proviso to section 1 of the Principal Act was in force on July 10, 1949; but the power to make a law for the time being in force was exercisable by the successor State. The High Court held that the second proviso was not applicable to the case in hand and that the power under section 1 1(2) was not exercised by a competent authority. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the provisions of Ch. IV were not in operation at all, and therefore the State Government could not be said to have the power conferred by any law for time being, in force until a notification was issued, and since no notification was made before Ch. III of the Act was repealed, there was no ceiling limit applicable to that case. HELD: (1) The second Proviso to article31A(l)(b) was introduced only with effect from July 1 1949 and not with effect on and from July 10 1949. [505 G] (2) The power to bring into force the provisions in Ch. V of the Constitution is exercisable by a successor State, and as such the power of the successor States under section I(3)(a) was exercisable only by the Government. [506 H] (3) The proviso to s. 1 1 (2), which was introduced with effect form July 10 1956, did not apply to the cases in hand. The power conferred on the successor states to make laws for the purpose of carrying out purposes of the provisions mentioned therein was a power in force only until a notified order was issued and was then repealed. [605 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1124 of 1966. Appeal by special leave from the judgment and order dated April 17, 1964 of the Kerala High Court in O.P. No. 14 of 1965. S. T. Desai, K. R. Nambiar and P. C. Bhartari for the appellant. M.C. Setalvad, Attorney-General of India, B. Sen, D. N. Mukherjee, and S. K. Das, for the respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Shah J. This appeal is directed against the judgment dated April 18, 1964 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court of Kerala in Writ Appeal No.. 14 of 1963. The appellant is a firm carrying on business at the head office of the Travancore State. It filed an application before the High court under article 226 of the constitution for the issue of a writ of certiorari to quash the order dated August 17. 1950, passed by respondent No. 1, the Commissioner of Income-tax, Kerala, in exercise or purported to be of the power vested in him under section l(3). The appellant contended that the impugned order was not an order made by the Commissioner under section 2(1)(a), and that it was not a law in force at all.

The widow of a Hindu widow of her husband died in the year 1955. She was a widow of the deceased husband. The widow executed a deed of gift in favour of the appellant, which was registered on April 1, 1956. On May 5, 1957, the widow executed an agreement to sell the property to the appellant. The sale deed was executed by the widow in favour her husband. On June 30, 1958, the appellant filed a suit for possession and recovery of possession against the widow. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the widow had no right to redeem the property during the widow's life time. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decree and held that the appellant was entitled to recover possession from her husband on the basis of the surrender made by the wife. In second appeal, a Division Bench of the High court held that in view of the provisions contained in Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, the estate of a widow is not liable to be surrendered to the reversioner and that the reversioners were entitled to redeem her properties on payment of the price thereof. The appellant filed an appeal against this judgment before this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The right of the widow to challenge the surrender by the husband was not extinguished by a surrender made subsequently by the deceased. [532 H] 1.2 In view of Section 6(3) of the Act, the reversioners are entitled to file an application for setting aside the order of the court and in case of alienation by a Hindu female, she is entitled to challenge it on the ground that the transferor has not made any such transfer. [506 G] 1: 2.1 In view thereof no question of fraud or collusion arises. The right conferred on the widow under Section 6 is only an incident of the estate and not a vested interest in her own property. [632 H; 506 A] 1 Whether a surrender is a voluntary act on the part of the husband, whether it is by a female Hindu widow or by a stranger acquiring title by adverse possession against her will is a question of fact. The court has no jurisdiction to impose conditions on the reversionary right of recovery of the property. The courts below were in error in holding that in the case before us no equitable considerations arise at all. [504 G] 2.2 The widow was not entitled to claim any interest in the properties during her lifetime on the principle of surrender by her husband and she is not entitled for any equitable consideration.

The appellant, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913 (hereinafter referred to as "the Companies Act") was formed with the object of carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling cotton textiles in the State of Uttar Pradesh. The Cotton Mills Company had been registered as a society under the Societies Registration Act, 1860. The Society was registered under the [Societies Registration Act] and it was registered as an Association of the members of the Society. The appellant was appointed as a Managing Director of the said Society on March 31, 1963. On April 1, 1964, the Cotton Mills Co. Ltd., the Cotton Mill Company, the appellant filed a petition before the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution praying for a writ quashing the order dated May 2, 1964 passed by the Collector of Kanpur in exercise of his powers under section 169 of the Act and also for a direction to the State Government to hold an inquiry into the affairs of the Cotton mills. The High Court held that the order of the Collector was not in accordance with law and quashed the order. On appeal by special leave, the matter was placed before this Court. HELD: (i) The order passed by this Court on February 1, 1985 was not a decree or order passed under section 168 of the Indian Contract Act. [655 G] (ii) The High court was in error in holding that the Collector had no jurisdiction to pass an order under section 170 of the Income Tax Act. The order dated April 2, 1965 passed by him was not an order passed on a petition filed by the appellant before the Collector and therefore it could not be treated as an order in exercise or purported to be made under section 17AA of the Industries (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951. [755 G B] (iii) The power conferred upon the State Legislature under Article 227 of the constitution is a legislative function and the High Courts have no jurisdiction in respect of such matters. [750 A] (iv) The appellant had not challenged the validity of the order passed in exercise o the powers under article 226 of Constitution. [751 G] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1579 of 1985. From the Judgment and Order dated 2.2.1985 of the Allahabad High Court in Misc. Writ Petition No. 890 of 1964. S.K. Bagga, R.N. Sachthey and B.D. Sharma for the Appellant. M.C. Bhandare, A.S. Bhasme, P.H. Parekh and Ms. Rani Chhabra for the Respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by KASLIWAL, J. This appeal is directed against the judgment dated February 2, 1985 passed by a Division Bench of the High court of Allahabad in Writ Petition Nos. 891 of 1964 and 890/64. The facts giving rise to this appeal are as follows: The appellant is a society registered under section 13(2) of the Societies Act. It has been established with the aid of its members by the Society on the basis of the membership of the society. The society was formed in accordance With the provisions of the [Industrial Employment (Development & Regulation) Amendment Act, 1964] (hereinafter called 'the Act') and it is a statutory body constituted under section 18AA of that Act. Section 18AA provides for the appointment of an Administrator to be appointed by the State Govt. in consultation with the Board of Directors of the Company. The appointment of the Administrator was made on the recommendation of the Board. The State Government has also issued a notification dated April 1 9, 1964 under section 19(1) of that act. Section 19(2)(b) provides for appointment of a Receiver to be called the Committee of Management of the Cooperative Society. Sub-section (3) of section 19 provides that the Administrator shall appoint an administrator in accordance therewith.

The plaintiffs filed a suit for declaration that the land in question was shamlat deh and they had purchased the same from the Panchayat. The Panchayat had also prayed for a decree for possession of the said land. The trial court held that the plaintiffs were entitled to the relief claimed by them. The High Court dismissed the appeal and affirmed the judgment of the trial court. In this case, the plaintiffs filed an application under section 13 of the Act praying that the suit land be declared as shamlat Deh. The Collector passed a decree in favour of the plaintiffs on the basis that the Panchayat was entitled to possession of it. The plaintiffs filed second appeal before the High Court which was dismissed by the impugned judgment. Hence this petition. It is contended by Mr. S.K. Jain, learned counsel for the petitioners-appellants that the High court had erred in holding that the property in question belonged to the Panchayat as shamilat deh and that the Gram Panchayat had not been impleaded as a defendant. The suit was filed against the Panchayat and the Panchayat had no right or title in it. It was further contended that the civil court had jurisdiction to try such suits. The learned counsel also submitted that the trial Court had erred by holding that there was no evidence on record to show that the plaintiff had purchased any land from the panchayat. In support of this contention, the learned counsel placed reliance upon the decision of this Court in [Ramanlal vs State of Gujarat] , referred to and relied upon. The facts of that case were that the defendant filed a civil suit against the Gram Panchayats for declaration and possession of their property which was decreed by the trial Judge. The plaintiff filed an appeal before this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The High court has erred in law in holding the Panchayat to be entitled to possess the land as shamat deh. [652D] 1.2 In the instant case, it is not disputed that the panchayat had been impleaded in the suit filed by the plaintiffs. It cannot be said that the Civil Court had jurisdiction under section 11 of the Code to try the suits. [650E] 1:3 The High Curt has erred by observing that the provisions of sections 13A and 13B of the Haryana Act have been inserted by the Haryana Legislature into the Act. [663F] 1.:4 In view of the fact that the dispute in this case was a civil dispute, it cannot be held that there is no evidence to show whether the Panchayat has purchased any property from the Gram panchayat or not. The Gram Panchayat has not been shown as a party to the suit. The question whether the plaintiff has acquired any right or not does not arise at all. [664F] 2:1 In view thereof, the civil Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit and the High C court was wrong in holding otherwise. [662G] 2.2 The provisions of section 13B have been introduced into the statute by the State Legislature into a Act. The provisions contained in sections 13B and 13C of the Punjab Act have not been amended so as to make it applicable to the facts of this case. [661F] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1533 of 1989. From the Judgment and Order dated 16.8.1989 of the High Courts of Punjab & Haryana at Chandigarh in C.M. No. 11090/89. S K Jain, M.K Sharma, R.N. Singh, V.K Jain, P.C. Kapur, B.D. Sharma, Ms. A. Subhashini and Mrs. A Verma for the Appellant. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by RANGANATHAN, J. This appeal is directed against the judgment dated 16th August 1989 of the Division Bench of the Delhi High Court in Civil Appeal Nos.

The petitioners are the consumers of electricity in the State of Rajasthan. They were granted energy by the Electricity Board to the consumers on credit with the Board. The Board issued a demand notice for payment of interest on the amount deposited by the consumer as security deposit. The petitioners filed an appeal before the Appellate Authority, which was dismissed. The respondent filed a writ petition challenging the order of the Appellate authority and also challenging the validity of the demand notice. The High Court held that the demand was illegal and quashed the demand. It was further held that in view of the provisions of Section 49(1) of the Act, it is not open to the Board to impose an unreasonable restraint on the consumer from charging interest at the rate of 12% per annum on the security deposit deposited with the Electricity board. The Court also held that there was no special reason why interest should be allowed as a reasonable demand. In this case, the Board has been directed to allow interest at 3 per cent per annum. The question whether the conditions of supply were not so unconscionable as to shock the conscience of the Court was not considered by the High Court. The appellants filed an application for review before the High court which was also dismissed. Hence this appeal. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 Section 49 of the Electricity Act is a beneficial provision and it provides that in case of default in payment of any amount due under the supply or on account of interest, interest at 12% shall be payable. [675 H] 1.2 The provisions of section 49 are not so harsh as to meet the ends of justice. It is only when there is a revision in the rate or tariff that it should be considered by a Court. If there is no revision in any amount, interest on security deposit can be allowed. [775 G] 2.1 The High court was in error in holding that the interest should not be allowed at the rates of 12%. [676 H] 2:2 In the instant case, it was not open for the respondent to impose a reasonable restraint. The conditions of the supply were also not so unfair as to make the demand unreasonable.

The petitioners are direct recruits to the Telecommunication Research Centre. They were appointed as Assistant Directors in the Telecommunications Research Centre on 1.1.1973 and they were promoted as Deputy Director, Assistant Director and Scientific and Technical Officers Grade I respectively with effect from 1.4.1974. The posts of Deputy Director and Assistant Director were redesignated as Assistant Director (Selection Grade) and Assistant Directors (Selection grade). The petitioners were appointed to the post of Assistant Director in the Telecom Research Centre in the year 1973. They joined the Tele Communication Centre on or about 1.7.1973. Thereafter, they were transferred to the Indian Telecommcommunication Service with effect form 1.9.1974 and they continued to work in the said service till their retirement on 31.3.1978. The petitioners filed a writ petition before the High Court of Delhi challenging the validity of the Recruitment Rules. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the petitioners were entitled to be promoted as Assistant director in the Telephone Communication Centre with effectfrom 1.10.1974, and that they should be paid the special pay at the same rates at which it was paid to the transferred officers. The appellants filed a Writ Petition before this Court challenging the constitutional validity of Rule 8(1) of the Indian Telegraph Service (Recruitment) Rules, 1954. This Court held that the said rule was ultra vires the Constitution and quashed the recruitment rules. It was further held that in view of the decision of this Court in [Union of India v. S.K. Sharma] , the petitioners are entitled to special pay as they were appointed by way of promotion to the posts of Assistant Directors, Selection Grade and Assistant Managing Director with effect on 1st July, 1973. The said judgment was challenged before this court by filing a Special Leave Petition. This court held that Rule 8 (1) was ultravires the Constitution. It is further held by this Court that in the case of promotion as Assistant Manager, the petitioners cannot be denied special pay for the period they were holding the posts. In view of this decision, the writ petitions were allowed and the respondents were directed to grant special pay to the petitioners with effect froth from 1st August, 1973, and to continue to pay it in future also as long as the transferred officer continued to get it. The present appeals are filed against the judgment of the High court. Allowing the appeals, HELD: 1. The power under Article 226 of the Constitution is not exercised by this court for denying special pay or special pay which is paid to a person who was appointed by promotion to a post in the service. [775 H] 2.1 The petitioners are not entitled to any Special Pay as they have been promoted as Assistants Director and the Special Pay at the relevant time. They cannot be deprived of the special Pay for the said period. [750 A] 2(i) The power to deny special pay is a discretionary power which can be exercised by the Court only in exceptional circumstances. It cannot be exercised for denying the special allowance to the persons who were appointed on or after 1st January, 1973 and who continued to hold the posts till their superannuation on 31st March, 1978. [751 B] 2.(ii) The petitioners have not been able to show that they are entitled for special pay in addition to their scale of pay. [751 D] 3.2 The power of this court under Article 32 is not an extraordinary power which could be exercised only by the Supreme Court. It can be invoked by the petitioners only if the petition is filed before this High Court. [764 G] 3.(i) In the case on hand, the Special Leave Petitions were dismissed by this Hon'ble Court and the petitioners have no right to claim special pay under Article 14 of the constitution.

The appellant was employed as a clerk in the office of the respondent, and he was dismissed from service on the ground that he had been guilty of misconduct. The respondent filed an application before the Labour Court under section 42(1) of the Act for reinstatement with back wages. The Labour Court held that the order of dismissal passed by the appellant was illegal and directed reinstatement of the workman with back-wages. On appeal, the High Court set aside the order and remitted the matter to the Labour court for fresh disposal in accordance with law. In this appeal, it is contended on behalf of the appellant that the Labour Courts have no jurisdiction to decide any dispute between the parties regarding an order passed by a Labour Court in respect of an order, matter or change referred to them under section 7 8 (1) and an employee who has been dismissed, removed, dismissed or retrenched, cannot be said to have committed any misconduct. It was further contended that the respondent had not been given an opportunity to show cause against the proposed action taken by him and that he was guilty of a serious misconduct. On behalf of respondent it was contended that in view of the solemn assurance given to this Court by Mr. K.B.N. Summary, the Labour Commissioner was justified in directing reinstatement with full back wages and that the appellant should not be allowed to continue with the proceedings. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The order of the Labour Officer dated December 10, 1970 is illegal and without jurisdiction. [775 H] 2. The Industrial Court has no jurisdiction under section 78(1)(b) of Act to decide whether an order of termination of service passed by an employer in a case where it was for misconduct committed by the employee which was not established or if it was possible to come to any agreement and an application to the labour court could only be resorted to after efforts had been made to settle the dispute. [750 H] 3. The scheme of section 78 (1)(a) is that disputes covered by paragraph A of sub section (1), (b) or (c) of section 78 must be settled as far as possible and primarily through conciliation and agreement, it does not stand to reason that an employee should be able to end the proceedings in terms of the proviso to sub section(4) of Section 7 8. [751 H] 4. The provisions of section 79(1), clause (b), sub section 2 of section 80, sub section 3 of section 81 and sub section 5 of section 83 are attracted only when an employee is dismissed or removed or dismissed or terminated in accordance With the proviso. [753 G] 5. In the instant case, the respondent was not given an option to continue in service after a proper enquiry into the allegations made against him by the employer. The appellant had no opportunity to prove that he should be deemed to have been dismissed from services. [764 H] 6. The question whether an employee has committed any act or omission in relation to the matters covered by sub section 1 of section 8 is a question of fact and not one of law. [754 G] 7. The High Court was right in holding that the provisions of sub sections (1-A) and (3) of [section 78(2)] are attracted when an order for reinstatement is passed against an employee, and that such an order can only be passed after a due enquiry into allegations made by the respondent. [752 H] 8. The proviso to section 7 does not apply where an employee was dismissed or discharged or terminated without holding any inquiry. [758 G] 9. The expression 'dismissal' in sub section 4 of section 10 is wide enough to include removal from service and termination of services of a workman who has not been dismissed or discharge or dismissed, as the case may be, shall not be deemed for all purposes to have taken place during the period of his dismissal or discharge, as required by that proviso. The appellants filed a suit for eviction of the respondents from the premises in question on the ground that they were tenants under the landlord. The respondent No. 1 was the tenant of the appellants. On the expiry of the period of one year prescribed by section 12(3) of the Act, the appellants instituted an application before the Munsif praying that the order passed by him be set aside and the matter be remanded to the trial court for fresh decision in accordance with law. The respondents filed a written statement contending that the tenancy was not terminated by the landlord on the expiry or the period specified in section 12 of the said Act, but it was terminated by way of an application under section 12 (3) and as such the order of eviction passed by the Munsif was illegal. The trial court held that the appellants were tenants within the meaning of section 2(1)(d) of Act No. 58 of 1972 and accordingly dismissed the suit. On appeal, the High Court set aside the decree passed by both the courts below and remanded the case to the District Judge for fresh disposal in accordance therewith. In the second appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that section 12 is a complete code in itself and as the order under section 11 or 12 has not been made by the court, the order should be treated as one passed under section 39 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that section 39 is a part of the statute and as it provides for an appeal against an order passed under [section 12], the order must be treated to be one passed by a court. [675 H] 2. Section 12(1) of this Act does not confer any power on the Court to make an order which is in excess of the powers conferred by section 39. The question whether section 12 has been made out or not was not considered by the High court and it was held that section 11 of the Bihar Act, 1947, must be read as a whole and as we have held that there is no point in asking the appellants to file an application for setting aside the order dated 30th May, 1972. [775 H; 776 B] 3. The provisions of section 12 are not exhaustive and they do not confer power on any Court to give effect to the provisions of the law. Section 39 is only a part and not a complete Code in itself. [750 D] 4. The order passed in appeal by the appellate court was illegal and without jurisdiction. [751 G] 5. The provision of section 39 does not create an absolute bar on the exercise of power by the Court. It merely provides for a procedure which is mandatory. [753 H] 6. Section 11 of Act, 1958, must receive the same construction as that of section 11. [764 D] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1566 of 1972. The appellant was the Secretary of the Society. The Society was registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860 and it had been functioning as a Secretary of that society. On March 31, 1966, the Society filed an application before the Registrar of Cooperative Societies for withdrawal of the suit under section 15 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The appellant contended that he was not a party to the compromise petition filed by the Society and that the trial court had no jurisdiction to cancel the order permitting the withdrawal of suit. The High Court held that Hari Narain Swami was not the Secretary and, therefore, the impugned order was passed on the basis of the consent given by the appellant. On appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) Section 15 1(1)(a) of the Act provides that a party may make an application for withdrawal under section 16 of the said Code of civil procedure, if he satisfies the court that the permission as a fact was not granted by it. [775 H] (ii) The High Courts in C.W.P. Beyond pointing out that Hari Narayan Swami was the elected Secretary and was, therefore entitled to withdraw the suit. [750 A] (iii) The appellant had no locus standi to file the application for withdrawing the suit as a result of the compromise decree. The question whether he was a party or not was a mixed question of law and fact. It was not open to him to make an amendment in his plaint after the withdrawal. [751 B] (iv) The trial court was wrong in dismissing the appellant's application under section 151 of the C.P Code. The order passed by the High Court was erroneous. [751 D] (v) The question as to whether Hari Narain was a Secretary or not and whether he had consented to it, was a pure question of fact. [754 G] (vi) The provisions of section 15 I of the code of Civil procedure are applicable only in cases where the consent is not given by a party. [752 D] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 879 of 1973. From the Judgment and Order dated the 10th May, 1973 of the Bombay High Court in Civl Appeal No, 9 of 1972. S. T. This appeal is directed against a judgment of the High court of Bombay dated October 10, 1973 in First Appeal No 9 of 1973 whereby the High-Court allowed the appellant' application filed under section 152 of the Civil Procedure Code and set aside the order passed on that application. The respondent was the plaintiff before the trial Court. The suit was instituted by the respondent for a declaration that he is a party thereto with a consequential relief. The trial Court dismissed the appellant"s application holding that the suit was not maintainable. The appeal filed by him was allowed and the suit of the respondent was decreed. The defendant filed an appeal to the High, Court against the judgment of acquittal passed by it in the first appeal. The State Government preferred an appeal against the order of acquittal before this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD (1) The order of the trial Judge dismissing the application under [section 152] of the CPC was erroneous and liable to be set aside. [764 G] 2. Section 15 I(1) of Code of Criminal Procedure is applicable only when the consent in writing given by an accused is not a necessary party.
