The appellant was a member of the Indian Civil Service and was appointed to the Indian Police Service on April 1, 1946. He was promoted as Deputy Superintendent of Police in the year 1947. On May 27, 1947, he was confirmed in the Indian Administrative Service with effect from April 1,. 1946. On June 28, 1948, he filed an application before the Chief Minister for a writ of quo warranto against the appellant and the High Court dismissed his petition on July 11, 1949. The appellant then applied to the High court for a certificate under Article 132(1) of the Constitution for being appointed as a member in the State Civil Service. On August 28, 1950, the High-Court allowed the application and quashed the order of the Chief Secretary. On September 30, 1951, the appellant filed an appeal before this Court against the judgment of the High' Court. The question which arose for consideration was whether the appellant could be appointed as member in a State Civil service or as a Member in a Union Civil Service under Article 233 of the constitution of India. HELD: (i) The appellant was not a member at the time when he was appointed as an Assistant Superintendent of police. He had to be confirmed in that post after the declaration of emergency by the President. [675 B] (ii) The order passed by the Chief Justice on September 30., 1951, was in operation between June 27, 1940 and April 1. 1946, and therefore, the period of his duration had to expire on April 28, 1946, i.e., before April 1., 1946. [776 C] (iii) The High Court was wrong in holding that the appellant was entitled to be appointed to a State civil service under Article 234 of the Government of India Act, 1935, and the order passed on September 29, 1951 by the Governor General was not in operation at all. [750 D] (iv) The appointment of the appellant as a District Judge was made by the High Commissioner in exercise of his powers under Section 72 of the 9th Schedule to the Government Of India Act. 1935. [751 G] (v) The period of probation of the petitioner was not fixed and he could be confirmed only after the expiry of the period specified in section 72 of that Act. [753 D] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1566 of 1966. The appellant, a member of the Indian Police Service, was convicted by the Court of Session, on charges under section 302 read with section 34 of the Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the death sentence passed by the trial court. The State filed an appeal against the order of conviction and sentence before this Court. The appellant, who was a member in the Indian Administrative Service, challenged his conviction and the sentence imposed on him by the Sessions Judge. The learned Judges of the High Court held that the death penalty and the judicial discretion vested in the Court regarding its imposition on an accused were 'erroneous' in principle 'and not 'indicative of an improper exercise of discretion '. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the High Courts had no jurisdiction to interfere with the sentence passed under section 368(a) of the Code and the Sessions Court had no power to pass any sentence which could be said to have been 'errorised' or 'unfair'. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The appeal must fail on the ground that there was no 'erreous' or "irregularity" in law. [775 H] 2.1 The High Courts were justified in confirming the death sentences passed under sections 302 and 354 of the Criminal Procedure Code read with sections 354(3) and 354(4) of Code of Criminal procedure, 1973. [750 A] 2:2 In the instant case, the appellant was convicted on charges which were 'enoughly' 'erred' in law but in fact he was 'errasided' in that behalf by the High court. [751 B] 3.1 There is no merit in the appeal and it must be dismissed. [753 D] 2(i) The High court has not committed any error in confirming death sentence to any of the two appellants, Dalbir Singh and Kulwant Singh. [754 A] (ii) The conviction and sentences imposed on the appellant are well merited and do not call for any interference.

The appellant was a member of the Indian Police Service. He was appointed as an Assistant Sub-Inspector of Police in the year 1942. On March 31, 1942, he was promoted to the post of Inspector of Police. On April 1, 1942 he was transferred to the State Police Service and on his appointment he was posted at the State police Service. On May 29, 1943, he served as an Inspector of police in the State Government service. On June 30, 1944, he filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the order passed by the State of Mysore. The learned Single Judge dismissed the petition holding that the appellant was not entitled to special leave under Article 136 of the Constitution. On appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The Special Leave Petition is liable to be dismissed on the ground that it was not maintainable. [775 H] (2) The order passed in the writ petition by the High court was not a judgment within the meaning of Article 226 of the constitution. It was not open to the appellant to question the correctness of the findings recorded by the departmental authorities. [750 A] (3) The special leave petition is liable for dismissal on the grounds that the Special Leave Appeal was not competent. [751 B] (4) The High Court was right in holding that there was no material before the Division Bench to show that the departmental proceedings were null and void. [75 H; 75 D] (5) The appellant was entitled to a special leave to appeal under Article 226. [76 E] (6) The question whether the departmental proceeding was null and invalid or not is a matter of trial. It is true that in the present case, the Special leave Petition was filed by the appellant after he had been transferred to this court. But, as the order dismissing the writ petitioner's petition was not an interlocutory order, it could be challenged before the Supreme Court. [754 D] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 15 of 1972. From the Judgment and Order dated the 29th July, 1970 of the Mysore High Court in Writ Petition No. 12 of 1970. S. T. Desai, R. N. Sachthey and B. D. Sharma for the Appellant. V. C. Mahajan, M. K. Ramamurthi, S. P. Nayar and R. H. Dhebar for the Respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Sikri, J. This appeal is directed against a judgment of the High, Court at Mysore dated December 29, 1970 in Writ Appeal No.. 12 of 1971. The appellant is an Inspector in the Government service and he was appointed to the Indian Administrative Service on April 1,. 1942. He served as Inspector of the State Public Service for a period of two years from the date of his appointment. On July 30, 1943 he was reverted to the cadre of Inspector by order dated June 30., 1944. The order of reversion was passed in exercise of powers conferred under Rule 8 of the Central Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1965. The respondent filed a petition before this Court on May 29. 1972 for quashing the order of his reversion. This Court dismissed the writ application holding that it could not be said that there is no material to show as to why the departmental enquiry was null & void. It held that the charge against the appellant did not amount to a misconduct and, therefore, he could not make out a case under Article 227 of theConstitution. The High court also held that there were no materials before it to show how the departmental inquiry was vitiated by any material whatsoever. In this appeal, it is contended on behalf of the appellant that the order dated July 30., 1943, passed by this Court in the Writ Petition filed by him, was not one under Article 32 of the Act and, as such, the High Courts were wrong in holding otherwise.

The appellant, a dealer in the goods of the respondent, filed a writ petition before the High Court of Andhra Pradesh challenging the validity of the contracts between the appellants and the M.M.T.C. The High Court held that the contracts entered into by the appellants with the foreign buyers were not integrated transactions in the course of export. The State Trading Corporation was directed to place the goods on board the ship. The appellant filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the Andhra Pradesh High Court for quashing the order dated December 5, 1982 passed by the respondent. The said writ petition was allowed by the High court holding that the contract between the appellant and the foreign buyer was not integrated with the contracts in question. The appellants challenged the correctness of the decision of the High. Court in a writ appeal before this Court. Allowing the appeals, HELD: 1.1 The contracts entered by the appellant with the M/s. T.C., were not composite contracts in the nature of integrated transactions and they were not interconnected with each other. [775 H] 1.2 The contracts between both the appellants were not a composite contract. They were integrated into one composite contract for export of goods under a separate contract with the appellant. The contracts were not complete as they were integrated. [750 A] 1:3. Under the contracts, the contracts were composite contracts and the purchase by the State Trading corporation was in the case of the appellant's goods. The purchase by it from the mine owner was in course of the export. [751 H] 2.1 There is no evidence on record to show that the goods were not transferred to the foreign seller. The contract between a dealer and the Corporation was not composite. The sales were not in the execution of contracts between a merchant and the corporation. The only evidence produced by the Sales Tax authorities was that the appellant had purchased the goods from the mines owner. [752 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 879 of 1982. From the Judgment and Order dated the 14th July, 1982 of the Andhra High Court in W.P. No. 1223 of 1982 and M.C No. 1 of 1982 in WMP No. 11 of 1982). V.S. Desai, S.K. Bagaria, P.N. Gupta, R.K Jain, K.R. Nagaraja, B.D. Sharma, A.K Gupta, Sridharan, Sreedharan, M.V. Goswami and G.L. Sanghi for the appearing parties. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by FAZAL ALI, J. This appeal is directed against a judgment dated April 14, 1982 in Writ Petition No.1223 of 1983 filed by the dealer. The facts leading to this appeal are as follows: The appellant is a dealer registered under the Andhra Sales Tax Act. He purchased the raw materials from the respondent and sold them to the appellant on board a ship. On the basis of the contract entered into between the parties, the purchase was in progress. The goods were transferred to foreign buyer. The sale by the seller to the buyer was in pursuance of the agreement between the dealer and his foreign buyer and, therefore, the purchases by the purchaser from the appellant were not the first purchase. The second purchase was made by the assessee from the owner of the ship and the second purchase by him from the lessee. The third purchase was also made by him on board an Indian ship. In the course thereof, the goods purchased by the foreign purchaser were transferred in the form of a separate agreement with the lessee and the lessee was liable to pay tax under the Act. The respondent filed a suit for recovery of the amount from the appellants. The suit was decreed by the trial court. The appeal was allowed and the suit was dismissed. The question whether the contracts of sale between the two parties were composite, was not considered in that case.

The appellant was employed as a workman in the respondent-company. He was appointed as a casual worker under the appellant on January 1, 1966. On December 31, 1967 he was retrenched from service by the appellant. The respondent raised an industrial dispute which was referred to the Labour Court for adjudication. The appellant contended that the retrenchment of the respondent was illegal and void and inoperative and that the order of retrenchment was not legal and valid. The Labour Court held that the termination of the services of the workman was illegal, but it was held that he was in continuous service for a period of one year and that he should be deemed to be in continuous employment for a further period of six months. On appeal by the respondent, the High Court held against the appellant and dismissed the writ petition. The Union filed an appeal before this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The order of the Labour court was illegal as it was passed without jurisdiction. [775 H] 1.2 The termination of service of the appellant was not in accordance with law. [750 A] 1:3. The question whether the termination is illegal or inoperative and whether the respondent continued to be a workman for a long period, depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. If there is an ineffective order of termination, it is necessary that he must be in service for one whole year. If the termination was illegal or void, inoperative and inoperative, the question of his being in continuous services for a specified period does not arise. [751 H] 2:1. The High Court was wrong in holding that the appellant continued to remain in service with all consequential benefits. [753 D] 1.:2. In the instant case, the termination order was illegal because it was made without jurisdiction and was void ab initio. [764 G] 2.2 There is no merit in this appeal and it is accordingly dismissed.

The appellant was appointed as a temporary employee in the office of the Deputy Commissioner, Ambala Division, on October 1, 1966. He was confirmed in that post by an order dated March 17, 1955, and he was dismissed from service on April 30, 1955. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging his dismissal. The High Court held that the order terminating his services was not passed under the terms of his employment but under the provisions of the Settlement Officer's order which had been made by the Settlement officer on March 30, 1956. The appeal was allowed and the order passed by Mr. Summary was set aside. In this appeal it is contended by the appellant that the High court erred in holding that the termination of the services of the appellant was not in accordance with the terms and conditions of his appointment and that the provisions contained in the Settlement Office Order dated March 30 1955, were not applicable to him. The order passed on March 17 1955, was an order discharging a public servant, and therefore, there was no stigma affecting the future career of the public servant by the order of termination. It is further contended that the appellant had been appointed as temporary employee and he had been confirmed in his post by the settlement officer on April 10, 1956, and that, therefore, the protection of article 311 (2) of the Constitution was not available to him and, therefore. the order dated April 30 1955 could not be sustained. The respondent contended that in view of the provisions in the settlement office Order dated April 10 1956, the appellant's services were terminated for unsatisfactory work and conduct. The Settlement Officer held that there was a misconduct on his part and that he had no evil consequences. On appeal by the State, Held, that the orders passed by the authorities were not in conformity with the principles of Ram Narayan Das 's case (supra). The order terminating the services was an administrative order which could be sustained only if it was made under the conditions of service applicable to the appellant. The termination of his services could be made only after complying with the provisions relating to the enquiry and the procedure prescribed by the rules governing the conduct of public servants for ascertaining whether disciplinary action should be taken against them. The provisions contained therein were not attracted to him, because he was a temporary servant. The fact that the appointment of the temporary employee was terminated on April 1, 1955 did not affect his right to hold the post and therefore the protection given by article 311(2) could not have been invoked in favour of the respondent. The decision in Ram Narayan Dass's case (1) was not applicable as the appellant did not satisfy the requirements relating to a probationer or an order terminating him for unsatisfactory performance of duties. The appointment of a temporary government servant was not a termination simpliciter but was only a termination simplicitor and not on the ground that it was in violation of any provision of the statute. The view taken by the High. Court was erroneous. The State Government had no authority to terminate the services without complying with provisions relating thereto. The orders passed on April, 10, 1955 were an order discharge simpliciter. The question whether there was any stigma affecting his future career was not decided in the present case. The second proposition of law is well settled that if a person is appointed as an employee and has been confirmed by an authority under the rules, he cannot be dismissed from the service without holding a regular enquiry.
