The appellant, a candidate for the post of Professor in the college, was appointed as a Reader in the College on November 15, 1968. He was selected by the Commission for appointment to the post. The State Government issued rules on November 16, 1968, for selections to be made to posts of Professors in the colleges. The Commission was required to interview all or any of the candidates, including the appellant, who had secured the highest marks in the written examination and also the minimum qualifying marks in respect of the viva voce test. The appellant was selected for appointment as a Professor in a college on November 17, 1968 and he was appointed to the said post on November 18, 1968 on the basis of the recommendation made by the Selection Committee. On December 14, 1968 the State Government referred the selections to the Commission under section 133 of the Constitution. The selection was made by it for appointment of Professors. The Selection Committee was constituted in terms of section 133(2) of the Act and the Commission was appointed on November 19, 1968 as a member of the Commission. On January 22, 1969 the State government issued rules for selections of Professors to posts in colleges. In accordance with the provisions of section 134 of the said Act, the Commission made selection by the State of the persons who had obtained the highest percentage of marks in written examination or interview and were selected by it. The appointment was made on November 29, 1968 by the Government. On April 1, 1969, the appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the rules. The High Court held that the selection made by itself was invalid for that reason. It further held that there was no infirmity in the selection and the selection was valid for that reasons. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Commission had not been consulted before making the selections and that the Selection committee was not consulted in the manner required by section 133 (2) (b). Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The power under section 134(1)(b) is a special power conferred upon the State to make rules for the purpose of carrying out the provisions contained in the Constitution and it cannot be exercised for any other purpose. [557 G] 2. The rules made by a statutory body are not required to be consulted before they can be said to have been duly followed. The rule making authority is required to consult the Commission before making selection. It is not necessary that the rules should be consulted in regard to the suitability of the candidate for promotion as Professor. [506 G] 3. The provisions contained therein are not mandatory and the Selection Board was constituted by the Governor under section 136 of the constitution. [504 D] 4. The procedure prescribed by section 134 (2)(b), which is a general rule, cannot be said in any way to have complied with the requirements of section133(1) (a). [566 G] 5. The proviso to section 133 makes it clear that the power under sub section (2), is not required by the rules to be exercised by the appointing authority for making appointments to posts and services of persons other than the members of the service. [657 H] 6. The provision contained in section 133 is mandatory and does not require that the appointment should be made on the recommendation of the Selection body. [UDF] 7. The requirement of consultation with the Commission in regard thereto is mandatory. [546 G] 8. The expression "in the opinion of the appointing Authority" used in section133 (1) has to be construed as meaning "in his discretion". [546 H] 9. The word "in" occurring in section 134 is not a general word and it should be understood in its ordinary sense. [547 A] 10. The words "in my opinion, the selection of the members for appointment" used therein are "in their opinion" and not "in any way". [548 G] 11.

The petitioner was elected to the Legislative Assembly of the United Kingdom on January 26, 1950. He was elected as a member of the House of Commons of the Parliament of the said United Kingdom and was elected in the year 1951. The petitioner challenged the election of the respondents on various grounds including that the proceedings were not conducted in accordance with the provisions of article 194(3) of the Constitution. The High Court held that the petitioner had failed to prove that he was a member or a member thereof, and that the House had no privilege to prevent publication of its proceedings without the authority of the Speaker. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the petition was not maintainable in view of the provisions contained in article 194 (3) as it stood prior to the Constitution, and, therefore, the petitioner was not entitled to succeed. The respondents were not members of the Assembly of a State, but they were members of a House of the Legislature of a States, and their acts or proceedings could be brought before the House only by virtue of the powers conferred on the Speaker under article 194. The provisions of section 3(1) of that Act were applicable to the petitioner as he was not a member, and the proceedings could not be brought in respect of the same matter. The petition was maintainable in law. The question whether the petitioner is a member and a member was a matter for the legislature to decide, and if so, whether it was open to the Legislature to make any order or issue in that behalf. The words "any person" were not defined by the Constitution and, as they were not included in the definition of "person", they must be construed accordingly. The word "person" is not defined in the Constitution but it has been used in the context of article 19(1)(a) to (e).

The appellant was appointed as a Reader in the Government College on April 9, 1966. He was confirmed in that post on July 30, 1970 and was drawing a salary of Rs.600/ per month. On June 10, 1971, he was promoted to the post of Reader. The Respondents were appointed as Readers in the College on May 7, 1972. They were confirmed in the post on April 8, 1973. On August 9, 1974, the Government issued an order under Rule 5(1) of the Orissa Education Service Rules, 1975, appointing the Respondents as Readers and directed them to be confirmed in their respective posts. The Appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the said order. The High Court held that the appointment of the Respondents was not on probation but on the ground that they were not eligible for appointment as Readers. It further held that since the Respondents had completed the prescribed period of service, their services could be considered for appointment to the posts of Reader and that the Appellant should be deemed to have been appointed as Reader in Government College. The said decision was challenged by the Respondents in a writ appeal before this Court. Allowing the Appeal, HELD: 1.1 The High court was right in holding that the Respondents were not entitled to be considered as Readers for appointment on the post. [775 G] 1.2 The Appellant was appointed on April 10, 1973 and he was drawing salary of a sum of Rs,600/and odd per month from July 30 1970. He had completed his prescribed period. The question whether he should be treated as a Professor or Reader in any Government College is not one of fact but it is a matter entirely for the due and proper consideration of the Public Service Commission. [750 G] 2.1 There was no justification for the Respondents to have appointed the Respondents on April 7, 1973 as Readers on May 10, 1972 and they were confirmed by the Public Services Commission in their appointments. The appointment of Respondents was made on April 6, 1973, and he could not be considered to be a Reader. [751 G] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1579 of 1977. From the Judgment and Order dated the 14th July, 1976 of the High court of Orissa at Cuttack in OJC No. 975 of 1972. S.K. Bagaria, P.C. Bhartari, M.N. Shroff, for the Appellant. V.M. Tarkunde, K.R. Nambiar, R.P. Singh and B.B. Singh for Respondent No. 1. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by RAY, J. This appeal is directed against a judgment dated April 14, 1976 passed by the High Curt in Writ Petition No.975 of 1973. The appellant was working as Reader on May 11, 1972 in Government college, Cuttack. He joined the Government college on July 10, 1970. On September 9, 1971 he was confirmed as a Readers in Government Colleges. On October 15, 1971 the Respondents filed an application before the Public service Commission for being appointed as Professors of Government College, Cuttack, to be appointed as Lecturers in Government colleges. The Public Service commission rejected the said application by its order dated November 14, 1972 on the grounds that the said appointment was not made on the basis of any selection or on the recommendation of the Selection Committee. On December 9, 1972 the Respondents moved the High Courts under Article 226 and 227 of the Constitution for a writ in the nature of mandamus directing the Public services Commission to appoint them as Readers from time to time. The learned Single Judge dismissed the said petition holding that there was no merit in the contention raised by the Appellant that he was appointed only on April 5, 1973 on May 8, 1972, and that he could be treated to have continued in service for a period of more than six years.

The appellants were appointed as drivers in the State Transport Authority, Madras. They applied for a temporary permit to ply their vehicles on the route for which they had applied for. The scheme was published by the Corporation under section 68F(1) of the Act and the scheme was approved by the State Government. On the basis of the approved scheme, the Corporation issued an order in exercise of power conferred by section 68 F(1)(C) read with section 68D(A) of that Act. The appellants applied for temporary permits to ply the vehicles on their route for a period of one year and thereafter they were granted temporary permits. On receipt of the applications, the State Road Transport Authority passed an order on 30th June, 1976, granting temporary permits in favour of the present appellants. On 7th July, 1976 the Corporation made an application for grant of temporary permit in respect of the area or route specified in the scheme and the Corporation granted temporary permit on the basis that the scheme had been published in respect thereof. The State Transport Appellate Tribunal and the High Court held that the permits were valid and they were entitled to ply vehicles on that route. On appeal by special leave, the appellants contended that the schemes were not published in the prescribed manner and therefore the Corporation was not entitled to grant temporary permits under section68F(2) of Act. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the permit issued to the present appellant was valid and the State transport Authority had no power to grant such a permit. [675 H] 2.1 The scheme is published in accordance with section 69-C of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939. Section 68F (1) provides that the State Roadways Authority may grant temporary permit for any area or class of vehicles specified in Schedule I to the Scheme and the conditions subject to which such permits are granted shall be as follows: "68F. Grant of temporary permits.- (1)(a) The State Government may, after considering the application made by the existing operators under section 69C(2), grant temporary stage permit to any person who is not eligible for the grant of a temporary permits or to any other person willing to operate vehicles to the maximum number of seats specified in that behalf by the said scheme. (b) The scheme shall be published in such manner as may be prescribed." [682 H] 3.1 In the instant case, the scheme is not published either in accordance therewith or in accordance With section 68-F(3)(a). It was published in terms of section 69D(B) of Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Act, 1976. The appellant applied for grant and renewal of temporary stage permits to the existing operator on the same route. [650 A] 3:2. Section68F (4) provides for grant or renewal of a permit to the new operators on the following conditions: "(1)(b) If the existing permit is not issued in accordancewith section 68C(1), the State government may, if it considers necessary, after giving an opportunity of hearing to the applicant, pass such orders as it deems fit." [650 D] 3(c) The High court was right. [643 H] 4.1 It is true that the Scheme is not a part of the scheme but it is a part and parcel of the Scheme. The Scheme is published by notification in accordance wit h the provisions of section 68B(1). [685 D] 4(d) The Scheme has to be published under section 70C(3) of Chapter V of the said Act. [786 H] 5.1 Section 68-D (4)(a), as amended, provides that no permit shall be granted in respect or renewal thereof for any period after the date of publication of the draft scheme. [750 B] 5.(e) The schemes are not published under sections 68C and 69D.

The appellant was a minor. He executed a will dated January 11, 1934 in favour of his maternal grandfather. The said will was registered on the basis that he had a son and a daughter. On March 31, 1934, the appellant filed an application for grant of probate in respect of the estate of the deceased. The High Court held that the property in suit was ancestral property and that the appellant was entitled to challenge the validity of the will. The appellant contended that the said will dated March 31., 1934 was not binding on him as he had no right to challenge it. It was further contended that under the Hindu law, a Hindu widow is entitled to maintain her sons against his maternal grand father and that in view of the provisions of section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, she cannot be given any rights in respect thereof. The trial court held that there was no evidence on record to show that the properties in suit were ancestral property. On appeal by special leave, the High Court reversed the decree of the trial court and dismissed the application for probate filed by the appellant. In this Court, it was contended that section 6(1) of the Act is not applicable to the case as the property inherited from a maternal grandfather is ancestral in the hands of a grandson. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The question whether the property was ancestral or not has to be decided on evidence and the onus lies on the party who seeks probate to prove that the estate in suit is ancestral. [675 H] 2. Section 6(2) of Act I of 1920 provides that a Hindu female shall be entitled to make an application to the Court for grant or refusal of probate or letters of administration in respect, of her property. The section does not say that the court has to decide whether the estate is ancestral or whether it is ancestral property or not. [775 H; 776 A] 3. Section 8 of the Indian Succession Act provides that the provisions contained in Chapter III shall apply to all persons who are not members of a Hindu family and who have no right, title or interest therein. The expression 'family' has been defined in section 2(1)(i) of this Act as meaning any person who is a member of a joint Hindu family. [750 B] 4. Section 9 of the Transfer of Property Act provides for the transfer of property by a female to her husband and not to the wife. The provisions contained therein are applicable only to the persons who have a right, interest in the property which was inherited from the maternal grandfather or father. [751 G] 5. In the instant case, the property is ancestral and the appellant has no right title to it. [751 H; 76 A] 6. Section 10 of the Code provides that where any person is a minor, his guardian shall be competent to make such application for the grant of letters of Administration in respect to the estate or interest of the minor. The proviso to section 10(2)(i), however, does not provide that the Court has to determine whether the right to sue survives on the death of the father. The decision of the High court is erroneous as it was based on a wrong appreciation of evidence and was not based on any evidence. [764 H; 771 A] 7. Section 11 of the Limitation Act provides, inter alia, that where the property has been acquired by a Hindu male or female, the period of limitation for filing an application under section 11 is three years from the date of the acquisition of the property and not five years from such acquisition. [774 B] 8. The right to file an application in respect thereto was not a vested right. It could be exercised only if the person claiming the right had no interest in it. In other words, the right was not vested in the son or daughter of the person who acquired the property. [781 A-B] 9.

The appellant was a member of the Indian Police Service. He was convicted by the trial court and sentenced to death. The prosecution case, as disclosed from the evidence, was that on the night between 10th and 11th June, 1967, at about 6 p.m., he had gone to his house to purchase some articles for him. At that time, he was in a position of trusted by the members of the family of the deceased. He had also taken away the gold ornaments belonging to him from the house of the accused. The appellant was arrested on the same day and was remanded to judicial custody. On the next day, he filed an application for bail before the Sessions Court which was dismissed. The High Court held that the offence under section 307 read with section 34 of the [Indian Penal Code] was not made out against him. It further held that in order to attract the provisions of section 307 of the I.P.C., it must be shown that the act had been done by the accused person, and so, he became punishable under section 302 read with sections 34 and 449 of the IPC. The State filed an appeal before this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The offence under [section 307] read with Section 34 of Indian Penal Code is not made a cognizable offence. It is not established that the accused had committed the entire criminal act. [557F] 2. The provisions of sections 302 and 449 are not attracted in this case. The question whether a person has committed the whole criminal act or not, depends upon the facts of each case. If it is found that the individual act was done by him alone, he becomes punishable under Section 307 readwith section 34 IPC. [506F] 3. The position is different when Matiullah is not acting alone but he and several others are acting jointly in furtherance of the common intention of all of them to kill Ebrar Ali. In order to bring the entire case within the purview of section 302, it must further be shown by the prosecution that the acts had been committed by the individual accused. [504F] 4. The provision of section 34 is not attracted if the act was committed by any one of the persons who were acting jointly with the members or the persons in furtherance thereof. [ 506G] 5. Section 307 of Indian penal Code is applicable only when it is proved that the person concerned had committed an offence under Section 302 readwith Section 34 IPC and so he became liable to be punished under section 324 read with [section 34] of the Penal Code. [UDD] 6. The expression 'in order' in section 34 does not mean 'to commit the whole of the criminal act'. It is only when the individual acts were done by one or more persons, jointly, he become punishable under [sections 302], IPC. If a person had committed a particular offence, he would be liable to suffer imprisonment for life and also liable to fine. [511F] 7. The section does not apply if it is established that a person was in fact accused of an offence. [Section 34] is applicable when the act done by any person is done by another person. [54H; 54A] 8. Section 302 IPC is attracted only when there is evidence to show that the particular act was being done by some other person. The word 'in the context' in the section does indicate that it must mean 'in law'. [55B] 9. The words "in order" in section 302 of the Code are not applicable where the individual offence was committed jointly with a member or persons in pursuance thereof. If the individual is liable to punishment under section 34, he cannot be convicted under section 326 read with the section 34. [56C] 10. Section 34 does apply only when a person is in fact guilty of an act done in furtherance or intention of another person and not otherwise. [57D] 11.

The appellant was a minor. He executed a will dated January 11, 1934 in favour of his daughter, the respondent. The appellant filed a suit for partition and separate possession of the properties in dispute on the ground that the said properties were ancestral and self acquired property of her father. The trial court held that the appellant had failed to prove that the properties were joint family properties and that the respondent was entitled to succeed to the properties as a result of the production of the Riwaj i am of 1913 and, therefore, the appellant was not entitled to claim any share in the said property. On appeal by the respondent, the High Court held that in view of the evidence on record it could not be said that the family of the appellant's father was joint and that she had failed in establishing that the property in dispute was ancestral. The High Court further held that as the appellant has failed to discharge the onus that was cast upon her by the will dated February 11, 1935, the question of the respondent being a minor did not arise. On this finding, the suit was dismissed. In second appeal before this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High court erred in holding that the trial court had failed and that in any event the respondent had failed miserably to prove the special custom of the Punjab which was followed by the appellant in her case. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The High court was right in holding the respondent to be a minor on the date of the alleged production of Riwraj i am the father of the plaintiff and that being so, the trial Court was not justified in holding otherwise. [557 D] (2) The question whether the respondent is a minor or not does not arise at all because the appellant did not prove that she was a major on the day of the marriage. She had failed only to establish that the custom of her husband was not proved by the evidence adduced by the parties. [506 G] (3) The trial Court erred in law in holding, that the suit filed by the father was not maintainable. [657 D C] (4) The respondent having failed to establish the special rules of the Evidence Act, the burden was on her to prove those special rules. [504 E] (5) The finding of the High. Court that the marriage between the appellant and the respondent did not constitute a valid marriage is erroneous. [54 D C; 506 A] (6) The findings recorded by the trial Judge were based on proper appreciation of evidence and there was no error in the judgment of the first appellate court which could be said to have been vitiated by any error of law. [55 G] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 15 of 1972. From the Judgment and Order dated the 14th September, 1970 of the Allahabad High Court in Second Appeal No 12 of 1970. S. K. Sinha, for the appellant. R. N. Sachthey, for respondent No. 1. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Hegde, J. This appeal is directed against the judgment and decree passed by the High Curt in second appeal No. 12 of 1971 dated April 14, 1970. The facts leading to this appeal are these: The appellant was married to one Bal Kishan Singh on January 11th, 1934. She died on February 10, 1934 leaving behind her two sons, namely, Ram Narain and Ram Narain. The respondent filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution in the High Courts of Allahabad and Lucknow Bench praying for a writ of certiorari quashing the order dated April 15, 1970 passed by a learned Single Judge of that Court in second appeals No.12 of 1970 and the order of the learned Single judge dated April 13, 1970 in second suit No. 11 of 1964. The said suit was filed by Bal Kishan Sing, the father, who died on January 10, 1935.

The appellant, a member of the family of one of the sons of the deceased, filed a suit for partition and separate possession of the properties mentioned in Schedule A to the plaint. The respondent contended that the properties described in Schedule B were purchased by him from his father and that he was entitled to execute a power of attorney in respect of all the matters in which he could act as trustee, executor or administrator. The trial court held that the power of Attorney executed by the appellant in favour of the respondent was not valid and that the said power of power of the attorney holder was competent to execute the power in respect thereof. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decree passed by the trial court and dismissed the suit. In further appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the instrument in question did not constitute a deed of conveyance but was executed by him in his individual capacity as trustee and executor of the trust and that therefore he was competent under section 5 of the Act to execute such power of authority. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the document in question constituted a deed executed by one of its executant and that it did not contain distinct matters to be dealt with as such so as to attract the operation of section 5. [557F] 2.1 The power of an attorney holder is not entitled to exercise all these powers in relation to the properties specified in Schedule C to the suit and that is the execution of a general power of agreement by the donor in favour or for his own benefit. [506G] 2(i) The power conferred on the attorney-holder under section 3 of the Indian Registration Act, 1908 was not a power to execute any general power or agreement by himself but was a power which he had to perform and that was not an instrument executed by a person in his personal capacity as such trustee. [657F G] 2.(ii) The document in respect whereof the power was given was not invalid because it did contain distinct matter to be treated as one of several matters to attract section 5 and that being so, the said provision was not applicable to the instrument executed under section 4. [757G] 3.1 It is true that the executant of the deed was a trustee and an executor or an administrator and that in his capacity as trustees, executor and administrator he was also entitled to act for him in all the capacities specified in the said Schedule C. But the power conferred upon the attorney by section 5 was not subject to any other provision of law. [750H] 3.(i) In the instant case, the power given to the attorney was not in his own name but was in his name and that could be done only by a special power of agent. The power given under section 6 of the said Act was not intended to be exercised by the attorney or executor or the executor or administrators of the beneficiary. [751G] (ii) In any event, the instrument was executed on behalf and in the name of the executant and he was bound to perform his duties as trustee. The said power was not required to be used for execution of such power. [753D] 3(i)(a) The question whether the power is a power conferred by section 6 does not arise at all because the power has been given to an attorney or an executor and that would be a matter of contract between the parties. [764F] (iii) In view of the terms of the instrument, the executant was bound by the said clause, and he could execute such instrument only in his favour. [754G] 4.(i)(b) The said provision is not applicable in the present case because the said document did contain separate matters to fall within the category of a deed which contains distinct matters.

The assessee, a firm carrying on business in the State of Bombay, was assessed to income tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, for the assessment year 1948-49. The assessee claimed that depreciation should be allowed as per the provisions of the [Indian Income tax (Amendment) Act, 1949], and that the depreciation should not be allowed if proper claim had been made by the assessee in respect of the assets. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim of the assessee on the ground that the amount of depreciation was allowable under section 10(5) (b) of the Saurashtra Income tax Ordinance, 1949, and that it was not a deductible amount in computing the written down value of the asset. On appeal by the Commissioner of Income tax, the Appellate Tribunal held that the sum of Rs. 1,00,000/- was allowable as depreciation under section 13(5)(b) and the High Court was wrong in holding that the assessee had not claimed depreciation under any law or rules of a Part B State relating to income-tax and super tax or any law relating to tax on profits of business. The Revenue appealed against this decision to this Court. HELD: (1) The words "any law relating" in section 13 of the Ordinance were wide enough to include the depreciation actually allowed under any laws or rules, of a part B State. [675 H] (2) Section 13(4)(b), as it stood before the amendment, provided that the provisions contained in sub section (1A) of section 10 of the Indian Incometax Act, 1961, shall apply to the written off value of assets under any other law or rule of a Schedule Bank. [775 H; 776 B] (3) The word "any" used in section 10 (5) is wide enough and it means that the words "or any law" should be construed accordingly. [750 D] (4) Section 10(6)(b)(i) of Saurashtra Act, 1947, was not applicable to the case before the High Courts. [751 G] (5)(a) The expression "any other law" in sub clause (c) of clause (ii) of sub section 2 of section 13 is wide and it includes any law which has a Part A State relating thereto. [75 H, 75 B] In the instant case, the assessee was assessed under the Saurashtra Act on the basis that the income of the firm was not allowable as per its provisions. The High Court rightly held that there was no question of applying the provisions in sub clauses (c), (d) and (e) of proviso to clause (iv) of subsection 2 of Section 13 of that Act. [76 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1124 of 1972. From the Judgment and Order dated the 30th July, 1971 of the Bombay High Court in Income Tax Reference No. 1 of 1970. S. T. Desai, K. R. Chaudhuri, M. N. Shroff, for appellant. V. C. Mahajan, for respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Shah J. This appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated November 30, 1971 passed by the High court of Bombay in Income tax Reference No 1 of 1971. The facts leading to this appeal are as follows: The assessee is a firm doing business in cotton, woolen goods, and has its head office at Bombay. The assessment year was 1948-48. During the accounting period relevant to the Saurashtra income tax Ordinance 1949, the Act was repealed by the Saurashtra Finance Act, 1950, and the provisions relating to the said Ordinance were made applicable to it. Section 13 (4)(a), as amended by the Gujarat Taxation Laws (Amendment and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act No. 10 of 1970, provided for the depreciation allowance in respect thereof.

The appellant was a contractor for the supply of certain materials and for the construction of the building. The respondent, who was an employee of the appellant, entered into an agreement with the appellant on April 1, 1966 for the execution of certain works in the building and for construction of a new building. On May 2, 1966, the appellant executed a contract for the sale of certain items of materials and materials to the respondent. The appellant completed the work and submitted his tender on June 30, 1966. Thereafter, the respondent filed a suit against the appellant for specific performance of the agreement. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant was not entitled to claim the benefit of the provisions of the Act. On appeal by the respondent, the High Court held that the contract was not in accordance with the provisions contained in the N.I.T. and that the conditions laid down in the said N. I.T., were satisfied. The High Court further held that as the appellant had no knowledge about the terms of the contract, the question of granting him a relief did not arise. On this finding, the suit was dismissed. Hence, this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1. Section 2(a) of the General Clauses Act defines 'agreement' to mean an agreement in writing signed by the parties before the commencement of the work or any part thereof and includes a written document signed by both the parties. [775 H] 1.2. The question whether the contract is in accordance or not, was considered by this Court in [K.P.C. Jain vs Union of India & Ors.] , ; , referred to. 1.3. Section 3(1) of General Clauses (Regulation) Act, 1951 provides that a contract may be in writing and signed by either party before the completion of the works or any parts thereof. The expression 'agreement in writing' is defined in clause (a) to mean a written agreement signed by all the parties to the contract. [750 H] 2.1 The question as to whether the appellant has not fulfilled the requirements of paras III, V and VI of the N.,I. T. and the question whether he had not fulfilled those requirements does not arise in this case because the appellant did not have any knowledge about it. [751 G] 2:2. Section 4(1)(a) provides that where a contract is not in writing but is signed by two or more persons, then the contract may, if the terms thereof are not reduced to writing, be in Form 'B' and the form 'C' shall be used. [75 H; 75 A] 2.(i) The question of whether the agreement was in accordance in law does not depend upon the interpretation of the words "agreement in- writing" or on the construction that the said words are not material for the purpose of determining whether the conditions prescribed by the said clauses are satisfied. [76 H] (ii) If the appellant is entitled to a relief under Section 4, he should be given an opportunity to show cause against the grant of the relief and if he is able to show that he was not satisfied with the terms in the agreement, then he should have been given an adequate opportunity to prove his case. [77 H] 3.1 In the instant case, the contract did not contain any stipulation as to the conditions of the contracts. The contract was in writing. [78 G] 3:2 It is true that the question as regards the applicability of the said provisions does not involve a consideration of the facts and circumstances of each case but it is also well settled that the terms laid down by the two parties are satisfied if they are in accordance therewith. [79 H; 80 A] 3(i) In the present case, there was no stipulation as regards conditions of contract. The agreement did not require that the condition laid down therein was fulfilled. [81 G] (iii)

The appellant was an employee of the respondent, the Custodian General, and was appointed as a Custodian. He was served with a notice under section 6(1) of the Act on the appellant asking him to show cause why he should not be confirmed in his appointment as a custodian. The appellant submitted his reply to the show cause notice. The Deputy Custodian General passed an order dated November 30, 1949, confirming the appellant's appointment as Custodian General. On December 9, 1950, the appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court of Judicature at Bombay challenging the validity of the order of confirmation and also the order passed by the Additional Custodian General on the ground that the order was not in accordance with law and that the orders of confirmation were illegal and void. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant had no jurisdiction to make an application for confirmation under section 27 of the said Act. On appeal, this Court held that the provisions of section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, did not apply to the case. In the result, the High court quashed the order dated December 9 1950 and directed the Custodian to confirm the appellant in his capacity as a public officer. The present appeal by special leave is filed against the said decision of the High. Court. Section 6 of this Act provides that "no person shall be appointed as an Custodian General unless he has been appointed by the Central Government." Sub-section (2) of section 27 provides that no person shall, after the date on which the Central Act XXXI of 1950 came into force, be confirmed as a Public Officer in any case where the Central Legislature has not made any law for the time being in force. Section 27(1)(c) provides that the Custodian shall have power to make such orders and give such directions as may be necessary or expedient for the purpose of giving effect to the order. Sub-sections (2), (3) and (4) of this section are material for our present purpose and they read as follows: "27(1). Where an order is made by the Custodian under sub-section(1), he shall, within a period of six months from the date of such order or such further period not exceeding one year as may have been allowed in that behalf, make an order confirming the appointment of the appellant and the respondent shall be confirmed. (2). Where any person is appointed as Custodian under subsection (1) he shall be deemed to have made an order under sub section (2)."

The Act was passed by the Central Government in exercise of its powers under s. 32 of the Act, and it received the assent of the President on April 1, 1965. The Act provided for payment of bonus to employees in certain circumstances. Section 32(1) of the said Act provided that "no employer shall make any claim for bonus or any other benefit by way of industrial adjudication or otherwise." The Act was amended by the [Industrial Disputes (Amendment) Act] No. 1 of 1965, and s.32(2) was substituted by the Amendment Act No. 2 of 1966. Section 33(1)(b) provided that no employer shall be entitled to claim bonus under the Act on any other ground except as to the payment of such benefit. The effect of this amendment was that the provisions of s.33(1A) were not attracted and so, the Tribunal was right in holding that the Bonus Act was a complete Code and was exhaustive of the subject matter of the statute. The High Court held that the Tribunal had jurisdiction to entertain claims for bonus under s, 32(2)(b). It further held that as the Bonus (Amendment Act No 1 of 1966) did not bar claims for payment by way other than those specified in s. 33(2), it was open to the workmen to make an express provision for bonus and so long as that provision remained in force, the same claim under a different guise (the Shops Act) could be maintained by the workmen. The Tribunal further held: "The question of bonus is not a matter of dispute between the parties but it is a matter which has been left open to them by reason of its provisions." In this appeal, Shri Pai, learned counsel for the appellant, raised two contentions; (1) that the bonus Act was not applicable to the subject-matter of the Bonus Ordinance and so the Tribunal could not have entertained the claim under s 32(l)(b), and (2) that as a result of the amendment made by the Amending Act No 2 of 1967, the bonus scheme was not in force. The first contention is that the Industrial Tribunal had no jurisdiction to adjudicate upon the claim for Bonus under s 33(3). The second contention is also without merit. Section 34 of the Industrial Disputes (Amending) Act, 1962 provides that "No employer shall, make any claims for Bonus or any Other benefit by virtue of any other provision of this Act". The Tribunal was not right in entertaining the claim on the ground that it was barred by the general principles of res judicata. [523D] (3) Section 32 of that Act is a complete code and is exhaustive of all subject matter under which the bonus is payable to the employees. It does not bar the application of the general principle of resjudicata in such matters. The second question, therefore, is answered against the appellant.

The petitioners were appointed to the Superior Judicial Service of Punjab on December 31, 1976. They were promoted as District Judges in the year 1976 and they were confirmed as District Judge in the month of August, 1976 on the basis of the respective dates of confirmation. The High Court by its order dated January 5, 1977 declared that the seniority of the petitioners and respondents 1 to 3 was fixed at the time of their confirmation. On December 31. 1976 the High Court issued a notification fixing the seniority in accordance with rule 12 of the Superior judicial Service Rules of Punjab. The petitioners were promoted to the Higher Judicial Service on April 9, 1976 and their promotion was made as District and Sessions Judges on May 1, 1977. The respondents were appointed by promotion and direct recruits on December 30, 1976, on the ground that they were promoted or appointed to a post in the service on or after December 31 1976. On August 25, 1976 the State Government issued an order fixing seniority of all officers appointed to Superior Judicial Services of Punjab from the date of their appointment. The seniority list was published on September 27, 1976 for the first time and it was published by the High court on October 28, 1976 in respect of the first two vacancies. On November 30, 1977 the High Courts issued a Notification fixing the inter se seniority of officers appointed or promoted to a higher post in accordance With the provisions of rule 12. The State Government also issued another notification fixing seniority in respect to the petitioners. On September 27. 1976, the High courts issued a fresh notification fixing their seniority in terms of rule 8 of the Rules of the Punjab and Haryana High Court. On October 28. 1976 a notification was issued by the Governor of Punjab under Article 309 of the Constitution for the appointment of District Judges on the post of District and sessions Judges. The said notification was published in the Punjab Government Gazette dated November 30. 1976. The appellants filed writ petitions before the High, court challenging the validity of the said notifications. The learned Single Judge dismissed the writ petitions holding that the rules were not in conformity with the provisions contained in rule 12 and the Rules were not violative of Article 14 of the constitution. On appeal to this Court, HELD: 1(i) Rule 12 is a part of the law of the State and does not violate any fundamental right of the appellants. [775 H] (ii) The High Courts have issued a new notification fixing inter se- seniority in pursuance of rule12. The rules are consistent with the principles contained in the said rules. [750 A] (iii) The power to fix the interse seniority is vested in the State under Article 162 of theConstitution and not in any other authority. [751 B] (iv) The rule making power has been conferred on the Governor by Article 309 and it cannot be exercised arbitrarily or capriciously. [75 H; 75 A] 2(i)(a) Rule 8 of Punjab Civil Service Rules, 1963 provides that the service shall be determined with reference to the date from which the rules are made. [76 B] 2.(ii) In the instant case, the rules have been framed by the State of Haryana under Article 234 of the Indian Constitution and they do not violate Articles 14 or 16 of the Act. [77 C] (v) The rules were made in accordance to the provisions in rule 8. [78 D] 3(i). Rule 12 provides that seniority shall be fixed in accordancewith the provisions therein. [79 E] 2.1 The High court was wrong in holding that Rule 12 does not offend any fundamental rights of the appellant. [80 H; 81 A] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1332 of 1977. From the Judgment and Order dated the 14th July, 1976 of the HighCourt of Punjab & Haryana at Chandigarh in C.W.P. No. 1125 of 1976. S.K. Bagga, for the appellants (in both the appeals). V.C.

The State of Andhra Pradesh, by an order dated November 30, 1975, issued a notification under paragraph 3(1) of the Order that the posts of Junior Assistants and Senior Assistant in the Civil Services of the State were abolished. The said notification was published in the Andhra Pradesh Gazette on January 1, 1976. The appellant, who was working as Junior Assistant in Civil Services, was promoted to the post of Junior Assistant on November 30. The promotion order issued by the Government under paragraph 2(1)(e) of G.O.Ms. No. But, as stated earlier, was not challenged by the appellant before the High Court. The High Court held that the notification dated January 1. 1976 was valid and did not suffer from any infirmity. It further held that in view of the provisions contained in paragraph 3 of the order issued under paragraph 4(1), it is clear that the power to organise class or classes of posts was vested in the State Government. The State Government, therefore, could not have exercised the power under paragraph 5 of the said order. The learned Single Judge held that there was no infirmity in the order passed by the State and the appellant was entitled to be appointed as Junior Assistants on November 1, 1975. The Division Bench also held that since the post in question was a cadre comprising of posts belonging to category in which the appellant had been promoted to that category, the power conferred under paragraph 6 of the Government Order dated October 30, 1976 was not exercised by the President and the State could not be said to have exercised its power under the said paragraph. The Letters Patent Appeal filed by the respondent was allowed and the order of the learned Single judge was set aside. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1.1 The Government Order issued on October 30. 1975 is valid and does not suffer any infirmity in law. [775 H] 1.2 In view of paragraph 3 (1) (e), it must be held that it was not necessary for the appellant to hold a post in the cadre of Junior Superintendent or Senior Assistant for the purpose of promotion to the said post. [750 A] 1:3 The power conferred on the State under paragraph 7 of the G. O.Ms., is only to create a division and maintaining separate seniority of Junior assistants and Senior Assistants for the purposes of recruitment, seniority or promotion etc., as the case may be. [751 B] 2.1 In view thereof, the Government order dated October 1, 1974 was valid. The power to create class or categories of posts in the service is vested in State Government and not in the appellant. [752 D] 2:2 It is true that the post held by the Junior Assistant and Senior Superintendent in Civil Service of the respondent is a cadre consisting of posts which are filled up by promotion etc. but the power given to the State to create separate seniority is only for the said purpose. [753 H] 2] In view, however, of the fact that the appellant has been promoted as Junior Superintendent on November 10, 1975 and he was promoted as Senior Assistant on December 30, 1974, it cannot be held by any stretch of imagination that the Government had exercised its powers under paragraph 8 of the letter dated October 29, 1975 in accordance with the provisions of paragraph 4 of the O.M. dated October 20, 1975 issued by Government of Andhra. [754 D] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1579 of 1988. From the Judgment and Order dated 2.2.1988 of the Andhra High Court in W.P. No.. 8774 of 1976. V.S. Desai, S.K. Bagga, R.N. Singh, M.R. Rao, P.H. Parekh, K.V. Mohan, A.K Gupta and B.B. Ahuja for the Appellant. Virender G. Joshi, Ms.

The appellant, who was the mortgagee in possession of a portion of the land in question, filed a suit for redemption of the mortgage. The respondents contended that the mortgagor had no right to redeem the mortgage and that the mortgage was not binding on them. The trial court held that the plaintiff was entitled to redeem his mortgage and accordingly decreed the suit. On appeal by the defendants, the High Court reversed the decree passed by the trial court and dismissed the plaintiff's suit. In this Court, it was contended that in view of the provisions contained in section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act, the mortgagor could not be permitted to redeem a portion only of the property in question. Held: (1) The mortgagor had a right to sell the mortgaged property by sale and he could not have sold the same without the permission of the court; (2) that the mortgagee was entitled under section 52 to redeem an interest in the mortgaged land in the usual course of management, the lease granted by him could not prevail against the plaintiff. The mortgagor was entitled only to the extent of the right conferred on the mortgagee by the Act and the mortgage had got extinguished. (3) that there was no provision for the sale of a part of the mortgaged properties in the ordinary course of the management by the mortgagor, that the provisions of section 52 were not applicable to the grant of a lease by the mortgagee and that as the mortgagor was not entitled to exercise his right of redemption, the mortgage could not operate against him. (4) that in the absence of any provision for sale of Gadi Sirampur including the four villages in question the plaintiff could not get khas possession of the lands in question without the sanction of the Court and the provisions relating to the sale were applicable to grant of permanent lease by a mortgagee.

The respondent entered into an agreement with the appellant for the construction of a building on the land and building. The appellant entered into a contract with the respondent for construction of the building. On the date of the contract, the appellant was in possession of the property. The respondent filed a suit against the appellant in the court of the Subordinate Judge, Ernakulam, for specific performance of an agreement to sell the property on the ground that the respondent had failed to perform his part of the agreement and that the appellant had not paid any amount to the respondent. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the agreement was void as it did not comply with the provisions of section 14 of the Limitation Act, The High Court held that the arbitration clause in the contract was a valid arbitration agreement and the respondent was entitled to rescind the contract. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) Section 14 of Limitation Act applies to arbitrations as it applies to proceedings before the court within the meaning of section 4 of the Indian Limitation Act. The provisions of the [Limitation Act] apply to arbitrations under the Arbitration Act. In order that an arbitration agreement may be terminated or rescinded, the parties have to show in writing that the contract has been performed and that there is no breach of contract. The words "if any" used in section 14(2) (b) are not intended to cover arbitration proceedings. [675 H] (ii) Section 4 of Indian Limitation act applies to an arbitration as it apply to proceedings under the Act. Section 14(3)(a) provides that where the dispute is referred to arbitration, the court shall appoint an arbitrator or arbitrators and refer the parties to arbitration. The expression "if" used only in section 4(2)(b), does not mean that the court has no jurisdiction to entertain the claim. [775 H; 776 A] (iii) Section 5 of the Act provides that if the dispute relates to any matter which is required to be referred to an arbitrator, the arbitration shall be commenced within a period of one year from the date on which the cause of action arises. The language used in the section shows that it applies only to proceedings pending before the arbitration and not to proceedings which are pending before him. [750 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1379 of 1987. From the Judgment and Order dated 4.8.1987 of the Kerala High Court in O.P. No. 8/87. S.T. Desai, V.M. Tarkunde, R.K. Jain and M. Veerappa for the Appellant. K. Parasaran, Attorney General, B.D. Sharma, P.H. Parekh and Ms. A. Subhashini for the Respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by VENKATARAMIAH, J. This appeal is directed against the judgment dated April 4, 1987 of the High Court of Kerala in OSA No. 9/87 whereby the High court allowed the appeal filed by the appellant and set aside the decree passed by the trial court on the basis that the suit was not barred by limitation. The facts giving rise to this appeal are as follows: The respondent entered upon an agreement for construction with the appellants for construction on the property in question on the date when the contract expired. On or about April 1, 1982, the respondent filed an application under section 14 (2) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') before the District Judge, Kottayam, praying that the award be set aside and the matter be remitted to the trial Court for fresh decision in accordance with law. The High court dismissed the appeal on the following grounds: (1) That the arbitration agreement was not a valid one; (2)(a). That the respondent did not pay any amount by way of damages to the appellant as alleged in the application under Section 14 (3) of Act and, therefore, the award is bad. (b).

The State of Uttar Pradesh acquired the estate of a deceased proprietor on April 1, 1956. The estate was assessed to tax by the Income Tax Officer on the basis that the estate had vested in the State and that the amount due to the proprietor was secured by a mortgage of, or is a charge on such estate. On March 31, 1957, the State Government issued a notification under section 3(1) of the Act declaring that the estates of the proprietor were liable to be proceeded against in execution of a mortgage decree against the estate. The appellants filed an appeal before the District Judge and contended that the provisions of section 4 (d) of Act No. 1 of 1956 were not applicable to them as they had no interest in the estate and therefore, the provisions contained in sections 7A and 16 of the said Act were inapplicable to them. The High Court held that the right of the State to proceed against the estates was a charge upon the estate which had vested under the State law and that it was not open to the appellants to take advantage of the provisions in section 4(d) as they stood prior to the date of vesting. It further held that section 4 of Act 1 of 1957 did not apply to them and that, therefore, section 4 was inapplicable to the case. The question for decision by the High Court was whether the provisions relating to the scaling down of the debts due by the proprietors and tenure holders were applicable to the cases in which the interests of the proprietors had vested or were a charge thereon. HELD: (1) Section 4(a) of this Act is not attracted to them because it does not apply only to execution proceedings in which decree was passed against the proprietor. [616 G] The provisions contained under section 4 are applicable to execution proceeding in which an estate has vested in State and no other person. It is open to a party to take benefit of the provision in section 5 of Act I of 1956, if he satisfies the requirements of that section. [717 D] (2) Section 6 of Act II of 1957 does not affect the operation of section 3 of Act III of 1956. It only provides for the transference to the State of the estate as specified in section 16 of this act. The provisions of sections 7 and 16 are applicable only to cases where the whole of the property mortgaged is an estate, there can be no doubt that the provision contained in section 6 is not applicable. [817 G] (3) Section 5 of the Punjab Act does not exclude the application of section 5. It merely provides for a remedy against the debts incurred by the proprietor and the tenure-holder. The right to proceed in execution proceedings cannot be taken away by the provisions made in section 3. [918 A] (4) The provisions relating thereto are applicable also to execution cases in where an estate is vested in a State and not to the estates which have vested under that State law. [1024 D] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 13 of 1972. From the Judgment and Order dated the 14th July, 1972 of the Allahabad High Court in Misc. Case No. 11 of 1972 and Civil Appeal Nos. 13-14 of 1972 From the judgment and order dated the 24th October, 1972, of the District judge, Lucknow in Misc.(J) Case No, 11 of 1973. S.K. Sinha, for the appellants. R. K. Garg, for respondent No.1. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by FAZAL ALI, J.-This appeal is directed against a judgment and decree dated April 14, 1972 passed by the Allahabad, High Court, Lucknow Bench in Misc (J) Appeal No, 13 of 1973, whereby the High court allowed the appeal filed by the appellants and dismissed the application for setting aside the order of the trial court.

The respondents, who were allocated to the I.P.S. and Central Services Group 'A' on the basis of the previous examination held for the services of the Indian Army, applied for the post of Assistant Commandant (Central Services) Group 'B' in the year 1988. The result of the written test was declared by the respondents on 15th May, 1989. The results were published on 30th June, 1990 and the applicants were allocated the said course to the CSE (Main) for the years 1987 and 1989 respectively. On a provisional basis, they were allocated for the period from 1st July, 1988 to 31st August, 1991. They were allocated training for the purpose of examination by the I P.S., Central Services, Group 'C' on 1st September, 1992. The respondents were allocated two years training course for the said period and they were allotted the said training course in the same year. On the basis thereof, they applied for appointment to the post in the Central Service Group 'D' on a provisional footing. They also appeared in the written examination held by the respondent on 15 th May, 1990. The applicants were not selected for the posts of Assistant Commandants (Central Service) Group B and they had been allocated to I. P. S. or the Central Services group 'A'. On their applications, they appeared in a competitive examination held on 30 th June, 1991 and they qualified in the said test. They did not join the said examination. The respondent filed an application for appointment of the applicants to the posts in the Indian Armed Police Service Group B on a regular basis. The Tribunal allowed the applicants' applications holding that the respondents were entitled to appear in the preliminary examination held in the years 1988 and 1989. In the appeal filed by the Union of India, the appellants contended that the respondent was not entitled to be allocated to any of the Central services Group 'E' for the year 1987 and 1990 respectively. Allowing the appeals, the Court, HELD: 1.1 The Tribunal has erred in holding that there is no provision in the C.S.(C) Rules, which provides for a candidate to sit for the main examination. [532F] 1.2 The respondent was allocated to a different service and he was allocated training course of a specified rank. He was allocated the training course by the A.P., Central Service, Group B. He had been allotted the training courses in the matter of examination held from time to time. He did not have to resign from the said service. [506F] 2.1 There is no merit in the contention that the applicants are entitled to sit at the main examinations for the examination conducted by the C&P Department, Group A. The appellants were not entitled for being allocated to an independent service. They had been assigned training course only for the purposes of examination and they did not possess any other qualification. [504F] 3.2 There is nothing in the rules which provides that a candidate must be allocated training courses. It is true that the ASCs are allocated to different services but the respondent cannot claim to sit in the main exam for the examinations conducted by them. The question of applying the rule does not arise at all.

The appellant was detained under Section 3(1) of the Conservation of Foreign Exchange and Prevention of Smuggling Activities Act, 1974. The order of detention was made on 25th November, 1986. The detenu was arrested on 26th November 1986 and he was remanded to judicial custody till 5th December, 1986 when the Advisory Board met on 5th January, 1987. On 6th February, 1987, the appellant filed an application before the Advisory board for permission to be represented by a lawyer before the Board. The request of the appellant was turned down by the Board on the ground that the detenu had no locus standi to file the present petition. The appellant then moved the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution praying for quashing the order of the Board and for a direction to the Government to permit him to be assisted by Sundararajan as a friend. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant had no right to appear through a legal practitioner in the proceedings before the advisory board. On behalf of the State it was contended that the Advisory Boards were not entitled to seek permission to represent the detenu before the Government and the order passed by the Advisory Committee was illegal. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The power conferred on the Advisory boards under Section 11 of the Act is a quasi judicial function and the Advisory Advisory Board has no jurisdiction to grant or refuse to grant permission to the appellant to be associated with the proceedings. [775 H] 2.1 The Advisory Board is not entitled either to seek or to appear before the appropriate Government in the proceeding before the detaining authority. It is open to the detenu to file an application for permission under Section 12 of the COFEPOSA Act and the Government has no power to grant such permission. [750 A] 2:2 In the instant case, the AdvisoryBoard had not given any opportunity to the petitioner to be heard before the order was passed by it. The Advisory board was not entitled in law to seek the assistance of a friend in order to ensure due observance of the policy of law that a detenu is not allowed to represent through a lawyer. [751 B] 2(i) The power under Section 9 of the Customs Act, 1962 is a quasijudicial function and it cannot be exercised by the Government without giving an opportunity to a person who is not a legal adviser before the date of the Advisory Boat. [751 D] (ii) The Advisory Boards are not entitled, as they have no jurisdiction or power to decide whether the detenu should be represented through a friend or a legal consultant. [764 G] 2.(iii) The order passed under Section 10(2)(i) of COFEPOSA is illegal and void. [754 A] 3.1 In the present case, there was no representation from the appellant before the Central Government on 6th January 1987. The question whether the Advisory Chairman had given any such opportunity to be present before the said Board was not considered by the High court. [752 B] 3.(i) There is nothing in Section 11(4) of FERA or Section 12A of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1973 which empowers the Government or the authorised officer to grant exemption from personal appearance before the concerned Advisory Board. [758 C] (iii) In the absence of any representation from a detenu before an Advisory Board, it cannot act as a legal advise on the substance of such representation. [759 D] 3(i)(a) The right conferred on a person by Section 11 is not subject to any limitation or restriction and the said right can be exercised only in accordance with law. [761 E] (iv) The appellant was not represented before the authorities before the High Courts. [765 G] (v) The question of personal appearance of the detenu at the Advisory Panel does not arise for consideration in this case. [763 D] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1427 of 1987.

The appellants, the owners of the two mills, and the mills, filed a writ petition in the High Court of Madras challenging the validity of the orders of requisition and notices of acquisition. The High Court held that the delivery orders were valid and binding on the mills as they were not delivered by the mills. The appeals to this Court were filed against the judgment of the High court. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: (1) The delivery orders in question were validly served on the owners and the goods were not ascertained till then, but were substantially the same. [775 H] (2) The order of requisition was made by the Government of India under r. 75 A (3) of the Rules of Procedure. It was not open to the appellants to contend that the order of requisitioning was invalid because it was not served on them. [750 B] (3)(a) The High court was right in holding that the service of the notices of requisition did not amount to service on the owner of the goods and that the orders were validly made. [751 C] (b) The power under r, 75 A(3) is a power which is exercised by the appropriate Government in the case of delivery orders. It is not open for the appellants either to contend before this Court or to contend otherwise. [75 H; 76 B] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeals Nos. 943 and 944 of 1972. Appeals from the judgment and order dated September 30, 1967 of the Madras High Court in Writ Petition No. 845 of 1966. S. T. Desai, K. R. Chaudhuri, M. C. Bhandare, V. N. Ganpule, B. D. Sharma, for the appellant (in both the appeals). A. K. Sen and P. H. Parekh, for respondent No. 1 (in all the appeals) The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Shah, J. These two appeals are directed against a common judgment of Madras High court in Writ Petitions Nos. 843 and 844 of 1966 dated September 29, 1967. The appellants were owners of two mills at the relevant time. They filed a petition under Art. 226 of the Constitution challenging the legality of the order passed by the State Government on December 30, 1962. The writ petitions were dismissed by the High Courts on September 30,. 1967 and November 30, 1968. The orders of detention were challenged in these appeals by special leave. The main contention raised before us is that the power under Art, 19(1)(f) was not exercised by a competent authority in the cases of delivery order and notices for acquisition and that as the appellants had not been served on their mills as owners of goods, they could not be said to have acquired the goods. It has also been contended that the High courts were wrong in holding the delivery order to be invalid because the delivery was not made by a person who was not a party to the proceedings before them and therefore the orders passed by them were valid. The contention is that as there was no service on them, they were entitled to raise an objection under Art.. 226 of Constitution. It may be mentioned that in the present appeals the appellants have challenged the validity and legality of these two orders. The question whether the delivery of goods was made or not has been considered by this Court in several cases. In the case before us, the appellants are owners of certain mills at Bombay and the delivery is not made to them as owners but they are the owners. The power to requisition and acquisition is conferred on the appropriate government under r.. 75A (3). The power is exercised in the first instance by a Government officer in the second place. It cannot be said that the appellants were served on these mills as owner of goods. The right to receive compensation was not taken away by the provisions of Art. 19(6) of Constitution and therefore it was open for them to raise objection under s. 5A (1).

The assessee is a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The assessee was assessed to income tax on its total income of Rs. 1,02,000. The Income Tax Officer, on an application made by the assessee under Section 23A of the Act, included in the total income the sum of Rs, 4,50,000 as a reserve and added it to the net income of the assessee for the purpose of computing its capital gains. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax officer. On further appeal, the Tribunal held that the amount of Rs 4,00,000 was not a reserve but was a reserve. In the appeal before this Court, the Revenue contended that the said amount was a provision and not a reserves and, therefore, to be taken into account against gross receipts in the P & L accounts and the balance sheet by way of deductions from the assets in the accounts of the company. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the provisions made in Section 23(A) were not a provision or a reserve nor was it a reserve as contemplated under Section 28 of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. [775 H] 2.1 The expression "reserves" is defined in Section 28 and the word "reserve" has been used in Section 29A to mean "a reserve". Therefore, the said term does not include any provision or reserve. [750 A] 2(i) The words "results" are not a word of indefinite import but have a definite connotation. It is a provision which is intended to be an exception to the general rule that the expression "relative" in Section 24(1)(a) means "the person who has given or agreed to give the benefit of any benefit under the Act". [750 B] 2.(ii) The word " reserve" is not a term of indefinite and therefore, it must be construed as a provision. [751 G] 3.2 In order that the words "referring to" in the context may be read as a deposit or appropriation, the expression used is "reservation" which means "a provision or an reserve". The word 'reservs' has been defined in the Act and it must include any provisions or reserve or appropriation. [75 H; 76 A] 3.(i) In order to bring the said expression within the meaning of Section 28, the legislature has used the expression 'reserve' which is a deposit. It cannot be read in the sense that the word 'refere to" is used in the statute. [76 B] (ii) If the words are not capable of precise and unambiguous construction, it would lead to an absurd result. [77 C] 3(iii) The expression 'relative' in Section 30(1) means a person who is a member of the family of the deceased or of any other person who was a member in the family. [78 D] (iv) In the instant case, the amount was not paid to the assessee as a special reserve and it was not an appropriation. The said amount had been paid by way 'of deduction' under Section 24 of the Companies Act. [79 E] 3:1. The expression used in sub section (2) of Section 29 is "any provision or any reserve" and not "residual". [78 G] 2:2. In order for the said purpose, it was necessary to consider whether the amount paid by the company as a general reserve was a special provision or not. [80 D] 3I;F] 3 (i) Section 24 does not contemplate any such contingency. It only provides that the sum is a reserve which is not an item of a reserve or an appropriation, and it cannot be said that the provision is a special one. [81 E] 4.1.

The petitioners were appointed as Assistant Engineers in the Indian Railways. They were confirmed in the post of Assistant Engineers on the basis of a competitive examination held by the Union Public Service Commission. The petitioners were absorbed into the Indian Railway Service of Engineers Class I with effect from 1st September, 1966. On the basis that they were appointed to the Indian Administrative Service of Engineering Class I, they were given the benefit of weightage of half of their length of service as temporary Assistant Officers subject to a maximum of five years, and were also given the weightage of one year for each year of service. The respondents filed writ petitions in the High Court challenging the validity of the impugned order of the Central Administrative Tribunal, contending that the petitioners were not entitled to be treated as Assistant Officers on the ground that they had been absorbed into Indian Railway Services of Engineers, Class I and were therefore not entitled for promotion to the post in question. The High Court held that the respondents were not eligible for promotion as Assistant Executive Engineers on account of their being declared surplus from the Indian Engineering Service. On appeal by special leave, this Court HELD: 1.1 The petitioners are not entitled either to be considered as Assistant Engineer or to be promoted as Assistant Divisional Engineers on a regular basis. [775 H] 1.2 The High court was in error in holding that the impugned orders of the Tribunal were illegal and without jurisdiction. [750 A] 1:3. The question whether the petitioners are entitled to promotion as Executive Engineers, was not raised before the High court. It is well settled that a party cannot be allowed to raise a plea which was not taken before the Tribunal. [751 B] 2.1 There is no merit in the contention of learned counsel for the appellants that the order of absorption passed by the Central Government was illegal and contrary to law. The impugned orders are, therefore, liable to be set aside. [753 H; 75B] 2:2 In the instant case, the petitioners have been absorbed as Assistant Works Officers on a substantive basis from the date of their absorption in the service. They cannot be treated to be appointed as Executive Engineer on the principle of 'equal pay for equal work' and they are not eligible to be given promotion as Superintending Engineers on regular basis on the plea that they have been appointed to a post by direct recruitment. [764 D] 2] 2nd May, 1978, the date when the petitioners had been appointed as Assistants in the Department of Telecommunications, was the date on which they were absorbed in the Service. The order of appointment of the petitioners was not challenged before the Central Administratia and the High Courts were right in holding otherwise. [754 D] 3:3 The impugned order is liable to set aside on this ground alone. [752 G] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1524 of 1983. From the Judgment and Order dated 20.1.1983 of the Andhra Pradesh Administrative Tribunal in O.A. No. 8 of 1979. V.S. Desai, S.K. Bagga and R.N. Sachthey for the Appellants. M.C. Bhandare, K.R. Nambiar, P.H. Parekh, A.K Gupta, B.D. Sharma, Ms. Rani Chhabra, M.M. Lal, M/s. Vineeta & Co., M.V. Goswami, S/o late Shri R.K.. Srivastava, R/o H.No. 1-1-8, Sector-2, Noida, Uttar Pradesh. The West Bengal Special Courts Act, was passed by the State Legislature in exercise of its powers under article 14 of the Constitution. The West Bengal Act was passed to provide for a special procedure for trial by Special Courts and for matters connected therewith. Section 11 of the Ordinance which provided that the Special Court constituted under the Act shall try offences or classes of cases specified therein, as the case may be, in accordance with the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (hereinafter referred to as "the Code") was amended by the West Bengal Amendment Act, 1976 and the West Ben. Act was amended on April 1, 1977. The State Government issued a notification under section 5(1) of the West BENGAL Special Courts Ordinance, 1976, which was published in the Official Gazette on May 2, 1977, and the notification was published on June 6, 1977 in the Calcutta Gazette on July 7, 1977 and the same was published as required by sub-section (2) of section 11 of that Act. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the notification issued under section 11(1)(b) of that Ordinance. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the notification dated June 6., 1977, which had been published in Calcutta Gazette, was invalid and ultra vires the Constitution as it did not comply with the requirements of sub-sections (2), (3) and (4) of [section 11] of the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1(i) The notification issued by the Government under section 3(1), read with section 5 (1) was valid and in force on the date of the publication of the said notification, the State Government had no power to make a classifi cation of "offences", "classes of offences" or "clasures" as the cases were covered by the provisions contained in the proviso to section 11 (1)(a) of Ordinance No. 1 of 1976. [775 H] 2(ii) The State Legislature had no competence to make any law with respect to "offenses" and that the said Act was not invalid on the ground that it did comply with sub-s.(2) ofs.11 of the Saurashtra Ordinance. [764 G] (iii) The power conferred by section 11 is a power in the State legislature to make rules for the purpose of carrying into effect the provisions mentioned therein and the Court cannot interfere with the decision of the State government unless it is shown that the requirements laid down in sub-ss.(2),(3) & (4), are satisfied. [771 H] 3(i)(a)(ii) If the notification under s. 5(l) was issued by a competent authority, the said act would be invalid and the State law will not be valid. [781 A G] 2.(iii) Section 11(2) is not a provision in the statute which provides for a class of offences or class of cases to be tried by the Special Courts. The power under section11 is not an arbitrary power. It is not necessary that the legislature should have intended that the State should make a special law with regard to " offenses" as defined in s. 11(3). [784 B] 3.(i)(b)(ii), (iii)(a), (iv) and 2(v) of s.11(2), are not provisions in the Act which provide for special procedure. [791 A] (ii) Section 12(1A) is a provision to be construed as a proviso to sub-sec.(3). The power to impose a special penalty under section 12(4) is an arbitrary and unguided power. [802 B] (iv)(a). The State legislature has no competence in making a law with reference to the provisions in question.

The appellants were convicted by the Sessions Judge for an offence under section 396 I.P.C. and sentenced to death. The prosecution case was that on the night of the occurrence, the accused persons were found in a room at the house of the deceased and they were found dead. On the basis of the information given by P.W. 1, the police registered a case under section 302 I. P.C., and after investigation submitted a charge sheet against the accused for an alleged offence under sections 396 I, 302 read with section 34 I.p.C.. The learned Sessions Judge acquitted all the accused but convicted them of an offence punishable under section 395 I.PC. and awarded sentence to each of them. On appeal by the State, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentences passed on the appellants. Hence this appeal by special leave. The only point urged before us is that the evidence of P.Ws. 1 and 7 was not reliable and that their evidence should be rejected as unreliable. It was also contended that the prosecution has proved the case against the appellants beyond all reasonable doubt and that the conviction of the appellants for an offense under section 397 I.Ps. cannot be sustained. The learned counsel for the State of U.P., however, supported the judgment of the High court and submitted that the High Curt was in error in reversing the order of acquittal passed by the learned Sessions judge and confirming the sentence imposed on the accused. It is not necessary to go into the question whether the evidence adduced by the prosecution is reliable or not. The evidence of the witnesses, P.w. 1 to 7 and 8 are consistent with each other.
