The High Court has rightly held that the appellants were found guilty for an offences under section 398 I.A.C.; that the case was proved against them beyond all legitimate doubts and that they have been convicted for an act which is not in the interest of the accused; and that therefore, the conviction recorded by the trial court and confirmed by the High F Court cannot be upheld. The question whether there was a reasonable possibility of the appellant being found guilty of an offenses under section 412 I. PC. is also not relevant. The fact that the accused were found to have committed an offence in the house at the time of the commission of the crime, does not affect their conviction for an endless and innocent act. The conviction recorded against them for an an offensilary offence under Section 396 I., P. C. is therefore, correct.

The appellant was appointed as a probationer in the respondent company on January 1, 1966. He was confirmed in that post by an order dated December 31, 1967. On November 30, 1967 he was dismissed from service and was directed to be reinstated in service with effect from December 31. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court of Orissa which was allowed by a learned Single Judge on January 14, 1968. The appellant challenged the correctness of the decision of the Labour Court before the Division Bench of the High court. The Division Bench held that the termination of the services of the appellant was bad and accordingly quashed the order of dismissal. On appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The expression 'retrenchment' in section 2(oo) of the Act means only the discharge of surplus labour or staff by the employer for any reason whatsoever. [775 H] (2) The word 'ret retrenchment' is not defined in the Act and it must be construed as including within its ambit all kinds of termination of service except those which have been embodied in the definition. [750 A] (3) The words 'retrenched' in the context of section 2 (oo) are wide enough to include all types of termination by way of punishment. [751 B] (4) The term 'ret retrenched' in s.2(oo)(i) means only a termination of services by the employers for any reasons whatsoever, and not otherwise. [753 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1524 of 1968. Appeal by special leave from the judgment and order dated September 14, 1967 of the Orissa High Court in Misc. Case No. 11 of 1967. S. K. Das, for the appellant. M. C. Setalvad, Attorney-General of India, B. Sen, R. N. Sachthey and D. N.. Sharma, for respondent No. 1. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Shah, J. This appeal is directed against a judgment of the Division bench of the Calcutta High Court dated September 15, 1967 in Misc Case No 11 of 1966. The question involved in this appeal is whether the termination order passed by the appellant terminating his services with effect form January 1. 1966, was bad or not and if so, whether it amounts to retrenchment within the meaning of section 25F of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act'). The appellant was a probationer and he was confirmed on December 31,. 1967. He filed an application before the Labour Officer for permission to join his service with the employer. The Labour Officer allowed that application and directed the appellant to be re-instated in service. On further appeal, the DivisionBench of the Patna High Court held that termination of his services without complying with the provisions of section 3(2) of Act 1947 was bad. In this view, the learned Single judge dismissed the writ petition. The order of the learned Judge is challenged by the present appellant on the ground that the order passed under section 25FFF of Act No. 1947 was not in accordance with law and therefore it amounts only to retrenchment. The contention of the respondent before us is that the expression 'termination for any cause' in [section 2(o)] means only an termination of employment by the, employer for a reason other than those specified in sub-clause (i) of clause (oo). It was contended on behalf of the respondents that the words 'termination' in sub section (2), 'retrench' and 'reinstatement' are wide and include all kinds or termination of any service by the. employer for reasons other than the one mentioned in sub clauses (a) to (e) of section 10 of the said Act. The learned Single Judges held that in view of the provisions contained in section 25 F, the order terminating the services was bad as it did not comply with the requirements of section 4(1)(b).

The appellant is a dealer in goods carrying on business of sale and purchase of scrap and unserviceable material. The assessee purchased the goods from the State Trading Corporation of India Ltd., Calcutta, for the purpose of manufacture of scrap. The Sales Tax Officer, who assessed the sales tax assessed the assessee to sales tax under the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941. The assessing authority held that the sale was not a "dealer" within the meaning of Section 2(c) read with Section 2 of the Bengal Taxation (Sales-tax) Act. The appellant filed an appeal before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner of Commercial Taxes, West Bengal and contended that the sales were not sales in the course of inter-State trade or commerce but were sales in which the goods were sold by the assessee and that the Sales Tax authorities had no jurisdiction to assess the sale. The Appellate Tribunal held that as the sales did not indicate that the Railway concerned was carrying on the business as carrier of the goods, the sale could be said to have been exempted from assessment under Section 56 of the Indian Railways Act. On further appeal by the appellant, the High Court reversed the decision of the Appellate Tribunal and allowed the appeals filed by the Revenue. The present appeal is directed against that order. The question raised in this appeal is whether the sales effected by the petitioner were sales within the scope of Section 56 read with Rule 2 of Bengal Finance(Sales Tax), Act, 1942. The High Court answered the question in favour of the assessee holding that the transactions did not disclose that the railway concerned was carried on business as a carrier of goods and if at all the Railway was carrying the goods there could be no sale of the said goods by the Railway. In this appeal it is contended that since the sales had been made by the dealer, the Sales tax authorities were competent to assess them under Section 11 of the Act. It is further contended that as a result of the sales, the assessee became liable to pay sales tax on the sale of scrap in which he purchased the said scrap and that therefore the sales could not be assessed to assessment under the Act because the goods did not contain any material for the said purpose. The contention is that since there was no evidence to show that the goods had been sold by him, the sales are not liable to assessment. In support of this contention reliance has been placed on the decision in the District Controller of Stores, Eastern Railway, Jodhpur vs The Assistant Commercial Taxation Officer and Another, ; , ; ; (1) [1962] 36 S.T.C. 423. (2) [1965] 36S.T., C. 823. (3) [1964] 36 T.C.. 423. In the case of the appellant it was held that since no evidence had been produced to show the said sale, the goods could not have been assessed to tax under Section 12 of the Bihar Finance ( Sales Tax)Act, 1941 and the High court answered the first question in the affirmative. The second question is whether on a true construction of the provisions of the [ Bengal Finance Act, 1940] the sales can be assessed under the said Act.

The appellant, a Director of the Company, was appointed as an auditor to audit the accounts of the Insurance Company. The appellant filed a return of his income and expenditure in respect of the assessment year 1955-56 on the basis that he had received the amount from Bhagwati Trading Company for the purchase of securities. On October 30, 1956, the Income Tax Officer, Delhi, issued a notice under section 34 of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922, to the appellant, calling upon him to show cause why he should not be directed to pay the sum of Rs. 1,10,000/- as short fall of securities and also to pay interest at the rate of 15% per annum on the amount of short fall from the date of the notice till payment. The Income Tax officer held that the appellant was entitled to a sum of money equivalent to the short fall in the stock of securities purchased by him from the Insurance company, and that he was not liable to pay any interest on the short rise from the period September 16, 1955 to October 30. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax Officer. The Tribunal held that there was no evidence to show that the amount was received by the appellant from Bhagwati trading Company for his own purpose and that the sum was received in cash or purchase of shares. The High Court on a reference made to it under section 66(1) of the Act, set aside the order passed by the Income-tax Officer and restored the order. In this appeal, it is contended that the Tribunal had erred in law in holding that the assessee was entitled only to a deduction of the shortfall from the amount received by him as short falls in the stocks of securities held by him for his personal use and that, therefore the sum received by Dalmia was not an income tax payable on the stock. The contention is that the finding recorded by the Tribunal is erroneous and must be set aside. It is further contended that there is no evidence on record to show the receipt of the amount by the Insurance Co., and that in any event the Tribunal has erred in holding the appellant to have received the short falls securities for his individual use. The question whether the sum is received by a Director or an employee of the Bank, is a mixed question of fact and law. It was contended that in the circumstances it was not open to the IncomeTax Officer to hold that the money was received from the Bank. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The finding recorded on the facts found by the Appellate Tribunal is correct. [557D] 2. The sum of short falls due from the appellant as short fell due from him for the Union Agencies to meet its losses. The amount was not paid in cash but was received at the close of the business and it was only a part of the balance of the stock that was left by the Bank and the balance was not given to the Bank on account of the Central Government. [506F] 3. The fact that the amounts were received from Bhagwati, Trading Company, is not a circumstance which would justify the conclusion that they are not paid for the purpose of the Union Agency. It cannot be said that there has been no evidence in this case to show payment of short fell securities for the Bank to meet the losses. [504F] 4. The Appellate Tribunal was right in holding otherwise. [457G] 5. The appeal is accordingly dismissed with costs.

The appellants were appointed to the posts of Assistant Secretaries in the Secretariat of the State of Gujarat. They were confirmed as Assistant Secretaries on November 1, 1956 and they were posted at the Headquarters of the Gujarat State Secretariat. The services of the appellants were absorbed in the permanent establishment of the Government of Gujarat by the order dated December 10, 1957. On January 30, 1958, the Government issued a notification under section 115(7) proviso to section 115 (7) read with article 309 of the Constitution and transferred the appellants to the Secretariat. On April 1, 1959, the State Government issued an order under section 116(7), directing that the services of all the officers in the secretariats of the States of Saurashtra and Kutch should be absorbed in permanent establishment in the ministerial cadre of the Saurashtra and Saurashtra States. The appellants were confirmed in the posts held by them on November 30, 1956. On December 10,. 1957, the appellants filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of the Central Government dated April 1. 1959. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellants had no right to be absorbed as Assistant Secretary in the department of Secretariat and that they were not entitled to be treated as permanent employees of the Secretariat with the consent of the Public Service Commission. On appeal, the High court held that the order passed by the Central government dated April, 1, 1960 was illegal and quashed the order. The State Government filed a special leave petition in this Court which was dismissed on September 30, 1963. Thereafter, the appellant moved the High Courts under article 226 of the constitution for quashing the order made by the State government dated May 10, 1959 and also for a writ of mandamus directing the appellants not to absorb them in the service of the respondent-State. The learned Judges held that since the appellants did not have any right to hold the posts in the 'new State which were equivalent and on terms which were not, unless the previous approval of the central Government was obtained, disadvantageous. In view of this finding, the appeal was allowed by the High. Court with costs. Hence this appeal by special leave. 3. The main contention of Mr. S. T. Desai, learned counsel for the appellants is that the orders passed by both the Central Governments are illegal and invalid as they were made without jurisdiction. In support of his contention he relied upon the decision of this Court in [State of Gujarat vs. Ramanbhai Naranbhai Patel & Ors.] , referred to. 4. The question whether the order was made by a competent authority or not is a matter for the State Governments to decide and if it is not, the Central Govt. can issue an order which is not in accordance with law. 5. In the instant case, the order issued by the Government dated May 11, 1959 was passed by a Competent Authority under section 6 of the Act and the appellants could have been absorbed in service in the regular establishment of Gujarat State or the State. The order was passed on April 1,. 1960 and it is clear that the appointment of the appellant was made as Assistant Commissioner of the department concerned. The contention of the learned counsel, therefore, cannot be accepted. 6. It is true that the Government has power to make an order for absorption in service of a person who had been appointed by the competent authority to the post of Assistant Commissioner and that such an order can be passed only after the Central Public Service Commissions are constituted under section 5 of the said Act. But, as pointed out earlier, the appointment was made on November 10, 1956, the date when the appellant could have exercised his option for absorption as Assistant Collector in the cadre of Deputy Secretaries to the Government. The appointment was not made by an officer who had no power to do so and therefore, the question whether he was absorbed in a permanent establishment or not does not arise. 7.

The appellant, a registered dealer, was assessed to tax under the Central Act on the purchase of goods made by him from outside the State. The tax was levied at the rate of one stage and that was reduced by the State Government by the notification dated December 7, 1966. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the levy of tax on the ground that the tax was not higher than six naye paise in a rupee. The High Court held that the sales were made by the first purchaser from outside and therefore the tax could be levied at one stage only. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The appellant is liable to pay tax under section 5(2)(a)(vi) of the Central Sales Tax Act on his purchase of declared goods. [775 H] (2) Section 5(1) of Central Act provides that no tax shall be levied or collected at more than one stage in respect of declared Goods. The State Government may, by notification direct that the rate specified in section 15(1)(vi), in respect thereof, is to be fixed and that stage shall be deemed to have been substituted for the original stage by a new rule made under section 15A. [750 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 12 of 1967. From the Judgment and Order dated the 30th September, 1966 of the Andhra Pradesh High Court in Writ Petition No. 923 of 1966. M. C. Chagla, S. K. Mehta and R. N. Sachthey, for the appellant. A. V. Viswanatha Sastri, B. D. Sharma and P. L. Vohra, for respondent No. 1. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Shah, J. The question involved in this appeal is whether the tax levied under section 3(1), (2)(b) and (vi) read with section 15-A of the Act on declared goods is at one time purchase in the State and that the stage of sale of such goods by the last dealer liable to tax is the sale of declaredgoods. The facts leading up to this appeal are as follows: The appellant was assessed under section 4(1). He filed a petition for refund of tax paid by him on his first purchase from outside. The contention of the appellant was that the levy was not at one point and therefore he was not liable to be taxed at more or less than six stage. The Andhra Pradesh Sales Tax Tribunal held that there was no sale at all in the case of imported goods and that it was not a case of sale at any time. The Tribunal held, relying on the decision of this Court in [The State of Andhra v. VST Industries Ltd.] , that "the sales tax is levied at two stages, namely, (i) purchase by the dealer from outside; and (ii) sale by him to the last purchaser liable to sales tax under this Act. The point for consideration before us is whether there was a sale at the first stage of the sale in the course of inter State trade or commerce. If it is not a sale, then the tax can be levied on the first purchase in respect whereof the tax has been imposed at one and the same rate. In the case before us, the appellant had purchased the goods from outside, but he did not pay the tax. The levy was at one end of the tax and therefore it is a case where the tax is not at all levied at more points than six stages. If the tax cannot be levied in respect thereto, then there is no sale or purchase at all. In this view of the matter, we are unable to accept the contention of Mr. Chagla that the appellant is not liable for payment of tax under Section 3(2) of Act.

The appellant, who was the owner of a house in which he had purchased the mortgaged property, filed a suit for recovery of money against defendants 2 to 7 on the ground that they were agriculturists and hence entitled to get the benefit of the provisions of the Agriculturists' Relief Act. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the mortgage debt was one and indivisible and not a debt and that the mortgagors had failed to repay the amount due under the decree. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decree and held that the mortgagee had become entitled to have his debts scaled down in favour of defendants 2 and 7 and that on payment of the amount directed by the trial court he would be entitled to avail himself of the benefit under the Act. In second appeal before this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court erred in holding that a purchaser could get the benefits of the Act only if a purchaser had not paid the amount ordered to be paid by defendants 2, 3 and 4. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding otherwise. [775 H] (2) The provisions of Section 29(3)(a) of the Indian Contract Act are applicable to the facts of the case and the question whether a purchaser can get the protection of the said provision depends on the finding that a purchase is one and the same as a result of the scaling down of the decree in favour or against defendants. [750 H] The High court was right when it held that a person who has become entitled under the provisions contained in the Act to get his debts, would be a purchaser. [751 A] (3) Section 29 of the Contract Act is applicable only to the transactions which are covered by the provisions thereof and not to the transaction which is one. [751 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1584 of 1987. From the Judgment and Order dated 20.8.1987 of the Allahabad High Court in Second Appeal No, 921 of 1986. S.K. Jain for the Appellant. V.S. Desai, R.N. Singh, A.K Gupta, B.D. Sharma, P.C. Kapur, M.M. Kochar and D.P. Mukherjee for the Respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by VENKATARAMIAH, J. This appeal is directed against the judgment dated October 20, 1987 passed by the Allahabad high court in Second appeal No. 921/1986. The appellant is a purchaser from defendant No. 2 who purchased the property in dispute on payment to defendants 2 & 7 and the sale deed executed by defendants 1 to 7 in favour the plaintiff was one of the purchasers. The High-Court has held that in view of the decision of this Court in the case of [Ram Chandra Singh vs State of U.P.] , the provisions relating to the said provisions have been made applicable to a transaction which are not covered by them and the suit filed by the appellant is liable to be dismissed. The facts leading to this appeal are as follows: The plaintiff purchased the house in dispute from defendant Nos. 2 & 3 on payment by defendants 4 to 7. On payment of Rs. 1,000/- by defendants 5 to 7, the sale-deed was executed and registered in favour defendants 2&7. The said sale deed was executed by the defendants 2 (the appellant) in respect of the mortgaged house in question. The plaintiff filed a civil suit for specific performance against defendants 1 & 2 on the basis of the mortgage decree. The defendant No 1, who is the purchaser, has not challenged the findings recorded by the High-court that the said sale was one among the purchasers and that it was a transaction between the parties which is not covered under the said Act. It is true that in the suit for possession filed by defendants 3 to 7 against defendants 4 & 5, the plaintiff had not impleaded defendants 2(a) to 6 as parties.

The appellants were tenants of the premises in question. They filed a suit for eviction against the respondents on the ground that they were tenants within the meaning of section 14 of the Act. The respondent filed a petition under Article 227 of the Constitution before the High Court of Bombay, praying for an order restraining the appellants from evicting any of the plaintiffs or their tenants and from evicting them in pursuance of the provisions of the [Bombay Rents, Hotel Rates and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947] (hereinafter referred to as "the Act"). The appellants contended that the suit filed by the respondent was not one between the landlord and a tenant but was one for possession. The High Court held that the plaintiffs were tenants under section 14(1) of the said Act and therefore they could not be evicted from the premises. It further held that in view of the decision of this Court in [Shanti Devi vs State of U.P.] , the suit was maintainable. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High court was wrong in holding that the City Civil Court had no jurisdiction to entertain a suit relating to possession. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The provisions of section 28 and 29 of the Bombay Rents, Hotels Rates and lodging House Rates (Control) Act, were not applicable to the present case. [775 H] 2. Section 14(2) of that Act provides that where any premises is in the nature of a title to the premises, the jurisdiction to try such a suit was vested in the courts specified in section 28. The words "any other" have been used in the said provision and it has not been shown that the appellants were the tenants within those provisions. [750 H] 3. Section 29 of Act No. 30 of 1947 provides that no suit relating thereto shall be instituted by or against the landlord for eviction of any of his tenants or for recovery of possession thereof. The appellants were not tenants under the said section and therefore their suit was not maintainable. [751 G] 4. The question whether the plaintiffs are the tenants under Section 14 (1) or 29 of that act is a question which has to be determined by the courts in the suit relating back to the provisions contained in Part 11 of the Schedule. [75 H; 76 A] 5. The City Civil Courts Act, was not applicable in the present matter and therefore the suit could not have been instituted by the appellants. [76 B] 6. Section 28 of the Indian Contract Act provides for a bar against the jurisdiction of courts specified therein. It is true that the provisions relating to suits relating to eviction of tenants are not applicable but the question whether they are in the form of a landlord or tenant under section 29 of Bombay Rent Act, would be a question arising out of the statute and therefore it was not necessary for the appellants to establish that the said suit was one between them. [77 C] 7. The fact that the defendants were tenants is not in dispute. The plaintiffs were the landlords. They were tenants only under section 28 of Bombay Act. [78 D] 8. Section 15 of the Transfer of Property Act provides a bar for the jurisdiction in respect of any suit relatingto possession of immovable property. [79 E] 9. The suit filed on the City civil Court was not a suit by or for possession of the property. It was not an action for recovery against the defendants. [80 G] 10. Section 30 of the Specific Relief Act provides as under: "30. Suit to recover possession of premises.- (1)(a) Where any premises are in possession of a tenant, he may sue for eviction thereof on the grounds specified in clause (b), clause (c) or clause (d) of sub section (2) and clause (e) of section 29, if the suit is not instituted within one year from the date of the service of notice of demand.

The appellant was a director of the respondent company. He was appointed as an additional director by the company on the basis of his appointment. The respondent was appointed to the post of a director in the respondent's place. On the expiry of his term, he was appointed by the Company as an Additional Director. The appellant was appointed a new director by order dated January 28, 1957. He continued to hold that position till March 31, 1958 when he was removed from the office of the managing director. On April 1, 1959, the respondent filed a petition under section 397 read with section 397 of the old Act before the High Court for quashing the order of removal and for a direction to the appellant to appoint him as an Assistant Director of the company. The High Court held that the appointment of the appellant was illegal and void and directed the appellant's reinstatement in service. On appeal by special leave, this Court reversed the judgment of the High court and held that there was no valid appointment of an additional Director by the respondent. In the present case Dadoba had power under the articles to appoint a person as an addition to his office. The question whether he was a member of the board or not was considered by this Court in [K.S. Paripoornan vs State of Kerala & Ors.] , and it was held that in order to make him a member, he must be appointed by a director who is appointed by an order made under section 86B of the new Act. The Court observed that the word "assignment" would include "appointment". In [Kutchy Lal vs State Of Punjab & Ors.], , , this Court held: "It seems to us that in view of section 86(1) read with sections 255 and 256 of the Act, it is clear that the words "appointment" or "promotion" are used in section 86 (1) of the said Act. In order to give a right to an additional person to have a say in the appointment, the shareholders must be given an opportunity to show cause against the appointment. If the appellant does not show any cause against his appointment he will be entitled to a hearing and the appellant will be heard by the High Courts on the question whether the appointment was made by him for the purpose of section 312 of the present Act."

The appellants are the partners of a firm, M/s. Adeshwar Glass Mart. They were carrying on business in the said premises as partners. The respondent landlord filed a suit against the appellant for eviction and recovery of possession of the said shop from the appellant. The trial Court decreed the suit holding that the appellants had sublet the shop to M/S. Aday Glass Mart and that the respondent was liable to pay rent at the rate of Rs. 1,000/- per month. The appellants filed an appeal before the High Court against the judgment and decree of the Trial Court. The High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the order of the trial court. In this appeal by special leave, it is contended by Mr. Nayar that in view of the provisions of Section 13(3)(i) of the Act, the respondent landlord was not entitled to get any relief under the said provision. It was further submitted that the High court erred in holding that there was no evidence in support of the appellants' case and thereby the finding of subletting was vitiated by an error apparent on the face of the record. In our view, this contention is without merit. Section 13 (3)(ii) of The Act provides that a tenant shall be liable to be evicted from any premises if he has sublet or transferred such premises to another person for a continuous period of one year and six months immediately preceding the date of the application. It is not in dispute that the appellant was carrying on the business at the said place for some time during which the appellants firm had ceased to carry on the said business. The question, therefore, is whether the respondent-landlord was entitled to claim any relief against the appellants under Section 13 of the Rent Act. In order to appreciate the contention raised by Mr, Nayar, it would be necessary to refer to the relevant provisions of the [Rent Act]. Section 13 provides that where a tenant has sublet the premises to a person other than the landlord, he shall be deemed to have sublet the same and such subletting shall not affect any right or liability of the landlord in respect of the shop. The proviso to this section provides that if the tenant is a partner of a partnership firm, he may be liable for eviction from the said property if he is carrying on any business in such premises. Section 14 provides that no suit for eviction shall be maintainable against a person who has sublet, transferred or otherwise parted with possession of any shop to another persons for a period of more than one year. The provisions of sub-section (3) of Section 14 are mandatory and the respondent is not entitled for the relief under Section 12 of the Delhi Rent Control Act. [Section 13(1)(i)] provides that in case of subletting, the tenant shall have to be deemed also to have been sublet the said and such sublet shall not be affected by any right of the parties in respect thereof. The expression "tenant" is defined in Section 2 (g) of Delhi Rent control Act, 1952. [The Act] provides for eviction of a tenant from any shop. It does not provide that the landlord has sublet any premises to any person other then the tenant. The only provision which is relevant in this behalf is sub-Section (3). [Section 14(3)] provides for an appeal against the order passed by the Rent Controller and it reads as follows: "14. Appeal.- (1) Any person aggrieved by an order of eviction under Section 11 or Section 12 may, within one year from the date on which the order is made, prefer an appeal to the High C Court. (2) The High court shall not entertain any appeal against an order under this section unless it is satisfied that the case involves a substantial question of law." [Section 15] provides that the Appellate Authority shall have power to call for and examine the record of the case and pass such orders thereon as may be necessary. [Sections 16] and 17 are mandatory.

The Andhra Pradesh Act was passed by the Andhra Pradesh Legislature on 1st January, 1975 and it received the assent of the President on 2nd May, 1972. The Andhra Pradesh (Amendment) Act, 1976 introduced section 7A in the Andhra State Act which provided for a partition between the members of the family and the land held by each member of the joint family. Section 7A was amended by the Amendment Act, 1977 and it provided that where any property is acquired by a person in excess of the ceiling area, he would be liable to be included in the family unit. The Explanation to section 7B provided that if any property which is not acquired by the person in whose favour the partition was effected is held by him as a joint family unit, then such property shall be deemed to have been transferred to and vested in the State Government free from all encumbrances. Section 8 of the Andhra Act provided for the computation of ceiling area. The relevant provisions of section 8 were as follows: "8. (1) Where any property has been acquired by or on behalf of a joint Hindu family, but no partition has taken place before 2nd day of May, 1973 and under that section, the property shall, in relation to such property, be deemed, for the purposes of this Act, to have vested in a member of such family. (2) Where an owner of any property acquired by him is not a joint owner thereof, he shall be liable for the partition of the property so acquired and the property held by the other members of his family shall be treated as the separate property of the other member of his own family." The Explanation was amended in 1976. It provided that the land which was acquired by an individual or a family unit would be deemed under section 3(f) of the Act to have become vested in him as part of joint family property. The effect of the amendment was that the lands held by a Hindu undivided family, which were not acquired on partition, were liable to tax. The High Court held that the Explanation did not apply to the land in question and that the properties acquired by such Hindu undivided families were liable for assessment under section 8(1)(a) of that Act. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The expression 'family unit' in section 3 (f) is a comprehensive definition and it includes any property owned by a joint member of a family. [775 H] 2. Section 4 of the Hyderabad Act provides for a division of the land into two classes of persons, namely, (i) an individual, and (ii) where such individual was not a member in his own right as a member or members of any other family unit and under section 4(2)(A)(a), the property would be treated to have devolved on him as one member. [750 H] 3. The words 'family' in the Explanation are not a comprehensive expression and it is only where an owner is not an individual that he would become liable to pay tax. [751 G] 4.1 In the instant case, the lands acquired by A-2 were held by A.2 and the lands of others were held jointly by A and B. The question whether the lands in question were held on partition was a mixed question of law and fact. [753 H] 5. Section 3(e) of Act provides that where an individual is not member of any family unit but his father or mother, the land shall be assessed to tax under section 7. [764 G] 6. The word 'family', in the context of the Explanation, means a person who was not an undivided Hindu family and under Section 4(1) of A Act would include a joint holding.

The Company was a registered trade union of workmen in the year 1953. The respondent, who was working as a clerk in the office of the Assistant Labour Commissioner, was dismissed from service on August 24, 1953, and he was reinstated in service by order dated October 1, 1953. On November 30, 1953 the respondent filed an application before the Industrial Tribunal for permission to dismiss Chattoraj. The Tribunal allowed that application and granted leave to the respondent. In the appeal to this Court it was contended that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to interfere with the decision of the Company on the ground that the order of dismissal passed by the Company was mala fide or amounted to victimisation. HELD: (i) The Industrial Tribunal had in fact considered the justification for absence without leave and the circumstances of the case, and it was not open to the Tribunal to interfere. [775 H] (ii)The Tribunal was right in holding that Chattorraj was guilty of misconduct. The order passed by him was justified. The Industrial Court was wrong in interfering with the finding of fact recorded by the Tribunal. [750 A] (iii)The Industrial Tribunal was not justified in interfering on the basis of the evidence adduced before it and it had no power to interfere under Article 226 of the Constitution. [751 B] (iv)The order passed in favour of Chattoraraj was not a finding of law but was a finding based on facts which were not established by the Industrial Court. The decision of this Court in Chattorgarh's case, referred to above, was not an authority for the proposition that the Industrial tribunal had no such jurisdiction. [751 D] (v)The question whether the order passed is mala fide and amounted to unfair labour practice was a mixed question of fact and law. It was not necessary for the Tribunal in this case to decide whether Chattorrai was guilty or not. The finding of the Tribunal that Chattaj was guilty, was based on evidence which were neither established nor proved by the evidence. [761 D C] (vi)The decision of a Tribunal is not an administrative order and it cannot be challenged as being mala fide. It is not open for the Industrial court to interfere in the matter. The question whether Chattraj was actuated by any corrupt or victimisation, was a pure question of law and no evidence was produced before the Tribunal which could have been considered by the Labour Court. [754 D] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1123 of 1966. Appeal from the judgment and order dated April 20, 1966 of the Bombay High Court in Misc. Petition No. 8 of 1965. S. N. Andley, for the appellant. M. C. Setalvad, Attorney-General of India, B. H. Dhebar, R. K. Garg, S. P. Nayar, for respondent No. 1. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Hidayatullah, J. This appeal is directed against an order passed on a reference under section 10(1) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') by the Government of Bombay. The appellant is a registered Trade Union of workmen employed in the respondent's factory at Ahmedabad. It filed an industrial dispute before the Labour Tribunal, Bombay, claiming that Chatrodaj was not guilty of any misconduct and that he was not paid his wages for the period from October 1 to November 30 and, therefore, he was entitled to reinstatement in service with full back-wages. The case of the respondent was that Chattaraj was a workman within the meaning of section 2(s) of Act No. 10 of 1947. The Labour Tribunal held that Chatrudra was not proved to have been guilty of such misconduct and accordingly, directed the appellant to pay him wages for that period. It also directed that he should be paid Rs. 1,000/- per month as compensation for the said period.

The appellant was appointed as a lecturer in Botany in the University of Rajasthan on a temporary basis for a period of six months. He was confirmed in that post by an order dated 10th July, 1978 issued by the Vice Chancellor of the University. On his appointment he joined the University on a regular basis and continued to work till he was appointed on probation for a further period of one year. The appellant was confirmed as Professor in Botsany in Bokot College, Jodhpur on a substantive post of Professor in the said college. He filed an application before the Vice-Chancellor of the respondent University praying that he be appointed as Professor of Botacin in Bore College, Jaipur and his appointment should be treated as regular appointment for the purpose of selection and appointment to the post of professor in Bogany. The Vice Chancellor allowed the said application by order dated 11th July 1983 and directed the appellant to join the University within a period one year from the date of the order. On appeal, the High Court held that the respondent was not entitled to be appointed on a permanent basis for the reason that he had joined the college after the expiry of the period of probation. The said decision was confirmed by the Chancellor in appeal. In further appeal to this Court it was contended that the ViceChancellor had no power to make an order of appointment of a teacher or an officer in a university and, therefore, the respondent could not be appointed to any post on a vacant post caused during the validity period of the said appointment. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court has rightly held that there was no merit in the appellant's contention that he was not appointed as professor in the Botopah College. [532E] 2.1 The Vice- Chancellor is a statutory authority and he can make an appointment of an officer or an employee in any post under the University and such appointment cannot be made for a long period of more than one year unless there are good reasons to do so. [506F] 2:2 In the instant case, the appellant was not selected by the Selection Committee for the post on probation and he was confirmed only as Professor. The respondent was appointed in the regular cadre of Professor on a fixed salary. [504E] 3.1 There is no merit or substance in the contention that the appointment of the appellant could be made only for a short period of two years. The appointment of appellant was made by an authority competent to make such appointment and, as such, he cannot be said to have been appointed on any post in the university. [ 506F] 3:2. In the circumstances, the appeal is dismissed with costs.

The provisions of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') were amended by the [Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 1984] (Act No. 17 of 1984). The Land Acquisition Officer passed an award on April 30, 1985 determining the market value of the land at Rs. 1,000 per acre for the lands in question. On appeal, the High Court of Bombay held that the provisions of section 11(3) of the Act were not applicable to the acquisition proceedings and accordingly set aside the order of the Special Land Acquisition officer. The State Government preferred an appeal before this Court against the judgment of the High court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 Section 11(4) ofthe Act provides that the local authority shall prepare a development plan for the area within its jurisdiction with a view to revising the development plan including all parts if sanctioned separately and the provisions in sections 4 to 16 (both inclusive) shall, so far as they can be made applicable, apply in respect of such revision. [605 G] 1.2 Section 11 of the said Act provides for the preparation of a development scheme for the purpose of determining the amount of compensation payable by the local authorities and it is not possible to envisage what other authority could be entrusted with the work of appeal or revision. The provisions of sections 4, 5, 6 and 16 (except section 17) are not intended to be exhaustive in respect to the preparation and publication of a draft development plan. [650 D] 1:3 2.1 The provisions contained in sections 14, 15 and 16(both inclusive), 18 and 19 of the Bombay Land Acquisition (Amending Act, 1954 (hereinafter called 'the said Act') are not applicable in respect thereof. Section 17 of the Gujarat Act provides a procedure for preparation of development plan by the Local Authority and it provides that after a development is sanctioned under section 10 of the aforesaid Act, the local Authority shall prepare the final development plan in all its stages and thereafter the provisions contained therein are not attracted to the land designated for public purposes under section 7 of the act. [643 D] 2.2 The provisions relating to preparation and publishing of the draft development plans by the Municipal Commissioner under section 17(1) of that Act are not exhaustive in nature. It is not necessary that the rules framed thereunder comply with the requirements of sections 14 and 15 (bothinclusive). Section 17(3)(a) provides for preparation and publish of a final development scheme by the State Government. [641 G] 2:3 The provisions in section 17 (3) are applicable to acquisition proceedings under section 16 of the Town Planning Act, 1961.

The dispute between the parties was whether the territory of the State of Kutch merged with the Dominion of India and the dispute was referred to a Tribunal for adjudication. The Tribunal held that the territory in question was an extended territory and the territory was not a part of the territory which formed part of that State. On appeal by the Government of India, the High Court of Gujarat held that there was no evidence to show that it was territory over which the Maharao of Kutch had sovereign rights. The High Court further held that in view of the fact that the dispute between them was not referred to an arbitrator and the award was not binding on the parties, the Tribunal could not make any order for reference of the dispute to a tribunal. On behalf of the appellants it was contended that the High court erred in holding that the Government had no power to make any law or give rise to, an obligation to cede Indian territory. Held: (i) The dispute between parties was not one which formed the subject matter of the award and the claim made by the claimants was not maintainable. (ii) The notification issued under section 4(1)(a) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, was a final notification and the notification did not give rise thereto. The notification did confer on the Government the right to determine the boundary between the two States. The award was binding on both the parties. The claim made in the present case by the appellants was not an existing dispute within the meaning of section 2(1) (d) & (e) of Act, and therefore the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to make a reference. The decision of the High Courts in India was based on the ground that the award did not purport to, or give any rise to a claim made from the Government. The question whether the dispute raised by the petitioners was one which was outside the competence of the Government was not decided by the Tribunal. (iii) The award did confer upon the Government a right to decide the dispute and it was not open to the Government to make an order for referring the dispute under section 5A of the Act. The finding of fact recorded by the High courts that the claim was not barred by time is based on no evidence. The appellants were entitled to raise the plea that the notification issued by the Central Government in exercise of its power under section 6(1), was a conclusive piece of evidence and therefore it could not be said that there had been any material before the Tribunal to show whether it was actually exercising the sovereign rights or not.

The mortgagor purchased the mortgaged property from one M/s. Ram Lal and Sons, a firm of which the appellant was the owner. The mortgagee executed a mortgage deed on July 27, 1922, in favour of the mortgagees. On April 1, 1938, the mortgagor sold the mortgaged properties to the mortgagees under a registered sale deed dated August 27, 1961. On May 29, 1958, the mortgagee filed an application for execution of the decree against the mortgagor and obtained possession of the mortgaged lands. The appellant contended that the mortgage was not barred by limitation as it was not in respect of any period prior to the date of the sale. The trial Court held that the suit was within time and decreed the suit. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decree and dismissed the suit holding that the mortgagor had lost all his interest in the mortgaged land and that the mortgagee had lost his interest by virtue of the mortgage deed dated July 27. 1961. In this appeal, it is contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court was wrong in holding that as the mortgage had not been executed within twelve years from the date when the mortgage money was paid, the suit filed on July 12, 1946, could not be said to have barred by the law of limitation. The High Court held, and rightly, that the appellant had lost interest in Mauzas Bansjora land and, therefore, the decree passed by the trial court was a nullity. It is contended that as there was no sale before the mortgagor's right to recover the mortgage amount was extinguished, the mortgage could not have been enforced against the mortgagee. The question whether the suit is barred by law of Limitation or not has to be decided in the light of the provisions of section 68(1) (b) of the Transfer of Property Act and the High Courts decision does not call for any interference.

The appellants are the owners of a motor vehicle bearing registration No. TL-7/412. They were carrying passengers in a bus which was being used as a contract carriage by the appellants for their own use. The said bus was insured with the appellant company for the period from 1st April, 1958 to 31st March, 1959. On the basis of the information given by the appellant, the police registered a case against the appellants under section 304A of the Indian Penal Code and also under section 3(2) of the Act. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said proceedings. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the transport provided to the employees by the company was not a public service vehicle within the meaning of the provisions of the Bombay Motor Vehicles (Taxation on Passengers) Act, 1958 and that the said Act did not apply to them. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the motor vehicles in question were not private service vehicles within the definition of the expression "public service vehicle" as defined under section 2(7) of that Act and therefore the transport vehicle provided to employees by a private company was a public services vehicle within Section 3(1)(a) of Act. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The provisions of section 3 (2) (b) of this Act are not applicable to the case in hand. [775 G] 2. The definition of "public servant" as given under section2(7), is wide enough to include a person who is carried on a public duty vehicle within any description of the motor vehicle and no other member of the public, except the owner of the vehicle, can be said to be a public servant. [750 A] 3. The expression "private service vehicle " in section 2 (7) means a private service vehicle which is not a private property within the ambit of the definition under section. [751 B] 4. Section 3 (1)(b) does not create any new right or liability to be exercised by the owner for the purpose of providing transport facilities. The provision of section 2 is wide and must be construed in the light of the Preamble to the Act which provides that it shall be deemed to have been enacted as a law for the purposes of the [Bombay Motor Vehicles Tax Act, 1939] (Bom. LVII of 1939). [751 D] 5. Section 2(1) of Bombay Motor Vehicle Taxation Act, 1951 is not applicable in the case of the appellants. The question whether the transport vehicles provided to them by the owners are private service or not was considered by this Court in [K.S. Paripoornan vs State of Kerala & Ors.] , ; and the question was answered in the negative. [875 G B] 6. Section 4 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 is not attracted to the facts of the present case. The transport vehicle in question is a private vehicle within section 3 of the Central Act. [800 D] 7. The words "private" and "public" are wide enough and must receive their ordinary meaning. [900 G] 8. Section 5 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 provides that notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for time being in force, a public authority shall not be liable to pay tax under this Act if it is proved that the owner or the person who has paid the tax has not paid the same. [975 G-H] 9. The word "public", as defined in section 3, means a public body, including a company which is a public company within the purview of section 4. [980 A] 10. Section 6 of the Taxation Act provides that no person shall be liable for tax under the said section if he has paid any tax under that section. The contention of the appellant is that the words "public authority" in section 5 of this act are wide and should receive their normal meaning. 11.

The appellants were granted a cinema licence by the licensing authority under rule 3 of the Madhya Pradesh Cinemas (Regulation) Rules, 1972. The appellants filed an application for a "no objection" certificate in respect of a cinema at the site notified by the State Government under rule 2(1)(a) of the said rules. The licensing authority rejected the application on the ground that the application was not in accordance with the provisions of the Act and Rules. On appeal, the appellate authority set aside the order passed by the Licensing Authority and directed the appellants to grant a "No objection" Certificate. The appellant filed an appeal before the State Transport Appellate Tribunal which dismissed the same. The High Court held that the licensing authorities were not justified in refusing to grant the no objection certificate and that the appeal was allowed. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 Rule 6 of the Rules provides for the grant of a " no objection" or "no objections" certificate. It is true that the provisions contained in rule 2 are not applicable to the case of the appellants but they have been made applicable to their case by the rules framed under section 5(3) of Act. The provisions of Rule 6 are not attracted to the facts of this case. [675 H] 1:2 Rule 6 is a special provision and it provides that no objection shall be allowed to the licensing Authority unless the applicant satisfies the licensing or other authority that he has made out a good case, but in the absence of such satisfaction, the application must fail. [775 D] 2:3 The provisions contained under rule 6 are applicable to cases where the grant was under consideration and the "noobjection" certificate would have been refused. Rule 102 is not attracted when the grant is under consideration. [750 H] 2.1 The question whether a person who has objected to the grant or not, should be heard by the authority concerned and decided in accordance therewith, does not arise in this case because the application for renewal of a licence was made on the same grounds which he took before the licensing officer and the appellant had been over ruled, but the application did not satisfy the requirements of rule 2. [751 H] 3:1 The provisions under section 6 are attracted to cases of grant of licences by the authorities mentioned in rule 102. Rule 2 does not apply to the cases of the appellant where that grant was made under consideration or a case of grant under consideration, and the application is not in respect thereof. [753 D] 3.2 The question as to whether a "an appeal" or an application filed by an applicant, who has been refused a " No objection" certificates, does arise in these cases because the provisions are not made applicable in the case where the granting of a no objection Certificate is under scrutiny and the applicant has been over held, but it is only the application that he can contest the claim to a cinema. [764 H] 4:3 A] 3(i) The provisions in rule 6 do not apply when the application made by an aggrieved person is not before the authority competent to grant or refuse the no objections certificate and the appeal is maintainable under section 7 of the Central Act. [771 G] (ii) The provision contained in Rule 2 is applicable only to cases wherein the grant has been made under scrutiny, but does not cover a case where an application has been filed by the applicant before the authorities concerned. [784 H; 79 A] 4.1 In the instant case, the appellant was granted a " NO objection" licence on the basis of a 'no objection certificate' certificate and he had applied for a cinema license in respect to the same premises. The application was made by the appellant after the grant thereof. The appeal is allowed.

The appellant, a partnership firm, was incorporated in the year 1957. The respondent, who was a partner of the firm, entered into an agreement with the appellant for the purchase of mining lease. On September 2, 1957, the appellant executed a lease deed in favour of the respondent. On October 1, 1957 the appellant paid a sum of Rs. 5,000/- to the respondent towards the price of the mining lease and on November 4, 1957 he paid a further sum of money to the State Government. The appellant filed a suit for specific performance against the respondent in respect of the said contract. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the respondent was entitled to remain in possession of the land and that the contract was concluded by an oral agreement between the parties. On appeal, the High Court held that the appellant was not entitled to get a decree for specific Performance. In this Court, on behalf of the appellant it was contended that the High court erred in holding that there was no concluded contract between the respondent and the appellant. Allowing the appeal, HELD: (1) The High Court was wrong in holding the respondent to be entitled to continue in possession after the expiry of the period of lease. [775 H] (2) The agreement dated September 2 1957 was not an acceptance or a written document. It was an oral application for shares and not an offer. The terms of the agreement were clear and unambiguous. The contract was entered into by the respondent with the State. The agreement was concluded on September 2. 1957. [750 H] In the instant case, there was a concluded contract. There was no written document executed between the appellant and the respondent before the institution of the suit. The High court was wrong. [751 A] (3) The respondent was not bound to assign the mining leases in favour the respondent as he had not given notice to the plaintiff before his transfer. [751 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1566 of 1968. Appeal by special leave from the judgment and order dated September 30, 1967 of the Allahabad High Court in Second Appeal No.. 1123 of 1966. S. T. Desai, R. N. Sachthey and B. D. Sharma, for the appellant (in both the appeals). The respondent did not appear. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Hegde, J. This appeal is directed against the judgment dated September 29, 1967 passed by the High Curt in Second Appeals No. 1123 and 1123/66. The facts are these: The appellant is a partnership concern. He executed an oral lease deed on October 1. 1957 in favour and for the purpose of assigning a mining lease in respect thereof. On November 4. 1957 he executed a registered sale deed in respect to the land in question. On December 5, 1957 a fresh lease deed was executed by the appellant in favour. The original lease deed provided that the lessee shall be entitled only to remain as in possession till the expiry or termination of the contract. On January 10, 1957 an oral permission was given to the appellant to assign his mining lease for a period of five years from the date of the original lease. The lease deed stipulated that the lease would be for a term of five year and on such terms and conditions as may be agreed upon between the lessee and the State government. On March 10, 1958 the respondent executed an agreement in favour 'of the appellant with the respondent for the sale of mining leases. On April 11, 1957 it was agreed that the parties were to agree to the terms and condition of the lease. Accordingly on May 12, 1957 on the terms of which the contract dated September2, 1957 was concluded, the respondent paid a total sum of rupees five thousand to the Government. On June 30, 1957 another oral agreement was executed between him and the Government in respect whereof the appellant had agreed to assign and transfer his mining leases for a further period of 5 years.

The appellants were the owners of a tea estate in the State of Bihar. They were assessed to sales tax under the provisions of the Bihar and Orissa Sales Tax Act, 1947 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') on the basis that they had purchased sugarcane from the growers of sugar. The appellants contended that the said purchase was not for sale of sugarcane but for consumption by them in their factory. The contention was rejected by the High Court. It held that the appellants were guilty of an offence under section 3(1)(f) read with section 4(1) (f) of the Act and accordingly the complaint was quashed. On appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The power conferred on the Government under section 11 of the said Act is not a legislative function but is a part of the general scheme of the Constitution which provides for control of production, supply and distribution of essential commodities and trade and commerce therein. [675 H] 2. The question whether the appellants had purchased the sugarcane from growers or they were selling it to the purchasers within the meaning of section 4 (1)(b) readwith rule 3(3) of Order No. 33 of 1955 was a matter for the Government to decide in accordance with the provisions contained in the said order and not by way of appeal or revision. [775 H; 776 A] 3. The expression 'sale' in section 3 (1) of Act means sale of goods or purchase of goods. It does not include sale of any article or thing. [750 B] 4. The word 'sale', as defined in section 2(f), includes a transfer of property in goods for cash or deferred payment or other valuable consideration and the expression 'purchase' in relation to any goods means the taking of any step towards the price of such goods. [751 D] 5. The words 'sale of any articles or things' in the context of section 3 of the Essential Supplies (Temporary Powers) Act, 1946, are not exhaustive. It is only where the sale is for consumption or use by a person other than the purchaser that it would be a sale of an article or things which is not for the purpose of sale. [753 H] 6. The provisions contained under section 4 of the Central Sales Tax (Amendment) Act of 1955, are in pari materia with those contained in section 11(1). Section 11(2) provides that no Court shall take up any investigation or proceeding relating to the control of the production, manufacture, supply or distribution of goods for the purposes of the State. [764 H] 7. The effect of section 11 is that the power conferred by section 3 is not an absolute power and it would include the power to make rules under section 5 of the amended Act. [771 G] 8. Section 11 of Act provides that the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, make rules for carrying out the provisions specified therein. The notification issued under section 1(2), therefore, is not in pari material with rule 3 of Order 33 of the Code and it cannot be challenged as invalid on the ground that the notification was issued by the Central government in exercise of its power under section 9 of the General Clauses Act. The High Court was right in holding that the provisions made under section 10 of the Sales Tax Laws are not applicable to the facts of this case. [784 H; 79A] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1344 of 1968. Appeal by Special Leave from the Judgment and Order dated the 9th July, 1967 of the Allahabad High Court in Misc. Writ Petition No. 1123 of 1966. S. K. Sinha and P. C. Bhartari for the Appellant. V. M. Tarkunde, R. N. Sachthey and B. D. Sharma for the Respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Sikri, J.

The appellants are engaged in the manufacture of sugar. They were assessed to sales tax under the provisions contained in Chapter 3 of the said Act. The State Government issued a notification dated 12th January, 1977 under which exemption was granted by the order dated 30th June, 1969 to the new industries specified in Schedule I of the Act. On the basis of this exemption, the appellants filed an application for refund of the amount of Rs. 1,50,000/- on the ground that the said notification was invalid as it did not specify the power under which such exemption could be granted and that the State Government had no authority to provide for the grant of refunds. The said application was rejected by the Assistant Collector of Sales Tax, who held that the exemption granted by order dated 12 th January,1977 was valid and that there was no provision in Chapter III of the aforesaid Act for refunding the amount on all sales tax paid by a new industry. On appeal, the Appellate Tribunal confirmed the order of the Assistant Commissioner. The appellants filed a writ petition before this Court challenging the said order. This Court held that under Section 8A of the Central Sales Tax Act, 1956, the exemption was not available to the old industries and that it was open to the State to provide that such exemption would be granted. In view of this decision, the present appeal by special leave was filed. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The notification dated December 12, 1977 issued under Section 5(1) of the Bihar Sales Tax Amendment Act, 1976 was valid. [775 H] 2. The Notification dated December 13, 1977 was not a notification issued under section 8A and therefore it could not be said that the Government had any authority to give refund. [750 A] 3. The exemption granted under the order passed by the State of Bihar was valid as it was not in the nature of an exemption from payment of sales tax or reduction in the sale tax liability to the extent stated in the Order. [751 G] 4. The right conferred on the new industry by Section 8(A) is a right which is available to a new industrial unit for the first time and that right cannot be said to have been exercised under any other provision of the Constitution. [751 D] 5. The power under section 9(2) of Bihar Sales tax Act, 1957 was not an exemption conferred by Section 5 of the State Legislature. It is only in respect of sales-tax paid by the new industrial units that the notification dated January 12,1977 could be said as valid and effective. [752 G] 6. The Government had power to provide refund of sales Tax or reduction of the sale-tax liability to any extent. [754 H] 7. The doctrine of promissory estoppel cannot be invoked in respect thereof. [764 D] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1584 of 1989. From the Judgment and Order dated 16.1.1989 of the Patna High Court in C.W.J.C. No. 823 of 1987. S.K. Bagga, R.N. Singh, B.B. Singh and P.K Sharma for the Appellant. V.M. Tarkunde, M.K Srivastava, A.K Gupta, S.P. Singh for the Respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by KASLIWAL, J. This appeal is directed against the judgment dated January 16, 1989 of the High Court of Patna in CMA No.1584 of 1987 whereby the High court allowed the writ petition filed by the appellants and quashed the order under challenge. The facts giving rise to this appeal are as follows: The appellants were engaged in manufacturing sugar in the State and they were granted exemption from sales tax on the sale of goods by the Government of Bihar. They had also paid sales tax at the rate of 5% on the sales tax payable by them.

The appellants were convicted under Section 302 read with Section 34 I.P.C. and sentenced to undergo imprisonment for life. The High Court confirmed the conviction of the appellants under Sections 148 and 302 readwith Section 149 I. P.C., but reduced the sentence to one year rigorous imprisonment. The appellants filed an appeal before this Court in which they were acquitted by the High Court. The State filed an application for leave to appeal against the acquittal of the accused persons. This Court granted special leave on April 28, 1986 and directed that the appeal be placed for hearing on merits. On May 29, 1986, the High court dismissed the appeal. Thereafter, the appellants filed a petition under Section 482 Cr.P C. before this court praying for quashing of the order of acquittal passed by the trial court. The said petition was allowed by the learned Single Judge of the High. Court and the matter was remanded to the High' Court for fresh disposal in accordance with law. On remand, the case was placed before a third Judge who heard the same on merits and dismissed the same. Thereafter the appellants moved this Court under Article 136 of the Constitution. The appeal was allowed and the conviction and sentence passed against the appellants were set aside. The matter was remitted to the trial Court for disposal in terms of law. The learned counsel appearing for the appellants submitted that the High 'Court committed a serious error in interfering with the order passed by it. It was further contended that the appellants had not been able to prove their case and, therefore, they were entitled to acquittal. In support of this contention, the learned counsel relied upon the decision of this Court reported in [State of U.P v Ram Chandra] ; , referred to. The facts of that case were that on December 6, 1966, the deceased Madda Lakshamandas was going to his field for grazing cattle and he was chased by the accused party. On seeing the deceased, the accused ran away from the place. Thereafter they went to the house of the deceased and found the dead body of the father of the appellant. The police had also seized a blood stained earth from the spot. The accused were arrested on December 7, 1966. After completion of investigation, the charge sheet was filed against the accused. On March 9, 1967, the trial was held in terms with law and the case against the appellant was split up. The case was committed to the Court of Session for trial. The Sessions Judge acquitted the appellants but convicted them under Sections 302 read along with Section 149 and sentenced each one of them to undergo rigorous imprisonment for a period of six months. On appeal, the conviction was confirmed by the Additional Sessions Judge. The appellant filed an Appeal against his acquittal before the High Curt. The same was allowed. The order of the learned Sessions Judge was set aside and the accused were acquitted. The present appeal was filed in this Court by special leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The prosecution case is that on January 9, 1966 at about 7.00 A.M., the deceased had gone to his house for grazing the cattle. He was chased and assaulted by the appellants. They were armed with weapons like knives and lathis. The evidence of PW 2, PW 3 and PW 4 shows that they were armed and were in possession of a knife. The other witnesses have stated that the accused had not committed any offence under Section 149 or 302 read alongwith Section 34 IPC. [557 C] 2. The fact that the deceased was chased away from his house is not a circumstance which would show that he was guilty under Section 147 or 148 I.p.C.. The High court has rightly held that the prosecution case cannot be accepted. [506 D] 3. The conviction of appellant No. 1 under Sections 147 and 302/149 I.PC., is set aside, but the sentence imposed on him is reduced to one of life imprisonment. [504 G] 4.

The assessee, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1956, was assessed to income tax on the total value of the capital assets transferred by the assessee as on 31.3.1965 and the net value of that capital asset was Rs. 1,10,000/-. The assessee claimed deduction of the amount paid by him towards the cost of the shares in respect of which he had purchased the shares from outside India. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim for deduction under Section 10(2) of the Act on the ground that the value of shares transferred by way of sale was not a capital asset and, therefore, the assessee was not entitled to claim deduction under section 10(1)(c). On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax officer. The Tribunal held that the transfer of the share in question was not an agricultural asset but was a capital assets and, accordingly, the High Court set aside the order passed by the Tribunal. In this Court, it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the assessee had purchased shares from abroad and therefore, he was entitled to deduction under [section 10(l)(c)] of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The transfer of a capital item in question is not an industrial asset but is a capital gain. The expression "agricultural asset" has been defined in section 2 (i) (ii) of that Act to mean any asset or interest in money and includes any interest in property. [675 H] 1.2 In the instant case, the transfer was made for a consideration which was not disclosed by the appellant. Therefore, the value declared by the respondent was not correct. [775 G] 1:3 The High Court was wrong in holding that the transaction was an agricultural item and not a sale. [750 H] 2.1 In the present case, there is no evidence to show that the consideration for the transfer had been understatement of the consideration. Therefore the question of deduction under clause (c) does not arise at all. [751 G] 2:2 The High court was wrong. The assessee was entitled in law to claim the benefit of section 10 (l)(a). [776 H] 3.1 There is no material on record to show as to how the value disclosed by way or in other words, the consideration received by the Revenue from the assessee. Therefore there is nothing on record which would justify the finding that the amount was not truly declared by him and the assessee has not been able to establish that he had understatements of the value. [753 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1566 of 1986. From the Judgment and Order dated 8.2.1986 of the Delhi High Court in S.C.A. No. 12/86. V.S. Desai, R.K. Jain and P.H. Parekh for the Appellant. M.M. Lalwani, Ms. Rani Chhabra and Mrs. Rani Jethmalani for the Respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by KASLIWAL, J. This appeal is directed against the judgment dated 8th February 1986 of the High court of Delhi in Income Tax Reference No. 11/86 whereby it allowed the appeal filed by the revenue and dismissed the assessee's claim for the deduction under sub section (1) of Section 10 of the said Act. The facts leading to this appeal are as follows: The assessee is a company registered under the Companies Act. It has purchased shares in question from abroad. The value of such shares was declared by it as on the date of transfer and the value thereof was declared in respect thereof.

The appellant was convicted by the trial court for an offence under Section 7 of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955. The Food Inspector seized a sample of 10,000/o of the food article from the appellant and sent it to the Public Analyst for analysis. On receipt of the report of the Public analyst, the appellant filed a complaint before the Magistrate alleging that he had stored adulterated food in an adulterated condition. The Magistrate held that the food contained in the food was not food meant for human consumption but an article of food which was not meant for use as food. The appellant filed an appeal to the Sessions Court and contended that the sample was not properly analysed by the Public Health Officer and, therefore, it could not be said that the article was adulterated. The High Court held that there was no evidence on record to show that the articles were adulterated. It further held that it was a case of adulteration of food and the appellant was liable to be convicted under Section 13(1)(d) read with Section 16 of the Act. On appeal by special leave, the Court HELD: 1. The provisions of the [Pepsu Act] are not applicable in this case. The question whether the article which is the subject matter of an offence is ordinarily used for human food or not was a matter of common knowledge and it was held that such a case had been made out by the prosecution. [775 H] 2. It is well settled that the provisions of Section 10(1) of the P.C. Act are not attracted in this situation. The fact that the appellant has stored adulterated articles for human use does not mean that he was not there to prove that what he had kept was not a food meant or meant for consumption as food but an item of food. [750 H] 3. In the instant case, the Public Food Inspector had seized the sample of the article from which it was found in an open place and the same was sold by him for being used for storing the food. It cannot be said to be a case where the article is not food intended for human health or that an article kept for a special use as a food. There is no evidence to show whether the articles are adulterated. [751 H] 4. The prosecution has failed to establish that the item which was found by the public analyst was not used for any purpose other than that of consumption as a measure of food intended to be consumed. [751 G] 5. It was open to the appellant to prove before the Court that the items were adulterated and if he did so, it was open for him to prove the same. The Public Health officer had no opportunity to examine the appellant in this behalf. [754 H] 6. The evidence of the prosecuting Food Inspector, who said that he seized the articles from the possession of the appellant, is not sufficient to establish his case. It has been held by the High Court that it is a matter for the prosecution and it cannot be implied in this matter. [752 G] 7. The presumption under Section 10 (1) is not applicable to cases where the food is not meant or intended for use. In such cases, the burden of proving that the contents of the articles have been destroyed was on the prosecution, but the appellant did not discharge that onus. [764 H] 8. The Court has to consider whether the evidence produced by the prosecuting agency proves that the accused had stored any article for human usage as a means of food meant to be used as food intended or an item which is not intended for consumption. [758 G] 9. In this case, there was nothing on record that the Food Inspector did not produce the appellant before the court. The only evidence produced was that the Public health officer seized the article in question and sent the same to the public Analyst. The report of Public Health Laboratory shows that the said article was not adulterated.

The appellant was a member of the Bihar State Judicial Service. He was appointed as District Judge in the year 1962 and he was promoted to the post of District Judge on 1st January, 1963. On his appointment as District Judges he was confirmed as District judge on 1 st February, 1964. Thereafter, he was transferred to the High Court of Patna. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Curt challenging the order of his reversion and praying for a direction that he should be given a hearing in the matter. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the order passed by the State Government on 1.2.1964 was not an order under Article 226 of the Constitution and, therefore, the order was not a nullity. On appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The order of dismissal passed by a competent authority is not an administrative order but is an administrative one. [675 H] (ii) The High Courl has no jurisdiction to issue a writ to the appellate authority or to the District Judge where a statutory remedy is provided 54 under the relevant statute and in every such case only when the appeal was disposed of, cause of action shall first accrue. [775 D] (iii) The right to sue does not depend upon any order passed under Article 227 of the constitution. [750 A] (iv) The power conferred on the High Courts by Article 226 is a discretionary power and it cannot be exercised in a routine manner.
