[751 B] (v) The appellant was appointed by the Central Government as District and Sessions Judge in 1962 and his appointment was confirmed by the appellate order of the State government dated 1st February, 1963 and he continued to hold that post till the date when the order dated 1.1.1964 became final. [753 D] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1566 of 1967. Appeal from the judgment and order dated April 2, 1966 of the Patna High Court in C.W.J.C. No. 8 of 1964. S. K. Sinha, for the appellant. R.K. Garg, for respondent No. 1. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Shah, J. This appeal is directed against a judgment and decree dated April 22, 1966 passed by Patna High court in Appeal from Order No. 2 of 1963. The facts giving rise to this appeal are as follows: The appellant is a member and working as District & Sessions Judge. He filed an application before the State of Bihar for a writ of certiorari quashing the order terminating his services. The learned Single Judge dismissed the petition holding, inter alia, that the appellant was not appointed by any competent authority and he had no jurisdiction. The Division Bench held that the appointment of the appellant as District Magistrate was illegal. The Letters Patent Appeal filed against this judgment was allowed by a Division Bench of the High court on April 2. 1966. The State Government preferred an appeal to the Supreme Court. The appeal was dismissed on April 22. 1966 and the order dismissing the petition was confirmed. The present appeal is by special leave. The only question that arises for consideration in this appeal is whether the appellant is entitled to be given an opportunity of being heard before the termination of his services as District Munsif. The respondent No 1 filed a counter affidavit in which he stated that the State had no authority to terminate his services and, in any event, the HighCourt was not justified in dismissing the writ application on the ground that the impugned order was passed by an incompetent authority. The point raised before us is that the learned Single judge has erred in holding that there was no valid order of termination of service as such. It is true that the Division Bench has held that there is no valid reason for not accepting the appellant's contention that the High courts have jurisdiction to entertain a writ application under Article 32 of the Act and it is not open to the appellant to raise this point in the appeal.

The appellant, a minor, filed a suit for partition and separate possession of the properties in dispute. The trial court decreed the suit on the ground that the appellant was entitled to get a decree for partition of his properties. The appellant filed an appeal against the decree before the District Court which confirmed the decree passed by the trial court. The High Court held that the decree was not a decree of affirmance and since the variation in the appellate decree was made in favour of one party, it was not necessary to pass a variation in regard to the order as well as the variation. In this appeal by special leave, the appellant contended that the High Court erred in holding that the variation made in the appeal was not an integral part of the decision or the decree and that the finding of the trial judge that the modification was not in favour or contrary to law was erroneous. The question whether the variation was a result of the nature of the original order or it was a variation made by the appellate court was not decided by the High court. It was held that if an appeal is allowed, the variation must be treated as a decree and only the party in whose favour the variation has been made would be entitled to go to the Privy Council. The correctness of this decision was challenged before this Court by special Leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: (1) The High court was right in holding the variation to be not a judgment of affirmances but it was an integral and essential part of that decision. [775 H] (2) The variation made on the basis of the appellate order was not merely a result in favour by the nature or the original decree but was a mere alteration in the original judgment. [750 A] (3) The finding of fact recorded by the first appellate court that the modified appeal was an essential part thereof was erroneous and it was rightly set aside by the lower court. [751 D] (4) The order passed by this Court on appeal was final and conclusive and no further question of law could be raised in the second appeal. [753 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1566 of 1968. Appeal from the judgment and decree dated April 10, 1967 of the Punjab High Court in First Appeal No.. 11 of 1965. S. K. Mehta, for the appellant. R. N. Sachthey, for respondent No. 1. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Shah, J. This appeal is directed against the judgment of the High C Court dated April 20, 1967 dismissing the second suit filed by the appellant for partition. The facts leading to this appeal are as follows: The appellant is a minor and he had been appointed guardian of his minor son. He filed an application under section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the order passed in the trial Court on the grounds that the appellate Court was wrong in holding, that the order of the first court was erroneous because it was passed by it without giving a hearing to the appellant and that it was therefore not necessary for him to pass an order of remand. The learned Judge held that there was no material before him to show that the appeal against his order was heard by the District Judge. He further held that in view of the provisions of section 11, the High Courts were right in setting aside that order. In the result, the appeal is dismissed with costs.

The respondent, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1956, was assessed to sales tax in respect of its sales by the Sales Tax Officer. The Sales Tax officer issued a notice under section 25, Provincial Small Cause Courts Act, calling upon the assessee to pay the amount of Rs. 1,00,000/and odd as tax due from him on the sale of his goods. On receipt of the said notice, the assessee filed a return of his income and claimed that he was entitled to the benefit of section 25 of the Provincial Small Causes Courts Act. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim by order dated March 31, 1979. He held that the sales were not liable to tax under section 115, Code of Civil Procedure. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax officer and dismissed the appeal. On further appeal, a Division Bench of the High Court allowed the writ petition filed by the assessee and quashed the order passed by the Income tax Officer. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the Sales tax officer had no jurisdiction to make an order under section 10, Code, of Civil procedure, as he had no power to make such an order. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the Income-tax Officer had no authority to make any order under Section 25, [Code of Civil Procedures] and the provisions of section 115 Code of civil Procedure were not applicable to the State of Uttar Pradesh. [557F] 2.1 The Sales tax Officer had jurisdiction to pass an order for payment of tax due by the dealer on the sales made by him. He could have passed an order in terms of section 10 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, but he did not do so. [506 G] 2:2 In the instant case, the Sales-tax officer had jurisdiction under section 5, Code to pass a final order under that section. The order passed under section 11, Code was not appealable under section 12 and no question could have arisen of invoking the revisional power of the State Government under section 35, [506 A] 2.[357A] 2I: 3.1 In the present case, there is no provision in section 115 of the code of Civil procedural law which empowers the High court to revise an order passed in exercise of its jurisdiction under that Section. The provisions of sections 25, 26 and 27 of the [Code] are not applicable in the State. [504F] 3.2 In any event, the sales could be assessed by a competent authority under section 8, Code. The power of revision conferred on the High Courts under section 15, Code is not available to the High courts under section 36, Code and the High Curt was right. [54 G] 4. Section 25 of Provincial Small cause Courts Act provides that no order passed or proceedings taken under the said section shall be called in question in any Court inferior to the District Court. The words "any court" occurring in section 25 are not relevant for the purpose of this case. [55 D] 5. In view of the provisions contained in sections 25 and 26, [55 G] 6. Section 35 of the Act provides for revision by the High or the State Governments under section 24. [56 H] 7. The powers conferred on a District Court under section 33 are not available in the case of the Government of Uttar pradesh. [57 D] 8. Section 5, Civil Procedure Code, does not apply to the cases of the Central Government and the State Legislature has no power under section 34 to make orders for payment or recovery of tax by the authorities specified therein. [58 G] 9. The sales tax officer is competent to pass any order in exercise o the revisional powers of the state Government under sections 25 to 26, Provincial Civil Courts Act and the rules made thereunder. [59 H] 10.

The respondents filed a writ petition before the High Court of Rajasthan challenging the notification issued by the State Government under section 52(1) of the Act on the ground that it was not necessary for them to file an appeal against the said notification. The High Court quashed the notification dated February 8, 1984 and directed the State to release the land in favour of the respondents. On appeal by the respondents, the Division Bench of the High court held that the notification under section 51(1)(a) of Act was not a valid one and accordingly set aside the order passed by the Special Officer, Town Planning Department, Jaipur. The State Government filed an appeal before this Court against the judgment of the Division bench of the Rajasthan High Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The notification under Section 52(2) of The Act is not a nullity in so far as it purports to be issued by a competent authority of the State. [775 H] 2.1 The notification issued under section 3(1), Town Planning and Urban Development Scheme, Jaipur was valid only for a public purpose namely, for the implementation of a development scheme at public expense viz., the Civil Lines Extension Scheme, The said scheme was not in existence at the time when the notification was issued by State Government. [750 A] 2:2 Section 52 (1) is an enabling provision and it empowers the State government to acquire land under section52(1). It does not confer any power on the State or its officers to proceed with the inquiry under section 53 of the said Act. The scheme framed under section 54 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 is a valid piece of legislation. [751 B] 2.(i) Section 52 of the Town Planning Act, 1956 provides that no person shall be entitled to acquire any land in contravention of the provisions of this Act or the rules made thereunder unless he has been given an opportunity of being heard. [75 H; 75 A] (ii) The notification dated March 13, 1984 issued under sub section (1), is not valid for a period of five years from the date of its publication and the notification is liable to be quashed on that ground alone. [76 B] 3.1 Section 52 is an important provision which empowers the Government to acquire lands in public interest by issuing a notification under sub-section (2) thereof. The power conferred on the Government under sub sections (1)(b), (1A) and (1B) of section 52 is not an enabling power but it is a power conferred upon the State and its officers.

The appellant was the tenant of a building in which he was residing. He filed a petition for eviction against the respondent on the ground that the respondent had committed default in payment of rent and damages for use and occupation of the building due from him. The trial court held that the appellant was entitled to the benefit of s.39 of the new Act and accordingly, dismissed the application. On appeal by the respondent, the High Court reversed the judgment and decree of the trial court and restored the order passed by the trial judge. In this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the provisions of s..39 of old Act were not applicable to a building which had become ten years old on the date when the revision petition was heard by the High court. HELD: (i) The provisions of sub section (1) of s.(2) of the old Act are mandatory and they do not confer any right on the tenant to claim the benefit under s. 39 of the Act. [775 H] (ii) Section 20 of the New Rent Act provides a bar to a suit for eviction on that ground. The provisions contained in sub section(1) are mandatory. If the tenant in default pays all arrears of rent due from the landlord, such damages for using and occupation as provided in the section would be payable by him. [750 H] In the instant case, the respondent was not entitled to claim benefit under S.39(2) because he had committed a default in paying the rent due by him under sub section 1 of s (1). [776 H] The provisions relating to arrears of rents and damages were mandatory and the landlord was entitled only to the protection of s,39 of Act. The respondent was entitled not only to claim that the amount of rent as directed by the Court was paid by him but he would be entitled to get the benefit thereunder. [751 G] (iii) The provision in sub-section (1)(a) of section 20 is mandatory and it does not confer a right on a tenant to recover damages for user and occupation from his tenant. [753 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1266 of 1967. Appeal by special leave from the judgment & order dated April 10, 1966 of the Allahabad High Court in S.C.A. No. 11 of 1965. A. K. Sen, for the appellant. R. N. Sachthey, for respondent No. 1. The Judgment of the Court delivered by Hegde, J. This appeal is directed against the judgment of the High,Court at Allahabad dated April 20, 1966 in S/s. (1), (2) and (3). The appellant was a tenant of the premises in which the respondent-landlord had been residing. On March 16, 1965, the Rent Controller passed an order for eviction of the respondent from the premises on the grounds specified in sub sections (1A) and(2). The respondent filed an application under s.. 20 of Act No. 13 of 1972 before the Rent Control Tribunal, Allahabad, praying that he should be evicted from the said premises. The appellant contended that the building was not a building within the meaning of s 2(e) of Act 13 of 1973 and that the order of eviction passed by him was illegal. The Rent Controller dismissed the petition on the basis of the ground specified in clause (a), (b) and clause (c). The Appellate Authority, however, held that there was no material before it to come to a conclusion that the said building was a building as defined in s 2 (e) and that it was not an "building" within the Act and therefore, the order for possession passed by it was illegal and void. The Appellate Tribunal also held that since the respondent did not pay the arrears of damages, the appellant could not be evicted on the said ground.

The appellant, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was incorporated in the year 1948. The appellant was an employee of the respondent company. He was appointed as a Director of the Company on April 1, 1948. On May 5, 1948, he executed a deed of assignment in favour of the appellant. The document was executed by the appellant in his capacity as the Managing Director of a company. On June 6, 1948 the appellant executed an agreement for arbitration in accordance with the provisions of section 35 of the Stamp Act. On July 7, 1948 he filed an application under section 34 of the Arbitration Act, 1940, praying that the award be set aside and the matter be remitted to the arbitrator for fresh disposal according to law. The arbitrator rejected the application on the ground that the agreement was not executed by a person who was authorised to do so by the Governor, and that the document was not an instrument in writing signed by both the parties. On appeal, the High Court of Calcutta held that the arbitration clause contained in the deed of assign was an instrument which was complete and effective as soon as it was amended and that there could be no question of any fresh reference to arbitration. The High Court further held that under section 35(1) of the Indian Stamp Act, the document is not a certified copy but a true copy. On the other hand, the agreement dated February 6,1948, was executed between the appellant and the respondent on April 5, 1949, and signed by the parties in token of its contents. The question whether the document could be validly registered or not came up for consideration before this Court in [K. K. Das vs The East India Commercial Co. Ltd.] , referred to above. In that case, the appellant was a partner of a firm which was incorporated under an agreement dated April 1. 1948. He executed a power of attorney on behalf of the firm in favour and in respect of the property in question. On August 7, 1949 he executed another power of Attorney in favour, of the partnership firm in respect to the property mentioned therein. The deed of transfer was registered on July 7. 1950. On September 6, 1950, the respondent filed an objection under section 48 of the Act before the arbitrator stating that the original document was a certified true copy and that it was not a true one. The trial court held that there was no valid reference to the arbitration agreement in question and accordingly dismissed the application. On further appeal, this Court reversed the judgment of the High court and held that as the original deed was not registered, the original was admissible in evidence and that if the document had been executed by an agent who was not authorised to act on behalf or for the purpose of the transaction, it could be used for collateral purposes. In the result, the appeal was allowed and the order passed by the High. Court was set aside. The respondent filed a special leave petition in this Court which was also dismissed. On behalf of appellant, Mr. S. T. Desai, learned counsel appearing on behalf Of the respondent submitted that the power to execute an agreement is not an original document and that as such it could not be used by the respondent for collateral purpose. The contention of the learned counsel for the respondent was that under s. 35(2) of Stamp Act the document cannot be registered in respect thereof. It was further contended that the High Courts decision in India was erroneous and should be setaside. On a consideration of the provisions contained in s.35, we are unable to accept this contention. The agreement dated May 5. 1948, was not entered into by the agent who executed the document. The contract was not one for which an arbitration clause could be incorporated in it. The arbitration clause is an instrument executed by two persons and the agreement is a registered document. Under s. 36 of the Contract Act, an agreement to refer to arbitration is an original contract.

The appellant was a Government servant. He was appointed as a Head Constable in the Department of Home, Government of Tamil Nadu on 1.7.1971. On his retirement from service he was promoted to the post of Head Constable by order dated 30.6.1972. The appellant filed a criminal complaint against him for offences under Section 120B read with Section 420 IPC and Section 5(1)(d) read with section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 (hereinafter referred to as "the Act"). On the basis of the said charge sheet, the appellant was charged for an offence under Section 5 (1)(e) readwith Section 5 of the Act. The trial court held that the prosecution had failed to prove the charges against the appellant and accordingly acquitted him. In appeal, the High Court set aside the order of acquittal and convicted the appellant under Section 6(1) of Prevention of corruption Act, 1988 (hereinafter called "the said Act"). The appellant was also found guilty of an offence punishable under Section 7 read with [Section 13(2)] of the aforesaid Act. On appeal by special leave, the Court held that there was no evidence to show that the accused had committed any offence and accordingly dismissed the appeal. In this appeal, it is contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court should not have quashed the prosecution on the ground that the public servant was prosecuted for an alleged offence under [Section 5(i)(d)] read with Sections 5(3) and 5(4) of Act. It was further submitted that the order passed by the High,Court quashing the prosecution is erroneous in law as it has been passed without application of mind to the facts of the case. The learned counsel for the respondent on the other hand supported the judgment of the High. Court. Section 6 of the General Clauses Act provides that no person shall be entitled to any benefit under a Government Servant or under a State Government, unless he is in possession of a valid licence and the said provision does not provide for any exemption from payment of tax. The question whether the public servants are liable to pay tax under Section 3(1), as against the public exchequer, was considered by this Court in [State of Punjab vs Ram Chander] , and it was held that in view of the provisions contained in Section 6 (1) read along with Section 5, the public officer is not entitled to claim exemption from the payment of any tax. In the present case, the prosecution has failed to establish the charges levelled against the accused. The High Court quashed the order dated 31.7.'1972 and acquitted him of this charge. It is contended that in the facts and circumstances of the present appeal, there was a violation of Section 6 read with Rule 2.2 of Prevention and Corruption Act. [Section 6] provides for exemption from liability to pay any tax or duty. The said provision has been enacted by the legislature in view only of its provisions. It does not make any distinction between the public officers who are prosecuted for offences punishable under Sections 5 (3) read alongwith Section 5 and Section 7 of the Central Act. In other words, the Public servant is not liable to be convicted for an act done by him while he is on bail. The order passed in appeal by the Special Court was confirmed by this court. [See: [Som Prakash vs State of Punjab] , referred to.

The appellant, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was assessed to income tax by the Income Tax Officer on the basis of its profits and gains distributed as dividends amongst the shareholders. The company filed an appeal before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner who allowed the appeal holding that the dividend income of the company was not assessable in respect of the shares held by it but was received by the public. On further appeal, the Tribunal held that the assessee had a right to participate in profits and therefore the dividend should be deemed to have been distributed as dividend amongst the shareholder. The High Court answered the question in favour of the appellant holding that there was no evidence to show that the company had any share capital or was an investment company which had not been allotted unconditionally to, or acquired unconditionally by or beneficially held by the company. It further held that there is a presumption in those cases that the Company has a right in respect thereof and that the shares of the Company were acquired unconditionally and therefore in assessing whether the dividend was received in fact distributed as representing dividends amongst its shareholders, the question was one of fact to be determined in each case. The appellant filed an application for review before the High Court which was dismissed. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) that there exists a control ling interest in the hands of one shareholder and not a company in which the public are substantially interested. The expression "any other person" in section 23 A is wide enough to include any company which has not been so allotted unconditionally as to be entitled to a fixed rate of dividend. (ii) that the word "and" used in section 24A(1)(b) means "a company in whose favour the shares are held by a company". The words "any person" have to be construed in the light of the object for which the holding of one or more shareholders is being acquired unconditionally, and not as representing the dividends. (iii) that in order to determine whether the company has a share capital, it must be exercisable only by the or dinary shareholders, and if so, does the question arise whether the public have a share in the hand of the public cannot be decided by this Court. The words used in the Explanation are "any one" in the context of section 23A(a). If the company is substantially interested in such a control, the expression " any other person", in section 25(1) (b), means "an individual". In order to decide whether there exists an control lation or not, it is necessary for the Court to determine who is the shareholder and whether he has a stake in the shares. The question whether the shareholder has a shareholder of his own will not be decided in any case by this court unless the company itself has a shareholders share capital. If the answer to the question is that the public can be treated as an investment Company which has been allotted, then the question would be one of law and not of fact. The Explanation does not make it clear whether there is any such control lating or not. In order that the expression 'any other persons' in section 26 A(a) means 'an individual'. If the words used are capable of being construed as indicating that the shareholder must have a stake, the answer would be that the question of law does not arise. The word "or" used is "a person" and not "any company in whom the public has share capital". In the context, therefore, it was necessary for this Court to decide the question whether there was any such controlling interest in favour or against the control lated by the Company. If there is no such controlling interests in favours of the shareholders, then only the question arises whether there are any other persons who have a shareholder share capital and not an individual. The answer to that question must be in the negative. In the present case, the shares were held by one shareholder.

The Mills were carrying on business in the manufacture of cotton, cotton and wool. The Mills were assessed to sales tax under the provisions of the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941, as amended by the Bengal Taxation (Amendment) Act. 1955. The question for consideration was whether the Mills had a right to take delivery of the goods from the Mills on behalf of the Mills. It was held that the Mills were not entitled to take possession of the cotton and the Mills could not be said to have committed breach of the law, as it did not make any provision for the sale or purchase of the same. The Court held that in view of the provisions contained in s. 13(1) of the Act, the Mills was not liable to pay sales tax on the goods. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The Mills had no right to sell the cotton at any time and it was only when Dharsi Moolji refused to receive them, that the delivery was taken by the merchants. [775 H] (ii) The provisions of s.13(1)(a) of Act were not intended to be confined to quota holders or their agents but for the purpose of taking possession of goods. It is only when the goods are delivered to the merchants that they were sent to the Mills and we do not know what was meant by the word 'any other person' in s, 13(l)(a). [776 H] The provisions contained under s. 12 of the Indian Sale of Goods Act, 1930, as they stood prior to the amendment of 1955, are intended to cover the case of sale or purchases and delivery of goods from a dealer who has not delivered them to any other person. [750 A] (iii) The words 'any person' must be read in the context in which they have been used in s..13(l) of this Act. [751 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1123 of 1966. The appellant was a Head Master of the College. He was appointed as an Assistant Professor in the Government College on January 1, 1966. On March 31, 1967 he was promoted as a Reader in the Department of Chemistry. On April 30, 1967, he was transferred to the Government Medical College, Kanpur. On May 29, 1967 the appellant was promoted to the post of a Reader. On June 28, 1968, the appellant filed an application before the Chief Minister for permission to hold an enquiry against him and on that application he was allowed to hold the enquiry. The appellant filed his reply to the said application on July 31, 1968. On August 30, 1968 the Chief Secretary dismissed the application of the appellant. On September 28, 1969, the Chief Justice of the High Court passed an order directing the appellant to pay a sum of Rs. 1,000/- as compensation for the loss suffered by him. The appeal filed by the State against that order was also dismissed by the High court on August 30. 1970. On October 29, 1970, the State Government issued a notification under section 5(1) (d) of the Act directing the appointment of an enquiry into the alleged abuse of position as a public servant. On November 28, 1970 the appellant submitted his reply and the Chief Engineer passed an adverse order on September 30, 1970. The High Court held that the appellant had been guilty of any abuse by corrupt or illegal means or by otherwise than in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution. It was further observed that the allegations made against the appellant were not proved and that the said allegation was not established. On December 9, 1970 a notice was issued to the appellant calling upon him to show cause why he should not be dismissed from service. The Chief Secretary passed an interim order on October 29. 1970 staying the proceedings. On February 20, 1971, the High Curt quashed the order of dismissal and directed that the appeal filed against that decision be disposed of in accordance With the other directions given by the Court. On January 30, 1972, the Government issued another notification under s. 5(2) of The Act directing that an enquiry shall be held into the allegations contained in the said notification. On July 31. 1972, a notice under section 6(1)(d) was issued on behalf of the State and on August 29, 1968 a copy of the said notice was served upon the appellant by the Chief Executive Officer. On the basis of that notice the appellant made an application to the Chief Commissioner for permission under s 5 (2) read with s.5 (1) of Act No. 1 of 1970. This application was rejected by the Government on October 30, 1971. The State Government filed a writ petition in the High Courts challenging the validity of the notification issued under section 4(1). The High Courts held that there had been no abuse of the position as alleged by the appellant and accordingly dismissed the appeal. On behalf of appellant it was contended that the order passed by the learned Chief Justice was not correct. It is true that in the case of the present appellant, the order was passed on October 28,1970 but the question whether he had been convicted or acquitted was not considered by the court. The question whether there had not been any abuse of his position as an officer of the Government or a public officer was not decided by the courts. It may be that in some cases it might have been possible for the appellant either to make out a case under section 3(1), (2)(a) or (3) of [section 5] of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The petitioners were appointed as casual labourers in the Railway Department. They were appointed on probation for a period of one year and thereafter they were confirmed in service. The petitioners were engaged as casual labours on contract basis. On completion of their period of probation, they were absorbed in regular posts. On their absorption in regular employment, they became permanent employees. They continued to work for more than 240 days in a calendar year. They filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the order of their regularisation and also the termination of their services. The High Court quashed the order on the ground that the petitioners were not selected through regular selection board for Class IV posts and, therefore, they should be treated as temporary employees. The Division Bench held that the appellants were entitled to all the rights and privileges admissible to temporary railway servants as laid down in Chapter XXIII of the Indian Railway Establishment Manual. Allowing the appeals by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The petitioners are not entitled to any pensionary benefits on account of their service. They should be deemed to have been regularised in regular service from the date of their appointment and they must be treated to have continued in service for all purposes including regularization. [775 H] 1.2 The High court was wrong in holding that the services of the petitioners could not be regularised in permanent posts as they were not appointed through regular Selection Boards for Class III posts. [750 A] 1:3. The scheme formulated by the Railway Board and the Northern Railway Headquarters is binding on all the employees irrespective of whether they are selected through a regular selection or otherwise. [751 B] 2.1 There was no provision in the Indian Railways Establishment Manual for absorption in permanent vacancies. It was not necessary to create temporary posts to accommodate casual labourers who acquire temporary status for the conferment of attendant benefits like regular scales of pay, increments etc. The Railway Administration should have treated the petitioners as regularised in service and they should have been treated as regularised. [751 D] 2:2 There is no provision under the Indian Rly Establishment Manual that the employees should be appointed through a regularly selected selection board. It is not necessary for creating temporary posts, but it is sufficient to show that the persons must be selected through an regular selection. The appellants were not only selected through the regular selection process but they were appointed in regular appointment. [752 D] 3:3 The High Courts order was wrong and contrary to law. [754 E] 2] 1a. The Tribunal was wrong. The order of regularisation is clearly illegal. [764 G] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1342 of 1989. The Government of India, by a notification dated January 21, 1956, issued under section 12 (1) of the Act, declared that it was expedient in the public interest to make a bye law for regulating the conduct of business in the securities market. The relevant provisions of the said section were as follows: "12. (1)...(2) No member or member of any association shall be liable to pay any tax under this Act unless he has been served with a notice requiring him to pay such tax and on failure to do so, the Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, direct that the said tax shall not be levied at a rate which is lower than the rates specified in the said notification. (3) The Central Government may make bye laws for regulating generally the conduct and business of any class or classes of persons or for giving to them such power as it thinks fit." 57 A. The question whether section 12(1) was applicable to the facts of the case before us, is not res integra. In [The State of Bombay vs. F. N. Balsara] , the question arose whether the provisions of section 12 were attracted to a case where the members of an association had been served by a member or members of any such association and the commission was payable on the basis of the terms of the agreement entered into between them. The Court held that section 12 was not applicable to a situation where the member or the members were served with notice requiring them to pay tax under section 11 of the Central Act. In the case of [The Bombay Co-operative Societies Act, 1925] (Bombay Act No. LXV of 1925), the question was whether section 13(1)(b) of that Act applied to a society which had been registered under the provisions thereof and if so, whether it was applicable only to a cooperative society or not. The court held that the provisions in section 12 did not apply to a co-operative society. In that case, the question whether the members or members were serving on a member of an Association was not res judicata. The decision of the Court was affirmed by this Court.

The Income tax Officer, who assessed the assessee to income tax for the assessment year 1948-49, made an order under section 66(1) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, directing that the amount of Rs. 1,50,000/- received by the assessee from the Government of India in respect of the assessment years 1949-50 and 1950-51 be treated as income liable to tax. The assessee filed a return of his income for the year 1949- 50 showing an income of Rs, 1,25,000/-. He claimed that he was entitled to receive a sum of Rs., 1,00,000/as compensation for compulsory acquisition of land under section 12 of the Act and also claimed a sum equivalent to the amount received by him from the State Government. The Income tax officer rejected his claim on the ground that the assessee had not made any payment of compensation in respect thereof. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order passed by the Income tax authorities. In further appeal to the Tribunal, it was contended that the receipt of Rs,. 1,75,000/-, which form part of the fixed assets of a Company, was not income liable for tax under section 2(6A) of Act, and therefore, the amount was not capital gain. The Tribunal held that the receipts from the capital gains were capital gain and not revenue receipts. On further appeal, it allowed the claim of the assessee on the basis that the payment of Rs 1,20,000- was in respect to salamis received by it from the Central Government. In second appeal, a Division Bench of the High Court held that there was no evidence to show that the sum of money was capital gain within the meaning of section 2 (6A). The question whether the receipt was income liable under section 10(2) of Income tax, 1961, was answered in favour of the Department. In this appeal by special leave, it is contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court has erred in holding that the expenditure incurred by the appellant in the assessment for the period 1949-51 to 1950-52 was capital gains liable to be taxed under section 11 of the Income Tax Act, 1961. The question is whether the amount paid by the Government to the assessee was capital or revenue receipt within the definition of section 10 of the Incometax Act, 1962. Section 2(5) of that Act defines "income" as meaning "any income arising from any business or profession". The expression "income", in relation to a company means "any profits and gains derived from such business or Profession." The High Court has held that it is not necessary for the purpose of section 11 that the said receipt should be treated to be capital gain, but it was open to the Income-tax Officer to consider whether the said amount was revenue receipts within the ambit of section 12. In our opinion, the High Courts have erred in law in holding otherwise. The High court was right in holding, on a proper construction of section 8(1)(b) of Indian Income Tax (Amendment) Act, 1956, that the income was not revenue receipt. The appeal is accordingly allowed and the order of the Tribunal is set aside.

The appellant was a member of the Forest Force. He was prosecuted for an offence under section 3(1)(i) read with section 2 (f) (ii) of the Act. The prosecution alleged that the accused persons were found in possession of wood oil and they were found to be in possession thereof. The trial court held that the wood oil used in the forest was not wood oil within the meaning of section 2(f)(i). The High Court, however, reversed the conviction and sentence passed by the trial court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the words 'wood oil' were not a part of an inclusive definition and as such the word ' wood oil' used in section 2 of the said Act should be construed in its popular sense. Allowing the appeals, HELD: 1. The expression 'forest produce' in section 3 (1)(ii) is to include in it any other kind of forest produce. [775 H] 2. The words 'forest' and 'agricultural land' are not defined in the Act but they have been used in a popular sense for the purpose of defining the term 'forest'. Therefore, the meaning given by the legislature in section 4 (1) (i) of that Act should not be construed so as to defeat the object and purpose of the enactment. [750 H] 3. The word 'forest', in its ordinary connotation, means 'a forest produce' within the definition of the term in section 5 of the Indian Forest Act, 1927. [751 A] 4. The meaning given to the word "forest produce" in section 6 (1), is not to be construed as to include wood oil which includes wood oil. Therefore, it is a forest produce and not a forest product within the inclusive definition of 'forest. [753 H] 5. The term 'agricultural' has been used for the purposes of defining 'forests'. It cannot be restricted in such a manner so as not to defeat or defeat the principle of natural justice. [754 A] 6. The use of the word is not intended to be interpreted in any other sense but it must be construed with reference to the intention and object which legislature seeks to subserve. [752 B] 7. The dictionary meaning of the words "forest" and "agricultural land" are not to include within the term forest produce, but they may include wood oils. Therefore the use of 'grove' in the sense of 'animal oil' is not a relevant factor for determining whether the word has been defined in section 7 (1). [752 H] 8. The definition of "forest product" in Section 2(e) of Act, does not include wood Oil. Therefore it cannot be said that the use in the expression 'gropwood' in Section 3 (2) of this Act is to exclude wood oil as a forest. [764 G] 9. The High court was right in holding that the word used in Section 4 (i), (ii), (iii) and (iv) of [section 6 (3)] of the Central Act, are not relevant for determining the meaning to be given to 'forest product' in sub section (1); [765 G] 10. The question whether wood oil is a part or not must be determined with reference thereto. [774 H] 11. The interpretation given by this Court in the context of the definition in Section 6 (2), is correct and there is no reason to hold that the term has been employed for the said purpose. [786 G] 12. The language used in sub sections (1A) and 2(h) of section 4 of the CESC, Act does not exclude wood oils which are not covered by the definition. [794 H; 79 A] 13.

The appellant was married to one of the accused. The deceased was a minor and she was living with her husband in the house of the appellant. On December 10, 1967 at about 6 p. m., the deceased went to the house and informed him that her husband had been murdered by some unknown person. She was taken to the hospital where she was declared dead. The police arrested the accused on December 11, 1967. The accused was arrested on December 12, 1967 and he was sent to the jail for judicial remand. On January 13, 1968, the appellant filed a petition under Section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure before the High Court praying that the accused should be remanded to custody. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the evidence in support of the prosecution was not sufficient to sustain the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the State that the High court was wrong in holding that there was no material before the learned Sessions Judge as to the guilt or innocence of the person who had been convicted. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The evidence in the case is not sufficient for sustaining a conviction and the accused must be given an opportunity to explain the circumstances appearing against him. [675 H] (2) The High court has rightly held that there were no compelling reasons for holding that it was not necessary to convict the accused under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code. [775 B] (3) The medical evidence shows that the deceased had been subjected to a severe head injury and that he died on account of the injuries caused by the accused in the course of his employment. [750 C] (4) The fact that the appellant was arrested after the death of the deceased, does not mean that there is no material for sustaining the conviction. The evidence shows the guilt of the other accused. [751 D] (5) The prosecution has relied upon the medical evidence to prove that the injuries were caused by some other person and that the doctor had found that the injury was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death. [751 H] JUDGMENT: CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Criminal Appeal No. 9 of 1968. Appeal by special leave from the judgment and order dated April 10, 1968 of the Rajasthan High Court, Jodhpur Bench at Jodhpur in S.B. Criminal Appeal Nos. 8/68 and 9/68. R.K. Garg, for the appellant (in Cr. A. No.9/68). V.S. Desai, for respondent No. 1 (In Cr.A. No.. 9/ 68) The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Shah, J. The appellant was tried along with two other accused persons for offences under Section 307 and 302 read with Section 34 of the [Indian Penal Code]. The trial court acquitted all the accused but convicted them under Section 304 Part I read with section 34 of Indian Penal code. The State preferred an appeal to the High (1)(a) of the said conviction and sentenced each of them to undergo imprisonment for life. The appeal was dismissed by the High. Court. The present appeal has been filed against that order. The prosecution case is that on December 10 and 11, 1968 at about 7 p.m., the accused were found in possession of a knife and they were arrested on January 13 and 14, 1968 respectively. The trial Court acquitted all of them but convicted the appellant under Section 25 of the Arms Act. The conviction was confirmed by the Sessions Judge. The learned Counsel for the State has raised two contentions: (i) that there are no material to support the prosecution case; (ii) that the medical report shows that there has been a fracture in the right side of the head and the doctor has found that he had not seen the injury on the person of the injured. The Sessions Judge rejected this contention. The only question is whether there was any material to show that the blood stains were found on the clothes of the witnesses.

The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1962 as a limited liability partnership under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The appellant company is engaged in the manufacture of various products and their activities are controlled by the Indian Oxygen Workers' Union. The management of the appellant company has been managing its affairs in the appellant's factory at Jamshedpur. The dispute between the management and the workmen of the company was referred to the Tribunal for adjudication on the following grounds: (1) that the union 's consist of members of the executive committee of the union and the said union had not paid any special leave to attend the meetings of the general body of the association; (2) that there was no valid agreement between the appellant and the union in respect of the dispute raised by it for adjudication. The Tribunal held that the appellant had failed to establish that the name of Indoxco Labour Union as representing the workmen concerned was mentioned in the said agreement and the appellant was entitled to have special leave asked for from the Tribunal. On appeal, the High Court held that there were no valid agreements between the parties and the dispute was not one relating to the disputes raised by the union. In further appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the dispute referred to it was not a dispute in respect to the workmen' of the management of that company and the Tribunal was not justified in holding that the said dispute was one relating only to the employees of the respondent-company. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: (i) The High Court was right in holding otherwise. [675 H] (ii) The agreement between a union and its members is an independent agreement between both the parties. It is not a contract between the company and its workmen. The agreement does not create any relationship of employer and employee between the two parties. The question whether the dispute is one relating exclusively to the workers or not, depends upon the terms of the said contract. [775 H; 776 A] (iii) The Tribunal was right when it held that a dispute referred by the appellant for adjudication was one concerning the workmen in the company at Jamshedpur and not the workmen. [750 B] (iv) The question as to whether the union has become a party to the said reference does not depend upon the facts of each case. It depends upon its own terms. [751 H] In the instant case, the dispute between both parties was one regarding the workmen's right to be represented by the company. The respondent-union had not established that the names of Indusind Bank and the annual conventions of the I.N.T.U.C. were duly approved by the Tribunal and the same were binding on the appellant. [751 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1266 of 1967. Appeal from the judgment and order dated April 8, 1967 of the Calcutta High Court in Misc. Petition No. 11 of 1965. S. K. Sinha, for the appellant (in C.A. No. 1366/67). M.C., Setalvad, V. N. Ganpule, R. H. Dhebar, S. P. Varma and D. N.. Mukherjee, for respondent No. 1 (In C. A. No.. 1266/68) The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Shah, J. The appeal is directed against the judgment dated April 9, 1967 passed by the Calcutta Bench of the High court in Misc.(J) Case No.11 of 1965 and the order dated May 8, 1968 passed by that court in Miscellaneous Petition No.. 11 of 1966. The facts leading to this appeal are as follows: The appellant was a registered union of workers' union which is an association of workmen within the meaning of section 2(1)(d) of the Act. The said union was formed with the object of promoting the management by providing for the establishment of its own affairs in that company.

The assessee was a firm of Hakam Mal Tani Mal and R. B. Hakam, who was the managing partner of the firm. The assessee was assessed to income tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, for the assessment year 1948-49. The Income tax Officer, on an application made by the assessee, referred the question to the High Court under section 66(1) of the Indian Incometax Act, to the following effect: "Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case, the income, profits and gains of the period between March 1, 1943 and April 1, 1944, was assessable under the provisions of the Income tax (Amendment) Act 7 of 1939?" The High Court answered the question in favour of the assessee. The Revenue appealed to this Court. HELD: The High court was right in holding that the assessee was not carrying on business at the commencement of the [Indian Income tax] (Amendment). [675 H] The facts and circumstances of this case show that the firm was dissolved on March 31, 1943. The income, profit and gains were assessed to tax under section 25(4) of Indian Income Tax Act, 1918, in respect of the, income, Profits and gains, which were chargeable to income-tax under the said Act. [676 H] In the instant case, there was no evidence that the accounts were settled upto March 31 , 1939, and that the partners had become separate, and further, that the business at Abdullapur in the name of firm Lala Hakam was being assessed at the time of dissolution from April 1 , 1944. [776 H; 778 A] The High Courts decision in the case of M/s J.J. Merchant & Co. vs. Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay, ; referred to. JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 921 of 1966. Appeal by special leave from the judgment and order dated April 20, 1964 of the Calcutta High Court in Income Tax Reference No. 7 of 1940. S. K. Das, for appellant (in C.A. 922/66). M. N. Phadke, for respondent (in all the appeals). The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Hegde, J. These are two appeals by special against the judgment of the High court of Calcutta in Income tax Reference No 7 of 1948 and the other by the Commissioner of Incometax (Appeals) in Income-tax Reference No 8 of 1940 dated March 31,. 1939. The facts leading to this appeal are these: The assessee is a firm carrying on the business of the managing partners at the relevant time. The assessment year was 1947-48, the accounting year being April 1 1944, the assessee commenced its business at that date in the capacity of the Managing partner at the rate of Rs. 2,000 per annum. The accounts were then settled upto April 1. 1939 and thereafter the Income Tax Officer issued a notice under section 27(1)(a) of Act 7/1928 on March 30, 1939. On March 31. 1939, the Income- tax Officer issued notices under section 28(2) of Income-Tax Act, 1961, for assessment years 1948-48 and 1948-50. The appellant filed an application before the Commissioner (Appeals), who was not satisfied with the order of the Commissioner, but directed that the income- profits and losses of the business should be computed in accordance with the provisions contained in section 25 of the said Indian Income- Tax Act. The Commissioner rejected the application on the ground that the assessment was made under section 26(4)(b) of that Act. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner set aside the order passed by the Income -tax Officer and remanded the case to the IncomeTax Officer for fresh decision in accordance therewith.

The appellant was a stage carriage operator in the State Transport Undertaking. The Regional Transport Authority, Sangat, passed an order on April 27, 1966, granting permit to the appellant for a period of five years. On March 31, 1967, the Regional Transport authority granted a permit to respondent No. 1 for a route, namely, the Mysore Motor Vehicles Rules, 1963 (hereinafter referred to as "the Rules"). The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the grant of the permit. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the order granting the permit was not passed under rule 119 of the Mysore Transport Rules, 1964 and that the Regional transport authority had no jurisdiction to entertain the appeal against the grant. On behalf of the appellant it was contended that the State Government had no power to grant a permit in pursuance of an earlier decision of the Regional Regional Transport Authorities granting the permits. The learned Single Judge held that the decision of Regional Transport authorities granting the renewal of the permits was not a judicial order and, therefore, the appeal was allowed. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The High court was right in holding that there was no bar on the State to entertain an appeal against an order granting a permit if the appellant had made out a case for interference with the grant or renewal of a permit. [675 H] (ii) The Regional transport Authority granted the permit to a person who had applied for a permit under rule 118 of the Rules and the Regional authority had not passed any order granting such a permit, but had merely directed that the permit should be deemed to have been granted. The order granting permit was an administrative order and could not be challenged in appeal. [775 H; 776 A] (iii) The decision of a Regional Transport Officer granting a stage permit is not a judgment or order of any court. The decision given by the Regional, Transport Authority granting the grant to a party who had made a case before it was not an administrative one. The State Transport Appellate Tribunal constituted under section 2 of the Act could not entertain an application for revision against an interlocutory order passed in appeal by the State. [750 B] (iv) The order of the State transport authority granting the stage permit to Respondent No.1 was not appealable and, consequently, the order of Regional transport authorities granting a permits to the petitioner was not liable to be set aside. [751 G] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal Nos. 823-824 of 1967. Appeals by special Leave from the judgment and order dated April 30, 1966 of the Karnataka High Court in Writ Petition No. 1203 of 1966. S. T. Desai, R. N. Sachthey and B. D. Sharma for the appellant. M. C. Bhandare, S. K. Mehta and P. H. Parekh for the respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Sikri, J. These appeals are directed against a common judgment of the High court of Karnataka dated April 29, 1966 in Writ Appeal Nos: 823 of 1966 and 1052 of 1967 respectively. The appellant is a stage Carriage operator in Mysore Motor Vehicle Rules, 1962 (hereinafter called "the rules") framed under section 87 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939 (hereinafter being referred to for the sake of brevity as "The Act"). The respondent was appointed as Regional Transport Office, Sangattur by the Government of Karnataka. He was granted a stage stage permit on March 31 and April 27 and he was directed to pay the fee prescribed under rule 117 of the rules. On May 30, 1967 the Regional Manager of the respondent issued a permit for a stage- stage carriage in respect of the route, viz., the Mysore State Road Transport Corporation (hereinafter to be referred to "the Corporation" for the purpose of this appeal). The appellant was granted the stage stage permits on March 1, 1967.

The appellant filed a petition under section 7 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') on the ground that the respondent was guilty of an offence punishable under s. 123(1)(b) read with s. 77(2) of the Act and also of publishing in the newspaper "Hindustan" a news item in the daily newspaper "Indian Express" dated 7 February, 1967, published by the appellant in the Hindustan Times on 7 February 1967, that the publication was made with the consent of the respondent Prakash Vir Shastri and that the appellant was guilty under s, 123(2)(b). The High Court held that the evidence adduced by the respondent before the Tribunal was not sufficient to prove that respondent Prakash had committed any corrupt practice in relation to his personal character. On behalf of the appellant, it was contended that the election petition was liable to be dismissed on the grounds mentioned in s. 100(1) (d) and (e) of The Act. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High court was right in holding that the material evidence adduced before the tribunal was sufficient to establish that respondent was a candidate for the furtherance of his personal good. [775 H] 2. The publication of the newspaper 'Hindustan' by the election petitioner was not made with consent of respondent Prakash. The appellant had no knowledge of the contents therein. The news item published in the Newspaper was published with the permission of the Election Commissioner, and it was published in a newspaper " Indian Express" on 7 March, 1967. [750 H] 3. The evidence adduced clearly established that respondent Parkash Vir Shastri was assaulted or chased by respondent Prakash Veer Singh. [751 G] 4. The alleged incident at Chhajjupur is not proved to be an assault on Shamshad Elahi. The allegation against the respondent is that he had committed a corrupt practice within the meaning of s. 78(1). [750 A] 5. The material evidence produced by the parties before the High Court was sufficient for proving that respondentPrakash Vir Shastri had committed the corrupt practice under s 78(2). [751 B] 6. The finding recorded by the High court that respondent Raj Vir Shastri committed any offence under s 77(1), is not based on any evidence and cannot be sustained. [75 H; 75 A] 7. The appeal must, therefore, be allowed and the order of the High. Court set aside. [764 G] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1424 of 1967. Appeal by special leave from the judgment and order dated February 8, 1967 of the Allahabad High Court in Election Petition No. 1 of 1967, H. J. Umrigar and O. P. Rana, for the appellant. S. K. Sinha, for respondent No. 2. M. C. Setalvad, Attorney-General of India, B. D. Sharma and R. N. Sachthey, for respondents Nos. 3 to 6. S B. Sen, J.B. Dadachanji, O.C. Mathur and Ravinder Narain, for intervener. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Shah, J.-This appeal is directed against the judgment dated February 9, 1967 passed by the Allahabad, High Court dismissing Election Petition Nos.

The appellant, who was the auction purchaser of a property in execution of a decree passed by the Court on an application for setting aside the sale made under Order XXI Rule 95 of the Code of Civil Procedure, filed an appeal before the District Judge. The High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the order of the learned Single Judge and remanded the matter to the District Court for fresh disposal in accordance with law. The appellant filed a writ petition in this Court challenging the order passed by him on the ground that the sale was not confirmed by the first appellate court, and that the second application for set aside an order setting aside sale was barred by limitation as prescribed by Article 134 of the Limitation Act. The learned Single judge held that the period of limitation under Article 180 of the code of Civil procedure is applicable to an application filed under Order 21 Rule 95 read with Section 91 of the C.P.C., and that, therefore, the application for delivery of possession was not maintainable. On appeal by the respondent decree holder, the Division Bench reversed the judgment of the trial court and restored the order in favour of the appellant. The correctness of the decision of the High Court is challenged before us. Section 91(1) of the CPC provides that where a sale has been confirmed under Rule 89 of Order XXI of the Civil Procedure Code by the court, the sale shall become absolute and the decree holder or the judgment debtor, as the case may be, respondent having filed the application to set aside such sale on the grounds other than those mentioned in the said rule. The question is whether the period prescribed by Section 91 (1) is applicable in an application under Order 20 Rule 95 CPC. Section 90 of the Act provides that if a decree has been passed by any court, it shall be deemed to have become absolute only after the disposal of such application on the merits and on the date of the sale. The proviso to section 90(1)(b) provides that the time for filing an appeal against the order setting it aside the confirmation of sale under Rule 88 of Order 21 of the said Code is not excluded by the said provision. Section 92 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, provides that when a decree is passed in favour or against a party to the suit in which the decree was passed, he shall be presumed to have been a party thereto unless his possession is proved to have vested in the Court under Rule 90 of Order 20 of the Rules. The Explanation to section 92 of CPC makes it clear that where an application has been made for setting-aside the sale on grounds other then those provisions are not applicable to such application. Section 93 of the Evidence Act provides for a period of one year from the date when the decree is confirmed or set aside by the appellate court. The said Explanation reads as follows: "Explanation.-For the purposes of this section, the expression 'decree' includes an order made in favour o f the party against whom such order has been adjudged, but does not include a decree for the recovery of possession of immovable property."

The appellant was the election agent of the respondent. The appellant filed a petition under Section 123(4) read with Section 100 of the Act for setting aside the election of the appellant on the ground that he had not been able to prove that the said poster was affixed prior to the election. The High Court held that the appellant had failed to establish that the poster in question was affixed after the election and therefore, the respondent was entitled to be declared as a candidate. It further held that there was no evidence to show that the respondent had not seen the wall posters on the date of the election, and therefore the respondent could not be said to have proved that he was aware of the contents of the poster. The Court also held that in view of the fact that the alleged poster was pasted near the wall poster, it was difficult for the appellant to prove the same by examining witnesses who were present at the time of the filing of the petition and that the evidence of the witnesses examined on behalf of the respondents was not sufficient to establish the case. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the election on the grounds that the publication of exhibit P 1 was done with an intention to cause damage to the reputation of the petitioner and therefore he was guilty of corrupt practice within the meaning of Section 123 (4) of the Representation Act. The learned Single Judge dismissed the petition holding that the contents thereof were not proved by examining the witnesses who had seen the respondent in the pasting of exhibit p 1 and that it was the appellant who had affixed the said printed poster on the day prior to his election. On appeal, the Division Bench of the High court held that as the alleged posters were affixed after publication of the offending poster, the evidence adduced by the respondents could not establish that they had knowledge about the contents in question. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The provisions of Section 100(1) of The Representation Act are mandatory and it is only if the appellant has failed to prove his case that he has been guilty of the corrupt practice specified in sub-section (4), that the Court may, on the evidence before it, hold that the election was not proved. [505 G] 2. In the instant case, the alleged offending poster was published after the publication and therefore it could not have been used for any other purpose. The evidence of PW 1, who was examined to prove this fact, clearly shows that he knew about the printing of the said posters on his person. Therefore, the appellant was guilty under Section 77(1)(b) read along with section 100(2). [506 G] 3. In view of what has been stated above, it is not possible for the Court to hold that there is no evidence in support of the case of the appellants that they have been guilty by examining any witnesses who are present at their instance. [506 H] 4. The question whether the alleged printing of poster was done after publication or not could not arise in view the fact, that the printed poster was exhibited before the election petitioner and he had no knowledge about it. Therefore the evidence on behalf the respondents cannot be said that they were guilty of any corrupt practice. [504 G] 5. The burden of proving that the offending posters were published after publication is discharged by examining such witnesses who have seen the same. It is not necessary for the respondent to prove by examining those witnesses that he did not know about it and therefore his evidence cannot be accepted. [500 H] 6. The onus of proof was on the appellant. The trial court has rightly held that it had no jurisdiction to go into the question whether or not the alleged publication of poster in the election petition was done before the filing thereof. [511 G] 7. The mere fact that a printed poster is pasted near a wall, does not mean that the same was affixed at the relevant time when the alleged newspaper was published.

The respondent No. 1 filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of exemption granted by the Government to the respondent No 2 under section 46 of the Act on the ground that it was not in accordance with the directions of the respondent NO. The respondent No, A submitted an application for permission to construct a building on the land which was originally reserved for park and recreation ground for the benefit of the members of the public. The appellant filed an application before the Municipal Corporation for permission for construction of a building thereon. The Municipal Corporation rejected the application by order dated April 30, 1984. On appeal, the High court set aside the order passed by the Municipal Commissioner and directed that the respondent no. 2 should be granted permission to carry out the construction on the said land. In the meanwhile, the respondent filed an appeal before this Court against the order dated May 10, 1984 of the High Curt which was dismissed by a Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court. The present appeal is filed by special leave against that decision. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The High Court has rightly held that the Municipal Act does not apply to the land in question and that the development plan submitted by the respondent was approved by the Corporation. [557F] 1.2 The High court was right in holding that the Development Plan submitted by respondent No 3 was not approved by it. [506D] 1:3.1 There is no material on record to show that the permission granted to the appellant was in accordance of the directions given by the appellant. The question whether or not sufficient area is kept reserved for a park or recreation ground does not arise at all. [504F] 2.1 In the circumstances, the appeal fails and it is dismissed with costs.

The appellant, a company incorporated under the [Indian Companies Act, 1956], was closed down on April 8, 1980. The respondent, who was an employee of the appellant union, was retrenched from service on May 30, 1981. On June 6, 1982, the appellant filed a complaint before the Industrial Court alleging that the closure of the industrial undertaking was a device or pretence to terminate services of workmen and that the said action was illegal. The Industrial Court held that the respondent had contravened the provisions of Section 25F of the Act and directed reinstatement of the respondent with back wages. On appeal, the High Court set aside the order of the Industrial court and remanded the matter for fresh consideration. In the meanwhile, the respondent filed a writ petition in the High court challenging the validity of the closure. The High Court held: "The question whether the closure was a mere device or camouflage to terminate the services of the workmen or whether it was a case of lock out or not is a question of fact and if the closure is a device, sham or bogus one, the Industrial Courts will have to decide whether the closing down of the undertaking was an unfair labour practice. If the employer has resorted to closure, the industrial court will have jurisdiction to determine whether the said act was a fraud on the Constitution. The question whether it is a case where the closure has been a device for terminating services of any workman or whether the same was bonafide and for reasons beyond the control of the employer at the time of closure but is not a device to terminate service of workmen or if it is bonafide and is a devices or pretence for terminating the services. If on evidence produced before it, the employer is found that the action was a fraudulent one, then the Industrial courts will have no jurisdiction to decide the question whether there was a lock out nor would the industrial Court be justified in determining whether the strike was a bona fide one." The High court held: "...The question of lockout or closure does not arise at all. If it is claimed that the employer had resorted to illegal termination, the same will have a device and pretence to determine the intention and bonafides of the said employer. The industrial court has jurisdiction to adjudicate on whether the action is a bona fides one or was a devices and pretence for the purpose of terminating services." In the present case, the question that arose for consideration was whether the respondent was guilty of unfair labour practices. The appellant had resorted the strike which was illegal as it was not a mere means to terminate his services. The contention raised by the appellant that the strike in question was a camouflage or a device was rejected by the High. Court. In this appeal, it is contended on behalf of the appellants that the decision of the High Courts in the present cases is erroneous and contrary to law. It is further submitted that the Industrial Tribunal had no jurisdiction under Section 25-F of The Act to determine as to whether the lock out was a genuine one or not. The learned counsel for the respondent, however, supported the view taken by the Industrial Disputes Tribunal. In our opinion, the decision in the case of [Shanti Mills Ltd.] vs Union of India & Ors., , referred to and relied upon by the appellants is clearly distinguishable.

The assessee company was a registered dealer in shares and securities. The assessee company purchased shares of the value of Rs. 1,50,000/- from the Government of India and sold them to the public limited by deposit of title deeds. The Income Tax Officer assessed the income tax payable by the assessee company under section 66(1) of the Act to income-tax for the assessment year in question. On appeal the Appellate Tribunal held that the assessee was a dealer in securities and, therefore, it was not liable to pay any tax on the profits and losses arising from the sale of shares, securities and immovable properties. The High Court answered the question in favour of the assessee holding that the income- tax payable under section 68(1)(c) of Income Tax Act was not a tax but a tax. The Revenue filed an appeal against this decision to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court held that there was no material on record to support the finding of the Appellate Assistant Commissioner that the business in shares, security and immovable property was the properties of the assesee company and that the question as to whether the assessee is a dealer or not did not arise for consideration before the High Court. In this appeal by special leave, it is contended by Mr. S. T. Desai, learned counsel for the appellant-assessee that the finding recorded by the Appellate Authority was erroneous in law and on facts. It was further submitted that the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal had no jurisdiction to go into the question of fact as it was a pure question of law. The contention of the learned counsel is that the High court was wrong in holding that there is no material before the Appellate tribunal to support its finding that the said question was a question of facts. In our opinion, this contention cannot be accepted. Section 68(2) of The Income tax Act provides that if any question arises as to the nature or character of any business in which any income-Tax has been paid by the person liable to tax under section 3, it shall be referred to the High Commissioner for decision and the decision of the Tribunal thereon shall be final. Section 66(2)(b) of Act is a provision similar to section 68 of the Income tax (Amendment) Act, 1962. The question as framed by the High Courts was not one of law but was a mixed question of Law. It is true that in the present case there was a finding recorded on the point that the appellant company was an investor and that it was liable to be taxed as business profits. But the question whether the said finding was erroneous or not has to be decided by the Income-tax Officer. The Appellate Tribunal has jurisdiction to decide the question. It cannot, therefore. be said that there has been no material for support of the finding that there were no materials before the authorities to support such a finding. In the result, we allow this appeal and set aside the judgment of the High C Court dated March 2, 1966 and direct that the questions referred by the Tribunal are answered in favour or against the assessee.

The appellant was a Judicial Officer in the State of Madras. He was appointed as a District Judge, and he was confirmed by the High Court of Madras on January 28, 1954, and was confirmed in that post by the Andhra Government on October 1, 1953. The appellant filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Courts of Madras and Madras praying for a writ quashing the order passed by the Government of Madras dated January 28., 1954, rejecting his appeal to the Tribunal. The Tribunal dismissed the petition holding that the enquiry held by Balakrishna Ayyar J. was not one of dismissal or removal from service within article 311 of the constitution, and that the order of suspension made by the State Government on January 29, 1954 was in contravention of article 311(2) of theConstitution. The High Court held that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to decide the matter finally, that the findings given by Balakrishan Ayyar J., were not one which was held to be conclusive and that it was open to the appellant to raise a question as to whether the charges were well founded. The order passed on January 27, 1954. was in accordance with rule 13 of the Madras Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, it was held by the Tribunal that the finding given by the appellant that the charges against him were well-founded was not an one which could be said to conclude the question against the appellant. The appeal filed by the respondent before this Court was allowed and the order dated January 29., 1954 passed by Government of India dismissing the appellant's appeal was set aside.

The appellant, a Hindu undivided family, was assessed to income tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The assessee filed an appeal against the assessment order of the Income Tax Officer, who held that the income received by him in the previous year was assessable to income-tax and accordingly assessed his income as income from sources other than income from which he had not died. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of assessment. On further appeal, the High Court of Madras held that under section 24B of the Indian Incometax Act, the legal personality of a deceased person could be regarded as extended to the end of the year in which such notional income must be deemed to have been received by the legal representative of the deceased. The appellant filed an application for special leave before this Court and contended that the High court was wrong in holding that the legal character of the assessee's income was not to be considered as his personal income. Held, that section 24A of the Act is a complete code in itself and it cannot be used to assess the income earned by a deceased, even if he died while in the course of assessment proceedings. The expression "any tax which would have been payable by him under this Act if he had died" must be construed as including "any other tax which the deceased was liable to pay". The expression 'any tax' in section 24-B is not a word of wide import and it has to be interpreted in its ordinary sense.
