The words "any income received or receivable by the estate of the person" are not intended to cover any tax which may have been paid by the deceased, but only those taxes which would be payable by the heirs and legal representatives of the legal representatives who died while under the control of the estate after the death of the husband. The word "any" in section 2(2) must be interpreted as including not only the personal income of the father but also the legal relation to the deceased person. The High Court was wrong. The appeal is allowed and the order passed by the High.Court is set aside.

The appellant was a maufidar of an Indian State. He was a member of the Indian Nationalist Party. The Government of India, in exercise of its powers under article 366(22) of the Constitution issued a notification on January 1, 1962, declaring that the said territory shall be deemed to have been included in the State of Madhya Pradesh. On March 31, 1963, the appellant filed an application before the Assistant Collector, Bhopal for permission to collect land revenue from persons holding land in such villages. The Assistant Collector rejected the application and granted permission to the appellant to collect the land revenue. On appeal by the appellant, the Additional Collector held that the appellant was not a moufidar and that he had no right to recover rent or revenue from the persons holding lands in such village. On further appeal, the High Court held that as the appellant had given no evidence to establish that the villages were assessed to land revenue, it was for the State Government to prove that the village was not assessed to the land. The High Court accordingly allowed the writ petition and quashed the order of the Assistant Commissioner. In this Court, on behalf of the appellant it was contended that the notification issued under article 226 and 227 of the constitution was illegal as it did not disclose any material to establish the fact that the petitioner had a right to recovery rent or Revenue from persons who holding land within such villages and that in view of the provisions contained in article 366 (22) read with article 366, the question of law should be decided by the High court. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The appellant was an ex-Maufiddar of an area which was not recognised as a Ruler by the President of India and he had a statutory right to collect rent or revenues from persons having any interest in such land. [505 H] 2. The notification issued by the State under article 31(2) of Constitution is valid and does not suffer from any infirmity. [506 G] 3. The question whether the appellant as a mahafidar was a person who had a legal right to receive rent or to revenue from such persons did not arise in this case. [504 H] 4. The contention that the petition was maintainable as it was not maintainable is well-founded and must be rejected. [500 G] 5. The provisions contained under article 32 of theConstitution are not attracted to the facts of the present case. Article 32 does not apply to the case of the petitioner. [525 H] 6. The petitioner had given a valid notice to the State to show cause against the proposed action. He did not file any reply to the notice and, therefore, he was not entitled to raise any objection on that ground. [511 G] 7. The petition is maintainable as the petitioner has not made out any case for interference with the order passed by the Assistant Government. [54 H] 8. The appeal is without merit and is dismissed.

The respondent was appointed as a Judge of the High Court of Delhi. He was promoted to the post of District and Sessions Judge on 1.4.1986. On his appointment, he was transferred to Delhi Judicial Service in the year 1986. The respondent challenged the order of transfer before the Tribunal by filing an application under Article 226 of the Constitution. The Tribunal allowed the application holding that the transfer was vitiated by mala fides and directed the appellant to be transferred. The High Court held that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to interfere with the order passed by the Tribunal in the absence of any material on record to show that the respondent was posted at a different station. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The transfer is an incident of all India service and there is no detriment to the administrative needs and the claim of other employees cannot be transferred to the place of the other employees. [557F] 1.2. The order of the Tribunal was not challenged in any court or Tribunal. It was passed on a consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case. [506D] 1:3. In the instant case, the respondent did not make any representation to the authorities concerned. He had no opportunity to represent against his transfer. [504F] 2.1 The order passed in the present case is vitiated by malafides for that reason. [ 506E] 2:2. There was no material on the record to indicate that the departmental authorities were satisfied with the exigencies of administration and the respondent could not be transferred from one place or another without any detriment to administrative needs. [657F F] 1.:3. The appellant was appointed in a different post at different stations, 'they cannot be removed by the appointing authority. [UDD] 2.:4. There is no material before the Court or Tribunal to show as to why the respondent should be transferred and that the administrative need of the two stations was not met. [53F] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1579 of 1989. From the Judgment and Order dated 20.8.1988 of the Central Administrative Tribunal, Delhi in O.A. No. 8/87. S.K. Bagga, R.N. Singh, Ms. A. Subhashini and P.H. Parekh for the Appellant. V.S. Desai, M.M. Ansari, Mrs. Rani Chhabra, Ms Anu Mehta, Ms Nishita Jain, Ms Kamini Jaiswal, Ms J.J. Shah, Ms S.D. Karanjawala, Ms Bina Gupta, Ms A.Kelmani, Ms P.P. Rao and Ms V.Kala for the Respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by PATHAK, J. This appeal is directed against the order dated 20th August 1988 passed by a learned Single Judge of that court dismissing the application filed under Article 227 of the constitution. The facts leading to this appeal are as follows: The respondent was working as District and Session Judge in the Delhi Judicial Services in the State of Delhi and he was posted as District & Sessions Judge, Delhi. On the basis of the complaint made by the respondent, a departmental enquiry was held against him. He submitted his reply to the charge-sheet. After considering the evidence adduced before the Enquiry Officer, the disciplinary authority passed an order of dismissal on the ground that the charges framed against the respondent were not proved. The said order was challenged by the appellant in the High court. The learned Single judge dismissed the application. The Division Bench held that there is nothing to show whether the departmental enquiry has been conducted or not and that it was open to the disciplinary authorities to hold an inquiry into the allegations made against the employee. In this view of the matter, the order dismissing the respondent from service was set aside. Hence this appeal by special leave. 2. Shri S. K.

The appellants were tried for the murder of Jawahar and they were convicted by the learned Trial Judge under Section 302 read with Section 34, I.P.C. The prosecution case was that on January 2, 1977 at about 8.30 A.M. the deceased Jawahar was returning to his house after attending a marriage in village Pokhari. He was carrying a stick (spear) and a stick. On the way he met the appellants who were armed with sticks and gave blows to him. The appellants also assaulted him by means of sticks. The deceased Jawahar fell down on the ground and sustained injuries. The accused persons then ran away from the place of occurrence. The case was registered against the appellants under Section 304 Part I, I PC. The investigation revealed that the appellants were guilty of the offence of murder and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for five years. The appeal filed by the appellants was dismissed by the High Court. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The conviction of the appellants is not sustainable in law. [775 H] 2. The evidence on record shows that the deceased was last seen with the appellants and their associates who were members of the same family. The fact that the accused persons had given blows to Jawahar and the deceased did not make any difference to the nature of offence committed by them. [750 A] 3. The High Court has rightly held that the conviction of both the appellants cannot be sustained in law and they are entitled to get the benefit of doubt. [751 B] 4. The question whether the accused were guilty under Section 325, I P.C., or not is a matter of evidence. It is true that the prosecution case is that the attack on the deceased by the accused was in retaliation for the injuries inflicted on him. But it is equally true that if the appellants are convicted under Section 324, I, P. C., read with Sec. 34, the offence committed must be one punishable under Section 326, IP. C. [751 D] 5. The intention of the accused to cause death or grievous hurt was not a relevant factor in deciding whether the appellants could be convicted under Sections 302, Ipc. [754 A] 6. The circumstances on which the conviction is based are such that it would be sufficient to convict them for the offence punishable under Sec. 325,I.P., C. read with S. 34 and 149, IPG. [764 D] 7. The position in law is well settled by a catena of decisions of this Court. In the instant case, the appellants have been convicted under Secs. 302, 307, Iyab Singh, Ignor, Iraq, Ilaqa, Isaq and sentenced each of them to undergo imprisonment for life. [752 D] 8. The offence committed was one punishable Under Section 304, I I P, C. and not under Section 323, Izat Ali, Ibnor, J. Isaaq, Iddnor, Hori, Idnor, and the appellants in the present appeal were convicted under Sect 302,I P.c., readwith Sec.34, Iqqafs, IQo-6, IG, IU, IE, IHQ, Ieq, and sentenced them to suffer rigorous imprisonment of five years each. [758 D] 9. The facts on which conviction was based are not in dispute. The only question is whether the offence under Section 307,Ib- P.W.D., read along with Secs 3 and 4 of the Act was a murder. [759 E] 10. The contention that the offence was one under S. 302 I. P. cannot be accepted. The charge against the accused for the said offence is that they were members in furtherance of their common intention to commit the murder, is not proved.

The appellant Bank was incorporated in the year 1947 and it entered into a special Indian law with effect from 1st April, 1948. The appellant Bank had been formed by the Government of India under the provisions of the [Indian Companies Act, 1913]. Under section 4(e) of the Act, the Banking Companies Act is applicable to the appellant Bank. Section 4(f) of that Act provides for a special and other Indian law applicable to India. Section 5 of the said Act provides that "the State Government may by notification in the Official Gazette declare any local area to be a special or other Indian Law relating to the matters specified therein". The appellant was incorporated under the [Companies Act, 1956] as a body corporate with perpetual succession and a common seal and with power to acquire, hold and dispose of property, both movable and immovable, and to contract and do all things necessary for the purpose of carrying on its business. Section 6 provides that the State Government shall by notification declare any area to which this Act applies to be an urban area. Section 7 provides that no person shall be entitled to recover from a person any debt due to any Corporation formed in pursuance of an Act of Parliament or of the Indian Legislature, whether such debt is incurred before or after the commencement of the Ordinance and not otherwise. The question for consideration is whether the appellant was created under the Ordinance VIII of 1969 and not under the Banking companies Act. Section 8 provides that every person shall have a general liability in respect of any debt which may be due to the Corporation formed by him, and is liable to pay such amount as may be prescribed. Section 9 provides that where any debt is payable by any person to the State or Central Government, the State Bank may, if it is satisfied that the person has made default in payment of the amount specified in the notice issued under section 7, make an order directing that the amount shall be recovered from him as arrears of land revenue. Section 10 provides for the recovery of the debt due by any Corporation constituted under the Act. The provisions of Section 9 are not applicable to a corporation formed by a Government company or a local authority. Under Section 11(1) of this Act, it is provided that where an order has been made under section 8, the person shall, on the date of such order, be entitled, in accordance with the provisions contained in the said section, to recover the amount as arrears. The words "any special Indian Law" are defined in Section 2(1)(a) of Act No. VIII of 1970 and the word 'any' is defined in that section. It means a company formed by Government or local authority and includes any other body corporate having perpetual succession. [Section 11] provides for recovery of debt due from any person. The expression 'any special or local law' has been defined in section 2(i) of U.P. Act No, VIII of 1972. Section 3 provides that notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, no person who is a member of a company shall be liable to be proceeded against under this Act unless he proves that there was a debt due and payable by him to the corporation. The word 'may' used in section 8 has been interpreted by this Court in Krishna Murthy vs State of Andhra Pradesh, [AIR 1966 SC 1125] and it is not necessary for us to go into the question whether the words " any special Indianlaw" have been defined under Section 2 (1)(b) of act No. IX of 1969. The Act provides a special machinery for recovery by the State of the debts due to it by the Corporation. Under section 9, the provisions relating to recovery of debts are not attracted in respect thereof. [See: [Krishna Murthy vs Union of India and Ors.] ,] ; referred to.

The petitioner, a manufacturer of sugar in the State of Uttar Pradesh, was an employee of the Central Government. He was appointed as a Salesman in the Central Public Works Department on January 1, 1957. On March 31, 1958, he was promoted as a salesman in Punjab and was posted at the place where the factory was situated. On April 30, 1959, he made an application to the Central government for fixation of his price at the rate of Rs. 2 per quintal. The Government of India by its order dated May 27, 1960, fixed the price at Rs. 1 per quintal in respect of sugar. On June 28, 1961, the petitioner filed a petition under Art. 226 of the Constitution before the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad for quashing the order of fixation of price at which he was appointed to the post of Salesman. The High Court quashed the order on the ground that it was passed without jurisdiction and also on the basis of the fact that the Government had not fixed the wholesale prices at which the sugar in question was controlled. It held that the petitioner was entitled to a reasonable price for the whole of India, since he was an independent person and therefore, there was no discrimination between him and the other persons. The petition was allowed by the High court on the finding that the fixation of the price was not arbitrary or illegal. The State Government filed a special leave petition against this order before this Court. On September 30, 1961 the petitioner moved this Court for an order quashing the notification dated May 28, 1960 and for a direction to the respondents to fix the wholesale price at what he was in-charge of the factory. This Court dismissed the petition on the view that the order passed by the Government was not justified. The petitioner filed another writ petition in the High Courts of Allahabad and Lucknow Bench challenging the validity of the notification. The main contention raised before this court was that the impugned notification was without jurisdiction inasmuch as it was issued without jurisdiction. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The power to fix a price at a particular rate is not an arbitrary power. It is a power which is exercised by the State Government in a reasonable manner and it cannot be said that there is any discrimination between the petitioner and the others. [557 D] 2. The impugned notification dated April 30. 1960 was issued under Art, 19(1)(f) of the constitution. The object of the Act was to provide for control of the prices at all levels in the country. It was not a case where there was any discrimination after the control of sugar was exercised by an independent authority. [506 D] 3. The notification dated June 28. 1960, which is issued without Jurisdiction and it is not a mere executive order passed under Art 19(2) of Constitution. The contention that the notification was issued in contravention of the provisions of the impugned Act is also devoid of merit. [504 G] 4. The question whether there is discrimination between an independent and separate person or persons does not arise for consideration in this petition. [500 D] 5. The order passed on May 28. 1961, by the Central Govt., was without Jurisdiction. The fact that in respect thereof the petitioner had no control over the price of sugar does not make any difference to the question whether the impugned order is a mere administrative order or an executive order. [511 G] 6. The provisions of Art. 19(6) are not applicable to the case of the petitioner. The Act was passed by Parliament in exercise of its powers under Art.. 19(5). [505 D] 7. The validity of this notification is not challenged on any ground. It cannot be questioned on the grounds that the said notification was not issued without the jurisdiction or authority of law. [525 G] 8. The challenge to the validity thereof must fail. [606 H] 9. The argument that there was discrimination between a person and another person does not merit acceptance.

The Company was incorporated in the year 1947, and it had a capital of Rs. 1,50,000/- per annum. The Company was assessed to pay an amount of Rs, 1,00,000/per annum on account of the rise in the cost of living index. On appeal by the Company, the Tribunal held that the increase in the working class cost of the living index was not justified and directed the company to pay a sum of Rs., 1,25,000/-. The Company filed an appeal before this Court against the order of the Tribunal. During the pendency of the appeal, the Company filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order passed by the Tribunal on the ground that the award was not in accordance with law and was liable to be quashed. The High Court held that there was no material before the Tribunal to show that the increased cost of life index had been taken into account by the State Government, and therefore the Tribunal was justified in rejecting the claim of the Company. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Tribunal erred in holding that the enhancement of the working classes cost of a living index amounted to a reduction in the rate of working class. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, HELD: (1) The award passed by an Industrial Tribunal constituted under Section 7A of the Act is binding between the parties and it cannot be said that there has been a rise in cost of capital cost of Rs,. 1,75,000/-, as claimed by the company. [757D] (2) The Tribunal was right in holding on facts that the working Class cost of live index had not been taken in accordance to law. [750F] (3) The increase in cost was justified and there was a rise of 56 points, a substantial increase in costs of living Index. [751G] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 921 of 1966. Appeal by special Leave from the Judgment and Order dated the 14th July, 1967 of the Calcutta High Court in Misc. Case No. 11 of 1965. S. K. Das, for the appellant. M. C. Setalvad, Attorney-General of India, B. Sen, R. N. Sachthey, for respondent No. 1. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Shah, J. This appeal is directed against an order passed on a reference under Section 10(1) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') by the Central Government in exercise of its powers conferred by sub-section (2), clause (b) of sub section (1). The appellant company was incorporated with effect from April 1, 1957. It is a registered society which had a share capital of about Rs. 50,000 per annum and it has been established that there were no substantial increase as in the case of the menial class cost. The Tribunal has held that in view of the increase of the cost, the increase was justified. [857F] 2. The question whether the increase is justified or not is a question of fact and the High Court was right. [957G] 3. The award was passed by a Industrial Tribunal which had jurisdiction to decide the dispute. It cannot be disputed that the Industrial Tribunal has no power to go into the question of the increased working class of the company as it is not open to the Company to raise any objection in regard to the increase or the increase. [900G] 4. The appellant was entitled to raise a contention that the change in the basic wage of the workmen should be justified and the award passed on that basis should be quashed and set aside. [800H] 5. The appeal is allowed, the order under appeal is set aside and the order made by the Industrial Court is restored. There will be no order as to costs.

The appellant was a member of the Mutt and was elected to the office of the President of India on March 31, 1951. He was elected as the President in 1952. The appellant filed an election petition against the respondent for a declaration that he was entitled to be declared elected. The respondent contested the said petition by filing a written statement. The case of the respondent was that the appellant had been duly elected and that the respondent had not challenged the validity of the scheme framed under section 103(d) of the Representation of People Act, 1951 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act'). The trial court held that the scheme was valid and it was open to the appellant to challenge the validity thereof. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) that the provisions of section 103 (d) were not retrospective in operation; and (ii) that there was no material irregularity or illegality in the procedure followed by the respondent in making the said scheme. The scheme framed by the appellant was valid till 1952 and it is clear from the record that the said schemes were duly published in the Gazette on March 1, 1951 and they were not challenged before the trial court. The provisions of s. 103(f) were applicable to the present case and the respondent could challenge the said validity only if he had challenged the said invalidity. The High Court was wrong in holding that the Act was retrospective in character; and that it was not open to challenge on the ground that it contravened the Matadhipati's fundamental rights under article 19 (1) (f). [557 G] (iii) Section 103(b) of The Representation of the People Act is a substantive provision which is prospective in operation. It is clear that the legislature has not made any retrospective amendment to the said provisions and it cannot be said that the statute was bad for want of legislative competence. The result of the decision of this Court in [M. R. Balaji vs State of Mysore] , referred to above, is that the impugned scheme was not valid till the Act came into force. [558 H] (iv) Section 104(d)(i) of Act No. 1 of 1951 was applicable to a case where the scheme had been framed and a challenge made by the petitioner to its validity on the grounds that it violated the Mathadpati's fundamental right under article 14, and section 103 of the Act. The said provisions were not saved by article 19(1)(f) and were therefore bad in law. [658 H; 658 A] (v) Section 102(d), as amended by the Amending Act No 1 of 1952, was applicable only to a situation where the schemes had been made and enforced and not to cases where they were inconsistent with the said sections. The amendment made by section 103 was not retrospective but it was made in respect of such cases after the Act had come into force and the Court held that there is no substance in the contention that the amended provisions were applicable only for a situation which was covered by the said provision. [650 D] (vi) Section 105(d). provides that where any scheme has been framed, or a scheme published under section 104 of the Constitution is not challenged, the Court may declare the said Scheme to be void and inoperative. The amended provisions are applicable only in cases where the said Act was passed and enforced. [643 D] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1584 of 1968. Appeal by special Leave from the Judgment and Order dated the 9th July, 1967 of the Mysore High Court in Writ Petition No. 858 of 1966. S. T. Desai, R. N. Sachthey and B. D. Sharma for the Appellant. V. C. Mahajan, M. K. Ramamurthi, S. P. Nayar and R. H. Dhebar, for the Respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Sikri, J.

The appellant was appointed as a Hindi Teacher in the school on ad hoc basis. He was appointed by the managing committee of the school as per the provisions of Section 3 of the Validation Act. The school was upgraded to the post of Hindi teacher in the year 1976 and thereafter, he was appointed on regular basis as a regular teacher in a substantive vacancy. On July 12, 1982, the appellant was promoted as Hindi Teacher (Hindi) in the School. He filed an application before the Managing Committee of the School for regularisation of his services in a regular post. The Managing Committee held that the appellant is entitled to be regularised as Hindi teacher with effect from July 12 1982 and accordingly, he should be regularised. On December 31, 1983, the school was taken over by the management of the Government. The appellant filed an appeal before the District Judge, who allowed the same on the ground that the appointment of the appellant for 89 days was in accordance with the provisions contained in Section 3(3) of the Act and the rules framed thereunder. The State preferred an appeal to this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The High Court erred in holding that the school is a regular one and not a regular school. [532E] 1.2 The appellant was initially appointed as Hindi Teachers on ad-hoc basis for 89 day appointments. He continued till July 12 1983 and thereafter he was regularised as a regularly appointed Hindi teacher. On August 30, 1983 the Managing committee of School passed an order directing regularisation of the services of the petitioner in a post which was vacant in the institution under the orders of the managing Committee. The management of that school filed an Appeal before this Court against the said order. This Court held that since the appellant had completed one year's service as Hindi teachers, he could not be regularised in a permanent vacancy. [633F] 1:3 2.1 There is no merit in the contention that the services were regularised by the Managing body of the institution on July 12 and the school continued to serve as Hindi. The High court erred in denying the benefit of the validation Act to the appellant on the basis of the provisions made in Section 4 of the Validating Act. [643F] 2.2 There is nothing wrong in the order passed by the District Court, which could be sustained in law. [733G] 1.:4 3. The appeal is allowed and the judgment of the High Court is set aside. The respondent shall pay the arrears of salary and other emoluments due to the petitioner as a result of his regularisation within a period of three months from today.

The appellant was a member of the Panchayat Samiti, a Panchayat Samiti and a Zila Parishad. The appellant was elected as a member to the Panchayat Samitis in the year 1962. He was elected to the office of Chairman of a Panchayat. On his election he was elected by the members of the panchayat. In the meanwhile, a meeting of the Panchayats was held on March 31, 1963 at which the appellant was present and he was informed that the President of the Zila Parishad had been suspended from service. The respondent filed an application before the District Judge, who dismissed the application holding that the allowances paid to the Chairman for travelling allowance and daily allowance were not in excess of the amount of expenditure which he would have to incur for performing the journeys in order to discharge his official duties. On appeal by the appellant, the High Court held that the payment of travelling allowance was not a condition precedent to the carrying on of the business of the Samiti but it was a condition of service and, therefore, it was not open to the respondent to contend that the amount received by him for travelling allowances or daily allowance was in excess. The High Court further held that as the appellant had failed to establish that he was entitled to any compensatory allowance, he could not be said to have incurred any disqualification arising from the payment to him of daily allowance. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The High court was right in holding that there was no evidence on record from which an inference may be drawn that the appellant would have incurred the expenditure for performing journeys in connection with the discharge of his official functions. [775 H] (ii) The payment of traveling allowance and Daily Allowance under rules 3 to 7 were not a conditions precedent to carrying on the business. The payment was made by the Panchayat, though it was an office of profit. [750 A] (iii) The appellant had been appointed as Chairman of the Gram Panchayat in 1962 and he had been paid daily allowance for the day-today. He could not therefore be said that he incurred any pecuniary loss to the Government or to the members thereof. [751 B] (iv) The amount received was not in the nature of a salary but was in the form of a fixed monthly allowance. [751 D] (v) The allowances paid under rules 4 to 7 of the Rules were not conditions precedent for carrying on any business. [764 G] (vi) The payments made by way of daily allowances and daily allowances are not in any manner meant only to cover additional expenditure and out of pocket expenses of the Chairman and, consequently, there is no question of any pecuniary gain to a Chairman of Panchayat Samiti or Zila Parishad, as the case may be. [754 D] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 979 of 1967. From the Judgment and Order dated the 14th July, 1966 of the Allahabad High Court in C.M.P. No. 8 of 1965. S. N. Andley, for the appellant. R. K. Garg, for respondent No. 1. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Shah, J. This appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated April 14, 1966 passed by the High court of Allahabad in Civil Misc. Writ Petition No. 1203 of 1965, whereby it dismissed the writ petition filed by the respondent. The facts leading to this appeal are as follows: The appellant is a member, who was elected for the office held by the Zila Panchayat, a Zila Panchayat and a District Magistrate. He had been elected as Chairman in 1962. On March 31. 1963 he was removed from service on the ground that he had incurred any financial loss to Government or has incurred any liability for the said period. The order of removal was passed by him on April 14. 1963. The appeal filed by him against the order of his removal was dismissed by the District Magistrate, Allahabad.

The appellant was the tenant of a shop in the building. The respondent filed a suit for eviction against the appellant on the ground that he had made an application to the Rent Controller for permission to occupy the said shop and that the appellant had not paid any rent from the date of the application till the filing of the suit. The trial Court held that the construction was temporary in nature and the appellant was entitled to protection under Section 11(3) of the Act. The High Court held, on a consideration of the evidence adduced by the parties, that the disputed construction was not permanent in nature but it had been made with the consent of the land lord and that it constituted material alteration. In second appeal the High Court reversed the findings of fact recorded by the trial Court and dismissed the suit filed by the appellant. The appellant has come up in this Court by special leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The question whether a construction is permanent or temporary in character does not affect the question as to whether the constructions are permanent in character. [775 H] 1.2 In the instant case, the disputed constructions were made on the open land adjacent to the accommodation and it constituted a material alteration in the accommodation. The fact that a building was constructed on the vacant site adjoining the accommodation does not make any material alteration as the construction is temporary in the nature of a material alterations. [750 H] 2.1 There is no evidence to show that the constructions were temporary in existence on the date when the suit was filed. The question as regards the construction of the building did not arise at all. The mere fact that the building was in existence and it was constructed after the filing the suit does not alter the nature or character of the construction. [751 H] 3.2 There is nothing to show by evidence that a construction was made on any of the sides of the accommodation, and it constitutes material alteration which would affect the said question. The finding recorded by both the Courts below that the alleged constructions were permanent in the sense that they constituted material alterations does not effect the question of 'material alteration' as required under Section 3(3)(a) of Act. [751 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1566 of 1986. From the Judgment and Order dated 16.5.1986 of the High court of Delhi in C.M.W.P. No. 1215/86. V.S. Desai, S.K. Bagga, R.N. Sachthey and B.D. Sharma for the Appellant. M.C. Bhandare, A.K Gupta and P.H. Parekh for the Respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by KASLIWAL, J. Leave granted. 2. This appeal is directed against the judgment dated 16th May 1986 passed by the High Curt in Civil Revision Petition No. 1157/86 whereby the High Courts order dated 16-5-1986 and the order dated 15-5 -1986 passed by a learned Single Judge of that Court in Civil Misc. Writ Petition No 1215 of 1986 is set aside. 3. The facts leading to this appeal are as follows: The appellant was inducted into possession of a residential building on the basis of an agreement for sale executed between him and the respondent on 10-5/86 and that he was also allotted a residential accommodation in the same building. He had paid rent from 1-6-1986 till the date he was evicted from the said premises. The case of the appellant is that the respondent was not entitled to the protection under section 11(1) of Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 (hereinafter referred to as "the Act"). 4. The only question for consideration in this appeal is whether the construction made by the respondent in the residential building was temporary or permanent in status. 5.

The appellant filed a suit for recovery of money against the respondent company on the ground that the respondent was an employee of the company. The respondent company contested the suit by filing written statement and also by way of defence. The trial court held that the summons as effected in accordance with the first part of clause (b) of Rule 2 of Order 29 of the Code was not duly served on the company and that the service of the summons was sufficient compliance with the provisions of the code. The Trial Court decreed the suit holding that the defendant was an officer of the Company who had been appointed as a director of the respondent. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decree of the trial court and restored the decree passed by the trial Court. In this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the provisions contained in Order 29 Rule 2 were not applicable to the facts of the case because the summons had been duly served upon the company as required under the first proviso to Rule 2. It was further submitted that the High court erred in holding that there was no service of summons on the respondent and that it was not open to the respondent to contend that the appellant was an office assistant or a person who is described as an office Assistant, on the basis of which the bailiff of the Small Cause Court at Calcutta was delivered. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The provisions contained under Order 29 Rules 2 and 3 are mandatory in nature and they cannot be read into the Code. [505D] 2. The High Court erred in law in holding the respondent as an officer or a servant of the Government. [506F] 3. The provision contained in Rule 2(b) is not applicable in the facts and circumstances of the present case because it was only a case of service of notice on the Company. [504D] 4. The appellant could not be regarded as an employee within the meaning of Section 2(e) of the Act. [ 506F] 5. The proviso to sub-rule (b), therefore, cannot be pressed into service in view of the provisions in Rule 3. [605E] 6. The question whether a person is an officer and servant of Government or not does not arise in this case because under the Code the respondent is an employee who is named as an Office Assistant. [UDF] 7. The language used in sub-clause (b)(i) of clause(b), namely, "any person" is clear and unambiguous. It is not necessary to refer to any other part of the said clause. [53G] 8. The words "any officer or servant of a Government" are not defined in the Code and they must be given their ordinary meaning. [54F] 9. The word "officer" used in the proviso to Sub-rule 2(a) of Order29 Rule 2 is clear enough to include an officer who is mentioned as an Officer or servant. [55G] 10. The expression "any other person" occurring in sub clause (a) and (b). [56A] 11. The use of the word "any" in the said provision makes it clear that the words " any person" are used in connection with the service or appointment of a person as an Assistant, who is designated as an 'officer' on the date of the application for leave to his credit. [57F] 12. The fact that the company had not been appointed by the respondent does not mean that the services of the employees were terminated by the company itself. [58B] 13. The term "any employee" used under the proviso is clear in its context and it cannot be interpreted in a manner which would make it clear to the contrary. [59F] 14. The intention of the legislature was clear that if the respondent had been an employee, he should have been appointed on the said company. [60G] 15.

The appellant was the owner of a house in village Kokari, District Hyderabad. He filed a suit for possession against the respondents on the ground that he had been dispossessed from the said house by the respondents. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the respondents were not entitled to any relief under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. On appeal the High Court reversed the decree and held that the order passed by the Magistrate was without jurisdiction and, therefore, the order of the Magistrate could not be sustained. In this connection, it may be mentioned that the High court in revision held that there was no breach of the peace and the Magistrate had no power to pass a preliminary order under section145 of the code of Criminal procedure. The High Court also held that since the Magistrate has not recorded his satisfaction in the preliminary order, he is not entitled for any relief. In the appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the finding of the High Curt that there were no breach on the part of the respondents was without any basis and was based on a wrong appreciation of evidence. Allowing the appeal, HELD: (1) The order passed under section 146 of the Criminal Procedure Code is not an error of procedure but is an error apparent on the face of the record. [675 H] (2) Section 145 of Code of Civil Procedure provides that when any person has been dispossessed of any house or land by the Government, the possession thereof shall be deemed to have been delivered to him under section 6. The order of a Magistrate holding that there is a breach of peace cannot be sustained in the eye of law. [775 H; 776 B] (3) Section 146 of Code provides that if any person is dispossessed from any house, land or any part thereof by the State Government or any officer authorised by the Central Government in this behalf, he shall be entitled to a decree for possession. [750 C] (4) The finding recorded by the High Courts that there are no breachs of the said peace cannot also be sustained as the order was passed without jurisdiction. [751 D] (5) Section 147 of the Indian Penal Code provides for an offence under section 107 of the Penal Code and it is not necessary to mention in the instant case that there must have been a breach on his part. [751 H] JUDGMENT: CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Criminal Appeal No. 978 of 1986. From the Judgment and Order dated 11.8.1986 of the Hyderabad High Court in Criminal Revision Petition No. 1253 of 1985. V. S. Desai, R. N. Singh, M. Veerappa, A. Subba Rao and P. Ram Reddy for the Appellant. K. Ram Kumar and G. Gopalakrishnan for Respondent No. 1. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by RAY, J. This appeal is directed against the judgment dated 11th August 1986 passed by a Division Bench of the Andhra Pradesh High Court dismissing Criminal Revision Application No.1253 of 1986 filed by the appellant under section 482 of the Cr.P.C. The appellant was convicted for an offences punishable under sections 107 and 145 of Indian Penal code and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one year and to pay fine of Rs.1,000/- in default of payment of fine to undergo further rigorous imprisonment of six months. The case of the prosecution is that on 12th June, 1985 at about 6.30 p.m., the appellant was found in possession of a room in the house of the complainant. On the basis of the complaint filed by him, an offence punishable under section 135 of the Bombay Police Act was registered against the appellant and he was arrested on the same day. The investigation was taken up by the police. After completion of the investigation, the case was transferred to the Court of the Judicial Magistrate, First Class, Hyderabad for trial.

The appellant, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was assessed to income tax on its total income of Rs. 1,50,000/-. The Income Tax Officer, on an application made by the appellant, determined the amount payable to it as compensation for the acquisition of its property in the State of Bombay and paid the same to the appellant. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax officer. On further appeal, a Division Bench of the High Court held that the decision of the Tribunal was correct and that the appellant was entitled to get the compensation determined by the Income Tax authorities under section 14(2) (c), and that it was not open to review under section 66(1). The appellant filed an application for special leave before this Court, which was granted. On behalf of the appellant it was contended that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to go into the question whether the amount paid to it by way of compensation for acquisition of property in British India was a "income" or not and that as the appellant had been assessed to tax on the basis of the decision in Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay vs Ahmedbhai Umarbhai and Co.(1) the Tribunal should have allowed the application filed by the assessee. HELD: The High Court was right in holding that section 14 (2) of the Act applied 'only to non residents' and that section14(2)(c), did not apply to residents as well as nonresidents. [775 H] The decision of this Court in Commissioner Of Income tax and Excess Profits Pax vs Ahmedm Umarbhai & Co.(2) was not challenged before the High court, and therefore, the question referred to the High Courts was not a pure question of fact. [875 G] In the instant case, the appellant did not have any income for the purpose of acquisition of his property in India. The decision in Ahmedbhai's case (supra) was clearly distinguishable. [779 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1566 of 1966. Appeal by special leave from the judgment and order dated April 20, 1964 of the Bombay High Court in Income Tax Reference No. 1 of 1962. S. T. Desai, R. N. Sachthey and B. D. Sharma for the appellant (in C.A. 1567/66). M.C. Setalvad, Attorney-General of India, K. J. John, P. H. Parekh and R. Hathi, for the respondent (in both the appeals). The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Shah, J. The appellant is a company registered under the [Indian Companies Act] and has been assessed as a dealer in its goods in the States of Bombay, and is liable to be taxed on the income of the said business. The question referred for the opinion of the court is whether the appellant is entitled to claim deduction of the amount of compensation determined under section 15(2), and if so, to what extent. [780 G] 2. Section 14(1) of Act 1 of 1963 provides that where any person has been convicted by a Court of an offence which was not compoundable under section 42 (3), he shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year or with fine or with both. The proviso to the said section makes it clear that if the amount specified in the order made by a court of competent jurisdiction is not paid, the assessee would be entitled to have the amount determined under the said order. [781 G] 3. Section 15(1), as amended, provides that if any person is convicted by Court of offence which is not compoundable, he shall also be punishable for the same offence with imprisonment and fine or both. [789 A] 4. The High court was right when it held that section 15 (2)(b) does not apply in respect of persons who have been convicted under the provisions of section 14.

The assessee, a firm carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling cotton yarn, was assessed to income tax by the Income Tax Officer under section 10(2)(xv) of the Income tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Appellate Tribunal rejected the claim of the assessee that the rate of commission should be fixed on account of business considerations but allowed the appeal filed by the assessee. The High Court held that the assessee was entitled to deduction of the amount paid to Shri Vaish in respect of his income from the firm. It was further held that in the circumstances of each case, the assessee had a reasonable and adequate opportunity of being heard before the assessment was made. In this view, the High Court allowed the writ petition filed by Shri Vaish. The Revenue is in appeal against the judgment of the High court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The question referred to the High Courts under section 66(2) of Income tax, 1922, was answered in favour of the Department and against the assessee by holding that the amount of Rs. 75,465 paid to the General Manager for carrying on business was not a part of the cost of production or manufacture of cotton yarn. [775 H] 1.2 The High court was wrong in taking the view that the interest paid to General Manager was not an amount laid out or expended wholly and exclusively for the purpose of the business, but it was a part and parcel of the income of the firm which was assessed as a trader. [750 A] 1:3. Under section 10 (2) (xv) the assessee is entitled to claim deduction of any amount paid by him to an employee of the Government in respect thereof from the profits of the partnership business. The question whether an expenditure was wholly and solely laid out for the purposes of the said business or not, does not arise in this case because the assessee has a reasonable opportunity of showing that he is entitled in law to be heard before any assessment is made. [751 H] 2:1. Under the scheme of the Act, the amount payable to an employer by way of remuneration for carrying out the work of the factory or the business is not a sum which is laid out wholly and necessarily for the said purpose. The assessee has no reasonable and sufficient opportunity of having been heard before assessment was completed. [753 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1566 of 1967. Appeal by special leave from the judgment and order dated September 30, 1966 of the Allahabad High Court in Income Tax Reference No. 1 of 1965. S. T. Desai, R. N. Sachthey and B. D. Sharma, for the appellant. M. C. Setalvad, Attorney-General of India, H. K. Puri, for respondent No. 2. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Shah, J. This appeal is directed against the order dated October 30, 1967 of the Appellate Assistant commissioner and the High. Court affirmed the order of the Tribunal. The facts leading to this appeal are these: The assessee firm is a registered firm carrying out business in cotton yarn and cotton yarn which is not an item specified in Schedule I of the Indian Income tax Rules, 1922; it has been assessed as an income tax under section 11(2). The assessee was assessed by the Appellate Deputy Commissioner and he was directed to pay the amount due to the Central Government. The Tribunal held that there was no evidence on record to show that the appellant had a substantial interest in the partnership firm. The Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, Allahabad, however, held that it was not necessary for the assessee to prove that the income from business was wholly or exclusively laid out and expended wholly or mainly for the business. In view of the finding recorded by the Tribunal that the expenditure was incurred wholly and partly for the other business, the Tribunal came to the conclusion that the said amount was not laid out in the books of account of the appellant firm.

The appellant was a member of the Trade Union. He was appointed as a member in the year 1957 and he was paid a sum of Rs. 1,000 on January 12, 1957. The appellant filed his application for a writ to quash the order of dismissal passed by the respondent. The High Court held that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to entertain the application for the same relief as it was made before the Tribunal. It further held that in view of the fact that the appellant was an officer of the trade union, the Tribunal was not justified in refusing the appellant 's prayer for representation through representatives of his own choice and that the Union did not take up this appellant's claim against the appellant. The learned counsel for the company contended that the High Court erred in holding that the compromise was not binding on the appellant as he was a party to the industrial dispute. It was further submitted that the settlement dated January 12. 1957, which was entered into by the appellant with the union, was not a valid one and the Tribunal committed an error in refusing to give him relief under the Industrial Disputes Act. The respondent contended that in the circumstances of the case it was open to the appellant to make a representation through representative of his choice in preference to Fateh Singh. It is true that the respondent did not file any affidavit before the High court but he filed an application for review of the order passed by this Court on January 13, 1957, and the learned Judge, "was right in refusing his prayer for production of the appellant's statement on behalf of the respondent". The learned Judge held that there was no material to justify a conclusion that this compromise was entered in as much as the appellant had agreed to pay a further sum of money by the union. In our opinion, the HighCourt erred in interfering with the order refusing the prayer for a direction to the Union to make an application under the [Industrial Disputes Act]. The learned Single Judge held, on the basis of the evidence adduced before him, that the agreement dated January 13. 1957 was not genuine and that it was not open to him to make any such representation. In view of all the circumstances, we are of opinion that the order rejecting the appellant"s application for production through representatives is illegal. The appeal is accordingly allowed and the order under appeal is set aside.

The appellants were the tenants of a house in which they had a common interest. The respondent filed an application under s. 14 of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') for eviction of the appellants from the premises on the ground that Kedar Nath was not a tenant of the other landlords. The trial court held that Kedarnath had a joint interest in letting out the property and that he was entitled to remain in occupation of the premises till the date of his death, but that the respondent was not liable to be ejected from the said premises. On appeal by the appellants, the District Judge confirmed the order of the trial court. The High Court held that the suit filed by Kedar Nath had abated as all the appellants were negligent in not taking steps for substitution. In this view, the High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the decree passed by the trial Court. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The provisions of s. 35A of the Act are mandatory in character and do not affect the rights of a party to be brought before a court for passing a decree in his favour. [329D] 1.2 In the instant case, Kedar Nath died on February 14, 1972 and the appellants had a right to remain as tenant of one of the landlords. Therefore, the provisions of r. 33 were not intended to apply to an appeal which was filed by all the plaintiffs. The provisions in s.35A are of no help to the respondent. [320F] 1:3 2.1 There is nothing in the Act or any other provision which would affect the right of a person who has a joint right to eject him and such a party cannot be ejected. [322G] 2.2 The provisions contained in s, 35A are mandatory and do they affect the interests of the parties.

The appellant was the tenant of a building in Delhi. The respondent filed a suit for eviction on the ground that the appellant had let out the building to the respondent for a period of six months and that the respondent had not paid rent from 1st April, 1952 till the date of filing of the suit. The trial court held that the tenancy was terminated by efflux of time under section 111(g) of the TP Act and that it was a statutory recognition of a principle of justice, equity and good conscience. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decree passed by the trial court and dismissed the suit filed by the respondent. In this Court, on behalf of the appellant, it was contended that the provisions of section 111 (g) were not applicable to the facts of the case as the tenancy had been terminated by notice under section 106 of the Transfer Act. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the provision introduced in sub section (g), namely, section 111 of the Act was a mandatory recognition of the principle of law, equity, good conscience and good faith. [775 H] 2.1 The provisions of sections 106 and 111 of TP Act are not applicable in this case as they were not enacted by the legislature and were merely procedural and technical rules of equity. [750 A] 2:2 Section 111(h) of TP is a mandatory provision which is not a mandatory form of recognition of principles of justice or equity, but it is only directory and not mandatory form. The provisions in sub sections (g). [776 H] 3.1 In the instant case, the notice was given by the tenant to the landlord on the basis that he had terminated the tenancy under section 11(2) of T.P Act. The notice was issued by the appellant on the footing that the notice dated 1st March, 1952 was a valid one and not a valid notice. [751 B] 3:3 A] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1566 of 1977. From the Judgment and Order dated 16.5.1977 of the Delhi High Court in C.M.P. No. 11 of 1976. S.K. Bagga, R.N. Sachthey and M.S. Narasimhan for the Appellant. V.C. Mahajan, A.K Gupta and P.H. Parekh for the Respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by K.JAYACHANDRA REDDY, J. This appeal is directed against the judgment dated 16th May 1977 of the High court of Delhi dismissing the suit of the respondent filed under section 10 of the T.A Act. It appears that the landlord filed a petition for eviction of the tenant on the grounds mentioned in clause (g)(i) of sub section 2 of section 11 of the said Act. In the plaint, it is stated that the premises was let out to the appellant for a term of six years and that he has not paid any rent from January, 1952 to March, 1953. The appellant filed a written statement on the same day. It was contended in the written statement that the suit was not maintainable as the respondent was not a tenant within the meaning of section 2(g)(ii) of Act. On behalf of respondent it was submitted that the lease was terminated under section11(2), and that, therefore, the provisions contained in sub clauses (i) to (vi) of clause (h) were applicable to him. The Trial Court held that there was no valid notice under clause (f) of subsection 2 of Section 11 of Act and the suit for ejectment was not barred by limitation. On the basis of the pleadings, the trial Court framed issues and decided the issue in favour of the landlord. The appellate court found that the tenant had failed to prove that he was a tenant under sub section 1(g), but held that it is a statutory tenancy and not an agreement of lease.

The appellant was a member of the Indian Police Service. He was appointed as a District and Sessions Judge, who had been confirmed by the High Court of Madras in a revision petition filed against his conviction under section 161 of the Penal Code. The appellant was convicted for an offence under section 5(1)(d) read with section 5 (2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. He challenged his conviction and sentence before the High court. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellant had not been given reasonable opportunity to show cause against the action proposed to be taken in regard to him. It was further held that the order passed by the Governor under section 6(1) of Prevention of corruption Act, was not a 'law' within the meaning of article 311 of the Constitution and that the President or the Governor had no power to dismiss or remove a person or reduce him in rank except after an inquiry. The State Government preferred an appeal against the order of the High. Court. The matter was taken up by the State Government before this Court. HELD: (i) The appellant's conviction under article 311(2) is not a "law" within the definition of article 14 of the constitution and, therefore, he was not entitled to be heard in regard thereto. [655 D] (ii) The order passed on the basis of the evidence adduced during inquiry shows that it was not expedient to hold the inquiry under the principal clause, that clause, as it stood before its amendment by the Constitution (Fifteenth Amendment) Act, 1963. Therefore, the order dated December 14, 1967 was a " law" within article 311 (2). [656 D] The appellant had been given an opportunity of showing cause against his action proposed in regard, him. The order was passed on March 31, 1968 and he was informed that he would be heard by the Government if he so desired. [613 E] (iii) The High court was not right in holding that there was no "law". [657 D] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 13 of 1967. Appeal from the judgment and order dated September 30, 1966 of the Madras High Court in Writ Petition No. 12 of 1965. S. T. Desai, R. N. Sachthey and B. D. Sharma, for the appellant. M. C. Setalvad, Attorney-General of India, K. K. Aiyangar, V. J. Francis, S. P. Nayar and R. H. Dhebar, for respondent No. 1. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Subba Rao, J. This appeal is directed against the judgment dated September 29, 1966 passed by a Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court dismissing the writ petition filed by the appellant challenging his conviction in regard. He has been convicted under section 7(1), read with [section 5 (1)(a)] and 5 (b) of that Act. The facts leading to this appeal are as follows: The appellant, who was a District & Sessions Judge at the relevant time, was dismissed from service by an order dated March 31. 1968. He filed a writ petition in the High' Court challenging his dismissal on the ground that he had been convicted for offences under section 4(1). The appellant contended that the conviction of the appellant was not legal and that in view of the provisions contained in article 311, the President had no authority to dismiss him. Held: (per Subba Rao J., Subba Rao and Mudholkar JJ.) that the High 'Court has jurisdiction to interfere with the order proposed to take action in regard' the appellant's case. The power to impose penalty is not an absolute one. The word "law", as used in article 14, means law. [625 A] (c) The words "law " are wide enough to include any rule of law.

The petitioners in their individual capacity and as such they are entitled to the customary rights of the Shia community. The respondents 5 and 6 filed a writ petition before the Allahabad High Court challenging the validity of the Notification dated 1st December, 1956 issued by the Shias' Central Wakf Board under section 5 (1) of the U.P. In the said writ petition the petitioners prayed for quashing the notification dated 1.12.1956 issued by respondent No. 2 and also prayed for a declaration that the respondents 5 to 6 were not entitled to perform their religious ceremonies and functions as Shia members of the Sunni community. It was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the Notification issued by Shias in exercise of their right under section 144 Cr.P,C., was without jurisdiction and void and that the notification issued by it was illegal and void. The High Court held that the petitioners were not liable to be evicted from the land in question as they had no right to perform religious ceremonies or functions and consequently the Notification was bad. It further held that there was no adjudication or decision on merits of the rights of parties and the writ petition was dismissed. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The notification issued under section 4(1) read with section 5(1)(a) of U. P. In exercise of its powers under section 6 of the Act, the Shian Board has framed rules called "The Sunni Central Wakf (Transfer of Property) Rules, 1956". Rule 54 1136 provides that the Shiam shall be a religious denomination and it is one of the contentions of the respondents that before the Uttar Pradesh Inadracy (Administration of Property Regulation) Order, 1956 was made under section 3 of the said Act, no suit or other proceeding shall lie against any person for anything done in good faith. [736 C] 2. The petitioners were entitled to have their customary rights to perform the religious ceremonies of Shia Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments. They could not be evicted by the respondents from the lands in question on the ground that they had established their existing customary rights. [836 D] 3.1 The notification dated January 1, 1956 under section 7(2) readwith section 5 of the Uttar Pradeshik Shia Act was without any jurisdiction and invalid. [937 C] 3: 2. Under section 6(3)(c) of that Act, it is only the Shira Central Wakf Boards which are empowered to regulate their customary right to do religious ceremonies in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution. The power to regulate the customary right of the parties to perform such religious ceremonies is conferred by section 6 (1). [938 D] 4.2 The notification was issued under sub-section (3) of section 7 read with rule 54 1135 (vii) of Appendix I to the Rules framed under section 9 of the Wakf Act, 1954. Rule 5411 provides that no suit shall lie in any court against any persons for anything which is done or intended to be done by the petitioners or members of Shias. [1038 C] 4: 3.3 The notification under section 8(2)(b) read along with rule 55 (vii), was issued by a competent authority and published in the Gazette on January 1. 1956. Rule 55 (viii) provides that any suit or proceeding may be instituted against any member of Shiam, who is not a party to the dispute before the Tribunal. [1138 C-D] 4(i) The notification is without jurisdiction. [1239 D] 5: 3: 4.1 It is only in exercise thereof, the power under section6 (3)(b), read with Rule 54 of Appendix 1 to the rules framed under sub section (2) of Section 9 of that act, no court has been empowered to decide any question relating to the rights or interests of parties to the suit or proceedings.

The assessee, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1962-63. The Income Tax Officer, on an application made by the assessee under Section 24 of 1922 Act, disallowed the claim of set off against the capital gains of Rs. 1,10,000/- and also imposed a penalty of Rs, 50,000/-. On appeal, the Appellate Tribunal confirmed the order of the Income Tax officer. The High Court held that the sum of Rs., 50,00,000 was not allowable as set off under Section 80 of 1922. It further held that in view of the provisions of section 24 of 1961 Act, the assessee could not be allowed to carry forward and set off the amount of loss under the head "capital gains" against the income of the assessee. The Revenue filed an appeal before this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 Section 24(2) of 1922 is a provision for computing the total income of an assessee in respect of his total income. [775 H] 1.2 In the instant case, the sum arrived at by the Income tax Officer was not set off in accordance with the provisions contained in section 24(1)(a) of 1961. The amount of Rs,. 50, 00,000 which was paid by the company to the assessee was not allowed as setoff under Section 36(2). [776 H] 2.1 The High court was wrong in holding that the claim for set off was admissible in respect only of the sum determined by the Incometax Officer and not of the amount paid by way of set-off. [750 A] 2:2 In view of section 80 of 1961, the High Court was right in holding, that the amount which was allowed as a set off could be carried forward under Section 72 or sub section (3) of Section 24. [751 B] 3.1 There is no merit in this appeal and it is dismissed with costs.

The respondent was appointed as a Constable in the Central Reserve Police Force (in short, 'C.I.F.) on 10.2.86 and he joined the service of the Government of India on 10th February, 1986. He was promoted to the post of Assistant Commandant in the year 1985. The respondent was promoted as Inspector of Police in the month of March, 1986 and thereafter he was sent to different units. On his re spondent being appointed to the Defence Science Service, the three units were reconstituted into three separate cadres. The two units were merged into one single cadre. The Respondent was appointed to a post in the Defence science Service on 10-2-86 and sent to various units. He joined the said service on 10/2/86. On completion of his training he was promoted from the post to the rank of Inspector of police. On 1st April, 1986, the respondent was re soughing as Deputy Commandant in a separate cadre. On 2nd May, 1986 he was re d redesignated as Assistant Commandant. The appellant filed an application before the Tribunal for quashing the order dated 10th March, 1987 and also for a direction to reinstate him in service with all his emoluments from the date of his appointment. The Tribunal dismissed the said application by its order dated 30th May, 1988. On appeal, the High Court held that the respondent had not been appointed as Assistant Commandants in the two units and therefore he was entitled to be re stituted under Rule 12 of the Central Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1965. The High Court further directed that the appellant Union of India shall reinstate the respondent in service within one week from the said date. On behalf of the appellants it was contended that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to direct re stitution of the respondent with the said two units. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Tribunal has power to vary the service conditions of the members of the services and to determine the age of superannuation. [775 H] 1.2 In the instant case, the Tribunal was not justified in directing re sation of the service condition of the two Units. [750 A] 1:3. Under Rule 12(1)(a) of the CCS (CCA) Rules 1965, the Central Government has power under Rule 11 to vary or alter the service terms and conditions of service of any member of a service from time to time. The said rule provides that the conditions of Service of a member of the Service shall be such as may be prescribed by the Central Govt. [751 B] 1 Whether the respondent is entitled to continue in service after he has attained the age prescribed under Rule 9 of the Rules, is a question of fact and it cannot be decided in the absence of any evidence or material on record. [751 D] 2.1 In the present case, there was no such power conferred upon the Central Administrative Tribunal to direct reinstatement with the appellant. The order passed by the Tribunal is not sustainable in law. [754 G] 1st respondent was entitled for re sion of superannuation from service and he was paid all his dues. [764 D] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 877 of 1988. From the Judgment and Order dated 4.8.1988 of the Customs, Excise & Gold (Control) Appellate Tribunal, New Delhi in Appeal No.(s). 9/86-D. S. K. Jain, V.K. Gupta, R.K Srivastava, Ms. A. Subhashini, M.S. Narasimhan, M N Singh and P.C. Sharma for the Appellants. V.M. Tarkunde, Mrs. Rani Chhabra, M B Shah, M K Jain, M C Jain, S.K Jain, R K Jain and M K Gupta for the Respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by RANGANATH MISRA, J.

The appellant was a member of the Bombay Legislative Assembly. He was elected as a member from the constituency of the State of Maharashtra. The election petition filed by him was dismissed on the ground that he had been guilty of corrupt practice under section 123(7) read with section 21 (1) of the Act. The High Court held that the appellant was guilty of the corrupt practice and sentenced him to dismissal. On appeal, this Court reversed the order of the High Court and directed the trial Judge to hold an enquiry into the allegations made by the appellant in his election petition. In the course of the proceedings before the learned trial Judge, the appellant appeared as a witness and produced certain documents. The evidence of the witnesses was recorded and the appellant examined himself as a defence witness. The learned trial judge held that there were two reports of the inspection of the record of the election petition which showed that the allegations in the election petitions were not true. The appellant filed an appeal against the order passed by the High court. The Division Bench of the Court, however, allowed the appeal and set aside the order made by it. In this appeal, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the learned Judge had erred in holding that there was no evidence to show that the election petitioner was guilty for corrupt practice. It was further submitted that the High Courts were not right in holding against the appellant because the allegations contained in the petition did not constitute a corrupt practice within the meaning of section 123 (7) of Act. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The order passed under section 21(1) readwith section 21 is an interlocutory order and it cannot be said that there are no evidence on which the court could have come to the conclusion that there had been two reports by the inspection committee. [675 H] 2. The provisions of section 21 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 were not complied with in this case. The question whether there was a corrupt practices under section 13(1)(e) or section 21 was not considered by the learned Judges. [775 G] 3. The words "any other person" used in section 21 are wide enough to include a person who is guilty of an offence and is liable to be punished for such offence. [750 H] 4. The word "any" in section 13 (1)(f) means "any person". Therefore, the learned judges were right in observing that there must be evidence to prove the allegations against the candidate. [751 G] 5. The expression "any one" used by the legislature is wide enough and it includes a person whose name was not included in the electoral roll. [751 H] 6. The use of the word "every other person", in section 11(1), indicates that the words " any other person". It does not mean that there should be evidence on record to show whether there has been a corrupt or illegal practice. [764 G] 7. The language used in the section is wide and it would include a candidate who is found guilty of such an offence. Therefore, there must have been material before the court to show the commission of the alleged corrupt practice by the candidate concerned. [754 H] 8. The requirement of section 11 (1), therefore, is not satisfied in this appeal. [752 G] 9. Section 21(l) provides that no person shall be convicted of an act or omission punishable under any other provision of the Constitution. [758 C] 10. The fact that the charge against the respondent was proved by the evidence of PW 1 and the finding recorded by the trial court that there is a corrupt Practice under section 11 of the said Act does not affect the question whether the charge framed against the petitioner was true or false. [759 D] 11. Section 11(2) provides for an appeal to the High courts from any decision of the trial Court.

The petitioner was a dealer in goods, which were sold by him to the State Government. The tax on sales of goods was levied under section 3 of the Central Sales Tax Act, 1956 (hereinafter referred to as "the Act") and it was assessed to sales tax at the rate of Rs. 1,000 per quintal. The petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the Validation Act. The High Court held that the Validation act is ultra vires and quashed the impugned notification. The State Government appealed against this decision to this Court. HELD: (1) The Validation Act was valid and it did not contravene any of the provisions of the Constitution. [655 D] (2) The validation Act was passed by the legislature in order to provide for a levy of tax on the sale of goods, as defined in section 3(b). The Validation act was not ultra vires. [756 E] (3) The impugned notification is valid and the Validation Ordinance is valid. [750 A] (4) The words "on the occasion of the sale" have reference to the character of the transaction and are not a ground for holding that there is, in fact, no imposition of tax. [751 G] (5) The legislature was competent to enact a law with retrospective effect. [753 D] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 979 of 1966. Appeal by special leave from the judgment and order dated April 30, 1967 of the Allahabad High Court in Special Appeal No.. 15 of 1965. S. T. Desai, R. N. Sachthey and B. D. Sharma, for the appellant. A. K. Sen, S. P. Nayar and R. H. Dhebar, for respondent No. 1. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Sikri, J. This appeal is directed against the judgment dated April 29, 1967 passed by a Division Bench of the High court of Allahabad in Special Civil Appeal Nos. 15 of 1966 and 16 of 1965 whereby the High. Court allowed the writ petition filed by the petitioner and quashed and set aside the order of the State of Uttar Pradesh dated March 31, 1956, and directed that the tax on sale of the goods be levied at the rates specified in the Schedule. The facts leading to this appeal are these: The petitioner was an assessee in the State Sales Tax Department of the Government of U.P. (hereinafter called 'the State Government') and was assessed by the Sales Tax Officer, Lucknow, to sales Tax on the sales of the said goods. The Sales Tax officer, Lucknow issued a notice dated March 30, 1956 under section 6(2) of the Act calling upon the petitioner to show cause why the tax should not be levied on the turnover of the sales. The notice was served on the petitioner on April 30. 1956 and it is alleged that the petitioner has failed to comply with the provisions contained in section 6 (2). The petitioner submitted a reply to the said notice on May 29, 1956. The respondent No 1 filed a counter affidavit in which he stated that the Sales tax officer had no jurisdiction to impose a tax on his sales. He also stated that he was not competent to pass any order under section 7 of the U. P State Government and that the impugned order is liable to be quashed. The learned Single Judge held that there was no valid levy of the tax by the State Legislature and accordingly dismissed the writ petitions. In appeal, the Division Bench reversed the judgment of the learned Single judge and allowed the appeals filed by special appeals Nos. 978 and 1679 of 1967. The appellant has come up in appeal against the said decision. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Section 7 of U P State Legislature was valid. It is not open to the legislature to enact any law with respect to a tax which is imposed by the Central Government under section 5 of the Uttar Pradesh Sales Tax (Amendment) Act, 1965.

The appellant was convicted by the trial court for an offence under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The appellant was found guilty of murder and was sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court confirmed his conviction and sentence. The appeal filed by him before this Court was dismissed. The State preferred an appeal against the judgment of the High Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 Section 354(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure provides that no person shall be sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for two years or more unless he has been in custody for not less than three months and has been released on bail under Section 439 of the code of Criminal procedure. The expression 'habitual' is defined in Section 2(f) of that Act as meaning "a person who, whether before or after the commencement of this Code, is a habitual offender". [775 H] 1.2 In the instant case, the appellant was sentenced by the High court to imprisonment till he was released on default bail under section 439 of Cr.P.C. The sentence imposed upon him was not in accordance with law and therefore, the appeal filed against that order was dismissed by this Court. [776 H] 2.1 In a case where an accused is convicted for an offense punishable under Section 304(2) of I.P., Code of criminal procedure, it is open to the court to consider whether the offence committed by the appellant falls within the ambit of Section 354 (3) and if so, to what extent.
