[750 H] In the present case, there was no evidence on record that the appellant had any intention to commit murder or to cause grievous hurt to his cousin 's wife. The question is whether the appellant has a reasonable prospect of shaping into a balanced person, given in the circumstances of this case. [751 G] 2:2 In a criminal trial, it may be difficult for an accused to prove that he was a habitual criminal and that he had no intention to cause death or grievous hurt. The offence committed is punishable under section 304(1) of IPC.

The appellant, a private limited company, was assessed to income tax by the Income Tax Officer on the basis of an agreement entered into between the Government and the assessee. The assessee claimed that he was entitled to compensation for his land acquired under the Land Acquisition Act in respect of the land acquired. The Collector awarded compensation at the rate of Rs.7,36,691/- per acre. On appeal by the State Government, the High Court held that the amount of compensation payable to the appellant was not on the date when possession of the lands was taken by the Government for the purpose of assessment to tax in the year of assessment and accordingly enhanced the compensation. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High court challenging the order of the Collector. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the compensation payable under the Act was on the actual date when the possession of land was taken and not on any date prior to the date of taking over of possession. The State Government preferred an appeal against the judgment of the High, Court. The Division Bench held that in view of the provisions of Section 18 of the Land acquisition Act, the right to receive compensation under the said Act accrued or arose to the assessee when he sought to get the compensation determined by the Collector and the amount was not payable on any particular date prior thereto. It further held that since the entire question, namely, whether the offer made by the LandAcquisition Officer was on a subsequent date, was decided in favour of the appellant, the decision of the Division Bench was confirmed. The present appeal is filed by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court HELD: 1.1 Section 18(2) of the Act provides that the right of the owner to receive payment is not on actual date but on a particular date.

The appellants filed a suit for eviction against the respondent on the ground of non-payment of rent. The respondent filed an application under Section 12(1) (f) of the Act for eviction of the appellant from the premises in question on the grounds mentioned therein. The trial court dismissed the application holding that the compromise was not legal and valid. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decree and held that the appellants were entitled to get a decree for eviction under Section 11(1)(e) of The Act. In further appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High court erred in law in holding that there was no ground for passing a decree in favour of the respondent. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The compromise decree is not legal but is a nullity and cannot be executed by a competent authority. [675 H] 2. The provisions of Section 12 (1) of Act are mandatory in character and do not confer any right on a party to get possession of the accommodation from a tenant whose tenancy has been governed by the Rent Restriction or Control Act. [775 G] 3. In the instant case, the compromise decree was passed on the basis of the compromise and it was binding between the parties. The appellants were ill advised to fight the litigation further and thus cause delay in the vacating of the shop by another five years. [750 H] 4. The question whether a suit has been adjusted by any lawful agreement or compromise is a question of fact which can be decided only on consideration of the terms of the consent decree. If the appellants are entitled to have a decree under Section 13(1), it is not open to them to get an order for eviction passed against a tenant who was in occupation of the premises as a result of the agreement between the appellants and the respondent, [750 A] 5. The High Court erred in holding otherwise. [751 H] 6. The consent decree was not a nullity because the compromise had been held to be legal by a court of competent jurisdiction. [751 D] 7. The fact that the appellant did not get possession from a third party does not mean that he became entitled to obtain an order under Section 10(2) of CPC for eviction. He is entitled to seek a decree on the strength of the said compromise decree. [764 G] 8. The agreement between a landlord and a tenant cannot be enforced by a Court of competent Jurisdiction unless it is proved that the same was in accordance with law. [754 H] 9. The terms of compromise are not binding on the parties and the question whether there was any ground for the compromise to be in favour or not does not arise at all. [752 G] 10. The appellant had filed a petition under Section 14(1). The compromise was in the nature of an agreement between two persons, namely, the appellants. It is true that the terms and conditions of the lease are not in dispute but the question as to whether there is any ground other than the one mentioned in the compromise or not would depend upon the facts of each case. [758 H] 11. The Court has no power to pass a decree which is not a decree. It cannot pass a preliminary decree. The court can pass a final decree if it is satisfied that the agreement was in terms of law. If there is no ground other then the compromise will be binding on both the parties, unless it can be shown that the said terms are not contrary to law. The courts have jurisdiction to execute the decree. In this case, therefore, the question of passing a preliminary order does not lie at all and the High Courts were right in holding so. [759 H] 12. The appeal is allowed. The judgment under appeal is set aside. The parties will pay and bear their own costs.

The assessee, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was assessed to income tax by the Income Tax Officer on the basis of the assessment made by him. The Income Tax officer held that the assessee had suffered a capital loss of Rs. 1,50,000/and he accordingly issued a notice under section 23A(1) of the Act calling upon the assessee to show cause why the amount of Rs, 1,00,000/- should not be assessed as income tax and super tax payable by it on the surplus of Rs., 1,25,000/-. The assessee filed its reply to the said notice. The Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals) held that in view of the provisions of section 23(1)(a), the amount was liable to be assessed under section 22A(2). On appeal, the Appellate Tribunal confirmed the order of the Commissioner of Incometax and dismissed the appeal. In further appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the sum of Rs 1,75,000/-, which was paid by the assessee in the year of account was not a capital receipt and therefore, the provisions were not applicable to the case of the assessee. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that the amount paid by way of dividend was not capital receipt but was a capital expenditure. [775E] (2) Section 23A of the Income tax Act provides for an assessment and recovery of super tax at the rate of one per cent in the case where the assessee has suffered a revenue loss of more than Rs.1,25000/-. If the assessee is able to prove that the value of the shares may not go up in future but whether the Directors were justified in not declaring dividends in view ofs. 23A (1), it would be difficult to arrive at a conclusion as to reasonableness on the said ground. [750F] (3) The provisions of s. 23(2)(a) are not applicable when the assessee was able to establish that the shares were not capital receipts but were held by the Directors as having been purchased by the company in the ordinary course of its business. [751G] (4) The amount paid under the head "capital loss" is a capital asset and therefore it cannot be said that the provisions are applicable to such an item. [753F] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1533 of 1967. Appeal by special leave from the judgment and order dated April 20, 1967 of the Allahabad High Court in Income Tax Reference No. 1 of 1966. S. T. Desai, R. N. Sachthey and B. D. Sharma for the appellant. M. C. Setalvad, Attorney-General for India, K. L. Hathi and R. H. Dhebar, for the respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Sikri, J. This appeal is directed against the judgment dated April 24, 1967 passed by the Allahabad, High Court dismissing the Income-tax Reference No 1 of 1967 filed by the Commissioner under section 66(1), Income Tax Act, 1922 (hereinafter referred to as "the Act"). The assessee is a company registered under the [Indian Companies Act] and has its head office at Kanpur. It is a registered firm carrying on business in the name of the Mills. The assessment was completed by the Incometax Officer on March 31, 1966. On April 30, 1966 the IncomeTax officer issued notice under sections 23A and 23(3) of that Act calling for an explanation from the assessee as to why he did not assess him to income-tax for the year ending December 31, 1967. The assessee submitted his reply to that notice on May 29, 1966 but the Commissioner rejected the same on the ground that the explanation was not satisfactory.

The appellant, a permanent resident of village Koker, was an Assistant Collector of the District of Sultanpur. He filed a suit for declaration that he had acquired rights under section 15 of the Act and that the order passed by him was illegal. The trial court held that the appellant was entitled to get the declaration sought for in his favour. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decree of the trial court and dismissed the suit. In this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that section 12(6) of the . Act provides a statutory arbitration and section 37 of the : Act does not apply to arbitrations under section 12 (4). It was further submitted that section 46 of the , Act provides for an appeal against the order of the Civil Judge modifying the award made by him. The High Court held that section 16 of the U.P. Act is a provision which gives a statutory recognition to an arbitration and that section 37 does not affect the finality of the award. In dealing with this contention, Wanchoo, J., observed: "The question whether section 12 of the Arbitration Act applies or not to an award under section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure is one of fact and if it is so read in the light of section 46, section 47, section 48 and section 49 of the said Act, it will be clear that what is made final is the decision of the arbitrator as it emerges after proper proceedings. The question whether the decision was by any competent Court or Tribunal does not arise for consideration in this appeal." In dealing on this point, Wanchoo J., held: "It seems to us that section 8 of the Limitation Act applies to arbitrations and that it provides a special form of application to the Civil Courts for the correction and revision of revenue records for villages under consolidation. It is clear from section 46 that the decision in the case of Attar Singh's case (supra) was not an award made final. The decision of this Court in Attar singh's case was concerned with the validity of the provisions of sections 8, 9 and 49 of that Act. In our opinion, section 12 does not operate to affect the jurisdiction of the civil court to make a correction or revision of the revenue records. It only provides for the decision by the arbitrator under sub section (4) of section 16. The words "any other matter" in section 8 are clear and unambiguous. The expression "any dispute" is defined in section 2(b) as meaning " any question relating to the rights conferred by this Act". In our view, section 8 does not make a provision for an arbitration or revision. It merely provides that the decisions of the arbitrators as it emerge after proper proceeding, if any, have been taken under the provisions contained in the [Indian Arbitration Act] and the decision is final. Section 46 of The Indian Arbitration Act, therefore, applies to an order passed under section 16(4) and not to a decision by an arbitrator as provided in section 46. In the case before us, we are concerned with section 8 which provides that where any dispute or difference between the parties to the agreement referred to in section 12 and the person who is entitled to receive the declaration made under section 8 has been referred to arbitration, the decision shall be final. It will be seen that section 9 does not provide for an award by a civil court. The only question which falls for consideration is whether section 16 does not bar the jurisdiction under section 46 or section 47 of the Indian Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996.

The petitioner was appointed as Assistant Engineer in the year 1962 and he was promoted to the post of Executive Engineer on 1.4.1962. He was promoted as Executive Engineer in 1963 and he joined service on 1st April, 1963. The respondent was promoted on 1 st May, 1964 as Executive Engineers. On the basis of the seniority list prepared by the Corporation, the petitioner was promoted from the post to the higher post of Assistant Engineer. The promotion order was passed on 1-4-1963. The petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the promotion order and also the subsequent proceedings. The High Court held that the promotion was not made as per rules but was made by way of executive instructions and therefore, the promotion could be made only by an executive instruction and not by executive instructions. It was further held that since the promotion had been made on a basis other than that in the case before the court, the authority can prescribe service conditions by executive instruction. The Court held: "The rule providing for service conditions is a rule of general application and it cannot be said to be arbitrary or unreasonable. In the absence of any rule or regulation the authority could not prescribe service condition on the basis thereof." It was also held that in view of the fact that the petitioner had been promoted as Assistant Engineers, he could not be treated as a separate category amongst Junior Engineers and therefore his promotion was illegal. The appellant filed a Letters Patent Appeal against the judgment of the High court which was dismissed by this Court. Hence this appeal. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The rule providing that service conditions shall be made by executive orders and not otherwise is violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. [775 H] 1.2 In the instant case, the post in question was a separate cadre and was created on the principle of seniority-cum-fitness. The rules framed by the respondent Corporation provide for service condition to be made on the ground that it is a separate class of posts. [750 A] 1:3. The rule provides that the recruitment grade in the same category shall be as specified in the regulations and this is what was done till the year 1988 and is also sought to be done since 1988 by the impugned resolution. [751 B] 2.1 In view of Rule 4(2) of the Rules, the respondent could not have been promoted on a post which was not filled up by way promotion. The order passed by the High Courts in the absence thereof cannot be sustained. [753 H; 75B] 2:2. The impugned resolution is clearly violative of Article 14 and is liable to be set aside. [764 G] 2.(i) The rule making authority has not prescribed service conditions for promotion. It is not permissible to prescribe service regulations for promotion unless the rules provide otherwise. [754 C] (ii) The respondent could have been considered for promotion only by a executive instruction but he was not promoted on the post which is not in accordance with law. [752 D] 2(iii) The impugned order passed in the present case cannot be upheld as it is contrary to the rules and regulations. [758 G] (iv) The High Courts have failed to appreciate that the rule making power of the respondent was exercised by executive authority and therefore the impugned order is liable for interference under Article 226 of the constitution. [759 D] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 877 of 1989. From the Judgment and Order dated 17.8.1988 of the Karnataka High Court in Writ Petition No. 1123 of 1988. V.M. Tarkunde, M.K. Rajendran, R.S. Sodhi, S.N. Prasad, P.H. Parekh, K.R. Nambiar, Ms. A. Subhashini and B.B. Singh for the Appellant. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by VENKATARAMIAH, J.

The appellant, a retired Judge of the High Court of Delhi, was appointed as a Judge of a High Court in the year 1962. He was appointed by the President of India on the recommendation of the Chief Justice of India. On his appointment he was transferred to the National Judicial Commission and was posted at Delhi. The appellant was appointed to the post of a Judge in the Delhi Higher Judicial Service in the State of Delhi. On the basis of the recommendations made by the Chief Justices of the various High Courts, the Government of India issued an order on the same day i.e., on the date of his appointment as a judge of the Supreme Court of India and forwarded to the President the proposal for the appointment of a person as a sitting Judge of that High Court. The Chief Justice, however, recommended the appointment by the Governor of the State in consultation with the Chief Minister of the States concerned. On receipt of the recommendation, the President issued an office order on June 30, 1962 appointing the appellant as a Member of the Delhi Judicial Service. On July 31, 1963, the appellant filed a writ petition before the High court challenging the validity of the appointment and the appointment. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appointment was not in accordance with the provisions of Article 233(2) of the Constitution. On appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The appointment of the appellant was not by way of consultation with a Chief Justice or a Judge but by way other than his appointment. [775 H] (2) The High court was right in holding that there was no consultation with any of the Judges of the Punjab High Court and the Chief justice of India was not required to consult the Chief Secretary of the Government concerned. [750 A] (3) The power of appointment vested in the President under Article 233 is subject to the provisions contained in Articles 233 and 234 of the constitution. [751 B] (4) The consultation with, or the opinion of, the Chief Judge of India is not a condition precedent for the exercise of the power of appointments by the State. [75 H; 75 A] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1579 of 1967. From the Judgment and Order dated the 30th July, 1967 of the Allahabad High Court, Lucknow Bench in Writ Petition No. 1126 of 1963. S. K. Bagga, for the appellant. M. C. Setalvad, Attorney-General of India, B. Sen, R. N. Sachthey and B. D. Sharma, for respondent No. 1. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Shah, J. This appeal is directed against a judgment dated November 30, 1967 passed by the High' Court of Allahabad in Writ Jurisdiction Case No. 1026 of 1962. The facts leading to this appeal are as follows: The appellant, who was appointed in the post in question as a Chief Judge in 1962, was transferred from the National Commission and he was posted there at Delhi on his appointment and was also posted at New Delhi. He filed a petition before this Court under Article 32 of theConstitution praying that the High Courts of Allahabad, Lucknow and Allahabad should be directed to appoint him as a member of the Commission. The learned Judge of this Court dismissed it. On further appeal by the appellant, the Division Bench of the said High Court held that the order of appointment was in accordance With law and accordingly set aside the order passed by this Court. In the appeal before us, the only point urged is that the appellant has been appointed as an Additional Judge of Delhi Judicial Services on the basis that he was appointed on the recommendations of the then Chief Justice. The question whether there was a consultation with or not is a matter for the High 'Court and if it is not so, the High- Court should have directed the appointment to be made by this court. In our opinion, the contention raised by the learned Attorney- General cannot be accepted.

The respondent was a member of the Bihar State Electricity Board. He was appointed as an Assistant Engineer in the year 1962 and he retired from service on 31.12.1962. On his retirement, he was re-employed as an Executive Engineer in a new establishment. The respondent was promoted to the post of Superintending Engineer in 1973 and thereafter he was promoted as Executive Engineer on 1.1.1974. He filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of his promotion. The High Court quashed the order passed by the appellant and directed him to pay '50% of the consequential benefits 'to which the respondent would be entitled on superannuation. The State Government preferred an appeal against this decision to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal holding that the order imposing punishment was bad in law. In the appeal filed by the State, it was contended that the High court was right in quashing the order dated 1.9.1974 and directing 'all consequential benefits' to be paid to the respondent. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: (1) The order of the High. Court is quashed and set aside. [775 H] (2) The respondent had retired from the service on 30.12..1962 and he was entitled to get all consequential benefits. [750 A] (3) The impugned order passed in the present case was not a punishment order but an order imposing penalty. [751 G] (4) The High court should have remitted the matter to the competent authority for passing fresh orders on the basis of the report of the Enquiry Officer. [75 H; 75 B] (5) In any event, the respondent had already retired from his service and he could not be given any benefits under the order which was passed by him. The order imposing the penalty was bad as it was passed without giving an opportunity to the appellant to show cause against the proposed punishment. [76 H; 76 C] (6) The appellant was entitled, in law, to get his salary and allowances from the date of his retirement. [77 D] (7) The Government order imposing a penalty was not bad in Law. [78 G] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1579 of 1987. From the Judgment and Order dated 20.1,1987 of the Delhi High Court in W.P. No. 1255/87. S.K. Bagga, R.N. Poddar and P.H. Parekh for the Appellant. V.M. Tarkunde, Mrs. A.K Gupta and Ms. Rani Chhabra for the Respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by KASLIWAL, J. Leave granted in all the matters. These appeals are directed against the judgment dated January 20, 1987 passed by a Division Bench of the Punjab & Haryana High Court allowing the writ petition filed by respondent No. 1 and directing him to give his salary from the year 1973 onwards. The appellant is an Assistant Executive Engineer. He retired from services on 30th December 1962 and was promoted in 1973 as Superintending Engineer. On the basis thereof, he retired on superannuation on 31st January, 1974. The impugned judgment of the Division Bench dated January 19, 1987 was passed in Writ Petition No.1255/1987. The learned Single Judge dismissed the writ petitions filed by respondents 1 to 3 holding that they were not entitled to any benefits as claimed by them. The Division Bench held that the respondent was entitled for all consequential reliefs including the arrears of salary and other allowances from his date of retirement. The appellants are aggrieved by the judgment of a Division bench of the same High Court. It is contended on behalf of the appellant that the impugned order imposing penalties was bad because it was not passed in accordance with law.

The appellant was the owner of a plot in the city of Delhi. The respondent filed an application under section 14 of the Development Act for permission to construct a building on the said plot. The appellant applied for permission for construction of a building thereon. The Corporation granted permission to the appellant to use the site for the purpose of the proposed building. On the basis of the plan, the appellant was permitted to use and constructed a building in the area specified in the Master Plan. The respondents filed an appeal before the Appellate Authority against the order of the Commissioner. The Appellate Authority allowed the appeal and set aside the order passed by the Commissioner and directed that the appellant should be given an opportunity of being heard. On appeal, the Appellate Tribunal held that the land was not covered by a road and therefore, section 14(2) of the development Act was not attracted. In further appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the provisions of section 14 were not applicable to the case as the appellant had constructed a new building in his own right and had constructed the building in accordance with the Master plan. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court was wrong in holding that the Development Authority was competent to impose a tax on the land or building in question. [775 H] 2.1 Section 14 of The Development Act provides for the levy of a tax and it is not necessary for the purposes of this section to specify the particular use of any land or buildings in a zone. [750 A] 2:2 It is well settled that the legislature has no power to impose tax on lands or building, as the case may be, in respect of which a development Act has been passed. The provisions of the Act have to be read with section 10 and the Development Authorities are competent to levy a tax. [751 B] 2(i) Section 14 is not attracted to the facts of this case because it provides for a different use of land in a Zone. [751 H] (ii) The Development Authority has no authority to impose any tax on land or any building in a zones. [752 C] (iii) The provisions contained in section 14 are not applicable in respect to the cases where a Master Plan is prepared for the area, before it comes into operation and, if that be so, there is no violation of section 15 of the General Clauses Act. [754 D] 2.(ii) Section 15 is attracted only when the Development authority has made a proposal regarding the use of the land in accordance therewith. [761 H; 754 A] (iv) The development scheme is not a development scheme and, therefore, it cannot be put to a different uses. [758 G] 3.1 It is true that the Act provides that the Planning Authority shall levy a fee on the construction of buildings in the zone. But the Development Scheme does not provide for any other use of lands or buildings. The Development Authorities have no authority under section 15 to impose such tax. The development authority has no jurisdiction to impose the tax. It is also true that there is nothing in the Act which provides for any different use and, in fact, it is a case where the Development Plan is not prepared for a particular area. [759 D] 3:2 Section 14(1) does not apply to the circumstances of the case. The provision contained in sub section (2) is not applicable if the Development Commissioner has made proposals regarding the width of the road or any other uses in a region. [761 G] 4.1 In the instant case, the Development Officer had made a plan for the development of the area and had also constructed a residential building in that area. The construction of the building was not permissible under section 16. [763 D] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1584 of 1987.

The appellant No. 1 was convicted by the trial court and sentenced to death by the Sessions Judge, Delhi, on a charge of murder under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. The prosecution case in brief is that on the night between 10th and 11th June, 1967 at about 6 p.m., the appellant No 1 was found in possession of a sum of Rs. 5,000/- and a sum Rs. 2,500/- as illegal gratification by the police authorities. On the basis of the information given by the appellant no. 1, a case was registered against him under section 161 I. P. C. The investigation revealed that the appellant had taken the bribe from the complainant and handed over to Nagindas and the money was recovered from the pocket of the appellant. The appellant No, 1 was arrested on the same day and his statement was recorded by the Magistrate. On completion of the investigation, a charge-sheet was filed against the accused persons for offences under section 120B read with sections 302/34 I.p.C., and section 5(1) (d) read with Section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The trial court acquitted the appellant Nos. 1 to 3 on the ground that the evidence given by them in regard to the demand of bribe was not sufficient to establish the falsity of the allegation made by the prosecution and that the witnesses had been rightly excluded from consideration. On appeal, the High Court held that the prosecution case was proved beyond reasonable doubt and accordingly acquitted the accused. The State filed an appeal against the order of acquittal before this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1. Section 164 Cr. P C. is not a substantive provision but it is a procedural provision which should be strictly construed. It is not mandatory in every case. [675 H] 1.2. The evidence given in regard thereto by the complainant was sufficient to prove the falsity and the appellant was rightly excluded therefrom. [775 B] 1:3. The High Court was right in holding that the charges were proved beyond all reasonable doubt. [750 D] 2.1 There is no merit in this appeal and it is accordingly dismissed.

The appellant was appointed as a Constable in the Punjab Police on 1.7.1965 and he was dismissed from service on 2.8.1966. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court of Punjab and Haryana challenging the order of dismissal passed against him by the Superintendent of Police, Ambala City, on the ground that the order dated 2.5.1967 was illegal as it was passed without giving an opportunity to the appellant to file his reply to the show cause notice issued against him. The writ petition was allowed by a learned Single Judge of the High court holding that the dismissal of the respondent from service was not in accordance with law and, therefore, he was entitled to be reinstated in service. The State filed an appeal before this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The order passed by the High Curt is clearly illegal as the order passed against the appellant was without giving him an opportunity of hearing. [775 H] 1.2 In the instant case, the order was passed on 2nd May, 1967 and the respondent filed the writ petition in the year 1984. The learned Single judge has rightly held that the appellant had not been given an opportunity by the respondent to file reply to show cause against the show-cause notice issued by him. [750 H] In the present case, there was no law of limitation applicable to suits where an order is impugned as being void. [751 A] 1:3 2.1 There is a clear distinction between a suit for declaration and injunction and a suit in which the order is passed without hearing the party concerned. The question whether the order should be set aside or not, has to be decided by the Court after giving an adequate opportunity to both the parties. [754 D] 1.:3 2:2 In a case where the order against the plaintiff was passed by an authority not competent to pass it, the High Courts' power under Article 226 of the Constitution is exercised only in cases where no law or practice of limitation is applicable to the case. The Court has jurisdiction to examine whether the case is one which should be decided finally at the motion stage itself and if it is so done, the question involved in this suit would not be a bar to the maintainability of the suit. [764 D C] 1;3 3:2 It is well settled that a writ of certiorari can be issued for correcting errors of jurisdiction committed by inferior courts or tribunals. [754 A] 2.3 The High Court has rightly observed that the power under Art. 226 of Constitution is not exercised in an appropriate case. [752 B] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1566 of 1987. From the Judgment and Order dated 20.2.1987 of the Punjab & Haryana High Court in C.W.P. No. 823 of 1984. V.S. Desai, S.K. Bagga, R.N. Singh, M.M. Sharma, K.L. Gupta, P.H. Parekh and Ms. A. Subhashini for the Appellant. Virender Kumar, S.,R. Yadav, R N. Sinha, B.D. Sharma and D.P Singh for the Respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by RAY, J. Leave granted. This appeal is directed against the judgment dated February 20, 1987 passed by a Division Bench of the Delhi High Court dismissing the writ application filed by the appellant. The appellant was working as a constable in the Police Department and he had been dismissed from the service on the basis of a departmental enquiry conducted against him under Rule 16 of the Central Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1965. He challenged the order terminating his services by filing a writ application before the Punjab and Chandigarh High Court which was allowed on February 20. 1987.

The respondent was a dealer in the goods in question. The respondent purchased the P.D.Os. from the appellant, a dealer under the Central Sales Tax Act, 1956. The sales were made by him to the dealers on behalf of the Government of Andhra Pradesh. The dealers sold the PDOs to the purchasers on behalf and for the benefit of the State Government. The goods were delivered to the respondent in pursuance of the contracts entered into by the respondent with the appellant. The Sales Tax Officer, who assessed the sales tax payable by the dealer under s. 24(1) of the Act, held that the transactions were not speculative transactions and accordingly he set off the loss against the profits made by the assessee. On appeal the Appellate Tribunal confirmed the order of the Assistant Commissioner of Income tax (Appeals). The High Court on reference answered the question in favour of the revenue and against the assessee and dismissed the writ petition filed by the appellant with costs. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court HELD: 1.1 The sales in question were not made to the buyers but only lay down that if there was no actual delivery, the loss in speculative business against the appellant could be set off against the profit of the assessee in any year. [675 H] 1.2 In the instant case, the transactions entered into between the respondent and the appellant were merely sales of delivery orders and not to the extent of the losses suffered by the Government. Therefore, the sale was not a speculative transaction. The High court was right in holding that the sales in respect of which the sales were effected were not mere sales but only laid down that where the goods were not physically delivered by the seller but only laying down that when the goods had been sold, the losses in speculative transactions which could be allowed to be setoff against a profit in a speculative business. [775 H; 776 B] 1:3 The High Courts decision is correct and does not call for any interference. [750 D] 2.1 There was no delivery order or delivery orders issued by the dealers to the appellant on behalf or for the use of the respondent. The transactions were only lay out of the goods which were delivered by him. Therefore the loss suffered by him in speculative trading could be a loss in a speculation business and not a loss. [751 H] 2:2 In view of the fact that the contracts were entered into with the dealers, it was not open to the Sales tax authorities to assess the sales under s 24(l) of Act. The question whether the transactions are speculative transactions or not did not arise in this case because the High Court held that there was a delivery order and delivery orders. [751 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1179 of 1968. Appeal by special Leave from the Judgment and Order dated the 14th July, 1967 of the Andhra Pradesh High Court in Writ Petition No. 1223 of 1966. M. C. Chagla, S. K. Kapur and R. N. Sachthey, for the appellant (in both the appeals). A. V. Viswanatha Sastri, for respondent No. 1 (in all the appeals) The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Shah J. The facts in Civil Appeal Nos. 1180-1181 of 1968 are similar to those in the other appeals. The appellant is a dealer and has been assessed to tax under s 8(1)(a) of that Act. In the assessment proceedings for the year 1959-60, the Sales Tax authorities found that the sale of PD Os was not effected by the selling agents. On the basis of the findings recorded in the said proceedings, the appellant filed a writ petition before the High court of Andhra. The learned Single Judge dismissed the Writ Petition holding that there is no delivery orders or delivery order issued by dealers to dealers and therefore the sales are not liable to tax.

The appellant, a candidate for election to the Legislative Assembly of the State of Bombay, filed an election petition challenging the election of the returned candidate. The respondent contested the election. He was declared elected by the Returning Officer and his nomination paper was accepted by the returning officer. On the basis of the result of the scrutiny, he was declared as the successful candidate. He challenged the validity of the election on the ground that the nomination paper of the respondent was improperly rejected. The High Court held that the appellant had failed to comply with the provisions of section 33 and that the Returning officer was not entitled to reject his nomination papers on the grounds mentioned in section 33. It further held that there was no valid nomination paper at the scrutiny stage and the defect could be cured by an application for amendment of the nomination papers. The appellant filed a writ petition challenging this order. The learned Single Judge dismissed the writ petition holding that the provisions contained in section 36 were mandatory and as such the election was liable to be set aside. On appeal, the Division Bench held that section 36 was mandatory and that it was not open to the Returning authority to reject the nomination of the candidate on the basis that he had failed in his own case. The Division Bench also held that since the appellant did not comply with any of the provisions mentioned in [section 33], he was entitled to challenge the validity thereof. On further appeal, Held: (i) Section 36 is mandatory and it provides that if there has been "any failure to comply" by an candidate or his agent or other person in the conduct of a election, the matter may be different from the one before us. The provisions contained therein are mandatory and they do not provide for any procedure which would be inconsistent with the Act and the Rules. (ii) Section 33 is mandatory but it does not create any right in favour of an candidate to challenge his nomination on the score that he has failed to fulfil the requirements of section33. [775 H] (iii) The provisions of sub-section (1) are mandatory, and as a result of such compliance, the election is liable to suffer disqualification under section 36. [750 A] (iv) Section 35 provides for an appeal against the order of rejection of nomination paper on the sole ground that there has not been " any failure to record" by the candidate or he has not complied with any provisions of the Act or the Rules and the procedure laid down in the Act is mandatory. [751 B] (v) The provision contained in sub-sections (1), (2) and (3) are directory and not mandatory. Section 36 provides for a remedy to be available to an election petitioner against the improper acceptance of any nomination paper. [75 H; 76 A] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1566 of 1987. From the Judgment and Order dated 16.8.1987 of the Bombay High Court in Election Petition No. 1 of 1987 in Election petition No. 2 of 1987 In the matter of an election dispute between the appellant and respondent No.1. V.M. Tarkunde, Ms. A. Subhashini, M.K. Dua, S.N. Prasad, R.B. Mehrotra, P.H. Parekh, K.R. Nambiar, B.D. Sharma, Mrs. Rani Jethmalani, M/s. Viziagram and M.S. Arora for the appellant. Virender Kumar, S.,V.K Jain, S,V.B Jain, R N Singh, P R E S E N T The following Judgment of the Court was delivered by B.C. RAY, J. This appeal is directed against the judgment dated 16th August 1987 passed by the High Court of Bombay in Election Appeal No 1 of 1988. The election petition filed by the appellant challenging the validity and the validity or otherwise of the decision of the Returning Authority rejecting his nomination for the seat in question.

The appellants were appointed as workmen of the Company on October 22, 1972 and they were confirmed in their services by an order dated September 26, 1972. On November 30, 1972, the appellants filed a petition before the Labour Court under Section 33-C(2) of the Act for approval of the action taken by the Company in removing them from service. The said application was dismissed by the Labour Commissioner on October 21, 1972 holding that the appellants had voluntarily abandoned their services and that they were not entitled to any relief. On December 31, 1973, the Company filed a writ petition before this Court challenging the order of dismissal. This Court held that the action of the appellants in removing the names of the workmen from the rolls was illegal and invalid. The appellants challenged the validity of the said order by filing a writ application under Article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that there was no abandonment of service on the part of the appellant and that the dismissal was not justified. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The appellants were entitled to be reinstated in their respective posts with effect from October 22. 1972. [675 H] 1.2 The termination of services of the employees was illegal as it was not in accordance with the provisions of the Certified standing orders by virtue of which they were deemed to have abandoned their service. [775 G] 1:3.1 There is no case that the workmen concerned had been employed elsewhere during this period and, therefore, there was nothing in the surrounding circumstances or the conduct of the parties indicating or suggesting an intention on their part to abandon their services. The termination was illegal. [750 H] 2:1. In the instant case, the order terminating the services of all the workmen was not a change in the conditions of service of the company and it was only a change of condition of service which could be inferred from the circumstances of the case. [751 G] 2.2 There is nothing in Section 33(C)(2) or Section 33B(2), which prevents the Company from terminating the service of any workman concerned in the matter of abandonment of his services by the company. The order of termination passed on October 25, 1972 was not challenged before this court and it could be said that there is no abandonment by the appellants. [751 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1533 of 1973. From the Judgment and Order dated the 10th May, 1973 of the Orissa High Court in Misc. Case No. 11 of 1972. S.K. Bagga, for the appellant. M.C. Bhandare, R.N. Sachthey and B.D. Sharma, for respondent No. 1. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by RAY, J.-This appeal is directed against a judgment dated October 10, 1973 passed by the Orissa Administrative Tribunal in O.A. No. 8 of 1972 whereby the appellant has been dismissed from service with effect form October 22 and he was removed from service on November 30. 1972 by an Order dated December 31. 1973. The appellant challenged the said Order before this High Court by filing writ petition under Article 227 of the constitution. The learned Single Judge quashed the order passed by him holding that no abandonment was made by the appellant in the year 1972 and that he had not abandoned his services. Hence, this appeal. The only point urged on behalf of the respondents is that there has been a change by the earlier order dated October 25. 1972 and as such there was a change which could not be inferred by virtue or under Section33B(1) of Act No. 13 of 1972 and the appellant had no right to continue in service. It was also urged that the termination of his service was illegal, invalid. In support of this contention, the learned counsel for the respondents has placed reliance on a decision of this Court in [Shalini Devi]'s case (supra).

The appellant, a member of the Bombay Public Service Commission, was appointed as an Assistant Registrar in the State Bank of India. He was promoted to the post of Deputy Registrar on July 1, 1962 and was confirmed in that post on August 30, 1963. On September 6, 1964, he was transferred to the office of the Registrar of Co-operative Societies, Bombay, and was posted at Bombay. On October 7, 1965, he filed a suit against the appellant for recovery of money due to him under the decree passed by the trial Court in his favour. The trial Court decreed the suit on November 30, 1966. On appeal, the District Judge set aside the decree holding that the earlier decision of the High Court was not binding on the appellant and directed the Registrar to proceed with the sale. On December 6, 1967, the Registrar filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High court for quashing the order of the District Court. The High Court dismissed the petition. On further appeal by special leave, Held: (i) that the previous decision of a Single Judge of the same Court was binding on a Division Bench of the Court and the Registrar could not have taken the view that the subsequent decisions of the Division Bench were not relevant for deciding the question. The order passed by a Single judge in favour of the appellant was not an order of reference to a Division bench. [775 H] (ii) The High court had no power to set aside a judgment delivered by a single Judge, if it is found that the decision of Bhagwati, J., was erroneous or contrary to law. The learned Judge could not go behind the judgment and decide the question of law arising before him. [750 A] (iii) The order of a Division Judge in favour or against a party under Article 227 of the constitution was not a judgment within the meaning of Section 165 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872. [751 B] (iv) The learned Single Judge had no jurisdiction to set it aside on the ground that the High Courts had no authority to interfere with the order passed in favour. [751 D] (v) The Division Bench was not right in holding that a judgment pronounced by a Full Bench of a High Court is binding on any other Court and, therefore, the subsequent decision of another Court cannot be treated as an order or decision of such a nature which could be regarded as relevant by Judges of the Supreme Court. [764 D] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1566 of 1967. From the Judgment and Order dated the 10th July, 1967 of the Gujarat High Court in Special Civil Application No. 12 of 1965. S. T. Desai, R. N. Sachthey and B. D. Sharma for the Appellant. V. M. Tarkunde, K. J. John and P. G. Gokhale for Respondent No. 1. The Judgment of the court was delivered by Shah, J. The appellant is a member in the Bombay Civil Service Commission. He filed an application under Article 32 of theConstitution praying that the order dated October 7. 1965 passed by him in favour, or against the Government of Gujarat be quashed and set aside. On January 9, 1966, the High-Court dismissed the writ petition. The respondent then filed a writ petition in this Court which was allowed on April 10, 1967. The State Government preferred an appeal to this Court against the judgment of the learned Single judge. This Court held that the impugned order passed under Article 136 of the Letters Patent was not appealable and accordingly dismissed the appeal. On August 30. 1966, this Court issued notice to the appellant to show cause why the writ application filed by him should not be dismissed. The respondents appeared in person and filed a counter affidavit. In the counter affidavit it is stated that the Government had no objection to the order dismissing the writ petitioner's petition.

The appellant was appointed as a temporary Assistant Engineer in the Public Works Department of the State of Tamil Nadu. He was promoted to the post of Executive Engineer on 1.1.1973 and he was confirmed in that post on 1st January, 1973. On his appointment as a permanent Assistant Engineer he was promoted as Executive Engineer with effect from 1.2.1974. The appellant filed an application before the Central Administrative Tribunal, Madras Bench, praying for a direction to the Government of India to re-determine the pension under Rule 2(2) of the Pension Rules and to give him all consequential benefits including arrears of pay and allowances. The Tribunal dismissed the application holding that Rule 2 (2) was not ultra vires Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution of India. On appeal, the High Court held that Rule 2046 was valid and inoperative. In further appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that Rule 2946 was invalid as it was inconsistent with Rule 2. The High Court observed that Rule 22(1) of Pension Rules was not applicable to the case because Rule 2 was not in existence at the time when the retirement was made and, therefore, the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to retermine pension under the Pension rules. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The order passed by the Central Government on November 30, 1962 is valid and operative. [775 H] 2. Rule 29 46 was not a part of the Rules but was a statutory rule. It was in addition to that of clause (h) of Rule 29-46 of the rules. [750 A] 3. The power to retire under Rule 20 46 was conferred by the said rule and as such the order passed on November 1, 1962 was valid. [751 B] 4. The provisions contained in Rule 2 were not applicable in the case of the respondent. Rule 2 is not a statutory provision but it is an executive instruction which can be issued to clarify the statutory Rules. [751 D] 5. The proviso to Article 309 of the constitution does not apply to the facts of the present case because the appellant was promoted on 1 st January,1973 and his confirmation was confirmed by the Union Government as a result of that appointment. [764 G] 6. Rule 20-46 was not an executive instructions but was merely a statutory one. The said rule was in existence when the respondent was appointed to the service. [754 D] 7. The expression 'existing' is not defined in the Act and, as such, it cannot be construed to mean that the power to make rules can be exercised by the President or the Governor of the Union. [752 G] 8. Rule 22 of the General Rules was a part and parcel of the said Rules. It does not confer any right on the appellant to continue in service after he has been appointed as Assistant Engineer. [758 H] 9. The respondent was promoted from the post which was earlier to the appellant, but he was subsequently confirmed in the post. He could not have continued in service till his confirmation. [759 B] 10. Rule 23 of the Indian Railway Establishment Code is a statutory Rule and it cannot apply to cases where the power under Article 309 has been exercised by an authority subordinate to that by which the power is conferred. [761 D] 11. The question whether Rule 22 was not made applicable to a case of retirement under Rule 22 or not, does not arise in this case because rule 22 is not applicable. [765 G] 12. The words 'existing'. are not defined and they cannot be read as 'existing', unless the context requires otherwise. [763 D] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1579 of 1987. From the Judgment and Order dated 16.3.1987 of the Madras High Court in Writ Petition No. 823 of 1986. V.S. Desai, S.K. Bagaria, R.N.

The assessee, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was assessed to income tax on its total income of Rs. 1,10,000/-. The Income Tax Officer, on an application made by the assessee, determined the loss in respect of the chargeable accounting period ending 31st March, 1943 to be Rs. 2,00,000/- and added the amount of Rs, 1,20,000/to the total income for the chargeable account year ending 31-3-1943. The Income tax Officer, however, disallowed the claim of the assessee on the ground that the excess profits were not taxable in the assessment year ending March 31, 1943. On appeal by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner, the Appellate Tribunal held that the loss was not liable to be set off under section 4(1)(a) of the Act and accordingly, directed the Income tax officer to compute the loss on the basis of the excess profit for the period ending 30th March, 1942 to 31st day of March, 1944. The assessee filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Appellate tribunal. The High Court held that since the excess income was not taxable under section 5 of the Income Tax Act, 1961, it was not open to the Income-tax Officer to compute such loss on that basis and accordingly directed the Tribunal to compute this loss. On behalf of the appellant, it is contended that the High court erred in holding that the assessee had suffered a loss in any other business than the one which the assessee carried on at Raichur and that the profits for the said period were not assessed to excess profits tax under section 7 of the Indian Income Tax (Amendment) Act, 1944, and therefore, the loss should be computed as per the provisions of section 4 of the said Act. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The question whether the loss is taxable in a particular year or not was a mixed question of law and fact. [775 H] 2.1 The High court was wrong in holding on facts that the amount which the appellant had received by way of excess profits was not assessed as income tax under the provisions contained in section 4. [750 A] 2(i) The loss was, therefore, liable to assessment under section 6 of the Finance Act, 1943 and it could be computed under section 8 of the Central Act. [751 H] (ii) The High Courts erred in law in holding otherwise. [751 D] (iii) The assessee had not suffered a losses in any particular year. The loss in question was not assessable to excess profit tax under Section 5 of that Act. The profits for that year were not liable for assessment under the said section. [764 G] 2.(ii) In the instant case, the excess amount of income was taxable under the head "excess profits" and therefore the assessee could be assessed as a loss. [754 H] 3(i)(a)(iii) Where the loss had not been assessed as per provisions contained therein, it would be open to an assessee to claim that loss in his case. [752 G] (iv) The question of computation of loss under section 10 of the Incometax Act was rightly decided by the High Courts and the Tribunal was right in holding so. [758 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1566 of 1972. From the Judgment and Order dated the 30th day of October, 1970 of the Bombay High Court in Income Tax Reference No. 1 of 1971. S. T. Desai, R. N. Sachthey and B. D. Sharma for the Appellant. V. C. Mahajan, M. K. Ramamurthi, RR. Gupta and A. G. Ratnaparkhi for the Respondent.

The Kerala State Electricity Board (hereinafter referred to as the 'Board') issued a notification dated December 7, 1970 under Section 4 of the Kerala State and Subordinate Services Act, 1958 (hereinafter called the 'Act' for short) declaring that the petitioner was eligible to exercise his option in terms of Section 5(1)(a) of the Act. The petitioner challenged the said notification by filing writ petitions before this Court. The High Court dismissed all the writ petitions on the ground that the KPSC had not given effect to the directions given by the learned Single Judge and that the Government was not entitled to exercise their option in accordance with law. In the appeals filed by the Board, it was contended that the Kerala Public Service Commission (hereinafter described as the "Board") did not have the power to prepare a common list and since there was no common list, the K PSC could not prepare separate lists for Civil Engineering graduates. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The KP SC was entitled to consider the objections of the petitioner in accordance to law. [775 H] 2. The Kerala Public Services Commission (for short the 'Commission') is a body constituted by the Government under Section 5 of the said Act and it has the power of making recommendations for appointment to the post of Assistant Engineers. [750 A] 3. The expression "the common list" in Section 5 (1)(b) of Act means that the common list should be prepared by the Public Service commission. [751 B] 4. The Government is not entitled, as it has no power to make any recommendations for the appointment of Assistant Engineer. [75 H; 75 A] 5. The object of the K.PSC was to prepare separate list and if there was any defect in the preparation of the same, the Government could have made a specific order for preparing separate lists. [76 B] 6. The power to frame a common List is vested in the State Government under Article 162 of the Constitution. [77 D] 7. The appointment of the persons mentioned in Section 4(1) (a) is not a matter which can be decided by the KPsSC and the KPC cannot make any recommendation for appointment. [78 G] 8. The word "the Common List" in [Section 5(2)] of the act means that it includes the common lists. The words "theCommon List" are not intended to include the common List. [79 H; 80 A] 9. The scheme of the two Acts is different and distinct. The two Acts are separate and distinct, though they may be applicable in the same situation. [80 D] 10. The question whether a particular list is prepared by public or private agency does not depend upon the facts of each case. [81 G] 11. The State Government has no authority to make an order for preparation of a common Select List. The fact that there was a common select list does not mean that the same should be done in accordance therewith. [82 D] 12. The decision of the High Court is correct and it cannot be said that the decision of this Court in the case of KPTC was erroneous. [83 G] 13. The order passed by the High court is clearly unsustainable. [84 H; 85 A] 14. The judgment of the learned single Judge does not suffer from any infirmity. [85 B] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1579 of 1981. From the Judgment and Order dated 11.11.1980 of the Karnataka High Court in W.P. No. 805 of 1980. V.M. Tarkunde, S.K. Mehta, R.C. Sharma, M.N. Shroff, K.R. Nambiar, P.H. Parekh, Ms. A. Subhashini and Mrs. Arundhati Jain for the Appellant. Virender Singh, S/o.

The plaintiff, a partnership firm, was carrying on business in the name and style of M/s. S.K. Jain & Co., a firm, which was registered under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932. The firm was assessed to tax by the Income Tax Officer, who assessed it to income-tax for the assessment year 1964-65. The assessee filed an appeal before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the same was dismissed on the ground that the valuation put by the plaintiff was arbitrary and unreasonable. On further appeal the High Court held that in view of the provisions contained in Section 7(iv)(f) of the Court Fees Act, it was not open to the trial court to examine the correctness of the valuation made by the appellant. The High Court also held that the plaintiff respondent had failed to prove that the suit was not maintainable and dismissed the appeal. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 Section 7 of the Act provides for determination of the value of the assets of a firm and where the valuation is so fixed as to make it reasonable and fair on such valuation. [675 H] 2.1 The High Courts in India have taken a different view that when a plaintiff is required to place the valuation on his claim he must state a valuation which need only be approximately correct but qualified it by saying that, "it must not be arbitrary or manifestly inadequate" [682 A] 1.2 In the instant case, the plaintiff-respondent did not produce any evidence in support of his claim and therefore, the trial Court was right in rejecting the valuation declared by the petitioner. [650 D] 2:1 The learned counsel for the appellant submitted that the High Courts have taken into consideration the statement in the plaint that the value put by him on the plaint was arbitrary or unreasonable. In any event, the High court has not considered the statement of the plaintiff in the suit and has not given a correct valuation of the claim at the inception of the suit. [663 H] 3:2 The learned Counsel for the respondent submitted that when the valuation was so fixed by the trial judge as to enable the Court to determine the value, it should have been done on the basis of the statement made in the application filed by the defendant before the High Curt and not on the facts of the case. [664 D] 3.3 The learned Single Judge has rightly held that when an issue was framed by the court, the court could examine the same and if it is found that the claim was not tenable, it shall pass an appropriate order under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. [666 F] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1579 of 1989. From the Judgment and Order dated 4.2.1989 of the Allahabad High Court in Second Appeal No 974 of 1987. S K Srivastava, for the Appellant. V.S. Desai, R.K Jain, A.K Gupta, P.H. Parekh, Ms. Rani Chhabra, M.N. Shroff, Ms Neeta Goel and Ms. A. Subhashini for the Respondent. The Judgment of the court was delivered by VENKATARAMIAH, J. This appeal is directed against the judgment dated April 4, 1989 passed by the HighCourt of Allahabad in Second Appeals No. 974/1987 and 1088/87. The appellant is a partnership Firm. The plaintiff respondent filed an application before the trial Judge for permission to amend the plaint under Order 7 Rule 11 CPC. The learned trial Judge allowed that application on the following grounds: (1) The valuation put up by the applicant was not in accordance with law; (2) the valuation of suit was arbitrary, unreasonable and manifestly inadequate; (3) the plaintiff has failed to show that the plaint is not maintainable; (4) the court fee paid was not adequate. [665 D] JUDGMENT OF THE HIGH COURT: (Per Krishna Iyer J.) 1. The appeal is allowed.

The notification dated 1st April, 1981 exempted the industries specified in the Schedule to the Notification from the operation of the exemption under section 12(1)(i) of the Act. The exemption was granted by the State Government on the basis of the recommendations made by the Industrial Advisory Committee and subject to certain conditions. The industrial units were registered as small scale industries with the Central Government. The notification dated 31st March, 1981 issued by the Director of Industries, Madhya Pradesh, was published in the Gazette on 1st May, 1981. The said notification provided that the exemption granted under section 11(1) of that Act would be subject to the conditions specified therein. The State Government issued a notification on 30th June, 1982 exempting the industries from the provisions of the said section 12 and also exempted the industrial units from the applicability of the notification. On or about 1st July, 1983, the Industries Department issued an exemption certificate in respect of the industries mentioned by it. The appellant filed its return for the period 1st March 1981 to 31st December, 1983. The respondent filed a return on 30-6-1983 declaring that the said exemption was not available to the industrial unit. On 29th June 1983, a notification was issued under section 10(1), which provided that if the exemption was to be granted in respect only of the industry mentioned by the appellant, a special provision in the shape of section 22 D was added in the notification and the procedure for grant of exemption was also prescribed. The respondents filed an application before the Industrial Tribunal on 30.6.1983 claiming exemption under the said notification. The Industrial Tribunal held that the notification dated 30th April, 1982 exempted the units mentioned by them from the purview of the Notification and that the appellant was entitled to the benefit of deferment of tax. On appeal, the High Court set aside the order of the Tribunal on the ground that the industrial undertaking had not provided for an exemption under Section 12(2) of Act. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The notifications issued by Government under section 2 and 3 are in conformity with the provisions contained in the Notification dated 30-4-1981. [505 G] 2.1 The notification issued under sub-section (1) was not a notification issued by an authority other than the Industrial tribunal or the State government. It is only a notification which can be construed as a notification and it cannot be read as a declaration of exemption granted to the industries in question. [506 H] 2:2 In the instant case, the industrial industry had set up the industry after the explicit instructions given by 12.1.1983. The Notification dated 1-4.1981 was issued by a notification under section 3(3) of this Act and it is clear that the benefit conferred on the industries covered by the said Notification was not applicable to the appellant. [504 G] 3:2 It is true that the Industrial Court has held that, in view of the express language of the notifications issued under Section 2 and the notification issued thereunder, the exemption is available to a particular industry only. But if the notification is read as it does not provide for an exempting notification, there is no scope for the assessee to invoke the doctrine of promissory estoppel. [405 H] 3.3 The notification was published on 30/4-1982 and the appellant had setup the industries after the specific instructions given in the said notifications. The question whether the exemption conferred by the Notification was available to it or not is a matter for the State legislature to decide. [406 G] 4:3 It is clear from the language of section 12 that the Government has to be satisfied that the industry covered by it is exempted under section12(2). [407 H] 5:1 The exemption granted by notification dated 29-6 -1982 was not in conformity to the provisions made in the Notifications issued under sections 2 and 4.

The petitioners were appointed to the post of Additional District and Sessions Judges on the basis of selection by the High Court. The appointment was made in consultation with the High Courts as enjoined by Rule 7(a) of the said rules. The appointments were made by promotion on the recommendation of the High court. The petitioners were promoted to the posts of Additional district and Sessions Judge on the recommendations of the Delhi Judicial Service. On the basis that the appointments were to be made in accordance with the provisions of Rule 7, the Government issued a notification dated December 16, 1966 under which the appointment of the petitioners was made by direct recruitment. The said notification provided for a quota of 1/3rd for direct recruits and promotees. The appellants who were appointed as Additional District & Sessions Judges were confirmed on the post in accordance With rule 8(2) of Delhi Judicial Services Rules, 1967. On December 16. 1966 the Government passed an order under Rule 7 (a) declaring that the appointment was to be by promotion from amongst the members of Delhi Higher Judicial Service and the promotees were appointed on the principle of seniority-cum-fitness. The High Court held that the petitioners were not appointed as Assistant District & Session Judges on their own merit cum seniority basis so as to entitle them to be confirmed in the post. On appeal, the Supreme Court reversed the judgment of the learned Single Judge and held that Rule 7 was ultra vires the Constitution. In this case, the appellants challenged the validity of the order passed by the Government under Rule 8(1) on the ground that it was not a rule which required a minimum of 10 years judicial service to be eligible for appointment. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The power conferred by Rule 8 is an exception to the rule and the power conferred on the Administrator under Rule 16(1)(b) is subject to the condition that the said power can be exercised only in consultation and with the District Judge as enjoined in Rule 7. [505D] 2. The proviso to Rule 7 provides for a minimum period of 10 year judicial service, which means that the appointing authority may appoint any person who is appointed on probation or otherwise to a temporary post in the service. The words "if he is appointed" are not defined and it cannot be said that the expression "if the appointment is made" has been used in Rule 16. [506F] 3. The word "is appointed" in Rule 8 must mean only an appointment by promotion or on the principles of senioritycum-merit. [504D] 4. The expression "in consultation with District Judge" in the proviso to rule 7(b) means that all appointments made by way of promotion from among the members, of Delhi High Court, shall be made on merit cumseniority basis so that persons found not fit for promotion are ignored as in the case of Shri C.D. Summary: [506B] 5. The provisions of sub-rule (2) and rule 8 are mandatory in nature and do not require a minimum service to qualify for appointment by direct recruits. [500F] 6. Rule 7 is an instance of a rule made under Article 309 of the Constitution which requires that the power to make rules conferred on Administrator by Rule 16 is subject only to consultation with State Government as enjoined under Rule 9(2). The proviso does not require that the Administrator must be appointed by promotion. [525F] 7. The provision in sub-rules (1) and (2), therefore, cannot be read into the said rule. [511D] 8. The rules framed under Article 234 of the constitution do not provide for a mandatory requirement of appointment by way either of direct recruitment or by promotion to the service and the proviso does so only provides that the Government may appoint such persons as it considers fit to fill in the vacancies which are required to be filled in by promotion, but the said provision is subject also to the conditions prescribed under Rule 10. [54E] 9.

The appellant, Debi Parshad, was a member of the family of Debi Paridies. The Income tax Officer assessed his income as income from business in the hands of DebiParshad and computed the income of the said business at Rs. 1,000 per annum. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the income derived by the assessee from the business of Calcutta Flour Mills was not liable to be taxed under section 28(1) of the Income tax Act, 1922. He also held that Debi Parhad had submitted the returns and the income in the name of Debi parshad for the assessment year 1964-65. The Commissioner of Income tax, however, allowed the appeal filed by the appellant. The Tribunal held that there was no evidence to show that the business was carried on by the Calcutta Flour Mill and that the Income Tax Officer had not assessed the income as a result of the assessment. The High Court held that in view of the finding of the Appellate Assistant commissioner that the assessee was liable to pay tax under section 27(1), the order of the Tribunal was correct. The appellant filed an appeal against the said decision before this Court. HELD: (i) Section 28(2)(c) of Income Tax Act, 1961 provides that where the income tax Officer is a member or a member, he shall be assessed to tax as income of an association of persons, of which on the finding ,of the Income-tax Officer, Calcutta, was not a member. [675 H] (ii) The Appellate Tribunal has jurisdiction to make the impugned direction. The power of the Commissioner under section 29(2) is not in any way affected by the finding that the said income is liable to tax. [775 B] (iii) Section 27(3)(c), as it stood at the relevant time, provided that where an assessment was made on a Hindu undivided family, the IncomeTax Officer shall assess the income from such family. The income in question was assessed by the Incometax Officer as income under section 23 of the Indian Income Tax and the Appellate Tribunal had jurisdiction to direct the Income. tax officer to make an assessment. [750 C] (iv) Section 29(3) of The Income Tax, Act, 1962 provides that if the income-tax officer is satisfied that any person has failed to pay the tax due under section 26 or section 27A, he may, by order in writing, direct that the whole or any part of the income or profits of such person shall be liable to assessment. Section 29 (3) provides that no order for the recovery of any sum from an association or persons shall be made unless the Income -tax Officer is satisfied on the basis of the evidence adduced before him that the tax payable by the association or the persons is not due under this Act. [751 H] The High Courts in revision have jurisdiction to pass orders under section 30(2).

The appellant was the owner of a house situated in the city of Madras. He had two sons, namely, his wife and one daughter. The respondent filed a suit for partition against the appellant on the Original Side of the Madras High Court. The appellant claimed that he should be assessed to court fees under section 7(iv)(b) of the Act. The trial court held that the plaintiff was entitled to get the value of the relief sought by him for the purpose of jurisdiction and accordingly, decreed the suit. On appeal the District Judge confirmed the decree passed by the trial court. In second appeal the High Court reversed the judgment of the first appellate court and dismissed the suit with costs. The High Court held that in view of section 7 (iv)(a) of Act, the plaintiff could not be assessed for the purposes of court fees. On further appeal to this Court, HELD: 1.1 Section 7(v) of The Suits Valuation Act provides that the value for the payment of court fee shall be Rs. 100 and that the court fee payable in respect of the suit shall be at the rate of Rs. 200 per month or part thereof. [636 C] 1.2 In view of the provisions of section 8 of the Suits Valuation (Amendment) Act, 1983, the value fixed for the relief claimed by the plaintiff for the determination of the value should be taken as the valuation for the sum of Rs, 100 and not as the value as per the valuation made by him. [736 D] 1:3 The High court was in error in holding that the valuation of the claim for partition was Rs. 2,000 and not Rs. 300. [700 C] 2.1 The plaintiff could be assessed only for the amount of court-fee payable on the plaint as well as memorandum of appeal. [750 D] 2:2 In the instant case, the appellant had filed a petition under section 8(iv) of that Act for the valuation and the valuation was Rs, 2,500. It is not in dispute that the suit was valued at Rs. 1,000. The plaintiff claimed that the said valuation should be fixed as the market value of his claim for the period from April 1, 1983 to March 31, 1984. [800 D] 3:3 In view thereof, the High court erred in holding otherwise. [836 G] 2] 2nd appeal was not maintainable and the High Curt was in errors of law apparent on the face of the record. The respondent 1 and 2 filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the sanction of the NDMC to construct a pedestrian walk way. The respondent 1, who was the owner of a portion of a building, constructed a road on the ground floor of the building. The construction was completed by the respondent 1 on 15th April, 1979. On the expiry of the period of two years from the date of sanction, the respondent 2 and 3 filed a suit in the Court of the Civil Judge, Delhi for a declaration that they were entitled to construct the pedestrian road on their respective floors. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the construction was not at the risk of the respondent1 and 2 and that the building plans submitted by them were not in conformity with the Bye laws 16.4.8 or 16.04.8, as interpreted by the NDMC and the failure to comply with the requirements of the bye laws and the provisions of the Byelaws 16.5.8 and 16. 4.9.1. The High Court held that the respondent was entitled to raise a construction on the floor of a road which was not in accordance with the bye law 16.2.8. The appellant filed an appeal against the judgment of the High court before this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The provisions of Bye laws 17.4 and 16(3) are mandatory in character and they do not violate any of the fundamental rights of the appellants under Article 19(1)(g). [557 D] 1.2 The respondent was bound to construct such a road as he had constructed on his property. He could not have raised, even if he had made a construction thereon. [558 F] 1:3. The provisions in Bye laws 18.4 are mandatory and they cannot be read in conformity therewith. [506 G] 1a. The appellants were entitled under the byelaw 16.1 to construct any road on any part of the property. They could not, therefore, raise a question of construction on their own without complying with the provisions contained in Bye law 16(1). [506 H] 1b. The provision for the construction of a pedestririan walkway is mandatory and it cannot be said that the appellants were prevented from constructing such a way. [504 G] 2.1 There was no violation of the provisions in the Byelaw 16(2) or 16(4). [504 D] 2:2. The contention of the appellant that the respondents had not raised any objection to the plans submitted to the NDMC, is without substance. The Municipal Corporation of Delhi has not filed a written undertaking before the High Courts to the effect that they would construct such an approach as they were in conformity to the Bye law16.
