The appellant was a Salt Works. The Salt Works were manufacturing salt works in the area of Bombay and were supplying salt to the workers. On July 12, 1949, the Salt Works entered into an agreement with the Government of India for the supply of salt to them. The salt works were to be carried on by the Salt Department. The appellant was required to construct a building for the purpose of carrying on the salt work. The materials used in the construction of the salt works included salt works and the salt Works were to carry out the necessary repairs. On August 12, 1950, the salt was supplied to the appellant. On September 9, 1951, the appellant filed an application before the Assistant Salt Commissioner, Bombay, for permission to construct the salt-works. The Assistant Salt commissioner rejected that application on the ground that the salt is not a factory within the meaning of the word "factory" in the Act. On appeal by the appellant, the appellate authority held that the Salt works were not covered by the definition of the term 'factory' and accordingly allowed the application. In further appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the expression " factory " in the context of the Act means a factory as defined in the Factories Act and that the appellant was entitled to the benefit of the provisions of the said Act. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The definition of 'factory" under the Act is wide enough to include any premises including the salt, and it includes the saltworks within the definition clause. [675 H] 2. The expression "factory " in Section 2(h) means a place where the affairs of the Salt are carried on. [775 G] 3. The word " factory" in Section 3(1)(i) is wide and covers not only the premises but also any other premises including salt works. [750 H] 4. The words "factory ", "factory", "a mine" and "any other premises" are wide enough and cover all the premises except the precincts thereof. [751 G] 5. The use of the expression ' factory " is not of any significance for our purpose. It is only a factory which is meant to be used by the person who undertakes the work. [751 H] 6. The term "factory ". in Section 4(2) does not include any other factory as mentioned in that section. [752 G] 7. The question whether the salt should be treated as an industry or not, has to be decided on the basis of the evidence adduced by the parties and not on the assumption that the said evidence is relevant for our purposes. [754 H] 8. The decision of the High Court in this case does not call for any interference. [764 G] 9. The High Court was right in holding that the words " factory ". were wide enough. [758 C] 10. The construction of a building or structure is not an industry within the Act and it cannot be said that the word 'factory " should be construed as including the premises for the purposes mentioned in the definition clauses. [759 H] 11. The language of Section 4 (2) is clear enough to show that the term " factory ", in relation to which the expression is used, includes any other place where it is not necessary to do so. [761 G] 12. The contention that the use of a particular word in the said section should be taken as an indication that the same words are used in another section cannot be accepted. The respondent was appointed as a Tailoring Instructor in the Department of Technical Education, on deputation from other Departments. He was confirmed in that post by an order dated November 28, 1949, issued by the Director of Technical education, which was subsequently modified to the effect that he would be absorbed permanently in the Engineering Department of the Government of Mysore. The respondent was promoted as a Senior Tailoring Assistant in the scale of pay of Rs. 260-400 and was confirmed on the post of Assistant Engineer in the said scale. On November 28. 1950, he was appointed in the post carrying the same scale of Pay as that of a Junior Tailor. He joined service on April 1, 1951, and was absorbed permanently with effect from November 28., 1949. The post of Senior Tailor was redesignated as Assistant Engineer. On December 12, 1949 he was confirmed as a Junior Matoring Instructor. On January 29, 1950, the respondent was absorbed in the Technical Education Department. He filed an application before the Tribunal for a direction that his absorption should be made to the Engineering department and that he should be given the revised pay scales applicable to the post held by him on deputation. The Tribunal dismissed the application holding that the respondent had no legal right to be absorbed in that Department. On appeal, the High Court held that the order of the Tribunal was erroneous and directed the appellant to absorb the respondent in the service of the Engineering Departments. In further appeal to this Court, it was contended by the appellant that the Tribunal had erred in holding that there was a break in his service for the period from November 1, 1949 to December 12 1955. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The order of dismissal passed against the respondent did not suffer from any infirmity and the High court was right in holding otherwise. [557 F] (2) The Tribunal had rightly held that there is no justification to depart from the principle of policy in the case of the respondent. [506 G] (3) The respondent having been absorbed permanently, he should have been given the pay scales admissible to him on the basis of his absorption in the department. [504 D] (4) The High Court was right. [657 H] (5) The appellant had no locus standi to file an appeal against the order passed by the Tribunal. The order passed against him was erroneous. [UDD] (6) The principle of law laid down in the cases referred to above, is applicable only to a case where there is a break and not to a period prior to the date on which a person is absorbed permanently. [457 H; 506 A] (7) The appointment of a Tailor in the same Department was made by an officer who was appointed temporarily as a junior Tailoring Supervisor in the pay scale of Rs 260- 400. The appointment was not made to a post carrying a higher scale of promotion but to a higher post. [357 H, 506 A B] (8) The decision of the High Courts in the above cases is correct and does not call for any interference by this Court. The appellant, a foreigner, filed an application for guardianship of his child before the court of competent jurisdiction under Section 7 of the Act. The respondent, a foreign national, filed a petition for guardianship before the High Court of Delhi. The High Court held that the appellant was not a foreigner and that he had no right to be given in adoption by the foreigner. The appellant filed an appeal against the order of the High court. The learned Single Judge of the Delhi High Court allowed the writ petition and directed the respondent to take the child in adoption, if he is willing to do so. The Division Bench held that since the appellant had not taken a child in the adoptive family, it was not open to the appellant to be treated as a foreigner. In appeal by special leave, the appellant contended that the High Courts should have considered whether the principles and norms laid down by us in this judgment were applicable to the case of the appellant. The question for consideration before the Division Bench was whether the appellant could be treated to be a foreigner within the meaning of Section 2(a) of the Foreigner's Act, as amended by the [Foreigners (Amendment) Act, 1976]. The High court held that in view of the provisions contained in Section 2 of the Indian Foreigner Act, the respondent was not entitled to get the child registered under the said Act. In this appeal, it is contended on behalf of the appellants that the provisions of the said section are mandatory and they should be complied with by the recognised social or child welfare agency for taking a child into adoption. The contention of the learned counsel for the appellant is that the respondent had not adopted the child as required under Section 2 (a) and therefore, the High courts should have taken into consideration the provisions relating to the said provision in order to decide whether the principle and norms as laid down in this case are applicable to a foreigner who has taken a Child in adoption. In support of his contention, the learned senior counsel for respondent relied upon the decision of this Court in [Shalini Devi vs Union of India & Ors.] , referred to and relied upon by the High Curt. The said decision was rendered on the basis that the child should be treated at par with a foreigner as defined under Section 3(1) of Foreigner's Act, if the biological parents are known. In the present case, the appellants had taken a plea that the said provisions were not applicable to them. The appellants also relied upon a decision of the Bombay High Court in the case [Silver Jubilee vs Union Of India & Anr.] , wherein it was held that when the child is not known as a citizen, it should be made available to him by the recognized social or the child welfare Agency processing the application for custody and from the child study report, they would normally have the child' study report. The decision of Bombay High court in the said case was affirmed by this Court. In view of this decision, the question for determination before us is whether the provisions made in Section 3 are mandatory or not. [Section 3(2)] of the Citizenship Act provides that a person shall be deemed to have been born in an Indian State if he has not taken any child in such State and if he does not have a child. The expression 'a foreigner' is defined under the Foreigners Act, which means a foreigner or a foreign parents who have taken a juvenile in adoption as defined in Section 5 of the Foreigners Act.

The Company was an employee of the appellant-Company. The Company had a total income of Rs. 1,50,000 from all sources including income tax and supertax. The Tribunal held that the Company was entitled to deduction of Rs 50,000 under section 37(1) of the Income tax Act. The High Court on appeal by the employer held that as the Company had not paid any amount towards bonus for the year 1964 66, there must be a provision in the Act for payment of bonus at 20% for the accounting year 1965 66. It was contended before this Court that the Tribunal was wrong in rejecting the claim of the Company for deduction of the available surplus and that the High Court erred in holding that the amount of Rs 1,25,000 paid by the Company to induce the workmen to retire prematurely was an item of expenditure incurred by the company on the ground that the said amount had not been accepted by the Income Tax Officer. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The Tribunal was right in rejecting this claim of deduction of any amount which was allowable under section 36(1)(c) of Income tax. [675 H] (2) The payment of compensation to induce a workmen to retirement prematurely was not an item for the next year, namely, 1965 66 and it is clear that the further direction in the Award regarding set on cannot be accepted. [750 A] (4) The amount of compensation paid to induce workmen to retiring prematurely was a sum of Rs 5,00,000 and not the amount which the Company would have to pay by way of bonus to make up the 14.02% for each year. [751 B] (5) The claim made by the Unions that after distribution of bonus, the balance amount that the company will have to bear in the sum of 25% was an expenditure allowable under Section 37(2)(c). [750 D] (6) The Company was not entitled to any deduction of this amount. [753 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1566 of 1967. The appellant was a member of the Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal, Madras. He was appointed as a Member of the Board of Revenue by the Government of Tamil Nadu in 1969. The appellant was promoted as Deputy Commissioner of Commercial Taxes on August 31, 1970 and posted as Member of that Board. On November 29, 1974, he was promoted to the post of Member of Sales Tax Tribunal. On May 7, 1975, the Government passed an order under section 11(1) of the Tamil Nadu General Sales Tax Act, 1959 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') imposing a penalty on him for failure to pay the arrears of salary due to him. The order was confirmed by the Appellate Tribunal and the appellant was reinstated in service. On June 30, 1976, he filed an appeal before the Government which was dismissed. Thereafter, he made a representation to the Government on May 7. 1977. The Government rejected his representation. He then filed a writ petition in the High Court of Madras challenging the order of the Government rejecting his representation and also praying for quashing the order passed by the State Government. The learned Single Judge allowed the writ petition holding that the appellant had not been served with any notice or show cause notice before he was reverted to the service. The Division Bench held that the order dated June 30 1976, passed by a competent authority, could not be sustained and quashed. The High Court also held that in view of the fact that an enquiry was pending against the appellant, the order retiring him from service was illegal. The State Government filed an application for review before the High court which was allowed on May 9, 1977. On August 30, 1977, the appellant filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the order dismissing his representation dated May 7/22, 1976. The writ petition was dismissed by the learned Single judge on June 29, 1977 holding that there was no substance in the contention raised by the appellant that he had not received any notice before the order was passed. On July 30, 1978, the State filed an affidavit stating that the Government was satisfied with the explanation offered by the petitioner and that the said explanation was accepted. The appeal was allowed by the Division Bench on May 11, 1977 and the writ appeal was dismissed on June 30. 1977 holding: "We are of the view that the explanation given by the respondent in his representation is not satisfactory and we see no reason to interfere with the order under challenge." On August 31. 1978, a petition for review was filed before the Division bench which was also dismissed. The present appeal has been filed against the judgment of the learned single Judge.

The appellants were the owners of a private bus which was being run by the State Transport Undertaking. The scheme framed by the Corporation under section 68C was published in the official gazette on April 1, 1962 and approved by the Government of Andhra Pradesh. The schemes were published in two newspapers on May 5, 1962. The appellants filed their objections to the scheme before the Regional Transport Authority which rejected them. On appeal by the appellants the State Government confirmed the scheme and directed that the scheme be revised. The appeals filed by the respondents were dismissed by the appellate authority. Thereafter the appellants moved the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution for a writ quashing the order passed by the Regional transport Authority on August 10, 1963 and also for a direction to the State to implement the scheme. The High Court quashed the order of the Regional authority on the ground that it was not in conformity with section 68F(1) but was in violation of section 68D(3). Allowing the appeals, HELD: 1. The Scheme framed by an authority under section68C is a part of the scheme which provides for the revision of the schemes and the rules made thereunder are to have effect notwithstanding anything in Ch. No doubt, in a State where there is no Regional Transport Authorities at all [vide para. 2(i) of the affidavit filed on behalf of the appellants in the High Courts, but there is some other authority which functions as the Regional Regional Transport Officer for the purposes of the Art. The Regional Transport Office has not been shown to be an authority competent under section 69C of the Act to grant permits by reason of section68F(3) and the Rules made thereunder. [557 C] 2. The object of the Scheme is that it should be implemented in a manner consistent with the provisions of section 69D(1). It is not necessary for the purpose of this case to show that the schemes are vitiated by non compliance with section68B or 68C. [546 D] 3. The power conferred on the State under section 70C is not an authority which function as the State transport undertaking. [547 F] 4. The provisions of s. 68F do not apply to the schemes framed by a competent authority. It is only in respect of schemes published under section 66C that the State can make rules and make regulations consistent with section 69B. [548 G] 5. The State Transport Authority has no power to issue permits by virtue of section 70A. [549 F] 6. The question whether the scheme is vitiated by noncompliance with section 67F(2) or section 68E does not arise in this case. [556 H] 7. The rules made under s.68C are not inconsistent with the Act and the Regulations framed thereunder. The regulations framed under s, 68C do not affect the rights of the parties to the contract. [558 G] 8. The right conferred on a person by virtue or in pursuance of a statute is not affected by reason only of the fact that he was not allowed to ply his buses on the routes under the respective permits granted to him. [560 H] 9. The decision of this Court in State of Mysore vs. Mysore Transport Corporation, , referred to. 5. Section 68F does not apply in respect to the Scheme framed under section 67C. It only applies to schemes published by a Competent Authority and approved or modified by the competent authority and does not affect any rights of parties to contract. The conditions laid down in s. 69D are not consistent with s. 67F. [559 H] 10. The provision for revision of schemes is not inconsistent therewith. [561 G] 11. The Act provides for a complete machinery for the implementation of the provisions contained in Chapter IV and the scheme framed thereunder is not consistent therewith. The procedure laid down under section 73C is applicable to the cases where the scheme has been sanctioned by the Competent Authority. [562 H] 12.

The appellant, a dealer in the goods of the class specified in the certificate of registration issued by the Sales Tax Officer, was assessed to sales tax under section 5(2)(a)(ii) of the Act. The assessing authority held that the sales were for the purposes mentioned in the said certificate of the Sales-tax Officer and therefore, the appellant was not entitled to exemption from payment of sales tax. On appeal by the dealer, the appellate authority confirmed the order of the assessing authority. In further appeal to the High Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the provisions of section 5 (2) (a)(i) of Act were inconsistent with section 5 and the rules made thereunder and therefore the exemption given under the said section was not in respect of sales which were for purposes mentioned therein. The High Court held that there was no provision in the Act or in the rules framed thereunder requiring a dealer to produce a true declaration in writing by the purchasing dealer or by such responsible person as may be authorized in writing in this behalf by such dealer that the goods in question are specified in his certificate of Registration and therefore it was not necessary for him to furnish a declaration in respect thereof. The appellant, therefore, filed an appeal before the High court. The learned Single Judge held that section 5 of the Orissa Sales Tax Act, 1947 was inconsistent with the provisions contained in section 5 read with section 6 of the said Act and the Rules made thereunder. The Division Bench also held that by virtue of section 4(2) of that Act, the exemption granted under the aforesaid section was in respect to sales which are for purposes specified therein. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) Section 5(1)(ii), as it stood before its amendment by the Orissa Act No. 13 of 1976, did not contain any provision similar to section 5. [505 G] (2)(i)(a) The words "and" and "or" were used in the proviso to section 4 of the Central Sales Tax (Amendment) Act, 1976. Therefore, the said provisions were inconsistent only with section 4 and the rule made thereunder was inconsistent therewith. [606 H] (3) Section 6(2), as amended by the Amendment Act No, 13 of 1977, did make it clear that the exemption under the proviso was in relation to sales specified in clause (a) of sub-section (1). The said provision was inconsistent only if the said provision contained a similar provision. [650 D] (4) Section 4(3)(b) of Central Sales Act, 1956 is inconsistent with and not inconsistent with that provision. The proviso to sub section (2), therefore, did have no effect in relation thereto.

The appellant was a member of the Bihar Police Service. He was convicted by the Magistrate under Section 395 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one year and to pay a fine of Rs. 500/- in default to suffer rigorous imprisonment, on account of his failure to furnish security to the satisfaction of the Magistrate. The appellant filed an appeal before the Sessions Judge, who dismissed the same. On the basis of the conviction and sentence passed by the Sessions Court, the appellant was convicted under Section 396 of the Penal Code. He preferred an appeal to the High Court which was allowed by the impugned judgment. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The provisions of section 167(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code are mandatory in nature and they do not require any objection to a lawyer at the time when he is produced before the Magistrate or the Sessions Courts. [775 H] 2.1 Section 167(1) of Cr.P.C. provides that if the accused is not released on bail, he shall be released on his own bond unless the Court considers that there are reasonable grounds for believing that he has been guilty of an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life and that he will not commit any offence while on bail. [750 H] 3.1 The provisions contained in section 167 (2) do not apply to a case where the accused person is not produced before a Magistrate or is released on default bail under Section 167 (1). [776 B] 2:2 In the instant case, the prosecution was pending for more than six months and therefore, the State Government should provide him a lawyer. The High Court has rightly held that there was no such requirement in law.

The appellant was a tenant of the land in dispute. The landlord filed an application under section 29(2) of the Act for eviction of the tenant on the ground that he had failed to pay rent to the landlord within one year from the date of notice. The Rent Controller held that the tenancy was terminated by the landlord after the expiry of the period of one year and therefore the provisions of section 34(2 A) were not applicable to the case. On appeal, the High Court allowed the application holding that the tenant had failed in proving that he was a deemed tenant under section 34 (1) of Act. The appellant filed an appeal against the order of the High court before this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The provisions of sections 34(1) and 34(3) are not applicable in cases where notice has been given before the commencement of the Amending Act. [675 H] 2. Section 29(1)(2) is a declaration to the tenant that he has become deemed tenant by virtue of sub section (2A). The effect of sub sections (1), (2B) and (3) is that the provisions contained in sections 34 (4) and 35 are applicable to all cases where notices have been given. [775 H; 776 B] 3. Section 34(4) is an exception to section 34 which provides for a deemed tenancy by virtue. The proviso to sub section(2A) makes it clear that the period during which the notice has not been given shall be the date on which the tenancy has terminated and the landlord acquires a vested right to obtain possession of the lands. [750 H] 4. Section 35 is an enabling provision and provides for the termination of the tenancy. The effect is that in respect of the cases where the tenancy had not actually terminated before the coming into force of the Amendment Act, the provisions relating to the termination are applicable. [751 G] 5. In the instant case, the notice under section34(1), was given on the date when the tenancy stood terminated and therefore it is a deemed transfer by the tenant. The question whether the notice should be given or not does not arise in this case. [753 H] 6. Section 36 of the Transfer of Property Act provides that where the landlord has acquired a vested interest under section 35, he shall be entitled to obtain the possession of such land from the tenant within one month of the date he has made the application for eviction. The words "or the landlord" in sub section 2A are clear and unambiguous. [764 H] 7. Section 37 is an exemption provision and it provides that no court shall take any proceedings under this Act against a tenant except on the grounds mentioned therein. [771 G] 8. In view of the provisions in sections 35 and 36, the question whether notice should have been issued does not affect notices already given by the tenants. The language of section 37 is clear and it is not necessary to go into the question as to whether the tenant has acquired any vested interest in the land. [781 H] 9. Section 39(2)(b) provides that if the landlord fails to pay or tender rent within one calendar month from the commencement date, the court shall have power to take possession of any land which is not a deemed land under section 36. [791 G; F] 10. The provision in section 39(3), therefore, does not apply to the facts of the case and it cannot be said that the notice was given before or after the commencement. [80 H] 11. Section 40 provides for an appeal from the order passed by the Rent Controller under section 37. [81 G] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1320 of 1987. From the Judgment and Order dated 25.2.1987 of the Calcutta High Court in C.R.P. No.

The petitioners, who were the sons of Khadim Ali, filed a suit in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Delhi, against the respondents for recovery of possession of their houses. The respondents contended that they had been given a larger share in the house by the will and therefore the petitioners had become entitled to the properties mentioned in the notification. They also contended that the property was not evacuee property but was an evacuee property. The trial Court held that the properties were evacuee property and, therefore, the petitioners were entitled to claim possession of the houses. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decree of the trial Court and dismissed the suit. In this Court, on behalf of the appellants, it was contended that in view of the provisions contained in section 12 of the Act, the Custodian had no jurisdiction to declare the property as evacuee property, and therefore, there was no question of the petitioners being entitled to any relief under the Act. It was further contended that since the properties in dispute were not evacuee properties, the respondents could not be declared to be evacuee property because they were not acquired by the Custodian. HELD: (i) The provisions contained inss. 12 and 13 of the General Clauses Act are applicable to the facts of this case. Section 12 provides that "on the publication of a notification under sub section (1), the right, title and interest of any evacuee in the evacuee property specified in the order shall, on and from the beginning of the date on which the notification is so published, be extinguished and the evacuee Property shall vest absolutely in the Central Government free from all encumbrances. The provisions of section 12 are applicable only to the persons who were in possession of evacuee properties specified in a notification issued under sub sec. (1) of section 7. [775 H] (ii) Section 12 does not affect the petitioners' rights in the property which the petitioners have acquired under the, Act. Therefore, the provisions of this section do not affect their rights. The petitioners were not entitled to possession of any property as they had become evacuee properties. [750 A] (iii) The respondents could only be declared as evacuee properties if they were acquired by them under the notification issued unders. 7 and therefore there was a question of law involved in the case. [751 B] (iv) Section 13 does not apply to the fact that the petitioners are entitled to get possession of houses which the respondents had been allotted to them. The Custodian has no jurisdiction. It is true that the provisions relating to the rights of an evacuee in a evacuee property are applicable, but the provisions do not apply. [751 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 884 of 1972. From the Judgment and Order dated the 9th May, 1971 of the Delhi High Court in C.W.P. No. 1123 of 1970. S. K. Mehta, for the appellant. R.K. Garg, for respondent No. 1. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by RAY, J.-This appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated September 9, 1971 passed by the High court of Delhi in CMA No. 12 of 1971. The appellants are the sons and daughters of Khazan Ali who had been appointed as a direct recruit to the Indian Army on the basis of an advertisement issued under s. 7 of the Indian Armed Forces Act, 1950 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') and was allotted a larger number of houses by the Government of India in the Ministry of Home Affairs. The respondent No 1 is the brother of Khazim Ali who was appointed as direct recruit on the ground that he had become an evacuee. He filed a writ petition before the High Courl, Delhi praying for a declaration that the Act and the Rules made thereunder are applicable. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. Hence this appeal by special leave.

The assessee is a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The assessee was an employee of the assessee Company and was assessed to income tax in respect of its total income from the sale of shares of the company. On the basis of the assessment made by the Income Tax Officer, the assessee filed a return of his income for the assessment year 1955-56 declaring that the profits of the business were not taxable under section 10(2)(xv) of the Act. The Income Tax officer assessed the assessee to income-tax in respect to its total receipts from sale of the shares of company and also to the extent of Rs. 1,50,000/- as income from other sources. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax Officer. In further appeal to the Tribunal, it was contended that the amount paid by the appellant to the agent was not a part of the sale price and therefore the said amount was not liable to be included in the total income of the appellant. The Tribunal held that the assessee was entitled to deduction under section 11(2) of Income Tax Act, 1961. On further appeal by special leave, the High Court held that as the assessee had failed to make any payment towards the sale consideration and therefore it was not entitled to claim deduction under [section 10(1)(xv)] of the said Act. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The question whether the amount in dispute was a part or whole of the income of an assessee is not a mixed question of law and fact but one which is required to be decided by the Tribunal on the basis that the alleged payment was made by it in the character of an agency to conceal the real intent and purpose the commercial venture. [775 H] 2. The High Court was right in holding that the sum paid by it to the assessee for the sale was not part of its income but was a share of the profits which were chargeable under section 12(2). [776 G] 3.1 The question as to whether the payment was a mere part or a whole of its own income is a mixed one and therefore an amount paid towards the price of the goods sold cannot be included for the purpose of deduction under Section 10(l)(xv). [750 H] 3:2. In the instant case, the agreement between the assessee and the assessee did not make any profit out of it but only made some payments towards the purchase of shares. The amount paid to the appellant was not in excess of the reasonable return as contemplated by section 10 (1) of Act.

The appellant, a resident of Bombay, was assessed to income tax by the Income Tax Officer, on his total income of Rs. 1,10,000. The assessee claimed that he had accumulated profits during the year in which the loans were advanced to the assessee. The Income Tax officer rejected the claim and held that the accumulated profits could not be taken into account while determining the accumulated profit. On appeal by the Appellate Tribunal, the High Court of Madras held that there was no provision for payment of interest on the accumulated income as on March 31, 1958. In further appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the provisions of section 256(1) of the Income tax Act, 1961 were applicable to the case and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner had not taken into consideration the question whether the accumulated losses could take in current profits. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that there is no provision in section 256 (1) for payment or deduction of interest under section 256. [6A] 2. Section 256(2) of Income Tax Act, 1922 makes it clear that the expression "accumulated profits" in the said section must be read as a whole and not as a mere reference to the question of law which is referred by the assessee to the High court. The words "accusulated profits", in the context of section 257(2), mean "a sum of money payable on account of interest". [6B] 3. Section 254(1)(b) of Act, 1962 makes it abundantly clear that there must be a provision for paying interest on accumulated profits. [650D] 4. The expression "actually" in section 255(2)(b), as used in the Explanation to section 256, means "a person who is entitled to receive from any other person any income or part thereof." [6E] 5. Section 257(1A) of Finance Act, 1987 makes it amply clear that if there is a provision in the Income-tax Act for payment and deduction under section 80HH of the said Act, the assessee must be entitled to claim interest on such amount from any person other than the assessee in the event of his being found to have accumulated profits within the meaning of section 255. [643D] 6. The question whether there is provision for making a reference or not is a matter which is required to be considered by the High Courts and the High courts. [64E] 7. Section 255(1), as it stood prior to its amendment, makes it absolutely clear that where there is an express provision in any of the provisions referred to above, the Income -tax Officer must specify the questions of law arising out of the order of the Appellate Authority under section 254. The Explanation to [section 256] of the Act makes it further clear that a person who has accumulated profits can claim interest under Section 256. The proviso to section 255 provides that where any question arises as to whether the amount of accumulated profits is a sum of tax payable on the total income, the Appellate authority shall refer the said question to the Court and if the answer to the said questions is in the negative, the question must be considered as answered in favour of the assessee and against the Revenue. [65F] 8. The language of section 254(2A) makes it obligatory for the Incometax Officer to specify the matters of law referred to him by the Tribunal. The word "act" in this context means " a sum payable on behalf" in respect of any income, profits or gains chargeable under the head 'Capital Tax' and includes interest. [66F] 9.

The plaintiff, the predecessor of the defendants, filed a suit for partition and separate possession of the lands in question. The defendants claimed that they were tenants under the Raja of Burdwan, and that they had been cultivating the lands for a long time without any interruption from the Government. The trial court held that the defendants were trespassers and that the plaintiff was entitled to assessment of fair rent. On appeal, the District Judge confirmed the decree passed by the trial court. In second appeal, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court had erred in holding that the plaintiffs were not tenants under a Lakheraj grant and that as they were trespassers, they could be assessed only for fair rent and that there was no evidence to show that they claimed to hold under a right of occupancy. The High Court held that in view of the provisions contained in section 6 of the Estates Abolition Act, the question of adverse possession did not arise. It further held that as the defendants had been in possession of their lands for more than a long period of time without interruption from Government, they were entitled to claim assessment of the fair rent on the basis of the entry in the record of rights. The respondents contended that the suit was barred by limitation and that it was not open to the appellants to raise this plea at any stage of the proceedings. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The provisions contained under section 6 are mandatory in character and they do not create a right in favour of the plaintiffs. [557 D] 2.1 The High court was wrong in holding on facts that the possession of an individual was not referable to a right which had accrued by adverse possession for long over the statutory period. [506 G] 2(i) The provisions of section 6 were mandatory and they did not create any right in the plaintiffs to claim the assessment of their fair rent or to the assessment thereof. [657 D F] (ii) The High Courts have erred in law in holding otherwise. The question whether the defendants claimed to be tenants under an estate does not arise at all, because the provisions of sections 6 and 6 are directory in character. [756 G] (iii) The plaintiffs were trespassers on the lands. They had been dispossessed from their possession for a considerable period without any resistance from the government. [750 A] 2.(iv) The defendants could be said to have asserted that they held under a title not referable by adverse title, and therefore, they cannot be said that they claim to hold over under a person who was not a tenant. [751 G] 3.1 There is no evidence on record to show the relationship of the parties to the suit lands between the plaintiffs and the defendants. The plaintiffs had been able to establish their possession as tenants. They were trespassers. [753 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1552 of 1968. From the Judgment and Order dated the 9th July, 1967 of the Calcutta High Court in C.A. No. 1623 of 1966. S. K. Sinha and P. K Mukherjee for the Appellant. R. N. Sachthey, for the Respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Hegde, J. This appeal is directed against a judgment of the High court of Calcutta dated September 9, 1967 in Second Appeal No.. 1623/66. The appellants are the defendants in this case. They filed a civil suit for possession of lands under a lease deed dated March 31, 1931, and also for assessment of rent on that basis. The suit was decreed by the Trial Court. The first appellate court affirmed the decree of the trial Court. In Second Appeal, the High (Court) reversed the judgment of both the Courts below. The only question which arises in this appeal is whether the appellants are tenants under another person who had been inducted as a tenant under an owner of the land.

The appellant filed a suit for specific performance of an agreement to sell the agricultural land in question. The respondent filed a written statement and contended that the plaintiff was not an agriculturist and, therefore, he was not entitled to purchase the land. The trial Court held that the defendant was not a agriculturist and accordingly decreed the suit. On appeal, the Additional District Judge confirmed the judgment of the trial court. In second appeal, it was contended by the respondent that the trial Court had no jurisdiction to settle, decide or deal with the question as required under section 63 of the Tenancy Act. The High Court held in favour of the respondent and dismissed the appeal. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 Section 65 of the Bombay Tenancy Act, 1939 provides that where a suit is instituted for specific relief which is not specifically mentioned in the Tenancy law, then the provisions of the said Tenancy Act shall apply to such suit. [675 H] 1.2 The High court was wrong in holding that the provisions contained in section 63 are mandatory and they do not require any interference by this Court under Article 136 of the Constitution. [775 B] 1:3. Section 65 is a special provision which provides that if the question arises whether the plaintiff is an agriculturist he is barred from purchasing the land, the jurisdiction of the civil court to settle or decide such question has been excluded. The provisions contained therein are mandatory in nature and they cannot be treated as mandatory in character. [750 D] 1.:4. Section 64 is a general provision which confers power on the Mamlatdar to settle the dispute between the parties. It does not require that the Mamlatdar should refer the issue to the competent authority under the Tenancy Law. The Mamlatdar has no jurisdiction or power to decide, whether the suit is maintainable or not. [751 D] 2:1. Section 66 of the Act provides that when a suit in respect of any matter specified in the Schedule is instituted by an agriculturist for specific purpose and the defendant appears and shows sufficient cause for his absence on the date fixed for hearing the suit, the Court shall proceed to hear and decide the suit according to law. [753 D] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 15 of 1986. From the Judgment and Order dated 16.1.1986 of the Gujarat High Court in Special Civil Application No. 12 of 1985. V.M. Tarkunde, S.K. Mehta, K.L. Tayal, Ms. A. Subhashini, M.S. Agarwal, R.N. Singh, Mrs. Shobha Dikshit, M/s. P.V. Desai and M.R. Shah for the Appellant. Viney Kumar, S K Jain, M K Jain and M K Gupta for the Respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by B.C. RAY, J. This appeal is directed against the judgment dated 16th January 1986 passed by the Gujarat State Appellate Tribunal in Special Appeal No 12 of 1986 whereby the High Court has dismissed the appellant's appeal. The appellant is a registered dealer under the provisions ofs. 64 of the [Bombay Tenancy Act] and the respondent is an agricultural land governed by the provisions thereof. The question involved in this appeal is whether the provisions made in the Bombay Land Revenue Code, 1879 (hereinafter referred to as the 'Act') are mandatory or directory in character? The appellant was a registered trader. He filed a return of his income for the assessment year 1964-65 and claimed that he was an agriculturist. The claim was rejected by the Assistant Collector on the ground that the respondent had not produced any evidence to show that he is an agriculturists. The Assistant Collector held that there was no evidence to prove that the appellant was an agricultural labourer. He also held that in view of the provisions under the Act, the Mamlatdar has jurisdiction to decide whether the appellant is an Agricultural Land Tribunal and if so, whether he is a person who is an agriculture labourer.

The assessee, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was carrying on business of manufacturing and selling articles in the State of Bombay. The assessee was assessed to income tax by an order dated April 1, 1948, under section 10(2) of the Income Tax Act, 1922. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Tribunal. In further appeal to this Court, it was contended that the two undertakings were not formed out of the earlier business and, therefore, the assessee was not entitled to exemption under section 15C. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in answering the two questions in the negative and against the assessee. [775 H] 2. The two undertakings are distinct and separate units and they are distinct. The fact that an assessee by reconstruction of the business is carrying on a particular business does not make him a new and separate undertaking. The only change which is necessary to be made in the section is that the new industrial undertaking is being carried on by the assessee on his own as a viable unit. [750 H] 3. The question whether an assessee has become a new industrial unit or not, is a question of fact and it cannot be said that the High Court is right in answer to the two question in the affirmative. [751 G] 4. The expression "new industrial undertaking" in section 15 C(2)(i) means the new undertaking which may be existing on the date of its commencement. [751 H] 5. The words "new and separate" used in section 10C(2), 'new industrial unit' used in clause (ii) of sub section (3) of section 15D are not conclusive to decide whether the new business is being run by the new company on account of which exemption under [section 15C] could be claimed. The word "new" used therein does not mean that the old and separate undertakings must be formed out from the earlier undertaking. [761 H; 76 A] 6. The position in law as it stood prior to the amendment of section 10 C(3) was that the assessee had become a newly existing industrial unit on account, of which he was carrying business to set up a new new industrial concern on account whereof exemption under clause (i) of subsection (3), and after the said amendment, the new undertakings were being carried out on account thereof. [771 H-775 B] 7. The language employed in section 5C(3)(ii) is clear and unambiguous to show that the newly existing business was being run on account by the old company on its own as an independent industrial undertaking. It cannot be disputed that the said two undertakings form part of the new commercial undertaking. Therefore, the question whether the old business is a new one or not does not arise in this case. [781 H, 771 A] 8. The contention that the words " new and distinct" used by the Legislature in section 11(2C) were conclusive to show the intention of the legislature was also without substance. [791 D] 9. The object of the amendment is clear from the language employed therein. The intention of Parliament was not to include the new industry as a new unit. The said two activities are distinct, separate and distinct. [802 G] 10. The provisions of section 11C(4) were intended to be applicable only in respect of the old industrial undertaking which is being wound up by the Government. [813 H; 83 A] 11. The effect of the said provision was that if an assessee had been carrying on any new business on his behalf on the basis of which the exemption under sub section(1) could not be claimed, he would be entitled to claim exemption under that sub section. [83 B] 12.

The inam lands were granted to the temple for the performance of services connected therewith. The inamdar was granted a lease of the land under section 44 B(2)(a) and the inamdars were tenants in respect of the lands under the lease. On the expiry of the period of the lease, the inamdar had resumed the inam lands. The Government issued a notification under section 4 of the Madras Estates Land Act (Madras Act III of 1908), declaring that the inam land was liable to be resumed under section 43 B(1) of the said Act. The appellants filed an application for resumption of the inam. The Assistant Settlement Officer, who had jurisdiction over the area in which the inam was granted, held that the lands were resumable under section 45 B (2)(b). On appeal, the District Collector confirmed the order of the Assistant Settlement Commissioner and dismissed the application. In second appeal to the High Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the grant of a permanent lease in respect to the inam did not amount to resumption of any land within the meaning of section 44B(2) (a). Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The grant of an estate by the Government under section 46 B is not a transfer of the Inam lands and the grant was not a sale or mortgage of it. [675 H] 2. Section 44 B (1) is attracted only when the holder of the grant has made an exchange, gift, sale or lease of any inam land for a term exceeding five years. The question whether an alienee from the inam is entitled to resume the lands in accordance with section 45B(1), does not arise for decision in this case. [775 H; 776 B] 3. Section 45 B(l) is applicable only when there is an exchange of land between the inam and the Government. The provisions of section 45-B are attracted only where the holder has made a surrender of the estate or the lands have been resumed by the inam authority. [750 D] 4. The right to resume land under Section 44B is not an alienation of any property within the purview of section 43B. It is only when an alienees from the grant are in enjoyment of the same, that the transfer of a patta made under section 47 B(3) is not prohibited. [751 D] 5. The mere fact that an alienor from the Inamdar has made surrender of his inam does not by itself create any right to resumption. [751 H; 75 A] 6. Section 46-B applies only when a person who has made such an surrender is in enjoyment thereof. [764 G] 7. The land was resumed under the provisions of the Act and the lands had been resumed under sections 44 B, 44 C and 47 B. [800 D] 8. The fact that the land was not alienated by the grantees does not make the grant a sale of it for a period exceeding five year. [875 H, H; 800 A] 9. Section 48-B is attracted when there are no transfers of any kind made under the said section. [900 B] 10. The lands were resumed under s. 47 B (3) and they were resuming the melwaram rights in the inam villages. [975 G] 11. The transfer of an inam land by the State Government to the grantee was not prohibited under section 48-A(1). [800 H; 876 A] 12. Section 49 is attracted where there is a surrender by the holder and the land has been resumed. [100 B] 13. The Act does not apply to the lands which were resold by the grantee. [1000 C] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 15 of 1971. From the Judgment and Order dated the 10th May, 1970 of the Bombay High Court in Writ Petition No. 11 of 1970. S. T.

The appellant Corporation was assessed to tax on the gross annual letting value of buildings and lands in the State of Madhya Pradesh. The appellant Corporation filed a return showing the total income of Rs. 1,10,000 for the assessment year 1952-53. The respondent filed a statement showing the net annual letting values of buildings as well as the gross rent assessed thereon. On the basis of the said statement, the respondent claimed that the tax was leviable on the basis that the gross yearly letting value was saved by sec. 2(c) and that the appellant Corporation had not adopted the said assessment list for the two assessment years 1953 54 and 1954 55. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim of the respondent and assessed the tax at 7% of the gross return. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax officer. On further appeal, a learned single Judge of the High Court held that the respondent was entitled to demand the tax on his gross annual tenancy under sec. 73(1) of the Act and accordingly, he directed the appellant to pay the tax assessed by the respondent. The said order was confirmed in appeal by the Division Bench of the Bombay High Court. On a certificate granted by the High court, the appellant has come up before us. 3. Section 73 of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') provides that the assessment list prepared for the year 1952 53 should be adopted conclusive evidence of the annual letting and the amount of tax assessed thereon and entitled the Corporation to collect the tax. The relevant portion of section 73(2) is as follows: "73. Assessment list prepared under this Act.- (1) If the assessing authority is satisfied that any person has, in his possession or control, made any assessment or reassessment on the net and not otherwise provided for by the 1954 Act it may, after giving him a reasonable opportunity of being heard, assess or reassess such person accordingly: Provided that no order shall be passed under this section unless the person concerned has been given an opportunity of making representation. (2) The assessing authority shall give to every person who is liable to pay tax under this Chapter a notice in writing stating the grounds on which it proposes to impose any tax and requiring him to furnish within such period as may be specified in the notice, not being less than thirty days from the date of service of the notice. (3) If any person fails to comply with an order made under sub-section (1), he shall be liable to a penalty which may extend to one thousand rupees and if the person fails so to pay within the period specified in that order, he shall also be liable for penalty which shall not be less than one hundred rupees. (4) If, on the other hand, any person is required to furnish any return under sub section (1)- (a) he shall, after making such enquiry as may appear to him necessary, submit a report in respect of the same to the assessing officer; and (b) if the assessing Officer is satisfied, after hearing the person, that the return submitted by him was not correct or incomplete, he may assess or re-assess the tax payable by the person. (5) If on the evidence adduced before the assessing or reassessed or reassessing the tax under sub sections (1)(b), the assessing and reassessed, the assessing, authority shall serve on the person liable to make payment of tax, interest at such rate as may from time to time be fixed by the Government, a notice containing all material statements and particulars referred to in section 73. (6) If upon the evidence produced before the officer or any other person having special knowledge of the facts which are not admitted, the authority shall record its reasons for doing so, he has to give an opportunity to the person to be heard.

The assessee Company was carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling chemicals and raw materials. The assessee company sold the chemicals and other raw materials to the buyers for a price which, with an under taking to discharge liabilities, formed the consideration for sale of chemicals and the raw materials were sold as a going concern. The sales were made by the assessee Company in the course of its business and were treated as sales in the ordinary way of business. The Sales Tax Officer held that the sales were not liable to tax. On appeal, the Appellate Tribunal confirmed the order of the Income Tax Officer. In further appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the Department that the sale was not a sale in the normal course of trade and that the assessee was not carrying on any trading activity. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the transactions were sales in which the assessee had no direct interest or control over the business and that there was no profit other than what results from the appreciation of capital. [557 D] 2.1 The sale was a commercial transaction and not a trading activity, and therefore, the assessee company was not liable for tax. [658 F] 2:2 In the instant case, the sales are not in the regular course of business but only as a result of the appreciation or capitalisation of capital assets. There is no evidence that the appellant Company was keeping the factory going, not on its own behalf but entirely on behalf and for the purpose of carrying on a trading busi ness. [650 D] 3.1 In the present case, there was only one sale of the chemicals in trade and was, therefore, liable to be taxed under s. 5(2) of the Act. The question whether the sales should be treated as a trading receipt or not is a mixed question of law and fact. [663 F] 3:2. In the circumstances, it cannot be said that there is a profit other way of trade than a trading loss. [664 D] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1566 of 1967. Appeal by special leave from the judgment and order dated April 20, 1966 of the Calcutta High Court in Income Tax Reference No. 1 of 1965. S. T. Desai, R. N. Sachthey and B. D. Sharma, for the appellant. M. C. Setalvad, Attorney-General for India, K. J. John, P. H. Parekh and R. Hathi, for respondent No. 2. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Hegde, J. This appeal is directed against the judgment dated April 24, 1966 passed by the Calcutta high Court in a reference under section 66(1) of that Act. In this case, it appears that the Income tax Officer had taken the stock of chemicals from the appellant company and paid the sales tax on the chemicals. The appellant company was carrying out the business as a dealer in chemicals and he was maintaining the factory at all material times. It is not disputed that the goods were sold by the appellant to the customers for a consideration which was not part of the sale price. The case of the appellant is that the Sales Tax Act, 1947 (hereinafter referred to as "the Act") does not apply to the facts of this case and that in any event, there is no material on record to show that the said sales were sales within the meaning of s. 2(a) of Act.
